title: Social Science, Class 9
subject: Social Science
description: NCERT Grade 9 Social Science, chapter by chapter.

chapters.title: Understanding Social Science
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what is social science?; understanding society through time and traditions; social science disciplines and geography; history and historical sources.

lessons.title: What Is Social Science?

activities.prompt: How does the world around us shape the way we live?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Studying Human Society
activities.body: Social Science is the systematic study of human society. This means careful study of how people live together. People's lives are influenced by their surroundings and one another. Social Science also studies institutions, cultures, and human interactions. It includes studying food, roads, schools, and electricity networks. Society does not develop by chance. Social scientists use observation, evidence, and logical reasoning.
keyPoints: Social Science studies human society.
People and surroundings influence one another.
Observation, evidence, and reasoning help answer questions.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect daily life with the careful study of society.

activities.prompt: Why does a simple meal need many people and systems?
steps: Much of our food comes from different parts of the country, because many people work together.
They bring food from farms to our plates, so simple meals depend on shared work.
Roads, schools, and electricity also matter, because daily activities depend on social and natural systems.
Social scientists use observation, evidence, and logical reasoning, because these help them find answers about society.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Main Subject
activities.prompt: What does Social Science study?
options: Human society
Natural sciences alone
Only daily habits
Only one family
activities.explanation: Social Science is the systematic study of human society.

activities.prompt: Human lives are influenced by their surroundings and by one another.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that surroundings and other people influence human lives.

activities.title: A Way to Find Answers
activities.prompt: Social scientists use ______, evidence, and logical reasoning to find answers.
activities.hint: This is one of three methods named in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Social scientists use observation, evidence, and logical reasoning.

activities.title: Systems Around Us
activities.prompt: Match each part of daily life with the system that supports it.
activities.explanation: Different people and systems work together to support everyday life.

activities.title: Daily Activities
activities.prompt: Which statement is true about simple daily activities?
options: They depend only on natural systems.
They depend only on social systems.
They can depend on social and natural systems.
They do not depend on any systems.
activities.explanation: Even simple daily activities depend on social and natural systems.

activities.title: Society Does Not Develop by Chance
activities.prompt: Why does the lesson say society does not develop by chance?
options: Public systems and shared work shape daily life.
Daily life depends only on natural systems.
Every change happens without human planning.
Food, roads, and schools never affect society.
activities.explanation: Public authorities, shared work, and educational policies show how people shape society.

activities.prompt: An electricity map shows one large network. What may happen if one part stops working?
options: Some homes may lose power, because the parts work together.
More homes may gain power, because the network keeps growing.
All homes must lose power, because one part controls everything.
Nothing may change, because each home works completely alone.

why.More homes may gain power, because the n: This mistake thinks a larger network must create more power.
why.All homes must lose power, because one p: This mistake thinks one broken part must stop everything.
why.Nothing may change, because each home wo: This mistake thinks homes do not depend on one another.

activities.explanation: Correct: connected parts of the network can affect other homes.

activities.prompt: A plate has foods from two different parts of the country. What does this tell us about food?
options: Our food can connect different places, because people work together.
Food comes only from farms near our homes, because farms feed us.
All food must come from one place, because country food is simple.
Different places have no shared work, because food stays nearby.

why.Food comes only from farms near our home: This mistake thinks all food must come from nearby farms.
why.All food must come from one place, becau: This mistake treats food from different parts as coming from one place.
why.Different places have no shared work, be: This mistake thinks shared work does not connect different places.

activities.explanation: Correct: shared work can bring foods from different places to one plate.

activities.prompt: A map shows many connected lines for electricity. What can we learn from this source?
options: Electricity needs a large network, because it reaches many homes.
Every home makes its own electricity, because the lines are local.
Electricity needs no workers, because the map shows wires.
Food and electricity share one system, because their maps look alike.

why.Every home makes its own electricity, be: This mistake thinks the map proves each home makes electricity.
why.Electricity needs no workers, because th: This mistake ignores the workers needed to run the network.
why.Food and electricity share one system, b: This mistake thinks similar maps mean different systems share one purpose.

activities.explanation: Correct: the map's many connected lines show a large electricity network.

activities.prompt: Two schools have different lessons and ways of working. Educational policies shape schools. Why might the schools differ?
options: Their school policies may differ, because policies shape schools.
Their weather must differ, because weather changes school lessons.
Their food must differ, because policies control what children eat.
Their roads must differ, because schools are found near roads.

why.Their weather must differ, because weath: This mistake connects school differences to the weather.
why.Their food must differ, because policies: This mistake connects school policies to children's food.
why.Their roads must differ, because schools: This mistake connects school differences to nearby roads.

activities.explanation: Correct: different educational policies can shape schools differently.

lessons.title: Understanding Society Through Time and Traditions

activities.prompt: How did the past help us understand society today?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Society Changes
activities.body: Society has changed greatly over thousands of years. Early people grew crops, domesticated animals, and built settlements. Villages became towns, and towns became cities. Early Indian thinkers valued questions, dialogue, and logical reasoning. They studied nature, public welfare, administration, taxation, and the economy. Social scientists study people’s lives through interviews and documents, and support explanations with evidence.
keyPoints: Society changes as people develop new ways of living.
Early thinkers valued questions, dialogue, and logical reasoning.
Social scientists support explanations with evidence.
activities.explanation: This lesson shows how society and knowledge have changed through the years.

activities.prompt: A family watches its village grow larger. What may happen next, and why?
steps: Growing crops and domesticating animals made settled life possible.
Building settlements helped these early communities form villages.
Village growth led to towns, and town growth led to cities.
These connected changes explain society’s change over thousands of years.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A Change in Society
activities.prompt: Which option describes a change in society?
options: Villages became towns, and towns later became cities.
Early people stopped building settlements and growing crops.
Social scientists stopped studying people and their documents.
Early thinkers stopped valuing questions and dialogue.
activities.explanation: Villages gradually developed into towns, and towns grew into cities.

activities.title: Early Ways of Living
activities.prompt: Early people learnt to grow crops and domesticate animals.
activities.explanation: Early people learnt to grow crops, domesticate animals, and build settlements.

activities.title: Supporting an Explanation
activities.prompt: Social scientists develop explanations that are supported by ______.
activities.hint: What helps show that an explanation is supported?
activities.explanation: Social scientists develop explanations that are supported by evidence.

activities.title: Systematic Thinking
activities.prompt: Which work shows systematic thinking about governance and the economy?
options: The Arthaśhāstra examined administration and taxation.
The Pañchamahābhūtas examined taxation and administration.
Vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam examined ancient city taxes.
Social scientists examined administration in ancient times.
activities.explanation: The Arthaśhāstra examined administration, taxation, and economic management.

activities.title: Nature and the World Family
activities.prompt: The Pañchamahābhūtas means that the whole world is one family.
activities.explanation: The Pañchamahābhūtas presents nature as a connected system. The whole-world family meaning belongs to Vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam.

activities.prompt: Two thinkers notice different clues about nature. How should they explore it?
options: Observe carefully, reflect, and talk together.
Guess quickly and avoid checking with others.
Accept the first answer and stop asking questions.
Argue loudly without listening to any reason.

why.Guess quickly and avoid checking with ot: This mistake treats a quick guess as careful thought.
why.Accept the first answer and stop asking: This mistake thinks questioning stops useful exploration.
why.Argue loudly without listening to any re: This mistake replaces dialogue and reasoning with loud argument.

activities.explanation: Right: They valued questions, observation, reflection, and dialogue.

activities.prompt: One part of nature changes, and other parts are affected. What does this show?
options: Nature works as one connected system.
Nature has separate parts that never affect each other.
Nature has only one part that can ever change.
Nature follows only orders given by people.

why.Nature has separate parts that never aff: This mistake treats nature’s parts as completely separate.
why.Nature has only one part that can ever c: This mistake limits all change to one part of nature.
why.Nature follows only orders given by peop: This mistake thinks nature cannot work beyond human orders.

activities.explanation: Right: The Pañchamahābhūtas presents nature as one connected system.

activities.prompt: Early thinkers linked political authority with public welfare. The Arthaśhāstra examines administration, taxation, and economic management. What do these facts show together?
options: Governance and the economy were studied systematically for public welfare.
Political authority had no link to economic management.
Early thinkers had no systematic ideas about taxation.
Public welfare mattered only to one powerful group.

why.Political authority had no link to econo: This mistake separates political authority from economic management.
why.Early thinkers had no systematic ideas a: This mistake ignores the systematic study described in the Arthaśhāstra.
why.Public welfare mattered only to one powe: This mistake limits public welfare to one powerful group.

activities.explanation: Right: Authority and economic management were studied systematically for public welfare.

activities.prompt: Social scientists study people’s lives through interviews and documents. What should an explanation do?
options: Use interviews and documents as evidence for it.
Ignore interviews and documents to keep the answer simple.
Choose one source without checking any other evidence.
Replace interviews and documents with guesses about people.

why.Ignore interviews and documents to keep: This mistake thinks simplicity comes from ignoring sources.
why.Choose one source without checking any o: This mistake thinks one chosen source is enough without checking.
why.Replace interviews and documents with gu: This mistake treats guesses as stronger than studied evidence.

activities.explanation: Right: Social scientists support their explanations with evidence.

lessons.title: Social Science Disciplines and Geography

activities.prompt: How do different social science subjects help us understand the world around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different Fields, One Social Science
activities.body: Social Science is a group of related subjects, not one subject. A discipline is a field of study. No single field can explain all human society. Its four core disciplines are Geography, History, Political Science, and Economics. Geography studies Earth and how people relate to their surroundings. It also asks why things lie in certain places. It examines how places affect one another through time.
keyPoints: Social Science includes related disciplines.
Geography studies Earth, people, and their surroundings.
Geography examines places and change over time.
activities.explanation: This lesson shows how Geography fits within the wider field of Social Science.

activities.prompt: Why can’t one subject explain why people live and act differently in different places?
steps: Human society is very complex because many things affect people’s lives.
Geography is useful because it studies how people relate to their surroundings.
History, Political Science, and Economics are related subjects that give other views.
Together, the disciplines explain more than any single field can alone.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose the Main Study
activities.prompt: Which description best covers the main study of Geography?
options: Earth, people, and surroundings
Only Earth’s surface processes
Only why things lie in places
Only maps, globes, and atlases
activities.explanation: You spotted it! Geography studies Earth and the relationship between people and their surroundings.

activities.title: Complete the Definition
activities.prompt: Geography studies the Earth and the ______ between people and their surroundings.
activities.hint: Think about the link between people and their surroundings.
activities.explanation: Well done! This relationship is the main focus of Geography.

activities.title: Match Geography’s Focuses
activities.prompt: Match each Geography focus to its description.
pairs: The relationship between people and their surroundings
Asking why things are found in particular places
Examining how places affect one another
Maps, globes, atlases, and Geographical Information Systems
activities.explanation: Great matching! These are important parts of Geography and the tools it uses.

activities.title: Processes Shape the Earth
activities.prompt: What does Geography study about processes shaping Earth’s surface?
options: How Earth’s surface is shaped
Why items have certain names
How people choose their jobs
When markets began trading
activities.explanation: Good thinking! Geography studies the processes that shape Earth’s surface.

activities.title: A Regional Project
activities.prompt: A project compares two regions and studies how each region affects the other.
options: Changes between places over time
The history of geographical knowledge
Life in one region only
Reasons for choosing map symbols
activities.explanation: Good thinking! This project matches Geography’s study of how places affect one another.

activities.title: Geography’s Wide Scope
activities.prompt: Which description best matches the full scope of Geography?
options: Earth, people, places, and change
Only Earth’s physical processes
Only maps and globes
Only life in one region
activities.explanation: Excellent! Geography connects Earth, people, places, and change over time.

activities.prompt: Your class wants to understand why people live differently in different regions. Which plan best fits Social Science?
options: Combine Geography, History, Political Science, and Economics together.
Use Geography alone to explain every part of society.
Choose one subject and ignore the other three.
Study only maps and leave society out of the work.

why.Use Geography alone to explain every par: This wrongly assumes Geography can explain every part of society.
why.Choose one subject and ignore the other: This wrongly assumes related subjects do not need to work together.
why.Study only maps and leave society out of: This wrongly treats maps as separate from social questions.

activities.explanation: This is right because no single field fully explains human society.

activities.prompt: Two maps show two places in two different years. Which question should guide their comparison?
options: How did these places affect each other over time?
Which map has the clearest picture of one place?
How many labels appear on both maps?
What is the name of each map maker?

why.Which map has the clearest picture of on: This compares how a map looks instead of change between places.
why.How many labels appear on both maps?: This counts map features instead of explaining their connection.
why.What is the name of each map maker?: This asks about map makers instead of relationships between places.

activities.explanation: This is right because Geography examines how places affect one another over time.

activities.prompt: A student uses a globe, an atlas, and a GIS to investigate a place. Which question best fits this work?
options: Why is this place found in this particular location?
What is the longest name shown for this place?
How many words are used in the place description?
Which tool has the biggest screen or page size?

why.What is the longest name shown for this: This focuses on names instead of explaining the place’s location.
why.How many words are used in the place des: This counts words instead of using tools to investigate the place.
why.Which tool has the biggest screen or pag: This compares tool sizes instead of asking a geographical question.

activities.explanation: This is right because Geography asks why things are found in particular places.

activities.prompt: Students learn about the atmosphere, climate, oceans, and major biomes. Which question focuses on the processes they are studying?
options: How do processes shape the Earth’s surface?
How can maps, globes, atlases, and GIS help?
Why does Social Science have four core disciplines?
Which region has the most familiar place names?

why.How can maps, globes, atlases, and GIS h: This focuses on investigation tools instead of Earth-shaping processes.
why.Why does Social Science have four core d: This focuses on the structure of Social Science instead of Earth processes.
why.Which region has the most familiar place: This focuses on place names instead of Earth-shaping processes.

activities.explanation: This is right because Geography studies the processes that shape the Earth’s surface.

activities.prompt: Students compare life in two regions with maps and GIS. Which question best fits Geography’s regional study?
options: How do people relate to their surroundings in each region?
Which region has the clearest labels on its maps?
How many tools did the students use to study regions?
When was the first geographical idea written down?

why.Which region has the clearest labels on: This focuses on map labels instead of life in different regions.
why.How many tools did the students use to s: This counts tools instead of exploring life across regions.
why.When was the first geographical idea wri: This asks about history instead of people and their surroundings.

activities.explanation: This is right because Geography studies people and their surroundings in different regions.

activities.prompt: Students read old and new ideas about the Earth. Which question belongs to Geography’s study of its own history?
options: How did people’s geographical ideas change through history?
How can maps, globes, atlases, and GIS work together?
Why do places affect one another over time?
Why are some features found in particular places?

why.How can maps, globes, atlases, and GIS w: This focuses on investigation tools instead of geographical ideas.
why.Why do places affect one another over ti: This focuses on relationships between places instead of geographical knowledge.
why.Why are some features found in particula: This focuses on why features occur instead of how geographical ideas changed.

activities.explanation: This is right because Geography includes the history of geographical knowledge.

lessons.title: History and Historical Sources

activities.prompt: How can we uncover the past and understand where we came from?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is history?
activities.body: History is the study of the human past. The past can be interpreted in several ways. Bharat’s itihāsa-purāṇa tradition is one of the oldest for preserving cultural memory. Modern history uses empirical evidence, meaning evidence that can be checked. Human genetics is one method. Carbon-14 dating and archaeology help historians study the past. Travelogues, memoirs, letters, and family records are historical sources.
keyPoints: The past can be interpreted in several ways.
Historical sources include records, traditions, and material remains.
Modern history uses empirical evidence and methods.
activities.explanation: This card introduces history, evidence, and different kinds of historical sources.

activities.prompt: You find old family letters and hear old stories. How can a historian use them?
steps: Letters and family records are historical sources, so they provide information about the past.
Folklore and oral traditions also provide information, so spoken memories matter.
Archaeology and carbon-14 dating help study material remains, so objects need different evidence.
The historian can use the written and spoken records as historical sources.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose the meaning
activities.prompt: What is history?
options: The study of human past
The study of living plants
The study of future events
The study of daily machines
activities.explanation: History focuses on the human past, as the lesson explains.

activities.title: Name the kind of source
activities.prompt: Material remains from the past are called ______ sources.
activities.hint: These are physical remains from the past.
activities.explanation: Archaeological sources are material remains from the past.

activities.title: Records from the past
activities.prompt: Travelogues, memoirs, letters, and family records are historical sources.
activities.explanation: All four can provide information about the human past.

activities.title: Sources and methods
activities.prompt: Match each source or method to its description.
activities.explanation: Each match is a source or method named in the lesson.

activities.title: Find the historical sources
activities.prompt: Which group contains only historical sources?
options: Human genetics, carbon-14 dating, archaeology
Cars, trains, and aeroplanes
Travelogues, letters, and family records
Weather, clouds, and sunlight
activities.explanation: Travelogues, letters, and family records are named as historical sources.

activities.title: Different interpretations
activities.prompt: Why can people interpret the same past in different ways?
options: The past has several interpretations.
All sources are exactly the same.
Material remains need no study.
Only one method offers evidence.
activities.explanation: The lesson says the past can be interpreted in several ways.

activities.prompt: A community uses the itihāsa-purāṇa tradition to preserve old stories. What result fits its purpose?
options: Cultural memory can be passed on through preserved traditions.
Cultural memory becomes useless because methods replace traditions.
The past becomes easier to date through carbon-14 alone.
The community must stop using archaeology to study its past.

why.Cultural memory becomes useless because: This mistake thinks modern methods make cultural memory useless.
why.The past becomes easier to date through: This mistake confuses preserving traditions with dating material remains.
why.The community must stop using archaeolog: This mistake thinks preserving traditions removes the need for archaeology.

activities.explanation: This is right because the tradition preserves cultural memory and passes on values.

activities.prompt: A pot is found in an old dig. What kind of source is it?
options: It is an archaeological source because it is a material remain.
It is a family record because it belonged to an old household.
It is an oral tradition because elders can describe the pot.
It is a travelogue because it shows where people once travelled.

why.It is a family record because it belonge: This mistake treats a household object like a written family record.
why.It is an oral tradition because elders c: This mistake confuses spoken memories with material remains.
why.It is a travelogue because it shows wher: This mistake thinks a record of travel includes any old object.

activities.explanation: This is right because a pot from the past is a material remain.

activities.prompt: An old site has material remains. Which pair of methods fits this evidence?
options: Carbon-14 dating and archaeology help study the remains.
Family letters and memoirs replace archaeology for material remains.
Revenue documents reveal objects more directly than archaeological methods.
Human genetics alone identify the meaning of every old object.

why.Family letters and memoirs replace archa: This mistake thinks written records study material remains directly.
why.Revenue documents reveal objects more di: This mistake thinks revenue documents replace archaeological methods.
why.Human genetics alone identify the meanin: This mistake thinks one method can explain every material object.

activities.explanation: This is right because carbon-14 dating and archaeology help historians study the past.

activities.prompt: One class studies folklore. Another reads revenue documents. What do both classes use?
options: They use different historical sources that provide information.
They use only material remains found below the ground.
They use family letters because every record belongs to families.
They use carbon dating because both records came from objects.

why.They use only material remains found bel: This mistake thinks only buried objects can provide historical information.
why.They use family letters because every re: This mistake believes every historical record is a family letter.
why.They use carbon dating because both reco: This mistake thinks carbon dating is the main method for studying records.

activities.explanation: This is right because folklore and revenue documents both provide historical information.

activities.prompt: A student traces India's past from early civilisation to now. Another studies colonialism and anti-colonial struggles across the world. What connects both tasks?
options: Both are parts of studying world history across time and place.
Both describe only one country's history in the same period.
Both require students to ignore evidence from other places.
Both prove that all historical periods followed one pattern.

why.Both describe only one country's history: This mistake ignores the world-wide study of anti-colonial struggles.
why.Both require students to ignore evidence: This mistake thinks history students should ignore evidence from other places.
why.Both prove that all historical periods f: This mistake thinks different periods and places followed one pattern.

activities.explanation: This is right because both tasks are major parts of studying history.

lessons.title: Political Science and Economics

activities.prompt: How do people share power and make choices when resources are limited?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Subjects, One World
activities.body: Political Science studies how power is shared and how decisions are made. It looks at constitutions, governments, and state institutions. It also studies social movements, nation building, and foreign policy. Economics studies how people use limited resources to meet their needs. It looks at how goods and services are produced, exchanged, and distributed. It includes markets, well-being, and fairness too.
keyPoints: Political Science studies power and decisions.
Economics studies limited resources and human needs.
Both subjects study fairness and the well-being of people.
activities.explanation: These subjects help us understand power, resources, and fair choices.

activities.prompt: How do a family's choices affect what a producer makes?
steps: The family has limited money because resources are limited.
It compares its needs because economics studies how people use limited resources.
It chooses some goods because consumers choose what to buy.
A producer makes more of a chosen good because producers decide what and how much to produce.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Sharing Power
activities.prompt: Which subject explains how power is shared and decisions are made?
options: Production and resource choices
Power sharing and decisions
Trade centres and industries
Consumer choices and markets
activities.explanation: This is Political Science because it studies power sharing and decision-making.

activities.prompt: Economics studies how people use limited resources to meet their needs.
activities.explanation: Economics studies how people use limited resources to meet their needs.

activities.title: Connect Each Idea
activities.prompt: Match each subject or group with its main decision.
pairs: What and how much to produce
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a subject or group with its main choice.

activities.title: Resources for Needs
activities.prompt: Economics studies how people use ______ resources to meet their needs.
activities.hint: Think about the amount available.
activities.explanation: Economics studies how people use limited resources to meet their needs.

activities.title: What Economics Examines
activities.prompt: Which is part of the work studied by Economics?
options: Sharing power and making decisions
Producing, exchanging, and distributing goods and services
Writing constitutions and running governments
Studying movements, nations, and foreign policy
activities.explanation: Economics examines production, exchange, and distribution of goods and services.

activities.title: Where Power Exists
activities.prompt: Political power exists only in formal institutions.
activities.explanation: Power also exists in social relationships and customs, not only formal institutions.

activities.title: Power as Responsibility
activities.prompt: Indian political thought treated power as a ______ rather than merely a privilege.
activities.hint: This means something you must properly take care of.
activities.explanation: Indian political thought saw power as a responsibility, not only a privilege.

activities.prompt: A shop sells many blue shirts, but few green shirts. What might the producer do next?
options: Make more blue shirts because shoppers choose what they buy.
Make more green shirts because shops stock many shirts.
Make fewer blue shirts because shoppers dislike all shirts.
Make fewer green shirts because producers dislike blue shirts.

why.Make more green shirts because shops sto: This mistake ignores what shoppers actually choose.
why.Make fewer blue shirts because shoppers: This mistake wrongly says that shoppers dislike every shirt.
why.Make fewer green shirts because producer: This mistake wrongly says that producers dislike blue shirts.

activities.explanation: This is right because consumers choose what they buy.

activities.prompt: A chart shows goods being made, exchanged, and sent to different people. What kind of questions does economics study?
options: How production, exchange, and distribution affect people.
Why constitutions give citizens a voice in local places.
How power is shared between formal institutions and customs.
Why social movements shape nation building and foreign policy.

why.Why constitutions give citizens a voice: This mistake describes political science and local democracy.
why.How power is shared between formal insti: This mistake describes political power and social customs.
why.Why social movements shape nation buildi: This mistake describes another part of political science.

activities.explanation: This is right because economics examines production, exchange, and distribution.

lessons.title: Why We Study Social Science and Its Future

activities.prompt: How can studying society help us shape a better future?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why Social Science Matters
activities.body: Social Science helps us understand the systems that organise daily life. It explains how houses, water systems, roads, schools, markets, and digital spaces affect different groups. It also connects the past, present, and future. Learning about it can build respect, support cooperation, and prepare you to participate responsibly.
keyPoints: Social Science explains how society manages important systems.
It helps us understand communities and their differences.
It prepares citizens to take an informed part in shaping the world.
activities.explanation: Social Science helps you understand society and prepare for responsible citizenship.

activities.prompt: A town must improve its shared water system. How should it understand different groups before changing the system?
steps: Study how the water system works, because society manages this shared system.
Examine how it affects different groups, because Social Science explains these effects.
Compare locations, pasts, customs, and economies, because these factors explain community differences.
Plan the changes carefully, because learning about differences builds respect and cooperation.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which group of places does society manage?
options: Houses, water systems, roads, and schools
Geographical, historical, cultural, and economic factors
Geography, History, Political Science, and Economics
The past, present, and future
activities.explanation: Society manages places and systems such as houses, water systems, roads, and schools.

activities.prompt: The course introduces Geography, History, Political Science, and ______.
activities.hint: This subject studies economic factors.
activities.explanation: Economics is one of the four subjects in the broad introduction.

activities.prompt: Match each subject with its related area in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each subject helps explain a different part of social life.

activities.prompt: What does learning about community differences help build?
options: Respect and cooperation
Houses and water systems
Government and public life
Careful questioning and reasoning
activities.explanation: Learning about differences builds respect and cooperation among communities.

activities.prompt: Put these parts of time in order.
activities.explanation: Social Science connects the past, present, and future in this order.

activities.prompt: How can Social Science help societies facing rapid change?
options: It prepares citizens to shape the world with knowledge.
It shows one community's way of life to everyone.
It connects society with its earliest memories only.
It removes the need to compare different perspectives.
activities.explanation: Social Science prepares citizens to take an informed part. It also supports work on climate change and sustainable development.

activities.prompt: A town’s water system is managed by society. The council wants changes that help different groups. What should it learn first?
options: How the system works and affects different groups.
How each group can avoid using the system.
Why some groups should manage every part.
How to stop studying the system before deciding.

why.How each group can avoid using the syste: This mistake assumes that people should avoid a shared system.
why.Why some groups should manage every part: This mistake assumes that only some groups should manage it.
why.How to stop studying the system before d: This mistake treats stopping study as a useful first step.

activities.explanation: This is right because it follows how the system affects different groups.

activities.prompt: An older map shows roads and markets. A newer map also shows schools and digital spaces. What can comparing both maps help students do?
options: Choose the map that is right in every possible detail.
Connect changes in society across different time periods.
Use the maps without checking any written sources.
Guess each group’s feelings from the map alone.

why.Choose the map that is right in every po: This mistake assumes one map can prove every fact.
why.Use the maps without checking any writte: This mistake ignores the need to check written sources.
why.Guess each group’s feelings from the map: This mistake treats a map as evidence of people’s feelings.

activities.explanation: This is right because comparing maps connects society across different periods.

activities.prompt: Society is changing rapidly. A community wants help with climate change and sustainable development. How can Social Science support it?
options: It predicts one certain future for every changing community.
It removes the need to understand different social groups.
It helps societies meet these needs and prepare informed citizens.
It keeps citizens from taking informed action in public life.

why.It predicts one certain future for every: This mistake assumes the future is certain and easily predicted.
why.It removes the need to understand differ: This mistake thinks social understanding becomes less important during change.
why.It keeps citizens from taking informed a: This mistake assumes studying society prevents responsible action.

activities.explanation: This is right because Social Science supports these goals and informed participation.

activities.context: A family buys vegetables and grains that come from different parts of the country. Farmers grow the food, and many workers transport it from farms along public roads before it reaches the family’s plates. Public authorities plan and maintain those roads. At home, electricity reaches the family through a large and complex network. The family sees that even a simple daily activity such as preparing a meal depends on social and natural systems and on people working together.
activities.prompt: If public authorities stopped planning and maintaining the roads used to transport food, what would most likely happen?
options: Food would have greater difficulty reaching the family’s plates because the roads support its transport.
Food would reach the plates more quickly because fewer roads would be used.
Electricity would stop reaching the home because roads and networks are identical.
Farmers would no longer grow food because roads do not affect agriculture.

why.Food would reach the plates more quickly: Public authorities are responsible for planning and maintaining these roads.
why.Electricity would stop reaching the home: Workers still need suitable roads to complete the food journey.
why.Farmers would no longer grow food becaus: The other choices confuse separate systems or ignore the role of roads.

activities.explanation: The roads support the movement of food from farms to plates.

activities.context: A family buys vegetables and grains that come from different parts of the country. Farmers grow the food, and many workers transport it from farms along public roads before it reaches the family’s plates. Public authorities plan and maintain those roads. At home, electricity reaches the family through a large and complex network. The family sees that even a simple daily activity such as preparing a meal depends on social and natural systems and on people working together.
activities.prompt: Which explanation best shows why the family’s meal is connected to Social Science?
options: It shows how people, institutions, and cooperation shape an ordinary daily activity.
It shows that ordinary activities depend only on natural processes and not on people.
It shows that electricity and food are important because society develops by chance.
It shows that one family alone controls every system involved in the meal.

why.It shows that ordinary activities depend: The meal depends on farmers, workers, and public authorities working together.
why.It shows that electricity and food are i: The case therefore connects ordinary life with wider social relationships.
why.It shows that one family alone controls: The other options ignore institutions, human cooperation, or evidence.

activities.explanation: Social Science studies society, institutions, cultures, and human interactions.

activities.context: A family buys vegetables and grains that come from different parts of the country. Farmers grow the food, and many workers transport it from farms along public roads before it reaches the family’s plates. Public authorities plan and maintain those roads. At home, electricity reaches the family through a large and complex network. The family sees that even a simple daily activity such as preparing a meal depends on social and natural systems and on people working together.
activities.prompt: If electricity stopped reaching the family’s home, what would be the most reasonable conclusion?
options: One important system would be affected, but daily life would still involve other social and natural systems.
Every daily activity would stop immediately because all of them require electricity.
The electricity network would have no connection with society because it is only a technical system.
Food would become unimportant, so the people transporting it would no longer be needed.

why.Every daily activity would stop immediat: Its failure would affect activities that depend on it, but not every activity.
why.The electricity network would have no co: Food and roads would remain parts of the wider systems supporting the family.
why.Food would become unimportant, so the pe: The other choices make claims that are too absolute or confuse different systems.

activities.explanation: Electricity reaches homes through a large and complex network.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Even a simple daily activity can depend on social and natural systems.
Reason (R): Food reaches the family through the work of many people and maintained roads, while electricity also comes through a large network.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason gives specific examples showing why the family’s simple daily activity depends on wider systems.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Public authorities plan and maintain the roads on which people travel.
Reason (R): Food can reach plates without roads or the work of people who transport it.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because the food journey depends on roads and many workers.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between Social Science and natural science, using the family’s meal as an example.
activities.answer: Social Science is the systematic study of human society. Unlike natural sciences, it studies society, institutions, cultures, and human interactions. The family’s meal provides an example because its food comes from different parts of the country and reaches the family through the work of many people. Public authorities plan and maintain the roads used in this journey, while electricity reaches the home through a large and complex network. Thus, the case shows how ordinary life is shaped by surroundings, institutions, and human cooperation. Social scientists examine these connections using observation, evidence, and logical reasoning rather than assuming that society develops by chance.
points: Defines Social Science as the systematic study of human society.
Explains that it studies institutions, cultures, and human interactions.
Uses the food journey and electricity network as examples.
Mentions observation, evidence, and logical reasoning.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A village has gradually developed into a town, and the town is beginning to grow into a city. Its leaders must connect political authority with public welfare while dealing with administration, taxation, and economic management. A social scientist wants to explain this change. The scientist studies people’s lives, conducts interviews, examines documents, and develops explanations supported by evidence. The town also considers the Pañchamahābhūtas, which presents nature as a connected system.
activities.prompt: What should the town’s leaders do as they guide the settlement’s development?
options: Study how the town is run, how taxes are handled, and how its economy is managed, with public welfare guiding authority.
Administer the town but avoid examining taxation or economic management.
Use political authority without considering how it supports public welfare.
Treat the Pañchamahābhūtas as a direct guide to administration and taxation.

why.Administer the town but avoid examining: Leaving out taxation and economic management weakens the systematic approach.
why.Use political authority without consider: Authority should be connected with public welfare.
why.Treat the Pañchamahābhūtas as a direct g: The Pañchamahābhūtas concerns nature as a connected system, not town administration.

activities.explanation: This joins administration, taxation, and economic management with public welfare.

activities.context: A village has gradually developed into a town, and the town is beginning to grow into a city. Its leaders must connect political authority with public welfare while dealing with administration, taxation, and economic management. A social scientist wants to explain this change. The scientist studies people’s lives, conducts interviews, examines documents, and develops explanations supported by evidence. The town also considers the Pañchamahābhūtas, which presents nature as a connected system.
activities.prompt: If interviews could not be conducted, what should the scientist do?
options: Study the available records and build an explanation that evidence can support.
End the study because interviews are the only valid source.
Use logical reasoning alone and ignore all evidence.
Use the meaning of Vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam as the complete explanation of the change.

why.End the study because interviews are the: Interviews are a method, but the lesson does not call them the only valid source.
why.Use logical reasoning alone and ignore a: Logical reasoning should remain connected with evidence.
why.Use the meaning of Vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam: The meaning of Vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam does not fully explain the town’s change.

activities.explanation: Documents and evidence can still support a careful explanation.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Systematic thinking about governance and the economy existed long ago.
Reason (R): The Arthaśhāstra examined administration, taxation, and economic management.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The Arthaśhāstra provides evidence for the existence of systematic thinking about governance and the economy.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Pañchamahābhūtas presents nature as a connected system.
Reason (R): Vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam means that the whole world is one family.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the meaning of Vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam does not explain the Pañchamahābhūtas.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between how social scientists study society and how early Indian thinkers explored governance and the economy?
activities.answer: Social scientists study society by examining people’s lives, conducting interviews, and examining documents. They then develop explanations that are supported by evidence. Early Indian thinkers explored knowledge through observation, reflection, and dialogue, and they valued questions and logical reasoning. Their thinking about governance and the economy was systematic, as shown by the Arthaśhāstra’s examination of administration, taxation, and economic management. Thus, both approaches seek careful understanding, but the social science approach in this lesson emphasizes evidence from people’s lives and documents.
points: Social scientists examine lives, interviews, and documents.
Their explanations must be supported by evidence.
Early thinkers used observation, reflection, dialogue, and logical reasoning.
The Arthaśhāstra shows systematic study of governance and the economy.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A group of students is investigating why the same kind of settlement appears in one location but not another. They compare maps, an atlas, and a globe, then use a Geographical Information System to display the areas and their links. Their teacher asks them to examine how these places affect one another over time and to explain why the findings differ from place to place.
activities.prompt: What should the students investigate next to develop a geographical explanation of the settlement pattern?
options: Test what caused the uneven pattern and how the locations influence each other across time.
Catalogue where the settlement occurs without investigating the cause of the pattern.
Compare only the present appearance of the places and leave change over time outside the investigation.
Use the displays to list the areas but do not frame a question about the pattern.

why.Catalogue where the settlement occurs wi: This records location but does not investigate why the pattern exists.
why.Compare only the present appearance of t: This ignores how places affect one another across time.
why.Use the displays to list the areas but d: This collects information without using it to answer a geographical question.

activities.explanation: This combines questions about causes with questions about relationships over time.

activities.context: A group of students is investigating why the same kind of settlement appears in one location but not another. They compare maps, an atlas, and a globe, then use a Geographical Information System to display the areas and their links. Their teacher asks them to examine how these places affect one another over time and to explain why the findings differ from place to place.
activities.prompt: Which conclusion best fits the class's investigation?
options: Location data and questions about causes and changing relationships can work together to explain the pattern.
The location alone fully explains why the settlement appears unevenly.
The tool used to display the areas is more important than the geographical question.
The history of geographical knowledge is the only suitable way to investigate the pattern.

why.The location alone fully explains why th: Geography asks why things occur in particular places, so location alone is insufficient.
why.The tool used to display the areas is mo: The tools are used to investigate geographical questions rather than replace them.
why.The history of geographical knowledge is: The history of geographical knowledge is included within Geography but is not its only part.

activities.explanation: The investigation uses both location and questions about causes and relationships over time.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Geography asks why things are found in particular places.
Reason (R): This question guides the class toward investigating why the settlement pattern differs.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains why the stated ability of Geography is useful in the case.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Geography studies only the Earth's surface and has no interest in the relationship between people and their surroundings.
Reason (R): Geography studies the Earth and the relationship between people and their surroundings.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because Geography does study the relationship between people and their surroundings.

activities.prompt: Explain why using maps, globes, atlases, and Geographical Information Systems supports a geographical investigation.
activities.answer: These tools support a geographical investigation because they allow students to study where things are found and ask why they occur in particular places. Maps, globes, atlases, and Geographical Information Systems can be used when investigating questions about the Earth and people’s surroundings. They also help students examine how places affect one another over time. This supports the study of processes that shape the Earth’s surface and connects questions about the atmosphere, climate, oceans, and major biomes with life in different regions.
points: Identifies all four geographical tools.
Explains their role in investigating where things occur and why.
Links the investigation to relationships between places over time.
Connects the tools with the study of the Earth’s surface and related topics.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Archaeology and carbon-14 dating are methods used to study the past.
Reason (R): Both are examples of travelogues and family records.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because archaeology and dating methods are not travelogues or family records.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Modern history depends only on beliefs rather than empirical evidence.
Reason (R): Human genetics is one empirical method used in modern history.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because modern history relies on empirical evidence, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Which subject studies the human past?
options: History
Geography
Economics
Political Science
activities.explanation: History studies the human past. The other subjects study different parts of society.

activities.prompt: Social scientists can use interviews and documents when studying people’s lives.
activities.explanation: Yes. Social scientists study lives, conduct interviews, and examine documents.

activities.prompt: Social Science is the systematic study of human ______.
activities.hint: Think about how people live together.
activities.explanation: Social Science is the systematic study of human society.

activities.prompt: Match each core discipline with the main question it studies.
activities.explanation: Each discipline has a clear focus. Matching them helps you see the whole chapter.

activities.prompt: Put the three world-history periods in time order.
activities.explanation: These periods move from earlier times to later times.

activities.prompt: Why should you learn about differences between communities?
options: To build respect and cooperation
To erase every local difference
To avoid questions about history
To choose only one way of life
activities.explanation: Learning about differences builds respect and cooperation among communities.

activities.prompt: Social Science mainly studies natural processes instead of human society.
activities.explanation: Not quite. Social Science studies society, institutions, cultures, and human interactions.

activities.prompt: Social scientists develop explanations that are supported by ______.
activities.hint: This helps a researcher check whether an explanation is reliable.
activities.explanation: Explanations must be supported by evidence.

activities.prompt: Put these settlements in the order in which they developed.
activities.explanation: Villages developed into towns, and towns grew into cities.

chapters.title: Shaping of the Earth’s Surface
chapters.summary: In this chapter: plate tectonics and the earth’s layers; weathering, erosion and gradation; running water, beaches and coastal landforms; glaciers, wind and underground water.

lessons.title: Plate Tectonics and the Earth’s Layers

activities.prompt: What makes the ground beneath our feet move and change?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Earth’s Layers Move
activities.body: Plate tectonics explains how large pieces of Earth’s crust move slowly over the molten mantle. The crust is the outermost layer, and we live on it. The lithosphere includes the crust and the upper part of the mantle. Below it, semi-molten asthenosphere allows tectonic plates to move. Convection currents in the mantle push and pull the plates. Where plates meet, you find plate boundaries.
keyPoints: Plate tectonics explains slow movement of Earth’s crust.
The lithosphere includes the crust and upper mantle.
Plate boundaries are where tectonic plates meet.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect Earth’s layers with the movement of tectonic plates.

activities.prompt: A family lives on Earth's crust and wonders why the ground can change over time.
steps: The family lives on the crust because it is the outermost layer.
The crust and upper mantle together form the lithosphere.
The semi-molten asthenosphere below it allows solid plates to move slowly.
Therefore, forces inside and on Earth can change the surface over time.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Earth’s surface stays unchanged because no forces act on it.
activities.explanation: Earth’s surface is constantly changing because of forces inside and on the planet.

activities.prompt: The lithosphere includes the ______ and the upper part of the mantle.
activities.hint: This is Earth’s outermost layer.
activities.explanation: The lithosphere includes both the crust and the upper part of the mantle.

activities.prompt: Match each part to its description.
pairs: The semi-molten layer below the lithosphere
activities.explanation: Each pair links a layer or boundary with its correct description.

activities.prompt: How do plates move at a convergent boundary?
options: Towards each other
Away from each other
Past each other
Without moving
activities.explanation: At a convergent boundary, two plates move towards each other.

activities.prompt: Put these layers in order from Earth’s surface downwards.
activities.explanation: The asthenosphere lies below the lithosphere, which includes the crust and upper mantle.

activities.prompt: What pushes and pulls tectonic plates?
options: Convection currents in the mantle
The semi-molten asthenosphere
The outermost crust
The upper mantle
activities.explanation: Convection currents in the mantle push and pull tectonic plates.

activities.prompt: A map shows arrows pointing away. What boundary is shown?
options: The plates are moving apart at a divergent boundary.
The plates are moving together at a convergent boundary.
One plate is sliding past the other at a transform boundary.
The plates are moving away at a convergent boundary.

why.The plates are moving together at a conv: This mistake treats movement towards each other as movement apart.
why.One plate is sliding past the other at a: This mistake reads arrows pointing away as sliding past.
why.The plates are moving away at a converge: This mistake mixes convergent movement with divergent movement.

activities.explanation: Arrows pointing away match movement at a divergent boundary.

activities.prompt: If the asthenosphere became completely solid, what would happen to plate movement?
options: Plates would likely slow down because the solid layer would restrict sliding.
Plates would likely speed up because the solid layer would push harder.
Plates would likely join because the solid layer would pull them together.
Plates would likely keep moving because solid rock always slides easily.

why.Plates would likely speed up because the: This mistake thinks a harder layer would make plate movement faster.
why.Plates would likely join because the sol: This mistake thinks the asthenosphere pulls plates together.
why.Plates would likely keep moving because: This mistake confuses solid rock with the semi-molten layer that aids movement.

activities.explanation: The asthenosphere allows plate movement because it is semi-molten, not solid.

activities.prompt: A drill enters the crust and upper mantle. What layer is this?
options: It is in the lithosphere, which includes both layers.
It is in the asthenosphere, which lies below the lithosphere.
It is outside the lithosphere because the crust has ended.
It is only in the crust because the upper mantle is separate.

why.It is in the asthenosphere, which lies b: This mistake treats every mantle layer as the asthenosphere.
why.It is outside the lithosphere because th: This mistake forgets that the lithosphere continues into the upper mantle.
why.It is only in the crust because the uppe: This mistake treats the upper mantle as separate from the lithosphere.

activities.explanation: Both the crust and upper mantle belong to the lithosphere.

activities.prompt: Mantle currents push and pull plates. What should result at Earth's surface?
options: The plates move slowly, changing Earth's surface over time.
The plates stay still, so Earth's surface never changes.
The plates turn into liquid, because they enter the asthenosphere.
The plates rise higher, moving completely above the lithosphere.

why.The plates stay still, so Earth's surfac: This mistake thinks convection currents have no effect on plates.
why.The plates turn into liquid, because the: This mistake confuses solid rock plates with the semi-molten layer below.
why.The plates rise higher, moving completel: This mistake confuses slow sideways movement with rising above the lithosphere.

activities.explanation: Moving plates help explain why Earth's surface is constantly changing.

lessons.title: Weathering, Erosion and Gradation

activities.prompt: How do rocks become soil, and where does all that material go?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Rocks Change and Move
activities.body: Weathering breaks surface rocks into smaller pieces. It does not move the material, but helps form soil. Physical weathering uses temperature changes, frost or wind. Chemical weathering changes minerals through reactions with water, air or acids. Biological weathering comes from plants, animals or micro-organisms. Erosion wears away soil and rocks and carries them elsewhere. Water and wind cause erosion. Gradation has main agents: running water, glaciers, wind, waves and groundwater.
keyPoints: Weathering breaks rocks down without moving them.
Water erosion and wind erosion are part of erosion.
Gradation has agents such as running water and glaciers.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect breaking rocks, moving material and gradation agents.

activities.prompt: Rock breaks at a cliff, and loose pieces later reach a field below. Which process caused each change?
steps: The rock broke into smaller pieces, so weathering happened first.
Weathering did not send them away, because it does not move pieces.
The pieces reached the field later, so erosion carried them elsewhere.
Therefore, weathering broke the rock, while erosion moved the pieces.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Does Weathering Do?
activities.prompt: What is the main job of weathering?
options: breaks rocks into small pieces
moves rocks to different places
changes rock minerals with acids
builds dams and canals on farms
activities.explanation: Weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces on Earth’s surface.

activities.title: Physical Weathering
activities.prompt: Physical weathering can break rocks because of changes in ______.
activities.hint: This is one cause of physical weathering.
activities.explanation: Changes in temperature can break rocks into smaller pieces.

activities.title: Types of Weathering
activities.prompt: Match each weathering type with its cause.
pairs: changes in temperature, frost or wind
reactions with water, air or acids
activities.explanation: Each weathering type has a different cause described in your lesson.

activities.title: From Breakdown to Movement
activities.prompt: Put these actions in order from breaking down to moving material.
items: Weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces
Erosion wears away soil and rocks
Erosion carries the material to another place
activities.explanation: Weathering breaks material down, while erosion wears it away and carries it elsewhere.

activities.title: Water Management
activities.prompt: Dams and ______ are water-management methods.
activities.hint: This helps carry water across land.
activities.explanation: Dams and canals are both water-management methods.

activities.title: Erosion and Farming
activities.prompt: What can erosion do to a farmer’s crop yields?
options: raises crop yields
lowers crop yields
adds fertile topsoil
stores more water
activities.explanation: Erosion removes fertile topsoil, so farmers get lower crop yields.

activities.prompt: A rock breaks into small pieces, but every piece stays in place. What is happening, and why?
options: Weathering, because the rock broke without moving.
Erosion, because the rock broke into smaller pieces.
Erosion, because the pieces stayed in their original place.
Weathering, because the pieces were carried to another place.

why.Erosion, because the rock broke into sma: Breaking alone shows weathering, while erosion also moves material.
why.Erosion, because the pieces stayed in th: Erosion carries material away, but these pieces stayed still.
why.Weathering, because the pieces were carr: Weathering does not carry pieces elsewhere; erosion does.

activities.explanation: Weathering breaks rocks without moving the broken pieces.

activities.prompt: Rain changes minerals in one rock. Frost breaks another rock into smaller pieces. Which statement best explains both changes?
options: One is chemical weathering, while the other is physical weathering.
Both are chemical weathering, because both rocks changed.
Both are physical weathering, because both rocks broke apart.
One is chemical weathering, while the other is biological weathering.

why.Both are chemical weathering, because bo: Frost breaking rock is physical weathering, even though both rocks changed.
why.Both are physical weathering, because bo: Mineral changes by reactions are chemical, not physical weathering.
why.One is chemical weathering, while the ot: Frost causes physical weathering, while biological weathering needs living things.

activities.explanation: Water reactions change minerals chemically, while frost breaks rock physically.

activities.prompt: One field loses its topsoil, and the farmer gets fewer crops. What best explains both changes?
options: Erosion removed fertile topsoil and lowered crop yields.
Weathering removed fertile topsoil but kept it nearby.
Erosion formed more soil, so the farmer got fewer crops.
Weathering lowered crop yields by moving soil elsewhere.

why.Weathering removed fertile topsoil but k: Weathering does not move topsoil away from the field.
why.Erosion formed more soil, so the farmer: Erosion removes soil; it does not form more soil here.
why.Weathering lowered crop yields by moving: Weathering can form soil, but it does not move it elsewhere.

activities.explanation: Erosion removes fertile topsoil and lowers crop yields.

activities.prompt: A map shows soil missing uphill and piled downhill. What does this map show?
options: Erosion moved the soil from one place to another.
Weathering broke the soil but left every piece uphill.
Erosion formed new soil where the farmer planted crops.
Weathering moved the soil from uphill to downhill.

why.Weathering broke the soil but left every: The missing and piled soil show movement, not only breakage.
why.Erosion formed new soil where the farmer: The map shows soil moving away, not new soil forming.
why.Weathering moved the soil from uphill to: Weathering breaks material without moving it to another place.

activities.explanation: Erosion wears away soil and carries the material elsewhere.

lessons.sceneAlt: Exposed lateritic rock formations are shaped by tropical weathering and erosion, showing reddish hues and rugged textures typical of iron-rich soils.

lessons.title: Running Water, Beaches and Coastal Landforms

activities.prompt: What might rivers and waves do to the land near us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Water Shapes the Land
activities.body: Running water shapes land by erosion, transportation and deposition. Erosion wears away land. Transportation carries material. Deposition drops it. In the upper course, rivers often make V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and rapids. In the middle course, rivers meander, which means bending. They form oxbow lakes and floodplains. In the lower course, rivers slow down and deposit sediment. This sediment can form a fan-shaped or triangular delta. Waves and currents reshape coastal land.
keyPoints: Rivers erode, transport and deposit material.
River courses create valleys, lakes and floodplains.
Sediment can form fan-shaped or triangular deltas.
Waves and currents reshape coasts.
Cliff retreat can leave wave-cut platforms.
Some coastal communities use beaches for fishing.
activities.explanation: Water keeps moving material and changing the land around us.

activities.prompt: A farmer sees a winding river and wants fertile farming land.
steps: The river is in its middle course, where it begins to meander.
It can form oxbow lakes and floodplains because its course bends.
Soil deposited along the banks is fertile, so it supports agriculture.
Therefore, farming beside the meander banks is a sensible choice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which landforms can form in a river's upper course?
options: V-shaped valleys
Oxbow lakes
Floodplains
River deltas
activities.explanation: Upper-course rivers often make V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and rapids.

activities.prompt: In the middle course, a river begins to ______ and forms oxbow lakes and floodplains.
activities.hint: This means bending in curves.
activities.explanation: A meandering river bends and forms oxbow lakes and floodplains.

activities.prompt: Match each river course or coastal feature with its result.
activities.explanation: Each course has features linked to the river's changing speed and actions.

activities.prompt: What does fertile soil deposited along meander banks support?
options: Crop growing
Fishing
Waterfall making
Cliff retreat
activities.explanation: Fertile soil deposited along meander banks supports agriculture.

activities.prompt: Put the river's courses in order from start to finish.
activities.explanation: The upper, middle and lower courses follow the river from start to finish.

activities.prompt: What can remain behind retreating cliffs after coastal erosion?
options: Wave-cut platforms
River deltas
Floodplains
Oxbow lakes
activities.explanation: Coastal erosion can leave wave-cut platforms behind retreating cliffs.

activities.prompt: A river erodes land in the upper course. Which landforms may form?
options: A V-shaped valley, waterfall, and rapids may form.
An oxbow lake and wide floodplain may form.
A fan-shaped delta and fishing beach may form.
A wave-cut platform and retreating cliff may form.

why.An oxbow lake and wide floodplain may fo: This confuses the middle course with the upper course.
why.A fan-shaped delta and fishing beach may: This mixes lower-course and coastal features.
why.A wave-cut platform and retreating cliff: This mistakes coastal erosion for river erosion.

activities.explanation: This matches the landforms formed in the upper course.

activities.prompt: A map shows a river bending in the middle course. Which landforms should it show?
options: A meander and oxbow lake near a floodplain.
A V-shaped valley and waterfall near high land.
A fan-shaped delta and a beach beside the sea.
A wave-cut platform beside a retreating cliff.

why.A V-shaped valley and waterfall near hig: These describe upper-course landforms, not middle-course bends.
why.A fan-shaped delta and a beach beside th: This mixes lower-course and coastal features.
why.A wave-cut platform beside a retreating: This describes coastal erosion, not a bending river.

activities.explanation: These are landforms formed in the middle course.

activities.prompt: A river slows in the lower course. What happens to its sediment?
options: It is deposited and may build a delta.
It erodes cliffs and leaves a platform.
It forms rapids and waterfalls in valleys.
It moves upstream to support farms.

This confuses coastal erosion with river deposition.
why.It forms rapids and waterfalls in valley: This describes upper-course erosion, not sediment deposition.
This confuses middle-course farming soil with lower-course sediment.

activities.explanation: The slower river deposits sediment, which can build a delta.

activities.prompt: Sea cliffs are retreating along the coast. What coastal feature may remain behind them?
options: A wave-cut platform may remain behind the retreating cliffs.
An oxbow lake may remain behind the retreating cliffs.
A fan-shaped delta may remain behind the retreating cliffs.
A V-shaped valley may remain behind the retreating cliffs.

why.An oxbow lake may remain behind the retr: An oxbow lake is a river landform, not a coastal feature.
why.A fan-shaped delta may remain behind the: A delta forms from river sediment, not retreating sea cliffs.
why.A V-shaped valley may remain behind the: A V-shaped valley forms in a river's upper course.

activities.explanation: Coastal erosion can leave wave-cut platforms behind retreating cliffs.

activities.prompt: A coastal community stands beside a beach. Why might the beach be useful?
options: The beach may be used for fishing by coastal communities.
The beach may be used for farming on a floodplain.
The beach may be used to make rapids and waterfalls.
The beach may be used to build a wave-cut platform.

why.The beach may be used for farming on a f: Farming on a floodplain is linked to rivers, not beaches.
why.The beach may be used to make rapids and: Rapids and waterfalls form in a river's upper course.
why.The beach may be used to build a wave-cu: A wave-cut platform forms through coastal erosion, not beach use.

activities.explanation: Some coastal communities use beaches for fishing.

activities.prompt: A river slows in the lower course and drops lots of sediment. Which shape may result?
options: A fan-shaped or triangular delta may form.
A V-shaped valley may form instead.
A retreating wave-cut cliff may form instead.
An oxbow lake may form instead.

A V-shaped valley forms through upper-course erosion.
why.A retreating wave-cut cliff may form ins: A retreating cliff forms through coastal erosion.
An oxbow lake forms in the river's middle course.

activities.explanation: River sediments can form a fan-shaped or triangular delta.
