lessons.title: Glaciers, Wind and Underground Water

activities.prompt: How do glaciers, winds, and hidden water reshape our world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Water Shapes the Land
activities.body: Glaciers erode valleys, leaving U-shaped valleys. They leave moraines of rock, soil and debris. They supply fresh water to rivers. Wind erodes rock into yardangs and piles sand into dunes. Dunes slow wind erosion and stop desertification. Underground water creates karst topography, land shaped by chemical weathering and erosion. Caves may have stalactites hanging from ceilings and stalagmites rising from floors. Caves and underground rivers provide fresh water and tourism.
keyPoints: Glacial erosion creates U-shaped valleys.
Moraines are deposits of rock, soil and debris.
Wind forms yardangs and dunes, while underground water creates karst topography.
activities.explanation: Water and wind slowly reshape the land in different ways.

activities.prompt: A town lies downstream from a glacier. The valley is U-shaped, and the river gives the town fresh water. What explains both?
steps: The valley is U-shaped because glacial erosion creates valleys with that shape.
The river has fresh water because glaciers provide fresh water to rivers.
The town can use this water because the river supports people downstream.
Thus, the glacier shapes the land and also supports people downstream.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A Valley Made by Ice
activities.prompt: Which landform can glacial erosion create?
options: U-shaped valleys
Sand dunes
Wind yardangs
Karst topography
activities.explanation: Glacial erosion creates U-shaped valleys and other related landforms.

activities.title: Deposits Left by a Glacier
activities.prompt: Glaciers leave behind rock, soil and debris called ______.
activities.hint: These deposits can form along a glacier's sides or at its furthest advance.
activities.explanation: Moraines form when glaciers leave deposited rock, soil and debris behind.

activities.title: Match Landforms and Descriptions
activities.prompt: Match each landform to its description.
activities.explanation: Each landform has a special location, shape or way of forming.

activities.title: Desert Landforms
activities.prompt: A desert has a sand hill and a wind-carved rock form. What formed them?
options: Wind made both forms
Water made both forms
Ice made both forms
Chemical weathering made both forms
activities.explanation: Wind piles sand into dunes and erodes rock into yardangs.

activities.title: Land Shaped Below Ground
activities.prompt: Underground water can create which landform through chemical weathering and erosion?
options: Karst topography
U-shaped valleys
Barchan dunes
Terminal moraines
activities.explanation: Karst topography forms when underground water causes chemical weathering and erosion.

activities.title: Benefits of Caves and Underground Rivers
activities.prompt: Caves and underground rivers can provide which two benefits?
options: Fresh water and tourism
Dunes and yardangs
Moraines and glaciers
People and valleys
activities.explanation: Caves and underground rivers can provide fresh water and tourism opportunities.

activities.prompt: A valley has a wide U shape. Which process created this valley?
options: Wind erosion shaped this valley.
Underground water shaped this valley.
Glacial deposition shaped this valley.
Glacial erosion shaped this valley.

This mistake confuses wind erosion with glacial erosion.
This mistake confuses underground water with glacial erosion.
This mistake confuses material left behind with land being eroded.

activities.explanation: This is right because glacial erosion creates U-shaped valleys.

activities.prompt: A map shows rock, soil and debris left by a glacier. What does its terminal moraine show?
options: The glacier's side deposits reached there.
The glacier's fresh water began there.
The glacier's wind erosion made it.
The glacier's furthest advance reached there.

why.The glacier's side deposits reached ther: This mistake confuses lateral moraines with terminal moraines.
This mistake confuses moraine debris with the source of river water.
This mistake confuses wind erosion with glacier deposition.

activities.explanation: This is right because terminal moraines mark the furthest advance.

activities.prompt: A desert map shows a barchan dune beside other sand ridges. What does this show?
options: Barchan is one type of glacier-made valley.
Barchan is one type of underground rock cave.
Barchan is one type of wind-formed desert dune.
Barchan is one type of wind-eroded rock ridge.

why.Barchan is one type of glacier-made vall: This mistake confuses glacial valleys with desert dunes.
why.Barchan is one type of underground rock: This mistake confuses karst caves with desert dunes.
why.Barchan is one type of wind-eroded rock: This mistake confuses yardangs, which wind erosion creates, with dunes.

activities.explanation: This is right because barchan dunes are one type of wind-formed desert dune.

activities.prompt: Sand dunes stand between a farm and strong desert winds. What benefit do they give?
options: They can supply fresh water to downstream people.
They can stop desertification and wind erosion.
They can create U-shaped valleys for farms.
They can leave glacier debris across the land.

why.They can supply fresh water to downstrea: This mistake confuses glacier water with dune protection.
why.They can create U-shaped valleys for far: This mistake confuses glacial erosion with dune protection.
why.They can leave glacier debris across the: This mistake confuses moraine deposits with dune protection.

activities.explanation: This is right because dunes stop desertification and wind erosion.

activities.prompt: A cave has an underground river. A family wants fresh water and a place to visit. Why is the cave useful?
options: It gives fresh water and tourism opportunities.
It gives glacier valleys and moraine deposits.
It gives wind-made yardangs and desert dunes.
It gives underground rivers and fresh glaciers.

why.It gives glacier valleys and moraine dep: This mistake confuses glacial landforms with cave benefits.
why.It gives wind-made yardangs and desert d: This mistake confuses wind landforms with cave benefits.
why.It gives underground rivers and fresh gl: This mistake confuses moraine deposits with cave benefits.

activities.explanation: This is right because caves and underground rivers provide fresh water and tourism.

lessons.title: Landforms and Disasters

activities.prompt: Have you ever wondered why rain, snow, wind, and earthquakes can reshape the land?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Disasters Linked with Landforms
activities.body: Landforms can be linked with landslides, avalanches, glacial lake outflows and dust storms. A landslide happens when natural and human factors make a slope unstable. An avalanche begins when snow becomes unstable on a steep mountain slope. A glacial lake outflow is linked with a lake dam’s collapse. Strong winds can lift loose, dry soil and sand into the air.
keyPoints: Landslides happen when slopes become unstable.
Avalanches begin with unstable snow on steep slopes.
Dust storms form when strong winds lift dry soil and sand.
activities.explanation: These are four disasters linked with landforms in this lesson.

activities.prompt: A house stands on a hillside. Heavy rain begins. What danger may grow there?
steps: Rainwater enters the soil and rocks, so their weight increases.
The extra weight and lower friction make the slope unstable.
Therefore, the hillside is at risk of a landslide.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which cause can form a dust storm?
options: Strong winds lifting dry soil
Melting snow on mountain slopes
Rainwater entering soil and rocks
Earthquakes shaking weak lake dams
activities.explanation: Dust storms form when strong winds lift loose, dry soil and sand into the air.

activities.prompt: Heavy snowfall adds ______ to the snowpack and can make it unstable.
activities.hint: Think about what heavy snowfall does to the snowpack.
activities.explanation: Heavy snowfall adds weight to the snowpack. This can make the snow unstable.

activities.prompt: Match each disaster with its linked cause.
activities.explanation: Landslides need unstable slopes. Avalanches begin with unstable snow. Dust storms involve wind lifting dry soil.

activities.prompt: Why can road building on hillsides raise landslide risk?
options: Disturbing the slope
Making the slope stable
Adding dry soil and sand
Melting the snowpack
activities.explanation: Road building on hillsides can disturb slopes. Disturbed slopes can become unstable and cause landslides.

activities.prompt: Put the landslide process in order.
activities.explanation: Rainwater increases weight and reduces friction. These changes can make a slope unstable and lead to a landslide.

activities.prompt: What can earthquakes, avalanches or landslides help cause?
options: A glacial lake dam collapse
A dust storm formation
Heavy snowfall on mountain slopes
Rainwater enters soil and rocks
activities.explanation: Earthquakes, avalanches or landslides can weaken a glacial lake’s dam. The weakened dam can collapse.

activities.prompt: A dry hillside receives heavy rain. What is most likely next?
options: Rain makes the slope more stable.
Rain makes the slope more likely to slide.
Rain removes all soil from the slope.
Rain turns the slope into a snowfield.

It reverses the effect because rain can weaken a slope.
It mistakes rain for a force that removes all soil.
It confuses rainwater with falling snow.

activities.explanation: Rainwater adds weight and reduces friction, making sliding more likely.

activities.prompt: An earthquake shakes a hillside where people live. What may happen next?
options: A landslide may start because the ground is shaken.
A landslide may stop because the ground is shaken.
An avalanche may form because the ground is shaken.
A dust storm may form because the ground is shaken.

why.A landslide may stop because the ground: It reverses the effect because shaking can make landslides more likely.
why.An avalanche may form because the ground: It confuses ground shaking with unstable snow.
why.A dust storm may form because the ground: It confuses ground shaking with strong winds lifting dry soil.

activities.explanation: Earthquakes can trigger landslides by shaking the ground.

activities.prompt: Heavy snow falls, then sudden warmth reaches a steep mountain. What may happen?
options: The snow may become unstable and start an avalanche.
The snow may become stable and stay on the slope.
The snow may turn into loose, dry soil.
The snow may strengthen a nearby lake dam.

why.The snow may become stable and stay on t: It mistakes added snow weight for a reason the slope becomes safer.
It confuses melting snow with dry soil lifted by wind.
why.The snow may strengthen a nearby lake da: It confuses melting snow with weakening a glacial lake’s dam.

activities.explanation: Heavy snow adds weight, while sudden warmth can melt snow and reduce friction.

activities.prompt: An earthquake shakes a mountain with a glacial lake. What may happen next?
options: The lake’s dam may weaken and collapse.
The lake’s dam may become stronger and safer.
The lake’s snow may turn into dry sand.
The lake’s slope may lose all its friction.

why.The lake’s dam may become stronger and s: It imagines shaking making the dam safer instead of weaker.
It confuses a glacial lake with a dust storm.
why.The lake’s slope may lose all its fricti: It confuses the lake’s dam with an unstable soil slope.

activities.explanation: An earthquake can weaken a glacial lake’s dam and make it collapse.

activities.prompt: A place loses much of its plants. Why might dust storms become more likely?
options: Sparse plants leave loose soil for strong winds.
Sparse plants make heavy snowpacks more stable.
Sparse plants make slopes unstable through shaking.
Sparse plants cause glacial lakes to melt quickly.

why.Sparse plants make heavy snowpacks more: It confuses vegetation loss with heavy snowfall.
why.Sparse plants make slopes unstable throu: It confuses vegetation loss with earthquake shaking.
why.Sparse plants cause glacial lakes to mel: It confuses vegetation loss with melting glacial lakes.

activities.explanation: Sparse vegetation can leave loose soil that strong winds lift into the air.

lessons.title: Internal and External Forces

activities.prompt: What shapes the land we live on, and how does it shape us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Forces that change the Earth
activities.body: Landforms include mountains, deserts, coasts and harbours. Internal forces work inside the Earth and change its surface. Earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, folding and faulting are internal forces. External forces, such as weathering, erosion and deposition, slowly wear down landforms. Plate tectonics helps us understand the changing Earth’s surface. It also helps identify likely earthquake and volcano regions. Human life is closely connected with landforms and their resources.
keyPoints: Internal forces change the Earth’s surface.
External forces slowly wear down landforms.
Human life is closely connected with landforms and their resources.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects changing forces with the landforms people use.

activities.prompt: The Thar Desert limits large settlements. A trader still needs to cross it. Why can trade continue?
steps: The Thar Desert limits large settlements, so a large town is difficult.
The desert encourages trade routes, so traders can pass through.
Therefore, settlement may be limited, but trade can continue.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which one is an internal force?
options: Earthquakes
Weathering
Erosion
Deposition
activities.explanation: Earthquakes are listed as internal forces.

activities.prompt: Human life is closely connected with ______ and the resources they provide.
activities.hint: Think about mountains, deserts, coasts and harbours.
activities.explanation: Human life is closely connected with landforms and their resources.

activities.prompt: External forces wear down landforms very quickly.
activities.explanation: External forces wear down landforms slowly, not quickly.

activities.prompt: Match each landform with an effect from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a landform with an effect stated in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Mountains can act as both barriers and protectors for human societies.
activities.explanation: Mountains can protect societies while also acting as barriers.

activities.prompt: Plate tectonics helps identify regions where earthquakes and volcanoes are likely.
activities.explanation: Plate tectonics helps identify likely earthquake and volcano regions.

activities.prompt: Weathering, erosion and deposition slowly wear down landforms. What will likely happen to a landform over time?
options: It will slowly become smaller and lower.
It will slowly become taller and larger.
It will stay exactly the same for ever.
It will suddenly move far away.

This confuses slow wearing with slow building.
This assumes these forces make no change.
This confuses landform change with sudden movement.

activities.explanation: Wear down means the landform becomes smaller and lower.

activities.prompt: Earthquakes and volcanic eruptions are internal forces. Plate tectonics explains why the Earth's surface keeps changing. It also finds likely earthquake and volcano regions. What do these ideas help us understand?
options: Why the surface changes and where events are likely.
Why the surface stays still and where events never happen.
Why landforms wear down and where trade routes grow.
Why mountains protect people and where settlements stay large.

why.Why the surface stays still and where ev: This wrongly treats a changing surface as one that never changes.
why.Why landforms wear down and where trade: This mixes plate tectonics with external forces and human trade.
why.Why mountains protect people and where s: This mixes mountain protection with settlement limits.

activities.explanation: This joins surface change with likely earthquake and volcano regions.

activities.prompt: The Thar Desert limited large settlements but encouraged trade routes. Coasts and harbours supported trade, travel and cultural contacts. What can we compare about these places?
options: Both influenced where people settled, moved, and traded.
Both supported large settlements and distant cultural contacts.
Neither encouraged trade, travel, or cultural contact.
Only one encouraged routes between different places.

why.Both supported large settlements and dis: This gives the Thar the coast's full effects.
why.Neither encouraged trade, travel, or cul: This denies the trade and travel that both places supported.
why.Only one encouraged routes between diffe: This treats the coast as the only place encouraging routes.

activities.explanation: Both places shaped settlement, movement, and trade.

activities.prompt: Mountains can protect human societies even when they act as barriers. A village lies beside them. Why might they still help?
options: They may protect the village while limiting movement.
They may stop all movement but give no protection.
They may protect the village and encourage easy travel.
They may affect the village only through trade.

why.They may stop all movement but give no p: This treats mountains as only barriers.
why.They may protect the village and encoura: This treats protection as making travel easy.
why.They may affect the village only through: This ignores their barrier and protective roles.

activities.explanation: Mountains can act as both barriers and protectors.

activities.prompt: Human life is closely connected with landforms and their resources. A community depends on one nearby landform. If its resources change, what should we expect?
options: The community's life will be strongly affected.
The community will not change at all.
The landform will depend on the community.
Only travel will change, not community life.

This ignores the close connection with resources.
why.The landform will depend on the communit: This reverses the connection between people and landforms.
why.Only travel will change, not community l: This thinks only travel depends on landforms and resources.

activities.explanation: Human life depends strongly on landforms and their resources.

activities.prompt: Different landforms are linked with landslides, avalanches, glacial lake outflows and sandstorms. A region contains several landform types. Which risks should planners check?
options: All four events linked with different landforms.
One event linked with every landform type.
No events linked with different landforms.
Events linked only with one chosen landform.

why.One event linked with every landform typ: This assumes one event must fit every landform.
why.No events linked with different landform: This assumes different landforms have no linked events.
why.Events linked only with one chosen landf: This ignores events linked with the other landforms.

activities.explanation: Different landforms are linked with all four listed events.

lessons.sceneAlt: A world map showing the major tectonic plates.
lessons.sceneCaption: A world map of the major tectonic plates, based on a USGS tectonic plates map.

sceneCredit.text: Tectonic Plates by Danny William Wilson, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Danny William Wilson

activities.context: A student is told that Earth’s surface changes because of forces inside and on the planet. The student learns that large pieces of crust move slowly over the molten mantle. Later, the class studies two plates moving apart at a boundary and two plates moving towards each other at another boundary. The student asks why these movements differ.
activities.prompt: The pair of plates moving towards each other is best described as:
options: A convergent boundary; the plates are getting nearer.
A divergent boundary; the plates are getting nearer.
A transform boundary; the plates are getting nearer.
A convergent boundary; the plates are sliding past each other.

why.A divergent boundary; the plates are get: Divergent describes plates moving away from each other.
why.A transform boundary; the plates are get: Transform describes plates sliding past each other.
why.A convergent boundary; the plates are sl: Convergent is correct, but sliding describes a transform boundary.

activities.explanation: Convergent describes plates moving towards each other.

activities.context: A student is told that Earth’s surface changes because of forces inside and on the planet. The student learns that large pieces of crust move slowly over the molten mantle. Later, the class studies two plates moving apart at a boundary and two plates moving towards each other at another boundary. The student asks why these movements differ.
activities.prompt: Another pair of plates slides past each other without creating or destroying crust. How should the student classify this situation?
options: A transform boundary; the plates slide past one another.
A convergent boundary; the plates slide past one another.
A divergent boundary; the plates slide past one another.
A transform boundary; the plates approach one another.

why.A convergent boundary; the plates slide: Convergent plates move towards each other.
why.A divergent boundary; the plates slide p: Divergent plates move away from each other.
why.A transform boundary; the plates approac: Transform is correct, but approaching describes convergent movement.

activities.explanation: Sliding without creating or destroying crust defines a transform boundary.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): At a convergent boundary, two plates move towards each other.
Reason (R): Plate boundaries are the edges where tectonic plates meet.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but naming plate boundaries does not explain the movement towards each other.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The semi-molten asthenosphere below the lithosphere allows tectonic plates to move.
Reason (R): The asthenosphere is the outermost layer on which people live.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because people live on the crust.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the lithosphere and the asthenosphere?
activities.answer: The lithosphere includes the crust and the upper part of the mantle. The crust is the outermost layer, and people live on it. The asthenosphere is a semi-molten layer below the lithosphere. This semi-molten layer allows tectonic plates to move. The main difference is that the lithosphere includes the crust and upper mantle, while the asthenosphere lies below it and has a semi-molten state that allows the plates to move.
points: The lithosphere includes the crust and upper mantle.
The crust is the outermost layer where people live.
The asthenosphere lies below the lithosphere.
The semi-molten asthenosphere allows plate movement.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After water flows across a farm, the farmer notices that soil and small rock pieces have been carried toward a lower area. The field has lost some fertile topsoil, and its crop yields are lower. The farmer wonders how the material was loosened before it was moved and wants advice on managing water after this loss.
activities.prompt: If the farmer does not manage the water, what is likely to happen?
options: More fertile topsoil will be removed, and crop yields will decrease.
The broken material will remain on the surface, and crop yields will increase.
The field will gain fertile topsoil, and crop yields will increase.
Only the rocks will be eroded, while the soil and crop yields will remain unchanged.

why.The broken material will remain on the s: Weathering alone does not move the broken material.
why.The field will gain fertile topsoil, and: Moving soil to another place does not guarantee that the original field gains fertile topsoil.
why.Only the rocks will be eroded, while the: Water erosion affects soil as well as rocks.

activities.explanation: Erosion removes fertile topsoil and lowers crop yields.

activities.context: After water flows across a farm, the farmer notices that soil and small rock pieces have been carried toward a lower area. The field has lost some fertile topsoil, and its crop yields are lower. The farmer wonders how the material was loosened before it was moved and wants advice on managing water after this loss.
activities.prompt: Why was the material easier to carry after it had been broken down?
options: Weathering loosened the material at the surface, and erosion transported it.
Erosion loosened the material, and physical weathering carried the pieces away.
Chemical weathering transported the material, and biological weathering loosened it.
Gradation loosened the material, and wind erosion formed the smaller pieces.

why.Erosion loosened the material, and physi: The statement reverses the roles of weathering and erosion.
why.Chemical weathering transported the mate: Chemical weathering changes minerals, while biological weathering is caused by living things.
why.Gradation loosened the material, and win: Gradation and erosion are different from weathering.

activities.explanation: Weathering breaks down rocks without moving the material, while erosion carries it.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Erosion can carry soil away from a farmer's field.
Reason (R): Erosion wears away soil and rocks and carries the material to another place.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why soil can be carried away from the field.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Physical weathering moves broken rock to another place.
Reason (R): Changes in temperature, frost or wind break rocks into smaller pieces.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement is false because physical weathering does not move material, while the reason correctly describes how rocks are broken down.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between weathering and erosion?
activities.answer: Weathering and erosion are different processes. Weathering breaks rocks on the Earth's surface into smaller pieces. It can happen because of changes in temperature, frost or wind, and it can also involve chemical reactions or activity by plants, animals and micro-organisms. However, weathering does not move the broken material. Erosion wears away soil and rocks and carries that material to another place. Erosion includes water erosion and wind erosion.
points: Defines weathering as the breakdown of rocks.
Explains that weathering does not move material.
Defines erosion as wearing away and transporting material.
Identifies water erosion and wind erosion.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A community stands beside a river that slows in its lower course, where sediment settles near the banks. Residents grow crops on some of the nearby land. Along the coast, waves and currents reshape the shoreline, and a platform lies beyond cliffs that are retreating. Some residents also use the beach for fishing. The community is studying how these processes change the land around it.
activities.prompt: If the river’s flow slows further in this area, what would most likely happen?
options: It would deposit additional sediment.
It would cut a deeper V-shaped valley.
It would form rapids and waterfalls.
It would remove more soil through erosion.

V-shaped valleys are associated with the upper course.
Rapids and waterfalls are typical of the upper course.
why.It would remove more soil through erosio: The lower course is associated with deposition rather than greater erosion.

activities.explanation: A slower river deposits more sediment.

activities.context: A community stands beside a river that slows in its lower course, where sediment settles near the banks. Residents grow crops on some of the nearby land. Along the coast, waves and currents reshape the shoreline, and a platform lies beyond cliffs that are retreating. Some residents also use the beach for fishing. The community is studying how these processes change the land around it.
activities.prompt: What does the platform beyond the retreating cliffs most clearly show?
options: It is evidence that coastal erosion has left a landform behind the cliffs.
It shows that waves and currents have built new cliffs there.
It shows that river sediment formed the coastal platform.
It shows that beach fishing has cut away the cliffs.

why.It shows that waves and currents have bu: The platform records erosion rather than the building of new cliffs.
why.It shows that river sediment formed the: River sediment can form deltas, but this platform is coastal.
why.It shows that beach fishing has cut away: Fishing is a use of beaches, not the cause of cliff retreat.

activities.explanation: Coastal erosion can leave wave-cut platforms behind retreating cliffs.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): In the lower course, a river deposits large amounts of sediment.
Reason (R): The river slows down in the lower course.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The slowing of the river explains why large amounts of sediment are deposited there.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Waves and currents mainly add large amounts of sediment to beaches.
Reason (R): Waves and currents move over the ocean’s surface and reshape coastal land.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true, but the stated effect on beaches is not supported by the facts.

activities.prompt: Explain how landforms differ in the upper, middle and lower courses of a river.
activities.answer: The upper, middle and lower courses of a river produce different landforms as the river’s actions change. In the upper course, rivers often form V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and rapids. In the middle course, a river begins to meander and forms oxbow lakes and floodplains. In the lower course, the river slows down and deposits large amounts of sediment. Together, these landforms show how erosion, transportation and deposition shape land along a river’s course.
points: Upper course: V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and rapids
Middle course: meanders, oxbow lakes and floodplains
Lower course: slowing and deposition of sediment
River processes include erosion, transportation and deposition
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A mountain valley has been shaped by glacial erosion, and a river below it receives fresh water from a glacier. Rock and soil lie along the glacier’s sides and at its furthest point. In a nearby desert, wind has formed a ridge of sand. Underground water has created a karst area with a cave, where formations hang from the ceiling and rise from the floor. People use the cave and underground river for fresh water and tourism.
activities.prompt: If a glacier leaves deposits at the place where it once advanced farthest, which landform would mark that location?
options: A terminal moraine at the glacier’s former furthest limit
A lateral moraine beside the glacier’s edge
A dune beside the glacier’s edge
A stalagmite at the glacier’s former limit

why.A lateral moraine beside the glacier’s e: Lateral moraines form along glacier sides.
why.A dune beside the glacier’s edge: Dunes are formed from wind-blown sand.
why.A stalagmite at the glacier’s former lim: Stalagmites rise from cave floors and are unrelated to glacial limits.

activities.explanation: Terminal moraines mark the furthest advance of glaciers.

activities.context: A mountain valley has been shaped by glacial erosion, and a river below it receives fresh water from a glacier. Rock and soil lie along the glacier’s sides and at its furthest point. In a nearby desert, wind has formed a ridge of sand. Underground water has created a karst area with a cave, where formations hang from the ceiling and rise from the floor. People use the cave and underground river for fresh water and tourism.
activities.prompt: If people remove the sand dunes from the desert, which effect would be most likely?
options: Less protection against desertification and wind erosion
More fresh water flowing to downstream people
A wider U-shaped valley
More stalactites forming in nearby caves

why.More fresh water flowing to downstream p: Dunes do not supply rivers with fresh water.
why.A wider U-shaped valley: U-shaped valleys are related to glacial erosion.
why.More stalactites forming in nearby caves: Stalactites are cave features, not products of dunes.

activities.explanation: Dunes act as barriers against desertification and wind erosion.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A dune can act as a barrier against desertification and wind erosion.
Reason (R): Wind-formed sand hills and ridges can reduce these harmful effects.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason correctly explains how dunes limit desertification and wind erosion.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Shaping of the Earth’s Surface

activities.prompt: Which boundary has two plates moving towards each other?
options: Divergent boundary
Transform boundary
Convergent boundary
Plate boundary
activities.explanation: At a convergent boundary, two plates move towards each other.

activities.prompt: Weathering moves broken material to another place.
activities.explanation: Weathering breaks down rocks but does not move the broken material.

activities.prompt: The semi-molten ______ below the lithosphere allows tectonic plates to move.
activities.hint: It lies below the lithosphere.
activities.explanation: The asthenosphere is semi-molten and helps tectonic plates move.

activities.prompt: Match each plate boundary with its movement.
pairs: Plates move away from each other
activities.explanation: Each boundary has a different kind of plate movement.

activities.prompt: Waves and currents can reshape coastal land.
activities.explanation: Waves and currents move over the ocean’s surface and reshape coastal land.

activities.prompt: Which feature rises from a cave floor?
options: Stalactite
Stalagmite
Moraine
Dune
activities.explanation: Stalactites hang from cave ceilings, while stalagmites rise from cave floors.

activities.prompt: Match each disaster with the landform or process linked with it.
pairs: Unstable snow on a steep slope
Loose dry soil lifted by strong winds
Collapse of a glacial lake’s dam
activities.explanation: These disasters are linked with unstable slopes, snow, dry soil and glacial lakes.

activities.prompt: Coasts and harbours supported trade, travel and cultural contacts with distant lands.
activities.explanation: Coasts and harbours supported trade, travel and cultural contacts with distant lands.

activities.prompt: Put these river courses in order from the upper course to the lower course.
activities.explanation: A river changes from its upper course through the middle course to the lower course.

chapters.title: Atmosphere and Climate
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the atmosphere and its composition; the layers of the atmosphere; weather and its elements; local winds and seasons in india.

lessons.title: The Atmosphere and Its Composition

activities.prompt: What makes the air around Earth so important to life?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is the atmosphere?
activities.body: The atmosphere is a blanket of air surrounding the Earth. Gravity pulls it down towards the Earth. It mixes many gases in different proportions. Nitrogen and oxygen are the most abundant gases. Other gases include carbon dioxide, argon, helium, neon, krypton, xenon, ozone and hydrogen. Water vapour and tiny dust particles are also present.
keyPoints: The atmosphere surrounds the Earth.
Gravity pulls the atmosphere towards the Earth.
Nitrogen and oxygen are the most abundant gases.
activities.explanation: The atmosphere is a mixture of gases and other tiny particles around us.

activities.prompt: Imagine Earth covered by a blanket of air. Why does this blanket stay close?
steps: The atmosphere is a blanket of air surrounding Earth.
Gravity pulls this blanket down towards Earth.
Because of this pull, the blanket stays close to Earth.
Therefore, gravity keeps the atmosphere close around our planet.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What pulls the atmosphere down towards the Earth?
options: Gravity
Oxygen
Water vapour
Dust
activities.explanation: Gravity pulls the atmosphere down towards the Earth.

activities.prompt: The atmosphere is a mixture of gases in different proportions.
activities.explanation: Yes, the atmosphere mixes many gases in different proportions.

activities.prompt: Water vapour helps in cloud formation and ______.
activities.hint: This happens when water falls from clouds.
activities.explanation: Water vapour helps in cloud formation and precipitation.

activities.prompt: What does the atmosphere do with some solar energy?
options: Lets it escape into space
Traps it near Earth
Changes it into dust
Turns it into water
activities.explanation: The atmosphere traps some solar energy and prevents it from escaping into space.

activities.prompt: What happens to the composition of the atmosphere as altitude changes?
options: It changes with altitude
It stays exactly the same
It becomes only oxygen
It loses every gas
activities.explanation: The composition of the atmosphere changes with altitude.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the atmosphere with its role or feature.
activities.explanation: The atmosphere has many parts. Each one has an important feature or role.

activities.prompt: A child compares sunlight below the atmosphere with sunlight in space. Which difference matters most for safety?
options: Harmful radiation is blocked below the atmosphere.
Some solar energy is trapped below the atmosphere.
Gravity pulls sunlight down towards the Earth.
Water vapour blocks sunlight from reaching clouds.

why.Some solar energy is trapped below the a: Trapping solar energy is not the same as blocking harmful radiation.
why.Gravity pulls sunlight down towards the: Gravity pulls the atmosphere, not sunlight, towards Earth.
why.Water vapour blocks sunlight from reachi: This confuses water vapour's cloud role with radiation protection.

activities.explanation: The atmosphere protects people from harmful radiation from the Sun.

activities.prompt: A diagram shows different gas mixes at two heights. What does the change show?
options: The atmosphere changes in composition with altitude.
Gravity makes every gas settle at the bottom.
Water vapour always stays near the ground.
The Sun adds harmful radiation to both rows.

why.Gravity makes every gas settle at the bo: This assumes gravity sorts gases into separate layers.
why.Water vapour always stays near the groun: This assumes water vapour remains only near the ground.
why.The Sun adds harmful radiation to both r: This mistakes sunlight for the cause of changing composition.

activities.explanation: The different mixes show that composition changes with altitude.

activities.prompt: Clouds form and precipitation follows. What atmospheric ingredient can help cause both?
options: Water vapour helps form clouds and precipitation.
Tiny dust helps form clouds and precipitation.
Nitrogen gas helps form clouds and precipitation.
Argon gas helps form clouds and precipitation.

why.Tiny dust helps form clouds and precipit: This confuses the presence of dust with water vapour's cloud role.
why.Nitrogen gas helps form clouds and preci: Being abundant does not make nitrogen the gas that helps form clouds.
why.Argon gas helps form clouds and precipit: Being listed as another gas does not give argon this role.

activities.explanation: Water vapour helps in both cloud formation and precipitation.

lessons.title: The Layers of the Atmosphere

activities.prompt: What makes each layer of our sky feel different as we climb higher?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Layered Atmosphere
activities.body: The atmosphere has a layered structure. Its layers are defined by changes in temperature and density as altitude increases. Altitude means height above Earth’s surface. Air density is highest near Earth’s surface. The troposphere has an average height of about 12 kilometres. The stratosphere extends up to 50 kilometres. The mesosphere extends up to 80 kilometres. Temperature rises very rapidly with altitude in the thermosphere. The exosphere is the uppermost layer.
keyPoints: Nearly all weather phenomena occur in the troposphere.
The stratosphere is cloud-free and suitable for flying aeroplanes.
Ozone filters harmful radiation from the Sun.
The exosphere is the uppermost layer.
activities.explanation: Changes in temperature and density help us understand the atmosphere’s layers.

activities.prompt: A child wants an aeroplane ride without clouds. Which layer should the pilot choose?
steps: The troposphere holds nearly all weather, so it is the first layer to check.
The stratosphere is free of clouds, so it suits aeroplane flying.
The pilot should choose the stratosphere for a cloud-free journey.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The atmosphere has a single, unchanged layer.
activities.explanation: The atmosphere has a layered structure. Its layers change with temperature, density and altitude.

activities.prompt: Which layer has nearly all weather phenomena?
options: Troposphere
Stratosphere
Mesosphere
Thermosphere
activities.explanation: Nearly all weather phenomena occur in the troposphere. That is the correct layer.

activities.prompt: The stratosphere extends up to ______ kilometres.
activities.hint: Think about the height given for the stratosphere.
activities.explanation: The stratosphere extends up to 50 kilometres above Earth’s surface.

activities.prompt: Match each atmosphere fact with the correct layer or substance.
pairs: Filters harmful radiation from the Sun
activities.explanation: Weather occurs in the troposphere, while aeroplanes fly in the cloud-free stratosphere. Ozone and the mesosphere also have special roles.

activities.prompt: Which layer is suitable for flying aeroplanes?
options: Stratosphere
Troposphere
Mesosphere
Exosphere
activities.explanation: The stratosphere is suitable for flying aeroplanes because it is free of clouds.

activities.prompt: What does ozone in the stratosphere do?
options: Filters harmful radiation from the Sun
Creates clouds for aeroplanes
Makes air densest near the surface
Causes nearly all weather phenomena
activities.explanation: Ozone in the stratosphere filters harmful radiation from the Sun. This protects Earth from radiation.

activities.prompt: Which option correctly describes the upper atmosphere?
options: The thermosphere warms rapidly; the exosphere is uppermost.
The thermosphere is uppermost; the exosphere warms rapidly.
The thermosphere is cloud-free; the exosphere filters radiation.
The thermosphere holds weather; the exosphere extends to 80 kilometres.
activities.explanation: Temperature rises very rapidly with altitude in the thermosphere. The exosphere is the uppermost layer.

activities.prompt: Put these facts in order from the lowest altitude to the highest altitude.
items: Air density is highest near Earth’s surface
The troposphere has an average height of about 12 kilometres
The stratosphere extends up to 50 kilometres
The mesosphere extends up to 80 kilometres
activities.explanation: This order follows increasing altitude, from Earth’s surface towards 80 kilometres.

activities.prompt: A balloon compares air near Earth's surface with air high above. Where is the air denser?
options: Near Earth's surface, where air density is highest.
High above, because higher air is always denser.
At every height, because air density never changes.
Only in the exosphere, because density rises upward.

why.High above, because higher air is always: This mistake thinks higher air is always denser.
why.At every height, because air density nev: This mistake thinks altitude does not change air density.
why.Only in the exosphere, because density r: This mistake limits density change to the exosphere.

activities.explanation: Air density is highest near the Earth's surface.

activities.prompt: A hiker compares low and high places inside the troposphere. Where should the air be colder?
options: At the low place, because temperature decreases as altitude rises.
At the high place, because temperature decreases as altitude rises.
At both places, because temperature stays the same there.
At neither place, because temperature always rises upward.

why.At the low place, because temperature de: Temperature decreases upward, so the low place should be warmer.
why.At both places, because temperature stay: This mistake thinks temperature stays constant inside the troposphere.
why.At neither place, because temperature al: This mistake reverses the decrease of temperature with altitude.

activities.explanation: The high place has greater altitude, so its temperature is lower.

lessons.title: Weather and Its Elements

activities.prompt: What makes our weather change from sunny skies to stormy surprises?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Weather Words Made Clear
activities.body: Weather is the atmosphere’s conditions from hour to hour and day to day. Climate is the sum of weather conditions and variations over a long period. Insolation means sunlight energy. It decreases from the equator towards the poles. Air pressure is air pushing on Earth’s surface. Altitude means height above sea level. Air pressure falls as height increases. Wind moves from high pressure to low pressure.
keyPoints: Humidity means water vapour in air. Warmer air can hold more water vapour.
Rain is commonest precipitation and lowers temperature. Precipitation includes drizzle, rain, snow, sleet and hail.
Prevailing winds, mountains and seasons affect precipitation.
activities.explanation: These words connect changing weather with long-term climate and the atmosphere.

activities.prompt: Why is one rainy afternoon called weather, but a long weather record called climate?
steps: Weather is short-term because conditions change hour to hour and day to day.
One rainy afternoon is only one short weather condition.
Over many years, weather conditions and variations add together.
Therefore, the afternoon is weather, but the long record is climate.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which statement describes weather?
options: Climate is weather measured over a long period.
Weather changes from hour to hour and day to day.
Air pressure is wind pushing on Earth’s surface.
Humidity is sunlight energy reaching the poles.
activities.explanation: Correct. Weather changes from hour to hour and day to day.

activities.prompt: Which direction shows a decrease in insolation?
options: From the poles towards the equator.
From high pressure towards low pressure.
From the equator towards the poles.
From sea level towards higher altitude.
activities.explanation: Insolation decreases from the equator towards the poles.

activities.prompt: Match each weather term with its matching phrase.
pairs: Weather conditions and variations over a long period
Presence of water vapour in the air
Drizzle, rain, snow, sleet and hail
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a weather term with its meaning in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Which statement about rain is correct?
options: Rain is rare and raises temperature.
Rain is commonest and raises temperature.
Rain is commonest and lowers temperature.
Rain is rare and lowers temperature.
activities.explanation: Rain is commonest precipitation and lowers temperature.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to show the pressure change.
items: Air pressure is highest at sea level.
Air pressure falls as height increases.
activities.explanation: Air pressure is highest at sea level. It falls as altitude increases.

activities.prompt: Warm air holds more vapour than cool air. Which room holds more?
options: Warmer room, because warm air holds more vapour.
Cooler room, because cool air holds more vapour.
Both rooms, because both hold the same vapour.
Neither room, because air cannot hold vapour.

why.Cooler room, because cool air holds more: This mistake thinks cool air holds more vapour.
why.Both rooms, because both hold the same v: This mistake thinks both temperatures hold the same amount.
why.Neither room, because air cannot hold va: This mistake thinks air cannot hold vapour at all.

activities.explanation: This is right because warm air can hold more water vapour.

activities.prompt: Insolation decreases from the equator towards the poles. Which place gets more?
options: Near the equator, where insolation is stronger.
Near the poles, where insolation is weaker.
At sea level, where insolation is strongest.
At high altitude, where insolation is strongest.

why.Near the poles, where insolation is weak: This mistake reverses the decrease in insolation towards the poles.
why.At sea level, where insolation is strong: This mistake mixes insolation with air pressure at sea level.
why.At high altitude, where insolation is st: This mistake mixes insolation with the effect of altitude.

activities.explanation: This is right because insolation decreases as we move towards the poles.

activities.prompt: Prevailing winds, mountains and seasons affect precipitation. What may change in a town?
options: The amount of precipitation may change over time.
The amount of precipitation will never change.
The amount of precipitation depends only on humidity.
The amount of precipitation depends only on air pressure.

why.The amount of precipitation will never c: This mistake thinks precipitation always stays the same.
why.The amount of precipitation depends only: This mistake thinks humidity alone controls precipitation.
This mistake thinks air pressure alone controls precipitation.

activities.explanation: This is right because these three factors affect precipitation.

lessons.title: Local Winds and Seasons in India

activities.prompt: Why do coastal winds change, and how does India divide its year?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Local Winds and India's Seasons
activities.body: India has a broadly tropical monsoon climate. The Indian Meteorological Department recognises four distinct seasons: winter, summer, monsoon, and post-monsoon. Sea and land breezes are local winds. During the day, a sea breeze blows from sea to land. At night, a land breeze blows from land to sea. These winds help create moderate climatic conditions in coastal regions.
keyPoints: Sea breezes blow towards land during the day.
Land breezes blow towards the sea at night.
India has four recognised seasons.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects local winds with India's four recognised seasons.

activities.prompt: A family visits the coast in December and stays overnight. Which winds and seasons fit?
steps: Daytime wind comes from the sea because sea breezes blow inland.
Night wind comes from the land because land breezes blow seaward.
These winds help because they make coastal climatic conditions moderate.
Therefore, December fits both winter and post-monsoon labels.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which named local wind blows from the land towards the sea at night?
options: Sea breeze
Land breeze
Monsoon breeze
Coastal breeze
activities.explanation: You are right. A land breeze blows from land towards sea during the night.

activities.prompt: A sea breeze blows from the land towards the sea during the day.
activities.explanation: A sea breeze blows from the sea towards the land during the day.

activities.prompt: The season generally spanning from June to September is called ______.
activities.hint: Its name comes from the monsoon season.
activities.explanation: Correct! The monsoon season generally spans from June to September.

activities.prompt: Match each season to its period.
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each season is joined to its usual period.

activities.prompt: Put the seasons in their usual order through the year.
activities.explanation: Well done! Winter comes before summer, monsoon, and then post-monsoon.

activities.prompt: How many distinct seasons does the Indian Meteorological Department recognise?
options: Two
Four
Six
Many
activities.explanation: Correct! The Department recognises four distinct seasons in India.

activities.prompt: A map shows night wind moving from houses towards the sea. Which breeze is shown, and why?
options: It is a sea breeze, because sea air moves towards land.
It is a land breeze, because land air moves towards the sea.
It is a sea breeze, because sea air moves towards the sea.
It is a land breeze, because land air moves towards land.

why.It is a sea breeze, because sea air move: This uses the daytime sea breeze, but the map shows night.
This gives the right breeze name but reverses its direction.
why.It is a land breeze, because land air mo: This gives the right breeze name but reverses its direction.

activities.explanation: This is right because night land breezes move from land to sea.

activities.prompt: An outing starts in winter and ends in the monsoon season. Which seasonal order fits the calendar?
options: Winter, then summer, then monsoon
Monsoon, then summer, then winter
Post-monsoon, then winter, then summer
Summer, then post-monsoon, then monsoon

why.Monsoon, then summer, then winter: This puts the seasons in the wrong calendar order.
why.Post-monsoon, then winter, then summer: Post-monsoon comes after monsoon, not before winter.
why.Summer, then post-monsoon, then monsoon: This begins with summer even though the outing starts in winter.

activities.explanation: This fits because winter comes before summer, and summer before monsoon.

activities.prompt: A family plans a coastal holiday in September. Which season and daytime wind should they expect?
options: Monsoon season, with a sea breeze during the day.
Monsoon season, with a land breeze during the day.
Summer season, with a sea breeze during the day.
Winter season, with a land breeze during the day.

why.Monsoon season, with a land breeze durin: The season is right, but a land breeze blows at night instead.
why.Summer season, with a sea breeze during: The breeze is right, but September is not in the summer season.
why.Winter season, with a land breeze during: September is not winter, and a land breeze belongs to the night.

activities.explanation: Correct: September is monsoon, and sea breezes blow by day.

activities.prompt: One poster says India has four seasons. Another says six traditional seasons. Which explanation fits both?
options: The department recognises four; tradition recognises six.
The department recognises six; tradition recognises four.
Both posters use the department's four-season rule.
Both posters describe the same traditional system.

why.The department recognises six; tradition: This swaps the department's count and the traditional count.
why.Both posters use the department's four-s: The second poster refers to tradition, not the department's rule.
why.Both posters describe the same tradition: The two posters use different seasonal systems.

activities.explanation: This is right because the department uses four and tradition uses six.

lessons.title: Understanding the Monsoon

activities.prompt: Why do the winds change direction and bring rain to India each year?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is the monsoon?
activities.body: The monsoon is a yearly change in wind direction. Ancient sailors were among the first to notice it. Arab traders named this change ‘monsoon’. Summer winds bring moist air from oceans towards land. They bring most rain to India. Winter winds are cold, dry and blow from land to sea. Heavy rain can cause floods. Weak monsoons can cause droughts.
keyPoints: Monsoon winds change direction during the year.
Summer monsoon winds bring moist ocean air towards land.
Winter monsoon winds are cold, dry and blow towards the sea.
activities.explanation: Monsoon winds change direction with the seasons.

activities.prompt: A farmer sees summer winds moving from the sea toward the land. Why can these winds be important for the fields?
steps: India's land heats faster than the oceans because land and sea heat unequally.
This unequal heating mainly causes the summer monsoon.
Moist winds blow from the ocean toward the land, so they bring rainfall.
Most Indian agriculture depends on monsoon rainfall, so summer rain is vital.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which change is called a monsoon?
options: A daily change in wind direction
A yearly change in ocean depth
A yearly change in wind direction
A daily change in cloud colour
activities.explanation: A monsoon is the seasonal reversal of wind direction during a year.

activities.prompt: Arab traders named the seasonal reversal of winds ‘monsoon’.
activities.explanation: Arab traders gave the name ‘monsoon’ to the seasonal reversal of winds.

activities.prompt: What mainly causes the summer monsoon?
options: Equal heating of land and sea
Unequal heating of land and sea
Unequal heating of air and clouds
Equal heating of ocean and air
activities.explanation: The summer monsoon is mainly caused by unequal heating of land and sea.

activities.prompt: Match each monsoon term with its correct description.
activities.explanation: Summer winds bring moist ocean air and rain. Winter winds are called the north-east monsoon.

activities.prompt: During winter, monsoon winds are generally:
options: Warm, wet and moving towards sea
Cold, dry and moving towards sea
Cold, wet and moving towards land
Warm, dry and moving towards land
activities.explanation: Cold, dry winter monsoon winds blow from land to sea. This monsoon is also called the north-east monsoon.

activities.prompt: What can a weak monsoon cause?
options: A drought
A flood
Colder ocean water
Stronger land heating
activities.explanation: Weak monsoons can cause droughts. Excessive monsoon rainfall can cause floods.

activities.prompt: During summer, India's land heats faster than nearby oceans. Moist winds then blow toward the land. What is likely to happen?
options: The land will receive monsoon rainfall.
The oceans will receive most summer rainfall.
Cold, dry winds will blow toward the land.
The land will stay cooler than the ocean.

why.The oceans will receive most summer rain: This wrongly sends summer rain away from the land.
why.Cold, dry winds will blow toward the lan: It mistakes winter wind conditions for summer winds.
why.The land will stay cooler than the ocean: It reverses the stated summer heating difference.

activities.explanation: Ocean-to-land winds bring rain to the land.

activities.prompt: A summer monsoon brings much more rain than usual to India's farms. Which problem may farmers face?
options: Their fields may flood from excessive rainfall.
Their fields may face drought from weak rainfall.
Their crops may receive no summer sunlight.
Their soil may become colder than the sea.

why.Their fields may face drought from weak: Weak monsoons, not heavy rain, are linked with drought.
why.Their crops may receive no summer sunlig: This confuses a rainfall problem with a sunlight problem.
why.Their soil may become colder than the se: The problem comes from too much rain, not cold soil.

activities.explanation: Excessive monsoon rainfall can flood fields.

activities.prompt: A summer monsoon is weak and gives little rain. What may happen to farms that depend on it?
options: Farmers may face drought because rainfall is too low.
Farmers may face floods because rainfall is too high.
Farmers may face drought because rainfall is too high.
Farmers may face floods because rainfall is too low.

why.Farmers may face floods because rainfall: Floods follow excessive rain, not weak monsoon rain.
why.Farmers may face drought because rainfal: It mixes up weak rainfall with excessive rainfall.
why.Farmers may face floods because rainfall: It mixes up floods and weak monsoon rainfall.

activities.explanation: A weak monsoon can cause drought, especially for farming.

activities.prompt: A map shows summer winds from ocean to land and winter winds from land to sea. What pattern does the map show?
options: A seasonal reversal of wind direction.
A constant wind direction through the year.
A reversal caused by equal land and sea heating.
A reversal caused by floods and droughts.

why.A constant wind direction through the ye: It ignores the opposite directions shown for the seasons.
why.A reversal caused by equal land and sea: It wrongly treats equal heating as the cause of reversal.
why.A reversal caused by floods and droughts: It mistakes rainfall effects for the cause of wind reversal.

activities.explanation: The map shows wind direction changing between summer and winter.

lessons.title: Climate Change and the Punjab Floods

activities.prompt: What made Punjab’s floods so severe, and how can we respond?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Connects Climate Change and Floods?
activities.body: Climate change means long-term changes in weather patterns. Burning fossil fuels mainly causes it. Human actions raise greenhouse gases. These gases trap heat and raise temperatures. Climate change harms health, agriculture and livelihoods. In Punjab, heavy monsoon rains caused severe floods in 2025. Rivers were already high, and weak embankments worsened damage. Buildings near rivers reduced floodwater space. A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gases released by human activities.
keyPoints: Climate change means long-term changes in weather patterns.
Human actions raise greenhouse gases, which trap heat.
Heavy monsoon rains caused Punjab's severe floods in 2025.
activities.explanation: These ideas explain both climate change and the Punjab floods.

activities.prompt: A family burns fossil fuels. Why might health and livelihoods suffer?
steps: Burning fossil fuels adds greenhouse gases, because human activities mainly cause climate change.
Long-term weather patterns change because greenhouse gases trap heat and raise temperatures.
Climate change harms health, agriculture, and livelihoods, so life can become harder.
Renewable energy lowers carbon footprints, so fewer greenhouse gases trap less heat.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does climate change mean?
options: Long-term changes in weather patterns
Short-lived changes in one day's weather
Only changes in rainfall during one monsoon
Changes in temperature on a single afternoon
activities.explanation: Good choice! Climate change means long-term changes in weather patterns.

activities.prompt: A carbon footprint is the total ______ gases released by human activities.
activities.hint: These gases trap heat and raise temperatures.
activities.explanation: Well done! A carbon footprint measures greenhouse gases released by human activities.

activities.prompt: Match each human action with its result.
activities.explanation: You matched the actions and results correctly!

activities.prompt: What caused Punjab's severe floods in 2025?
options: Dry monsoon winds
Light monsoon rains
Heavy monsoon rains
Short monsoon bursts
activities.explanation: Yes! Heavy monsoon rains caused Punjab's severe floods in 2025.

activities.prompt: Put these Punjab flood events in order.
items: Farmland and paddy crops were damaged
activities.explanation: Good ordering! The rivers were high before the heavy rains and floods.

activities.prompt: Which condition made the Punjab floods more harmful?
options: Strong and new embankments
Weak and old embankments
Rivers flowing at low levels
Homes and farms far from rivers
activities.explanation: Correct! Weak and old river embankments made the floods more harmful.

activities.prompt: Factories burn fossil fuels and add greenhouse gases to the atmosphere. What is the likely chain?
options: The gases trap heat, temperatures rise, and climate change harms livelihoods.
The gases trap heat, temperatures rise, and climate change helps farming.
The gases release heat, temperatures fall, and climate change harms livelihoods.
The gases release heat, temperatures rise, and climate change helps farming.

why.The gases trap heat, temperatures rise,: This mistakes climate change's harm to agriculture as a benefit.
why.The gases release heat, temperatures fal: This reverses the greenhouse effect because the gases trap heat.
why.The gases release heat, temperatures ris: This reverses both the greenhouse effect and climate change's harm to farming.

activities.explanation: Right: greenhouse gases trap heat, and climate change harms livelihoods.

activities.prompt: In 2025, Punjab's rivers were already high before heavy monsoon rains. Homes stood near rivers. What followed?
options: Less space for floodwater will make the heavy rains cause worse floods.
Rivers will fall lower, so the heavy rains will cause milder floods.
Heavy rain will dry the rivers, so no floodwater will remain.
More space for floodwater will make the heavy rains cause milder floods.

why.Rivers will fall lower, so the heavy rai: This wrongly suggests heavy rain makes rivers fall lower.
why.Heavy rain will dry the rivers, so no fl: This wrongly treats heavy rain as drying rivers instead of adding water.
why.More space for floodwater will make the: This reverses the effect of having less room for floodwater.

activities.explanation: Right: high rivers and nearby homes leave less space for floodwater.

activities.prompt: A map shows old embankments and homes beside Punjab's rivers. What does it suggest?
options: Weak embankments and less river space will make floods more harmful.
Strong embankments and more river space will make floods less harmful.
Old embankments and nearby homes will make floods less harmful.
Nearby homes and old embankments will give floodwater more space.

why.Strong embankments and more river space: This reverses both weak embankments and reduced space for floodwater.
why.Old embankments and nearby homes will ma: This treats weak embankments and close homes as flood protections.
why.Nearby homes and old embankments will gi: This reverses the effect of building homes and farms close to rivers.

activities.explanation: Right: weak old embankments and nearby buildings reduce floodwater space.

activities.prompt: A community uses renewable energy and protects forests. How can this help against climate change?
options: Fewer greenhouse gases trap less heat, so climate harm can become smaller.
Fewer greenhouse gases trap more heat, so climate harm can become smaller.
More greenhouse gases trap less heat, so climate harm can become smaller.
These actions add greenhouse gases, so global temperatures rise less.

why.Fewer greenhouse gases trap more heat, s: This reverses the effect of greenhouse gases trapping heat.
why.More greenhouse gases trap less heat, so: This reverses the link between more gases and more trapped heat.
why.These actions add greenhouse gases, so g: This mistakes helpful actions for sources of more greenhouse gases.

activities.explanation: Right: renewable energy and forests can reduce greenhouse gases and trapped heat.

activities.prompt: Community A reduces its carbon footprint. Community B keeps using fossil fuels. What difference should we expect?
options: A releases fewer greenhouse gases, so less heat should be trapped.
A releases more greenhouse gases, so less heat should be trapped.
B releases fewer greenhouse gases, so more heat should be trapped.
Both release the same greenhouse gases, so equal heat should be trapped.

why.A releases more greenhouse gases, so les: This reverses the meaning of a smaller carbon footprint.
why.B releases fewer greenhouse gases, so mo: This swaps the communities and reverses the trapped-heat effect.
why.Both release the same greenhouse gases,: This wrongly assumes every community releases the same greenhouse gases.

activities.explanation: Right: a smaller carbon footprint means fewer greenhouse gases are released.

activities.prompt: Floods damage paddy in Punjab. Why can this hurt a farming family?
options: Their crops and farmland are damaged, so their livelihood is harmed.
Their crops are protected, so their livelihood is not harmed.
Their farmland is damaged, but their livelihood is not harmed.
Their paddy crop grows well, so their livelihood becomes safer.

why.Their crops are protected, so their live: This reverses the stated damage to crops and farmland.
why.Their farmland is damaged, but their liv: This wrongly separates farmland damage from harm to livelihoods.
why.Their paddy crop grows well, so their li: This wrongly treats flood damage as better crop growth.

activities.explanation: Right: damaged crops and farmland can harm a family's livelihood.
