chapters.title: State and Society up to 1000 CE
chapters.summary: In this chapter: society, state and the vedic beginnings; from janapadas to kingdoms and republics; ethics, dharma and social groups; family, women, religion and education.

lessons.title: Society, State and the Vedic Beginnings

activities.prompt: How did societies, states, and the Vedas begin to shape life together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How societies and states began
activities.body: People sharing territory, culture and belonging form society. Customs and practices guide it. A state is an organised political system based on rules and laws. Political systems developed gradually. The Vedas are the earliest known Indian literature. They were passed down orally for centuries. Each Veda has four sections, called samhitā, brāhmaṇa, āranyaka and upaniṣhad. Vedic kinship groups were called janas. Vedic texts mention assemblies called sabhā, samiti and vidhata.
keyPoints: Society shares territory, culture and belonging.
Political systems grew as societies became more complicated.
Vedas were oral, janas were kinship groups, and texts named three assemblies.
activities.explanation: This card connects society, states and early Vedic beginnings.

activities.prompt: A neighbourhood shares land, food habits, and belonging. A nearby town has an organised political system based on laws. Why are the two groups different?
steps: The neighbourhood is a society because people share territory, culture, and belonging.
Its customs and practices mainly guide it rather than formal written laws.
The town is a state because its political system is organised.
Its rules and laws explain why it differs from the neighbourhood.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Understanding society
activities.prompt: Which statement best explains society?
options: A system guided only by formal laws
A system of relationships among people
A group without shared territory
A collection of ancient literature
activities.explanation: Society connects people who share territory, culture and belonging.

activities.title: The meaning of state
activities.prompt: A state is an organised ______ system based on rules and laws.
activities.hint: Think of a system that organises political life.
activities.explanation: A state is an organised political system based on rules and laws.

activities.title: Why political systems developed
activities.prompt: Why did political systems develop gradually?
options: After all Vedas had been written down
Before people began sharing any culture
As societies grew larger and more complicated
While oral traditions had completely ended
activities.explanation: Great thinking. Larger and more complicated societies needed political systems.

activities.title: Match each idea
activities.prompt: Match each idea on the left with its meaning.
activities.explanation: You matched the main people, ideas and texts from the lesson.

activities.title: Where the Ṛigveda was composed
activities.prompt: Where was the Ṛigveda composed?
options: Southeastern part of the Indian subcontinent
Northeastern part of the Indian subcontinent
Northwestern part of the Indian subcontinent
Southwestern part of the Indian subcontinent
activities.explanation: Well done. The Ṛigveda was composed in the northwestern part.

activities.title: Use the lesson's terms correctly
activities.prompt: Which statement uses the lesson's terms correctly?
options: Vidhata was a part of each Veda
Samiti was an early Indian Veda
Janas were kinship groups in Vedic society
The sabhā was early Indian literature
activities.explanation: Correct. Janas were kinship groups, while the other names were assemblies.

activities.prompt: Ravi’s neighbours share land, food habits, and a strong feeling of belonging. What kind of group is this?
options: It is a society because people share territory, culture, and belonging.
It is a state because people share territory, culture, and belonging.
It is a state because neighbours mainly follow customs and practices.
It is a society because it must use formal written laws.

why.It is a state because people share terri: This confuses a society with a state, which has organised political rule.
why.It is a state because neighbours mainly: This mistakes customs for the rules and laws that define a state.
why.It is a society because it must use form: This wrongly assumes that a society must use formal written laws.

activities.explanation: This matches the shared territory, culture, and belonging that define a society.

activities.prompt: The Vedas are the earliest known collection of Indian literature. It was passed orally for centuries before being written. Why could it continue without written copies?
options: Teachers could pass it down orally for many centuries.
Teachers could pass it down through written copies from the start.
Teachers could pass it down orally after it was written.
Teachers could pass it down only through books and never aloud.

why.Teachers could pass it down through writ: This wrongly assumes written copies came before oral teaching.
why.Teachers could pass it down orally after: This reverses the order of oral teaching and writing.
why.Teachers could pass it down only through: This wrongly says oral teaching happened only after writing.

activities.explanation: Oral teaching explains how the literature continued before it was written.

activities.prompt: A map shows where the Ṛigveda was composed. The marked place is in the northwest. What does this tell us about its origin?
options: The Ṛigveda was composed in the northwestern Indian subcontinent.
The Ṛigveda was composed in the northeastern Indian subcontinent.
The Ṛigveda was composed in the south-central Indian subcontinent.
The Ṛigveda was composed in the southeastern Indian subcontinent.

why.The Ṛigveda was composed in the northeas: This wrongly changes the marked direction from northwest to northeast.
why.The Ṛigveda was composed in the south-ce: This wrongly places the composition in the south-central region.
why.The Ṛigveda was composed in the southeas: This wrongly places the composition in the southeastern region.

activities.explanation: The map places the Ṛigveda’s composition in the northwest.

activities.prompt: Imagine a town with an organised political system. Its decisions must follow clear rules and laws. Which description fits best?
options: The town is a state because its political system uses clear laws.
The town is a society because its political system uses clear laws.
The town is a state because its people mainly follow shared customs.
The town is a society because its members share territory and culture.

why.The town is a society because its politi: This confuses a society with an organised political system.
why.The town is a state because its people m: This mistakes shared customs for the rules and laws of a state.
why.The town is a society because its member: This wrongly treats shared territory and culture as the only signs of a society.

activities.explanation: This matches an organised political system based on rules and laws.

activities.prompt: A community is slowly growing. Its political system is also changing step by step. What best explains this pattern?
options: Political systems develop as societies become larger and more complicated.
Political systems stop changing when societies become more complicated.
Political systems change only when societies become smaller and simpler.
Political systems develop before societies become larger or complicated.

why.Political systems stop changing when soc: This wrongly assumes that complexity does not lead to political change.
why.Political systems change only when socie: This reverses the link between larger societies and political systems.
why.Political systems develop before societi: This wrongly places political development before social complexity.

activities.explanation: This matches the gradual change linked with larger, more complicated societies.

lessons.title: From Janapadas to Kingdoms and Republics

activities.prompt: How did small communities grow into powerful kingdoms and republics?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Political Organisation Changed
activities.body: Janapadas were larger territorial units that developed from Vedic clans. Kinship means family ties. Identity now rested on territory, not family ties. Mahājanapadas were larger political formations that appeared between about 600 BCE and 300 CE. Sources usually mention sixteen mahājanapadas. Magadha, in present-day Bihar, gradually became the most powerful mahājanapada. Northern India had monarchies and republics. A republic has no monarch.
keyPoints: Janapadas changed identity from kinship to territory.
Mahājanapadas were larger political formations.
Magadha gradually became the most powerful mahājanapada.
activities.explanation: Political organisation grew from clans into larger territorial powers.

activities.prompt: Clans join larger areas on a map. Why does political identity change?
steps: Clans gradually joined larger territorial units because political organisation was growing.
People began sharing a territory instead of tracing kinship because political belonging changed.
These larger units were janapadas, so territorial identity had replaced family identity.
Later, still larger mahājanapadas developed, showing that political units kept growing.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which change helped Vedic political organisation develop?
options: Clans formed smaller family groups.
Territorial units split into clans.
Clans joined larger territorial units.
Clans lost their shared identity.
activities.explanation: Vedic political organisation gradually developed from clans into larger territorial units. Good spotting!

activities.prompt: Janapadas changed identity from ______ to identity based on territory.
activities.hint: Choose the word meaning family ties.
activities.explanation: Kinship means identity based on family ties. Janapadas made territory more important.

activities.prompt: Match each political group with its description.
pairs: Earlier political groups in Vedic organisation
activities.explanation: Janapadas introduced territorial identity. Mahājanapadas were larger, and Magadha became the most powerful.

activities.prompt: Which region became the main centre of Vedic culture?
options: The Deccan
The Ganga plains
The Tamil areas
Magadha
activities.explanation: During the later Vedic period, the Ganga plains became the main centre of Vedic culture.

activities.prompt: Put these stages of political development in order.
activities.explanation: Political organisation developed from clans into janapadas. Larger mahājanapadas appeared later.

activities.prompt: Which statement matches the changes in identity and political size?
options: Janapadas used kinship; mahājanapadas were smaller.
Janapadas used territory; mahājanapadas were clans.
Janapadas used kinship; mahājanapadas were equal in size.
Janapadas used territory; mahājanapadas were larger.
activities.explanation: Janapadas changed identity towards territory. Contemporary texts describe mahājanapadas as larger than janapadas.

activities.prompt: Magadha grew powerful. The Ganga plains became Vedic culture's centre. What differs?
options: Magadha became culturally central, while Ganga plains became politically weak.
Both areas became the main centres of Vedic political power.
Neither area had any political or cultural Vedic importance.
Magadha became politically powerful, while Ganga plains became culturally central.

why.Magadha became culturally central, while: This swaps the political importance of Magadha with the Ganga plains.
why.Both areas became the main centres of Ve: This changes a cultural centre into a centre of political power.
why.Neither area had any political or cultur: This denies both Magadha's power and the Ganga plains' cultural role.

activities.explanation: This is right because Magadha gained political power while the Ganga plains became the cultural centre.

activities.prompt: Mahājanapadas formed between about 600 BCE and 300 CE. Sangam literature records kingdoms between 300 BCE and 300 CE. What overlaps?
options: The Sangam record began before any mahājanapadas formed.
The two periods overlap between 300 BCE and 300 CE.
Both periods began in exactly the same year.
The Sangam record ended before mahājanapadas formed.

why.The Sangam record began before any mahāj: This places the Sangam record before the mahājanapada period began.
why.Both periods began in exactly the same y: This mistakes overlapping periods for periods starting together.
why.The Sangam record ended before mahājanap: This wrongly places the Sangam record before the mahājanapada period.

activities.explanation: This is right because both periods include the years from 300 BCE to 300 CE.

lessons.title: Ethics, Dharma and Social Groups

activities.prompt: What shaped life and law in early India, and how did social groups grow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Ideas Shaped Indian Society
activities.body: Ethics formed the basis of early Indian law and life. Samatva taught that all bodies and forms of consciousness share the same basic reality. Aśhoka’s edicts promoted dhamma through morality, non-violence and compassion. Jātis are social groups. They arose partly through intermarriage, migration and territorial differences. The number of varṇas stayed four, while jātis could keep growing. Rulers had varied backgrounds. Inscriptions record changing occupations.
keyPoints: Ethics shaped early Indian law and life.
Samatva taught a shared basic reality.
Social groups and occupations could change.
activities.explanation: Notice how these ideas connect conduct, thought and social life.

activities.prompt: After people move, marry across groups, and settle in different areas, why can jātis change?
steps: People moved, married across groups, and settled in different territories.
These three changes partly caused jātis to arise.
Jātis could keep growing, while the number of varṇas stayed four.
So, jātis could increase without adding more varṇas.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Basis of Ethics
activities.prompt: What did ethics form in early Indian thought?
options: the basis of law and life
the cause of all social migration
the reason all work stayed fixed
the limit on rulers from new groups
activities.explanation: Ethics formed the basis of law and life in early Indian thought. You spotted the key idea.

activities.title: The Idea of Samatva
activities.prompt: Samatva taught that all bodies and forms of consciousness share the same basic reality.
activities.explanation: Samatva taught that all bodies and forms of consciousness share the same basic reality. You followed the shared idea well.

activities.title: Aśhoka’s Message
activities.prompt: Which set of ideas did Aśhoka’s edicts promote?
options: morality, non-violence and compassion
trade, migration and territorial differences
intermarriage, occupation and migration
ethics, law and social change
activities.explanation: Aśhoka’s edicts promoted dhamma through morality, non-violence and compassion. You identified the three guiding ideas.

activities.title: How Jātis Arose
activities.prompt: Jātis arose partly because of intermarriage, migration and territorial differences.
activities.explanation: Intermarriage, migration and territorial differences partly shaped the rise of jātis. You matched the causes well.

activities.title: Varṇas and Jātis
activities.prompt: The number of varṇas stayed ______, while the number of jātis could keep growing.
activities.hint: Think about how many varṇas remained.
activities.explanation: The number of varṇas stayed four, while jātis could keep growing. You spotted the difference.

activities.title: Connect the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its related lesson point.
pairs: Basis of early law and life
activities.explanation: Each pairing connects an idea with its meaning. You matched them neatly.

activities.title: Social Categories Were Flexible
activities.prompt: What does the varied social background of rulers show?
options: Social categories were not rigid.
Occupations always remained fixed.
Rulers came from similar backgrounds.
Social groups could never grow.
activities.explanation: Rulers came from many social backgrounds. This shows that social categories were not rigid.

activities.title: Evidence from Inscriptions
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order.
items: A brāhmaṇa becomes a land manager.
This shows that occupations could change.
activities.explanation: The inscription records a brāhmaṇa becoming a land manager. This is evidence that people changed occupations.

activities.prompt: Two students say a body and a thought are completely separate. What does Samatva ask them to consider?
options: They may share the same basic reality.
They must use completely separate realities.
They can never be compared with each other.
They always share every kind of experience.

why.They must use completely separate realit: This wrongly treats their reality as completely separate.
why.They can never be compared with each oth: This wrongly says they cannot be compared.
why.They always share every kind of experien: Sharing a basic reality does not mean sharing every experience.

activities.explanation: Samatva says bodies and consciousness share one basic reality.

activities.prompt: An inscription says a brāhmaṇa became a land manager. What can this source tell us?
options: That people could change their occupations.
That every brāhmaṇa managed land for life.
That only land managers became brāhmaṇas.
That no brāhmaṇa ever held other work.

why.That every brāhmaṇa managed land for lif: It gives one example, not a rule for every brāhmaṇa.
why.That only land managers became brāhmaṇas: It does not show that only land managers became brāhmaṇas.
It does not show that no brāhmaṇa held other work.

activities.explanation: The inscription directly records a change of occupation.

lessons.title: Family, Women, Religion and Education

activities.prompt: What were families, women, religion, and education like in the Vedic period?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Life in the Vedic period
activities.body: Families lived in villages, and groups of villages formed a viśha. The four āśhramas were life choices: student life, householder life, forest life and renunciation. The four goals of life were dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣha. Women joined learning, rituals, chariot races and social gatherings. They also worked in farming, crafts, household management and religious practices. Education was part of life and taught knowledge and moral values.
keyPoints: Families lived in villages, and groups formed a viśha.
Women joined learning and continued many kinds of work.
Education taught knowledge and moral values.
activities.explanation: This lesson shows how families, women, religion and education fitted together.

activities.prompt: A student asks a teacher for help after a lesson. Why is the teacher seen as a guide?
steps: A student learns facts and hears how to act rightly.
This matters because education joined knowledge with moral values.
A teacher guides learning and choices, so the bond goes beyond lessons.
Therefore, the teacher-student relationship is regarded as sacred.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did groups of villages form?
options: A viśha
A family
An āśhrama
A goal
activities.explanation: Groups of villages formed a viśha. A village contained several families.

activities.prompt: The four goals were dharma, artha, ______ and mokṣha.
activities.hint: This goal comes between artha and mokṣha.
activities.explanation: The four goals of life were dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣha.

activities.prompt: Match each āśhrama with its life choice.
activities.explanation: These were the four āśhramas: student, householder, forest and renunciation.

activities.prompt: Why was the teacher-student relationship regarded as sacred?
options: The teacher was seen as a guide.
The teacher avoided learning.
The teacher led chariot races.
The teacher rejected moral values.
activities.explanation: The teacher-student relationship was sacred because the teacher was seen as a guide.

activities.prompt: Put the four āśhramas in the order shown in this lesson.
activities.explanation: The four āśhramas were student life, householder life, forest life and renunciation.

activities.prompt: Which set shows activities women took part in during the Vedic period?
options: Learning, rituals, chariot races and social gatherings
Only farming and household management
Only crafts and religious practices
Only chariot races and social gatherings
activities.explanation: Women took part in learning, rituals, chariot races and social gatherings.

activities.prompt: An old map shows several family homes inside one village. A second map groups several village marks under one outer ring. What does the second map suggest?
options: The grouped villages together form a viśha.
The outer ring marks one family's home.
The village marks show four āśhramas.
The family homes show four life goals.

This confuses a group of villages with one family.
This confuses village grouping with the four āśhramas.
This confuses village grouping with the four life goals.

activities.explanation: This matches groups of villages forming a viśha.

activities.prompt: Group A has women farming, making crafts, managing homes, and doing rituals. Group B has people rejecting comforts and wandering as ascetics. What is the main difference?
options: Group B combines everyday work with religious practice.
Both groups reject material comforts and always wander.
Group A combines everyday work with religious practice.
Neither group has any work or religious practice.

why.Group B combines everyday work with reli: This wrongly treats wandering ascetics as household and ritual workers.
why.Both groups reject material comforts and: This wrongly says that both groups reject everyday and religious work.
why.Neither group has any work or religious: This wrongly denies both the work and religion in Group A.

activities.explanation: Group A does everyday and religious work, while Group B rejects comforts.

activities.prompt: A student learns a subject and then uses it to act honestly. Why is this education in the full sense?
options: Education includes subject knowledge but ignores moral values.
Education includes moral values but ignores subject knowledge.
Education includes only training for material comfort.
Education includes knowledge and moral values together.

why.Education includes subject knowledge but: This mistakes knowledge for education without moral values.
why.Education includes moral values but igno: This mistakes moral values for education without knowledge.
why.Education includes only training for mat: This mistakes education for training only in material comfort.

activities.explanation: This matches education teaching both knowledge and moral values.

activities.prompt: A student says, “Teacher, please guide my choices.” A classmate says, “My teacher only gives me information.” Which student better understands the old teaching, and why?
options: The first, because the teacher was a sacred guide.
The second, because teaching meant only passing information.
The first, because students needed no teacher guidance.
The second, because teachers had no sacred role.

why.The second, because teaching meant only: This mistakes information-giving for the teacher's full guiding role.
why.The first, because students needed no te: This wrongly treats guidance as something students did not need.
why.The second, because teachers had no sacr: This wrongly removes the sacred meaning of the relationship.

activities.explanation: The first matches the teacher as a sacred guide.

activities.prompt: One person wants to run a family home. Another wants to give up comforts and wander. Which āśhramas suit these choices?
options: Student life and forest life.
Forest life and student life.
Student life and renunciation life.
Householder life and renunciation life.

This confuses householder life with student life.
This confuses forest life with student life.
This confuses householder life with student life.

activities.explanation: Running a home is householder life; wandering without comforts is renunciation.

activities.context: A settlement’s families share a territory, culture and sense of belonging. Their daily shared life is guided mainly by customary practices, while a nearby state governs through organised rules and laws. As the community grows larger and more complicated, it may develop more formal political arrangements. The community also preserves Vedic literature through oral transmission before it is written down. Early Vedic texts describe kinship groups called janas and assemblies called sabhā, samiti and vidhata.
activities.prompt: A resident asks what should guide the settlement’s customary behaviour. Which response is most accurate?
options: Give priority to established customs rather than formal legal rules
Use only the rules and laws of the organised state
Allow each household to choose without considering shared customs
Treat formal laws as the only guide whenever customs and laws differ

why.Use only the rules and laws of the organ: A state is based on rules and laws, but that does not make it the main guide of society.
why.Allow each household to choose without c: Shared customs are not replaced by separate household choices.
why.Treat formal laws as the only guide when: Customs remain important even when formal laws also exist.

activities.explanation: Society is mainly guided by customs and practices.

activities.context: A settlement’s families share a territory, culture and sense of belonging. Their daily shared life is guided mainly by customary practices, while a nearby state governs through organised rules and laws. As the community grows larger and more complicated, it may develop more formal political arrangements. The community also preserves Vedic literature through oral transmission before it is written down. Early Vedic texts describe kinship groups called janas and assemblies called sabhā, samiti and vidhata.
activities.prompt: Students discover old Vedic verses that have been recited for centuries but have not yet been written down. What best explains their status?
options: They belong to the orally transmitted Vedic tradition
They are formal laws issued by an organised political system
They are the names of the four divisions within one Veda
They are the three assemblies named in early Vedic texts

why.They are formal laws issued by an organi: Oral literature is different from the rules and laws of a state.
why.They are the names of the four divisions: The four Veda divisions are specific textual parts, not general names for every verse.
why.They are the three assemblies named in e: The three assembly names refer to assemblies, not to Vedic verses.

activities.explanation: Vedic literature was passed down orally before it was written.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Political systems developed gradually as societies became larger and more complicated.
Reason (R): A larger and more complicated society creates a need for organised political authority based on rules and laws.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why political systems developed as societies grew larger and more complicated.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Vedic literature was passed down orally for several centuries before it was written.
Reason (R): All Vedic literature was composed in the northwestern part of the Indian subcontinent.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Only the Ṛigveda is stated to have been composed in that region, not all Vedic literature.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between society and the state, and why political systems developed gradually.
activities.answer: A society is a system of relationships among people who share a territory, culture and belonging. It is mainly guided by customs and practices rather than formal written laws. A state, by contrast, is an organised political system based on rules and laws. Political systems developed gradually as societies became larger and more complicated. This difference explains why customs can guide everyday social behaviour even when a state also exists. Society therefore concerns shared relationships and customs, while the state concerns organised political rule through laws.
points: Defines society as relationships based on shared territory, culture and belonging
Explains that customs and practices mainly guide society
Defines the state as an organised political system based on rules and laws
Links gradual political development with societies becoming larger and more complicated
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Ravi is preparing a short report on political organisation in ancient India. His notes show that kinship-based communities gradually gave way to territorial communities and that some much larger regional powers appeared later. One source usually names sixteen of them. Magadha, in the area now called Bihar, had grown especially influential. Ravi must decide which terms, sequence, and geographical details belong in his report.
activities.prompt: Which sequence correctly shows the development of political organisation in Ravi’s report?
options: Clans → Janapadas → Mahājanapadas
Clans → Mahājanapadas → Janapadas
Janapadas → Clans → Mahājanapadas
Mahājanapadas → Janapadas → Clans

why.Clans → Mahājanapadas → Janapadas: Larger mahājanapadas emerged from this development.
why.Janapadas → Clans → Mahājanapadas: The order reverses the historical progression.
why.Mahājanapadas → Janapadas → Clans: This order places the largest units first.

activities.explanation: Clans developed into territorial janapadas.

activities.context: Ravi is preparing a short report on political organisation in ancient India. His notes show that kinship-based communities gradually gave way to territorial communities and that some much larger regional powers appeared later. One source usually names sixteen of them. Magadha, in the area now called Bihar, had grown especially influential. Ravi must decide which terms, sequence, and geographical details belong in his report.
activities.prompt: If a small community accepted a territorial identity instead of a kinship identity, what change should Ravi expect in the way its members understood belonging?
options: They would increasingly regard the region they occupied as their shared political home.
They would continue to identify only with the clan to which their relatives belonged.
They would immediately treat their territory as one of the largest mahājanapadas.
They would identify with a republican state rather than with any territorial community.

why.They would continue to identify only wit: Kinship identity was the earlier basis.
why.They would immediately treat their terri: A territorial community did not become a mahājanapada immediately.
why.They would identify with a republican st: Republican states were a separate political system in northern India.

activities.explanation: Territorial identity made the occupied region the basis of belonging.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Janapadas marked a change from identity based on kinship to identity based on territory.
Reason (R): Vedic political organisation gradually developed from clans into larger territorial units.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The development of larger territorial units explains why political identity shifted from kinship to territory.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Sangam literature records early Tamil kingdoms between 300 BCE and 300 CE.
Reason (R): The Satavāhana Empire replaced Mauryan rule in northern India.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because the replacement occurred in much of the Deccan.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between a janapada and a mahājanapada, and what change in identity accompanied the earlier stage?
activities.answer: A janapada was a territorial political unit that developed as clans and kinship-based organisation gave way to larger territorial organisation. The important change was that people began to identify with the territory they occupied rather than only with relatives. A mahājanapada was a still larger political formation of the kind that arose between about 600 BCE and 300 CE. Contemporary texts describe them as bigger than janapadas, and historical sources usually mention sixteen of them.
points: Janapadas were larger territorial units that developed from clans.
Political identity changed from kinship to territory.
Mahājanapadas were larger than janapadas.
Historical sources usually mention sixteen mahājanapadas.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A school group is preparing an exhibition on early Indian thought. One display explains that ethics formed the basis of law and life, while an edict of Aśhoka promotes dhamma through morality, non-violence and compassion. Another display notes that jātis arose partly through intermarriage, migration and territorial differences, although the four varṇas remained unchanged. The group is also considering evidence that rulers came from different social backgrounds and that some people changed occupations.
activities.prompt: A student plans to show exactly four jātis because there are four varṇas. What should the student change in the display?
options: Keep the four varṇas, but allow the number of jātis to increase.
Show only four jātis because each jāti must match one varṇa.
Remove the varṇas because additional jātis must reduce their number.
Base the display on occupations because they determine the number of varṇas.

why.Show only four jātis because each jāti m: Four varṇas do not limit society to four jātis.
why.Remove the varṇas because additional jāt: Growing jātis do not require reducing the varṇas.
why.Base the display on occupations because: Occupational changes do not determine the number of varṇas.

activities.explanation: The number of varṇas remained four while jātis could grow.

activities.context: A school group is preparing an exhibition on early Indian thought. One display explains that ethics formed the basis of law and life, while an edict of Aśhoka promotes dhamma through morality, non-violence and compassion. Another display notes that jātis arose partly through intermarriage, migration and territorial differences, although the four varṇas remained unchanged. The group is also considering evidence that rulers came from different social backgrounds and that some people changed occupations.
activities.prompt: The exhibition places Aśhoka’s edict beside the statement that ethics formed the basis of law and life. Which explanation best fits both ideas?
options: The edict presents dhamma as relevant to the moral guidance of law and life.
The edict presents dhamma and ethics as opposing principles.
The edict makes compassion unnecessary in public conduct.
The edict indicates that social rank is the only basis of law and life.

why.The edict presents dhamma and ethics as: The edict promotes morality rather than opposing ethics.
why.The edict makes compassion unnecessary i: Compassion is one of the edict’s stated moral principles.
why.The edict indicates that social rank is: The case does not make social rank the basis of law and life.

activities.explanation: Morality, non-violence and compassion connect dhamma with ethical guidance.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Social categories were not rigid.
Reason (R): Rulers came from many different social backgrounds.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The varied backgrounds of rulers provide direct evidence that social categories were not rigid.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Aśhoka’s edicts promoted dhamma through morality, non-violence and compassion.
Reason (R): Jātis arose partly because of intermarriage, migration and territorial differences.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reasons for jāti growth do not explain how Aśhoka’s edicts promoted dhamma.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between varṇas and jātis in early Indian social organization.
activities.answer: The lesson distinguishes varṇas from jātis. The number of varṇas remained four, but the number of jātis could keep growing. Jātis arose partly because of intermarriage, migration and territorial differences. Therefore, identifying every jāti with one of the four varṇas would be incorrect. The evidence about social categories supports this distinction: rulers came from many social backgrounds, and inscriptions show people changing occupations. Social categories were therefore not rigid, even though the four-varṇa arrangement remained.
points: The number of varṇas remained four.
The number of jātis could continue to grow.
Jātis arose partly from intermarriage, migration and territorial differences.
Rule and occupation changes show that social categories were not rigid.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a village, several families lived close together, and groups of nearby villages formed a viśha. A girl attended lessons, took part in rituals, joined chariot races and visited social gatherings. She also helped with farming, crafts, household management and religious practices. Her teacher taught knowledge and moral values and was respected as a guide. A wandering renunciant rejected material comforts and spoke to students about the goals of life.
activities.prompt: If the teacher stopped teaching moral values and taught only knowledge, what would most likely happen?
options: Students would gain subject knowledge but miss the moral guidance expected in education.
The sacred teacher-student bond would remain complete because knowledge alone is enough to guide students.
Students would be better prepared to choose among the four goals of life.
The teacher would remain a moral guide even though moral teaching had been removed.

why.The sacred teacher-student bond would re: The sacred bond required a teacher who could guide pupils.
why.Students would be better prepared to cho: Removing moral teaching does not improve the four goals.
why.The teacher would remain a moral guide e: A teacher of only facts would not fulfil the full guiding role.

activities.explanation: Moral values were an essential part of education.

activities.context: In a village, several families lived close together, and groups of nearby villages formed a viśha. A girl attended lessons, took part in rituals, joined chariot races and visited social gatherings. She also helped with farming, crafts, household management and religious practices. Her teacher taught knowledge and moral values and was respected as a guide. A wandering renunciant rejected material comforts and spoke to students about the goals of life.
activities.prompt: If the girl were allowed lessons and gatherings but had to stop all farming, craft and household work, what would likely change?
options: Her contribution to farming, crafts and household management would end, while lessons, rituals and social gatherings continued.
Her lessons and social activities would end because household work must come first.
Only chariot racing would continue, while learning, rituals and work stopped.
Nothing would change because women’s work and social participation were separate from education.

why.Her lessons and social activities would: The facts do not make household work more important than learning.
why.Only chariot racing would continue, whil: Nothing requires learning and social participation to stop with work.
why.Nothing would change because women’s wor: Women participated in both kinds of activity.

activities.explanation: The proposed change affects only her work.

activities.context: In a village, several families lived close together, and groups of nearby villages formed a viśha. A girl attended lessons, took part in rituals, joined chariot races and visited social gatherings. She also helped with farming, crafts, household management and religious practices. Her teacher taught knowledge and moral values and was respected as a guide. A wandering renunciant rejected material comforts and spoke to students about the goals of life.
activities.prompt: If the wandering renunciant began collecting valuable possessions, what would happen to his way of life?
options: His ascetic and wandering way of life would no longer follow the example of early renunciants.
He would become a householder without changing any of his values.
He would remain a wandering ascetic because owning possessions does not affect ascetic life.
He would still reject material comforts because collecting possessions does not alter his choice of life.

why.He would become a householder without ch: Ownership alone does not make someone a householder.
why.He would remain a wandering ascetic beca: Possessions directly affect the ascetic way of life.
why.He would still reject material comforts: Rejecting comforts is inconsistent with collecting possessions.

activities.explanation: Collecting possessions conflicts with rejecting material comforts.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: State and Society up to 1000 CE

activities.prompt: Which statement best shows the difference between society and a state?
options: Society shares customs; states have rules and laws.
Society has written laws; states share customs.
Society is a political system; states share culture.
Society has no people; states organise relationships.
activities.explanation: Society connects people through shared life and customs. A state is an organised political system with rules and laws.

activities.prompt: A ______ is an organised political system based on rules and laws.
activities.hint: Think of the political system in the lesson.
activities.explanation: A state is an organised political system based on rules and laws.

activities.prompt: Match each clue to the correct term.
activities.explanation: Early Vedic society had kinship groups called janas. The texts also mention sabhā, samiti and vidhāta. Student life was one āśhrama.

activities.prompt: Put these political formations in the order they developed.
activities.explanation: Political organisation grew from kinship groups into territorial units called janapadas. Larger mahājanapadas rose later.

activities.prompt: What important change did janapadas mark?
options: Identity based on kinship
Identity based on territory
Identity based on occupation
Identity based on wealth
activities.explanation: Janapadas marked a shift from identity based on kinship. People’s shared identity now centred on territory.

activities.prompt: Magadha in present-day Bihar gradually became the most powerful mahājanapada.
activities.explanation: Yes. Magadha gradually became the most powerful mahājanapada in present-day Bihar.

activities.prompt: Which idea formed the basis of law and life in early Indian thought?
options: Ethics
Samatva
Dhamma
Dharma
activities.explanation: Ethics formed the basis of law and life. Samatva taught that all forms of consciousness share one basic reality.

activities.prompt: The four goals of life were dharma, artha, kāma and ______.
activities.hint: This was the fourth goal of life.
activities.explanation: The four goals of life were dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa.

activities.prompt: Put these stages in the order described in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Political systems developed gradually as societies grew larger and became more complicated. This gradual change led to more organised political life.

chapters.title: Democracy
chapters.summary: In this chapter: democracy and the constitution; popular sovereignty, rule of law and rights; types and systems of democracy; democracy in practice and the citizen’s role.

lessons.title: Democracy and the Constitution

activities.prompt: How does a democracy give people the power to shape their country?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Makes India Democratic?
activities.body: Democracy is a form of government where citizens hold power and authority. Citizens choose representatives through free and fair elections. India is the world’s largest democracy. Its Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950. It protects the Fundamental Rights of all citizens. India’s democratic ethos grew slowly through a long historical process.
keyPoints: Citizens hold power and authority in a democracy.
Representatives are elected through free and fair elections.
The Constitution protects the Fundamental Rights of all citizens.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the main ideas of the lesson.

activities.prompt: Our class needs a representative. Should the teacher choose alone, or should students vote?
steps: Students should have a say because democracy gives citizens power.
If the teacher chooses alone, students do not hold that power.
Free and fair elections let citizens choose representatives.
Therefore, the class should hold a free and fair election.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: India’s Democratic Journey
activities.body: India’s democratic ethos did not appear all at once. It developed gradually through a long historical process. This means its democratic ways grew slowly over time. The Constitution of India came into force on 26 January 1950. It protects the Fundamental Rights of all citizens. India is the world’s largest democracy.
keyPoints: India’s democratic ethos developed gradually.
India’s Constitution protects all citizens’ Fundamental Rights.
India is the world’s largest democracy.
activities.explanation: These points show that India’s democracy developed over time.

activities.prompt: In a democracy, who holds power and authority?
options: teachers
citizens
judges
soldiers
activities.explanation: In a democracy, citizens hold power and authority.

activities.prompt: Representatives are chosen without free and fair elections.
activities.explanation: Citizens elect representatives through free and fair elections.

activities.prompt: Match each important idea with its correct detail.
pairs: Held by citizens in a democracy
Chosen through free and fair elections
When India’s Constitution came into force
Protected for all citizens by the Constitution
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an important idea with the lesson.

activities.prompt: Which statement about India is correct?
options: India has no democratic government.
India’s democracy began in one day.
India’s Constitution protects only some citizens.
India is the world’s largest democracy.
activities.explanation: The lesson states that India is the world’s largest democracy. Its democratic ethos also developed gradually.

activities.prompt: India’s democratic ethos developed quickly through a short historical process.
activities.explanation: India’s democratic ethos developed gradually through a long historical process.

activities.prompt: Which answer correctly links democracy, elections and the Constitution?
options: Officers hold power, elect representatives freely and fairly, and keep protected rights.
Citizens hold power, elect representatives freely and fairly, and keep protected rights.
Judges hold power, elect representatives freely and fairly, and keep protected rights.
Citizens lose power, elect representatives freely and fairly, and keep protected rights.
activities.explanation: Well done! Citizens hold power and elect representatives freely and fairly. The Constitution protects their rights.

activities.prompt: A town hall shows citizens choosing representatives through free and fair elections. What does this show?
options: The town is democratic because citizens hold power through representatives.
The town is undemocratic because a leader makes every choice.
The town has no democracy because citizens chose representatives together.
The town became democratic only when its Constitution began.

why.The town is undemocratic because a leade: This mistake assumes a leader can hold power without citizen choice.
why.The town has no democracy because citize: This mistake thinks citizens must make every choice themselves.
why.The town became democratic only when its: This mistake links democracy only to the Constitution’s starting day.

activities.explanation: This is right because elections support citizens’ power through representatives.

activities.prompt: Place A holds free and fair elections for representatives. Place B lets a leader make every choice. Which place is democratic?
options: Place A, because citizens hold power through chosen representatives.
Place B, because democracy gives a leader all authority.
Place A, because elections remove power from the people.
Place B, because choosing representatives weakens citizens’ power.

why.Place B, because democracy gives a leade: This mistake believes democracy gives a leader all authority.
why.Place A, because elections remove power: This mistake thinks elections remove citizens’ power.
why.Place B, because choosing representative: This mistake believes representatives reduce citizens’ power.

activities.explanation: This is right because citizens elect representatives and hold power.

activities.prompt: A class must choose a representative. Which plan best follows a democratic choice?
options: Hold a free and fair election where every student can vote.
Let the teacher choose secretly and give students no vote.
Choose a student who promises gifts to receive classmates’ votes.
Make a student decide for everyone without an election.

why.Let the teacher choose secretly and give: This mistake treats the teacher’s choice as better than citizen voting.
why.Choose a student who promises gifts to r: This mistake thinks promises are a fair way to choose representatives.
why.Make a student decide for everyone witho: This mistake believes a student should hold power over everyone.

activities.explanation: This is right because citizens choose representatives through free and fair elections.

activities.prompt: People can influence government by choosing who will represent them. Why does this matter in democracy?
options: It lets citizens hold public power by electing representatives.
It lets a leader take power away from all citizens.
It makes elections needless because representatives should act alone.
It prevents citizens from holding any public authority.

why.It lets a leader take power away from al: This mistake thinks power should be taken away from citizens.
why.It makes elections needless because repr: This mistake believes representatives should work without any election.
why.It prevents citizens from holding any pu: This mistake thinks elections stop citizens from holding authority.

activities.explanation: This is right because citizens elect representatives and hold power.

activities.prompt: A timeline shows India's Constitution starting on 26 January 1950. What does this tell citizens?
options: The Constitution protects their Fundamental Rights as citizens.
The Constitution protects only the rights of powerful leaders.
The Constitution removes Fundamental Rights from all citizens.
The Constitution makes elections unnecessary for citizens’ power.

why.The Constitution protects only the right: This mistake believes only powerful leaders receive Fundamental Rights.
why.The Constitution removes Fundamental Rig: This mistake thinks the Constitution ended Fundamental Rights.
why.The Constitution makes elections unneces: This mistake assumes elections were the only way to protect citizens’ rights.

activities.explanation: This is right because the Constitution protects Fundamental Rights of all citizens.

lessons.title: Popular Sovereignty, Rule of Law and Rights

activities.prompt: What connects your voice, the laws, and your rights in a democracy?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Where Does Power Come From?
activities.body: In a democracy, the people are the ultimate source of power. The state gets its authority from the people. Citizens vote to elect governments and representatives. An elected government makes policies and implements laws. The voting right given to all eligible adults is called Universal Adult Franchise. The Rule of Law prevents misuse of power and protects citizens’ rights. The Constitution protects six categories of Fundamental Rights.
keyPoints: The people are democracy’s ultimate source of power.
The state gets its authority from the people.
The Rule of Law protects rights and prevents misuse of power.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect people, government, rights and lawful power.

activities.prompt: Your town will vote for people to make laws. Why should voters have the final say?
steps: Citizens use voting to elect governments and representatives, because people choose leaders.
Making laws shows why elected leaders must answer to the people.
The state gets authority from the people, not from rulers.
Therefore, people are the ultimate source of power, which is popular sovereignty.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who is the ultimate source of power in democracy?
options: the people
the state
the elected government
the Constitution
activities.explanation: The people are the ultimate source of power in democracy.

activities.prompt: Who gives the state its authority?
options: the Constitution
the people
the Rule of Law
the elected government
activities.explanation: The state receives its authority from the people.

activities.prompt: The voting right for all eligible adults is called Universal Adult ______.
activities.hint: This voting right has a special name.
activities.explanation: Universal Adult Franchise means voting rights for all eligible adults.

activities.prompt: What does the Rule of Law do?
options: Stops misuse and protects rights
Creates adult voting rights for all
Elects governments and representatives
Changes where state authority comes
activities.explanation: The Rule of Law prevents misuse of power and protects citizens’ rights.

activities.prompt: Match each idea to what it describes.
activities.explanation: The people hold power, and they give authority to the state.

activities.prompt: Put the democratic steps in order.
activities.explanation: Voting elects representatives, who then make and implement laws.

activities.prompt: All eligible adults can vote in elections. Which result is most likely?
options: More people can help choose their own government.
Fewer people can vote in future elections.
Rulers no longer need support from the people.
The government will stop making laws.

why.Fewer people can vote in future election: This mistake confuses giving everyone the vote with limiting voting.
why.Rulers no longer need support from the p: This wrongly treats government authority as separate from the people.
This wrongly assumes that electing a government ends lawmaking.

activities.explanation: Voting lets citizens elect governments, so more people can choose leaders.

activities.prompt: In Place A, all eligible adults vote. In Place B, only some can vote. Which gives citizens a stronger democratic role?
options: Place B, because smaller groups can choose leaders.
Place A, because more eligible adults can choose leaders.
Both places, because representatives still set policies.
Neither place, because voting removes public authority.

why.Place B, because smaller groups can choo: This mistake treats a smaller voting group as more democratic.
why.Both places, because representatives sti: This mistake assumes representatives remove citizens’ voting role.
why.Neither place, because voting removes pu: This wrongly believes voting takes authority away from the people.

activities.explanation: Universal Adult Franchise gives all eligible adults the chance to choose leaders.

activities.prompt: An official breaks rules to help a friend. What should the Rule of Law do?
options: Stop the misuse of power and protect citizens’ rights.
Allow the favour because the official wants to help.
Let the official decide which rules should apply.
Make every citizen responsible for the official’s choice.

why.Allow the favour because the official wa: This wrongly treats friendship as a reason to ignore the law.
why.Let the official decide which rules shou: This wrongly lets one official control the law.
why.Make every citizen responsible for the o: This wrongly makes every citizen responsible for an official’s misuse.

activities.explanation: The Rule of Law prevents misuse of power and protects citizens’ rights.

activities.prompt: People vote to elect representatives. Why does this give citizens influence over government?
options: Because citizens choose leaders who make policies and laws.
Because representatives make laws without needing public support.
Because voting ends the people’s role in government.
Because only elected leaders hold political power.

why.Because representatives make laws withou: This wrongly treats elected authority as independent of the people.
why.Because voting ends the people’s role in: This wrongly assumes that voting removes citizens’ influence.
why.Because only elected leaders hold politi: This wrongly denies that citizens hold ultimate political power.

activities.explanation: Voting lets citizens elect the leaders who make policies and laws.

activities.prompt: A government is elected by citizens. It then makes policies and implements laws. Where does its authority come from?
options: From the government itself, because it makes the laws.
From its officials, so they can use power freely.
From the people, who chose the elected government.
From citizens only while voting, not afterward.

why.From the government itself, because it m: This wrongly makes government authority independent of the people.
why.From its officials, so they can use powe: This wrongly treats officeholders as the source of public authority.
why.From citizens only while voting, not aft: This wrongly believes public authority ends when voting ends.

activities.explanation: The state gets its authority from the people who elected it.

activities.prompt: The Constitution protects six categories of Fundamental Rights. Which situation most clearly needs this protection?
options: A community elects representatives through voting.
An elected government implements new policies.
An eligible adult votes for a representative.
A citizen seeks protection from misuse of power.

why.A community elects representatives throu: This mistake confuses choosing leaders with legal protection.
why.An elected government implements new pol: This mistake confuses making policy with protecting rights.
why.An eligible adult votes for a representa: This mistake confuses voting with protection from misuse.

activities.explanation: This fits the Constitution’s protection of rights and the Rule of Law.

lessons.title: Types and Systems of Democracy

activities.prompt: How can people have a say in government, and what choices do they make?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Democracy Models
activities.body: Democracies use different models. Choices depend on citizen participation and political power organisation. Direct democracy lets citizens take part in most decisions directly. Representative democracy lets people elect representatives instead. Periodic elections are regular elections in this system. Government remains accountable to the people. Presidential democracy has an elected president, accountable to the people. India and Canada are parliamentary examples. Federalism shares power and responsibilities between union and state governments.
keyPoints: Direct democracy lets citizens take part in most decisions directly.
Representative democracy includes regular elections and government accountability.
Presidential democracy has an elected president, accountable to the people.
India and Canada are parliamentary examples; federalism shares power between union and state governments.
activities.explanation: Different models organise citizen participation and political power in different ways.

activities.prompt: A child asks why people in a large country choose representatives instead of deciding directly.
steps: Direct democracy lets citizens join in most decisions themselves.
Because direct choices can be hard to follow in a large country.
So representative democracy lets people elect representatives instead.
Periodic elections and accountability keep these representatives answerable to the people.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Spot Direct Democracy
activities.prompt: Which statement about direct democracy is correct?
options: Citizens take part directly in most decisions.
People elect representatives instead of governing directly.
Union and state governments share power.
The people elect an accountable president.
activities.explanation: Direct democracy means citizens take part directly in most decisions.

activities.title: A Large Country
activities.prompt: Direct democracy can be difficult to follow in a large country.
activities.explanation: A large country can make direct participation difficult to follow.

activities.title: Who Is Elected?
activities.prompt: In representative democracy, people elect ______ instead of governing directly.
activities.hint: These people speak and govern for the people who elected them.
activities.explanation: People elect representatives instead of governing directly.

activities.title: Match Models and Features
activities.prompt: Match each democracy model with its description.
pairs: Citizens take part directly in most decisions
Union and state governments share power
activities.explanation: Each description matches a feature of citizen participation or shared political power.

activities.title: Find the Parliamentary Examples
activities.prompt: Which pair is given as examples of parliamentary democracy?
options: India and Canada
India and the United States of America
The United States of America and Canada
India alone
activities.explanation: India and Canada are given as examples of parliamentary democracy.

activities.title: Shared Power
activities.prompt: Which system shares power and responsibilities between union and state governments?
options: Federalism
Direct democracy
Presidential democracy
Parliamentary democracy
activities.explanation: Federalism shares power and responsibilities between union and state governments.

activities.prompt: Direct decisions are hard to follow in a large country. Which model fits better?
options: Direct democracy, because every citizen must make each decision.
Representative democracy, because citizens elect people to decide.
Presidential democracy, because citizens vote in every meeting.
Federalism, because citizens elect leaders for union and states.

why.Direct democracy, because every citizen: Right: elected representatives help when direct decisions are hard to follow.
why.Presidential democracy, because citizens: This mistakes a presidential election for a vote on every decision.
why.Federalism, because citizens elect leade: This confuses federal power-sharing with elections at two levels.

activities.explanation: This confuses representative voting with direct decisions by every citizen.

activities.prompt: A representative ignores the people who elected them. Which rule can hold the representative accountable?
options: Periodic elections keep the representative accountable to the people.
Direct voting removes the need for representatives and elections.
Federal sharing gives the representative unlimited government power.
Presidential leadership makes the representative answer to nobody.

why.Direct voting removes the need for repre: This confuses direct participation with representative government and its checks.
why.Federal sharing gives the representative: This turns federal power-sharing into a source of unlimited personal power.
why.Presidential leadership makes the repres: This mistakes one leader's power for the accountability of representatives.

activities.explanation: Right: representative democracy includes elections and accountability to the people.

activities.prompt: A country has elected representatives and shares power between union and states. What can citizens expect?
options: They elect representatives, and power is shared at two levels.
They make most decisions, and power stays with one government.
They elect only a president, and states hold no power.
They join every decision, and all power belongs to states.

why.They make most decisions, and power stay: This confuses representative elections with direct decision-making.
why.They elect only a president, and states: This confuses a presidential election with the absence of state power.
why.They join every decision, and all power: This confuses direct participation with federal power-sharing.

activities.explanation: Right: representatives are elected, and federalism shares union and state power.

lessons.title: Democracy in Practice and the Citizen’s Role

activities.prompt: What does democracy look like when every citizen participates?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Democracy at Work
activities.body: India had over 96.8 crore registered voters in 2024. It has over 2,800 registered political parties. Indian elections use 22 scheduled languages and several other languages. Sometimes, a polling station serves only one voter. Grassroots participation makes democracy more responsive, inclusive and effective. Responsible and informed citizens strengthen democracy by joining public life. Challenges include illiteracy, misinformation, inequality and weak law implementation.
keyPoints: India has a large number of registered voters and political parties.
Grassroots participation makes democracy more responsive, inclusive and effective.
Responsible citizens strengthen democracy by participating in public life.
activities.explanation: This card introduces how voting, participation and citizen action support democracy.

activities.prompt: One voter finds it difficult to reach a usual polling station. What can be done?
steps: One voter may struggle to reach a usual polling station.
A special station for that voter makes voting easier.
Removing this barrier can protect that citizen’s participation.
Thus, special polling stations can make democracy more inclusive.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Citizen’s Role
activities.body: Responsible and informed citizens help democracy remain strong by participating in public life. Grassroots participation makes democracy more responsive, inclusive and effective. India also faces challenges such as illiteracy, misinformation, inequality and weak law implementation. Citizens can help by learning about public issues and joining public life.
keyPoints: Responsible citizens participate in public life.
Grassroots participation improves democracy.
Illiteracy, misinformation, inequality and weak law implementation remain challenges.
activities.explanation: Your informed participation can help democracy become stronger.

activities.prompt: How many scheduled languages are used for Indian elections?
options: one
activities.explanation: Indian elections are held in 22 scheduled languages and several other languages.

activities.prompt: Sometimes, a polling station is created for only one voter.
activities.explanation: Yes. Sometimes, a polling station is created for only one voter.

activities.prompt: Indian elections are held in 22 scheduled languages and ______ other languages.
activities.hint: Think of a word for more than one, but not a fixed number.
activities.explanation: Elections are held in 22 scheduled languages and several other languages.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its matching detail.
pairs: Sometimes created for only one voter
Illiteracy, misinformation, inequality and weak law implementation
activities.explanation: Each detail matches the correct idea about democracy in India.

activities.prompt: Which action matches the citizen’s role in a strong democracy?
options: Ignoring public life
Keeping public life private
Avoiding group work
Joining public life
activities.explanation: Responsible and informed citizens strengthen democracy by participating in public life.

activities.prompt: During the Emergency of 1975–77, the press was free from censorship.
activities.explanation: During the Emergency, the press was censored and many Fundamental Rights were suspended.

activities.prompt: Put these years in order from earliest to latest.
activities.explanation: The Emergency lasted from 1975 to 1977, so 1976 came between them.

activities.prompt: Grassroots participation makes democracy more responsive, inclusive and effective. Why should responsible citizens join public life?
options: It helps democracy stay strong when citizens act responsibly and stay informed.
Only elected officials should make every decision in a democracy.
Voting and public participation have no effect on democracy.
Citizen action matters only when everyone agrees with it.

why.Only elected officials should make every: This mistake assumes that only elected officials have a democratic role.
why.Voting and public participation have no: This mistake believes that voting and public participation do not matter.
why.Citizen action matters only when everyon: This mistake thinks democratic action matters only when everyone agrees.

activities.explanation: This is right because informed citizens strengthen democracy through public participation.

activities.prompt: A map marks a polling station serving only one voter. India had over 96.8 crore registered voters in 2024. What can we learn from both facts together?
options: One small voting group can exist inside a very large electorate.
One polling station must serve every registered voter in India.
One voter proves that India's registered electorate has only one member.
Every registered voter must live beside the same polling station.

why.One polling station must serve every reg: This mistake assumes one station must serve the whole country.
why.One voter proves that India's registered: This mistake reads one voter as the country's total electorate.
why.Every registered voter must live beside: This mistake assumes all voters must live beside one station.

activities.explanation: One-voter stations can exist inside a huge registered electorate.
