activities.prompt: Which office is chosen through indirect elections, where representatives select the leader?
options: The President
A Lok Sabha member
The Chief Electoral Officer
A Vidhan Sabha member
activities.explanation: Citizens choose representatives who then select the President.

activities.prompt: Periodic elections let voters hold their representatives accountable.
activities.explanation: Periodic elections give voters regular opportunities to hold representatives accountable.

activities.prompt: Under FPTP, the candidate with the ______ votes wins the seat.
activities.hint: Compare the votes received by each candidate.
activities.explanation: The candidate with the most votes wins the seat under FPTP.

activities.prompt: Match each electoral route to the body or office it fills.
activities.explanation: FPTP applies to the Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha. Proportional representation applies to the Rajya Sabha.

activities.prompt: Which law covers the conduct of elections and later disputes?
options: The 1950 Act
The 1951 Act
The Model Code of Conduct
activities.explanation: The Representation of the People Act, 1951 covers election conduct and later disputes.

activities.prompt: Delimitation seeks a nearly equal ratio of seats to ______.
activities.hint: Think about people living in constituencies.
activities.explanation: Delimitation seeks a nearly equal ratio of seats to population.

activities.prompt: Anyone may vote even if their name is absent from the electoral roll.
activities.explanation: Only a person whose name appears on the electoral roll can vote.

activities.prompt: Which qualities must a meaningful election have?
options: Inclusive, impartial and trustworthy
Inclusive, partial and secret
Impartial, private and local

chapters.title: The Problem of Choice
chapters.summary: In this chapter: choices, needs and scarce resources; the production possibility curve; what economics deals with; the three key economic questions.

lessons.title: Choices, Needs and Scarce Resources

activities.prompt: How would you choose if you could only have one wish fulfilled?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Choices, needs and wants
activities.body: Families, businesses and governments must often choose between different alternatives. A market is where products and services are bought and sold. Needs are important requirements like food, water and shelter. Wants are things people would like to have. Human wants are unlimited and change over time.
keyPoints: Families, businesses and governments make economic choices.
A market is where products and services are bought and sold.
Needs are requirements; wants are desired items.
activities.explanation: This card introduces choices, markets, needs and wants.

activities.prompt: Your family has enough money for either a holiday or a new gadget, but not both. Which should it choose?
steps: Both choices are wants, because the family would like them.
Limited money means the family must choose between them.
Choosing one gives up the value of the other.
Therefore, choose the most valued option, because resources should be used well.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Scarce resources
activities.body: Resources are the factors used to produce goods and services. Natural resources include water and coal. Human-made resources include capital and technology. Both types are limited in quantity, so scarce resources can be used for many alternative purposes. People and economies try to use them in the best possible way. Opportunity cost is the value of the option given up when a choice is made.
keyPoints: Resources produce goods and services.
Natural and human-made resources are limited.
Scarce resources can have many alternative purposes.
activities.explanation: Scarce resources require choices because their quantity is limited.

activities.title: What is a market?
activities.prompt: Where are products and services bought and sold?
options: A market
A resource
A need
A want
activities.explanation: A market is a place where products and services are bought and sold.

activities.title: Resource pairs
activities.prompt: Match each resource idea with its detail.
pairs: The factors used to produce goods and services
activities.explanation: Water and coal are natural resources. Capital and technology are human-made resources. Both types are limited in quantity.

activities.title: The cost of choosing
activities.prompt: What is opportunity cost?
options: The value of the option given up
The number of wants
The type of resource
The place for buying
activities.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the option given up when a choice is made.

activities.title: Limited resources
activities.prompt: Both natural and human-made resources are ______ in quantity.
activities.hint: They do not have unlimited amounts.
activities.explanation: Both natural and human-made resources are limited in quantity.

activities.title: Changing human wants
activities.prompt: Which statement about human wants is correct?
options: They are unlimited and change over time.
They are limited in quantity.
They are used to produce goods.
They are important requirements.
activities.explanation: Human wants are unlimited and they change over time.

activities.title: Many uses for resources
activities.prompt: What can scarce resources do?
options: Be used for many alternative purposes
Change only with human wants
Remain unlimited in quantity
Need no economic choices
activities.explanation: Scarce resources can be used for many alternative purposes. Their limited quantity creates a need for choices.

activities.prompt: A child buys a gadget. Later, another gadget appears for sale. What will likely happen?
options: The child will want the new gadget too.
The child will stop wanting the first gadget.
The child will have enough gadgets forever.
The child will need fewer other resources.

why.The child will stop wanting the first ga: It confuses changing wants with losing interest in the first one.
why.The child will have enough gadgets forev: It mistakes unlimited wants for unlimited resources.
why.The child will need fewer other resource: It wrongly links wanting more goods to using fewer resources.

activities.explanation: New wants can appear even after an earlier want is met.

activities.prompt: A map marks water and coal in one area. What can we tell about the area?
options: It has two natural resources.
It has two human-made resources.
It has two unlimited resources.
It has two wanted resources.

It mixes natural resources with human-made ones.
It mistakes limited resources for unlimited ones.
It treats resource types as things people simply want.

activities.explanation: Water and coal are both natural resources.

activities.prompt: A government must divide water between food production and street cleaning. What should it consider?
options: Which choice gives the best value.
Which choice wastes the most water.
Which choice needs no resources.
Which choice turns water into a want.

This focuses on wasting water instead of choosing its best use.
Every choice to provide water still uses resources.
Water is a resource, while wants are things people would like.

activities.explanation: Scarce resources should be used in the best possible way.

activities.prompt: A town uses water for food production instead of street cleaning. What is the opportunity cost?
options: The value of cleaning the streets.
The value of water used for food.
The value of food produced with water.
The value of a holiday for the town.

It confuses the chosen use with the option given up.
It confuses the benefit received with the value given up.
It names an unrelated want instead of the alternative water use.

activities.explanation: The value given up is cleaning the streets.

activities.prompt: Two families each want a holiday. One gives up a gadget. Why might it have chosen the holiday?
options: It valued the holiday more than the gadget.
It believed the gadget had no value.
It wanted to avoid making any choice.
It believed holidays use no resources.

It assumes a chosen item has no value at all.
It mistakes a necessary trade-off for avoiding choices.
It thinks a holiday can be produced without using resources.

activities.explanation: The family chose the option that it valued more.

lessons.title: The Production Possibility Curve

activities.prompt: How can a farmer find the best balance between two crops?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is a Production Possibility Curve?
activities.body: A Production Possibility Curve, or PPC, shows combinations of barley and wheat. Barley is on the horizontal axis, and wheat is on the vertical axis. Plotting combinations creates a downward-sloping curve. It shows the trade-off between crops. More barley requires giving up some wheat. The wheat given up is the opportunity cost of more barley. Every point shows greatest output without wasting resources. The PPC helps enterprises and governments decide.
keyPoints: The PPC shows combinations of barley and wheat.
More barley requires giving up some wheat.
The wheat given up is the opportunity cost.
activities.explanation: The PPC helps you see choices, trade-offs and efficient resource use.

activities.prompt: A farmer wants more barley. How should the farmer balance it with wheat?
steps: The farmer can plan different combinations because the PPC shows possible trade-offs.
Growing more barley requires some wheat to be given up.
That lost wheat is the opportunity cost of growing more barley.
Therefore, choose a PPC point because it avoids wasting resources.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Read the graph
activities.prompt: Which crop is shown on the horizontal axis?
options: wheat
barley
both crops
neither crop
activities.explanation: The horizontal axis shows the quantity of barley grown.

activities.title: Check the axis
activities.prompt: The vertical axis shows the quantity of wheat grown.
activities.explanation: The vertical axis shows the quantity of wheat grown.

activities.title: The cost of more barley
activities.prompt: When a farmer grows more barley, the farmer gives up some ______.
activities.hint: It is shown on the vertical axis.
activities.explanation: Producing more barley requires some wheat to be given up.

activities.title: Match the PPC ideas
activities.prompt: Match each item to its correct partner.
activities.explanation: The PPC links each crop to its axis and shows what trade-offs mean.

activities.title: Make more barley
activities.prompt: What must happen when a farmer produces more barley?
options: Some wheat is given up
Some wheat is gained
Barley output stays unchanged
Resources are wasted
activities.explanation: Producing more barley requires some wheat to be given up.

activities.title: Use the PPC
activities.prompt: How does the PPC help enterprises and governments?
options: Plan without limits
Plan and make decisions
Avoid all choices
Hide resource trade-offs
activities.explanation: The PPC helps enterprises and governments plan and make decisions.

activities.prompt: Last year, a farmer grew more barley. This year, the farmer grows more wheat. Why?
options: Less barley made more wheat possible.
More barley always made more wheat possible.
More wheat removed the trade-off between both crops.
The farmer now wastes fewer resources on barley.

why.More barley always made more wheat possi: More barley requires wheat to be given up, not more wheat.
why.More wheat removed the trade-off between: Changing the combination does not remove the trade-off.
why.The farmer now wastes fewer resources on: The change alone does not show that barley production became efficient.

activities.explanation: Giving up some barley allows more wheat to be produced.

activities.prompt: A farmer wastes some resources while growing both crops. What should the farmer change?
options: Choose a point on the PPC, because it avoids wastage.
Grow more wheat, because wastage only affects barley.
Keep the plan, because wasted resources still count.
Grow both crops together, because this removes the trade-off.

why.Grow more wheat, because wastage only af: This mistake thinks resource wastage only happens with barley.
why.Keep the plan, because wasted resources: Keeping a wasteful plan does not make resource use efficient.
why.Grow both crops together, because this r: Growing both does not remove the trade-off or resource waste.

activities.explanation: Every PPC point gives the greatest output without wasting resources.

activities.prompt: Barley is on the horizontal axis. Wheat is on the vertical axis. What does the downward curve show?
options: More barley comes with less wheat.
More barley always comes with more wheat.
The farmer can ignore the trade-off.
Both crops grow more without anything being lost.

why.More barley always comes with more wheat: This mistake ignores the trade-off shown by the curve.
The curve shows a trade-off, so it cannot be ignored.
why.Both crops grow more without anything be: Growing both more would remove the trade-off shown by the curve.

activities.explanation: A downward-sloping curve shows that more barley needs less wheat.

lessons.title: What Economics Deals With

activities.prompt: What can we learn about making wise choices in everyday life?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is Economics?
activities.body: Economics comes from the Greek word oikonomia. It originally meant managing a household. Families and nations have limited resources, but unlimited wants. They must plan how to use these resources well. Individuals, enterprises and governments also choose between competing uses. Economics studies these choices. It explains how people interact, work, earn wages and how market prices are determined.
keyPoints: Economics began with household management.
Limited resources require careful choices.
Economics studies interactions, work, wages and market prices.
activities.explanation: Economics helps people and groups make wise choices.

activities.prompt: A family has limited money and several needs. How can it choose which needs to receive the money?
steps: The family must plan because its money is limited while its wants are unlimited.
It should compare alternatives and possible outcomes because economists do this before giving advice.
It should use data and analysis because good economic decisions should not rely on guesswork.
Therefore, the family should choose carefully, because resource allocation affects the well-being of people and society.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does Economics study?
options: Choices with limited resources
Rainfall across different states
Religious festivals in villages
Different types of housework
activities.explanation: Limited resources and unlimited wants make choices necessary.

activities.prompt: Economics comes from the ______ word oikonomia.
activities.hint: The lesson gives the language name.
activities.explanation: The lesson says Economics comes from the Greek word oikonomia.

activities.prompt: Economics originally referred to the management of a household.
activities.explanation: Economics first described managing a household and its resources.

activities.prompt: Match each beginning with its meaning.
pairs: interact with governments and financial institutions
activities.explanation: Each pair links a word or phrase to the lesson's meaning.

activities.prompt: What do economists study before giving advice?
options: Weather and seasons
Schools and hospitals
Alternatives and outcomes
Music and sports
activities.explanation: Economists study alternatives and possible outcomes before giving advice.

activities.prompt: Which approach supports good economic decisions?
options: Using guesswork and hope
Using data and analysis
Ignoring all information
Avoiding careful study
activities.explanation: Good economic decisions rely on data and analysis rather than guesswork.

activities.prompt: A family has limited money and several competing needs. How should it choose one need first?
options: By comparing needs, trade-offs and possible outcomes.
By choosing the need that uses the least money.
By choosing the need that seems most exciting.
By giving equal money to every competing need.

why.By choosing the need that uses the least: This mistake thinks the smallest cost settles the choice without comparing outcomes.
why.By choosing the need that seems most exc: This mistake relies on feelings instead of data and analysis.
why.By giving equal money to every competing: This mistake thinks equal shares avoid making a choice.

activities.explanation: This is right because economists study alternatives and possible outcomes before advising.

activities.prompt: Earlier, a village used scarce food for one need. Later, it used food for another need. What should economists compare?
options: Only how much food each choice used.
Only how much each village member wanted food.
The alternatives, opportunity costs and possible outcomes.
Only how quickly the village made each choice.

This mistake focuses on one visible input instead of the whole choice.
why.Only how much each village member wanted: This mistake measures wants but ignores scarce resources and alternatives.
why.Only how quickly the village made each c: This mistake values speed instead of analysing the economic choice.

activities.explanation: This is right because economists study alternatives, opportunity costs and possible outcomes.

activities.prompt: A government has limited funds and two useful projects. What should it study before choosing one?
options: Only the project that needs the least money.
Only the project that officials like best.
Every useful project equally, without choosing.
The alternatives, opportunity costs and possible outcomes.

why.Only the project that needs the least mo: This mistake thinks lowest spending alone is enough, without comparing outcomes.
why.Only the project that officials like bes: This mistake uses personal liking instead of data and analysis.
why.Every useful project equally, without ch: This mistake treats equal attention as a decision instead of making one.

activities.explanation: This is right because economists study these points before giving advice.

activities.prompt: A worker wants advice about two jobs. Good economic decisions need facts and analysis. What should the adviser use?
options: Data and analysis comparing both jobs carefully.
A quick guess about which job seems better.
The job name that sounds most exciting to the worker.
The adviser's favourite job, without checking facts.

why.A quick guess about which job seems bett: This mistake uses guesswork instead of facts and analysis.
why.The job name that sounds most exciting t: This mistake chooses by sound instead of careful evidence.
why.The adviser's favourite job, without che: This mistake follows personal liking without checking facts.

activities.explanation: This is right because good economic decisions rely on data and analysis.

lessons.title: The Three Key Economic Questions

activities.prompt: How can we make choices that help people and the planet?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Three key questions
activities.body: The lesson introduces three key economic questions. First, what goods and services should be produced, and in what quantities? Second, how should they be produced? Third, for whom should they be produced? These questions guide production, resource use and distribution. They also help producers balance present gains with long-term sustainability.
keyPoints: Goods and services, with quantities.
Land, labour, capital and technology.
Who benefits from production.
activities.explanation: These questions guide choices about production, methods and consumers.

activities.prompt: A farmer is deciding between sugarcane, which can give high profits, and millets and pulses, which save water. Which choice is best?
steps: Sugarcane can give high profits, so this is one possible reason to choose it.
Millets and pulses save water and improve soil health, so they support sustainable agriculture.
The opportunity cost of sugarcane includes the benefits gained from saved water.
The farmer must balance short-term economic gains with long-term sustainability, so profit alone is not enough.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Production decisions should meet the ______ of the economy over a given period.
activities.hint: Think about what production decisions should meet.
activities.explanation: Production decisions should meet the economy's needs over a given period.

activities.prompt: Match each key question to its lesson meaning.
pairs: Goods and services, and their quantities
For whom should it be produced?
Who benefits and how goods are used
activities.explanation: Each question has a different focus: products, methods and consumers.

activities.prompt: Which crop pair saves water and improves soil health?
options: Millets and pulses
Sugarcane
Sugar
Profit and sugar
activities.explanation: Millets and pulses save water and improve soil health.

activities.prompt: Which differences do producers consider when choosing consumers to serve?
options: Needs, income, tastes, lifestyles
Needs, income and production
Tastes, lifestyles and outputs
Income levels and quantities
activities.explanation: Producers consider needs, income levels, tastes and lifestyles.

activities.prompt: Put the production decisions in order.
items: Select land, labour, capital and technology
activities.explanation: Producers first decide what to produce, then how, and select a suitable mix.

activities.prompt: A farmer wants high profits but must protect long-term farming. Which idea should guide the choice?
options: Balance short-term gains and sustainability
Focus only on high-profit sugarcane
Ignore water-saving benefits
Choose only for short-term gains
activities.explanation: Farmers must balance short-term economic gains with long-term sustainability.

activities.prompt: A farmer chooses sugarcane instead of millets and pulses. What is part of the opportunity cost?
options: The benefits gained from saved water.
The high profits gained from sugarcane.
The support given to sugar industries.
The needs of the economy over a given period.

This mistakes the chosen crop's gain for the cost of the alternative.
This is a benefit of sugarcane, not a lost alternative benefit.
why.The needs of the economy over a given pe: This is a wider production rule, not the lost alternative's benefit.

activities.explanation: These benefits are part of sugarcane's opportunity cost.

activities.prompt: A farm's production decisions must meet the economy's needs over a given period. Which choice best follows this rule?
options: Balance short-term economic gains with long-term sustainability.
Choose only the option with high short-term profits.
Choose only the option that saves water and improves soil.
Choose based only on consumers' needs, incomes and tastes.

why.Choose only the option with high short-t: This follows short-term profits but ignores long-term sustainability.
why.Choose only the option that saves water: This follows sustainability but ignores short-term economic gains.
why.Choose based only on consumers' needs, i: This focuses on one consumer group and ignores wider production needs.

activities.explanation: Balancing both goals best supports needs over a given period.

activities.prompt: Sugarcane can give high profits and support sugar industries. Millets and pulses save water and improve soil health. Which choice is most balanced?
options: Balance sugarcane profits with the long-term value of saving water.
Choose sugarcane profits and ignore the long-term value of water.
Choose millets for high profits and ignore the long-term value of water.
Choose sugarcane for water savings and millets for high profits.

why.Choose sugarcane profits and ignore the: This takes short-term gains but ignores long-term sustainability.
why.Choose millets for high profits and igno: This wrongly says millets give high profits.
why.Choose sugarcane for water savings and m: This swaps the stated benefits of sugarcane and millets.

activities.explanation: This balances high profits with the benefits of saving water.

lessons.title: Economic Systems and the Government's Role

activities.prompt: How should the government balance freedom and fairness in our economy?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How economic systems work
activities.body: An economic system organises how goods, services and resources are produced, consumed and distributed. A planned economy is led by central government decisions. A market economy is mainly guided by demand and supply. A mixed economy combines both. India moved towards a market-oriented system, but government still plays an important role.
keyPoints: Central government makes major economic decisions.
Demand and supply guide most market decisions.
Mixed systems combine planned and market features.
Government still plays an important role in India.
activities.explanation: Each system shares decision-making in a different way.

activities.prompt: A bakery keeps making old cakes, although customers want new ones. Why?
steps: The government sets production targets, so the bakery follows them.
Private firms often follow targets instead of demand, explaining the unchanged cakes.
Strict controls can limit competition, so firms may improve less.
Therefore, stable production may result from targets and weaker market pressure.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Meaning of an economic system
activities.prompt: What does an economic system organise?
options: Production, consumption and distribution
Factory ownership and worker wages
Government rules and public spending
School lessons and local elections
activities.explanation: This is the full meaning of an economic system.

activities.title: Government-led decisions
activities.prompt: In a ______ economy, central government authority makes the major economic decisions.
activities.hint: A system guided by central government authority.
activities.explanation: A planned economy puts major economic decisions with central government authority.

activities.title: Match features to systems
activities.prompt: Match each economic feature to its system.
activities.explanation: Each feature belongs to the system described in your book.

activities.title: Effects of limited competition
activities.prompt: What may happen when competition is limited?
options: Motivation to improve may reduce
Firms may gain stronger motivation
Competition may become stronger
Market demand may disappear
activities.explanation: Limited competition can reduce the wish to improve quality or innovate.

activities.title: Effects of India's reforms
activities.prompt: The reforms reduced excessive ______ and encouraged private enterprise.
activities.hint: Rules that control business activity.
activities.explanation: These reforms encouraged private enterprise by reducing excessive rules.

activities.title: India's economic change
activities.prompt: What best describes India's economic change after the reforms?
options: Markets with an important government role
Central planning with almost no government role
Complete markets with no public sector role
State ownership with almost no private enterprise
activities.explanation: India moved towards a market-oriented system, while government continued to play an important role.

activities.prompt: A planned economy has a central authority making major decisions. A market economy uses demand and supply with little government intervention. What is the main difference?
options: Government choices guide production, while buyers and sellers guide most decisions.
Every shop makes all choices without any limits from the government.
Government owns every factory, shop and piece of land in both systems.
Both systems let football referees set every production target.

why.Every shop makes all choices without any: This wrongly suggests that shops control production without government limits.
why.Government owns every factory, shop and: This ownership pattern fits planned economies, not both systems.
why.Both systems let football referees set e: This wrongly gives football referees the power to set production targets.

activities.explanation: Planned decisions are government-led, while market decisions mainly follow buyers and sellers.

activities.prompt: A large public sector company operates beside private shops in one economy. Which feature does this show?
options: Market and planned features exist together in the same system.
Only government decisions exist, because private shops have no role.
Only private ownership exists, because public companies have no role.
Government targets have ended all choices by private enterprises.

why.Only government decisions exist, because: Private shops can exist because the economy mixes both features.
why.Only private ownership exists, because p: Public sector companies can still play an important role.
why.Government targets have ended all choice: This wrongly treats following targets as removing every choice.

activities.explanation: This is the defining feature of a mixed economy.

activities.prompt: Demand and supply guide most market decisions with little government intervention. The government acts like a football referee. What does this suggest?
options: It guides the rules without making most economic decisions.
It owns all shops and factories and chooses all products.
It has no role because private companies make every decision.
It sets production targets for every private company.

why.It owns all shops and factories and choo: Factories, shops and land largely belong to individuals and private companies.
why.It has no role because private companies: The government still acts like a referee in a market economy.
why.It sets production targets for every pri: Market decisions are mainly guided by demand and supply, not government targets.

activities.explanation: The referee role suggests guiding play while leaving most decisions to others.

activities.prompt: A bakery in a planned economy gets a government target for cakes. Customers prefer a different cake. What is the bakery most likely to do?
options: It follows the government target because that guides its production.
It follows customers because market demand always overrules government targets.
It takes control of banks and transport to set a new target.
It changes freely because strict controls do not limit competition.

why.It follows customers because market dema: This reverses the rule that private firms often follow government targets.
why.It takes control of banks and transport: Governments usually own resources and sectors such as banks and transport.
why.It changes freely because strict control: Strict controls can restrict competition among private enterprises.

activities.explanation: Private enterprises often follow government targets instead of market demand.

activities.context: A family runs a business near a market, where products and services are bought and sold. The family needs food, water and shelter, while its wants include a holiday and a gadget. The business uses water and human-made resources such as technology. These resources are limited and can serve different purposes. When the family uses them to produce goods, it gives up another use. It should consider the value of that option.
activities.prompt: Before using its resources to produce goods, what should the family consider?
options: Which alternative use of the resources will be sacrificed.
Which new want might appear because human wants are unlimited and change over time.
Whether the resources can be used without producing goods or services.
Whether the market can make the limited resources unlimited.

why.Which new want might appear because huma: Future wants may affect decisions but do not identify the option given up.
why.Whether the resources can be used withou: Resources are used to produce goods and services.
why.Whether the market can make the limited: A market does not remove the limited quantity of resources.

activities.explanation: This identifies the alternative use given up by the choice.

activities.context: A family runs a business near a market, where products and services are bought and sold. The family needs food, water and shelter, while its wants include a holiday and a gadget. The business uses water and human-made resources such as technology. These resources are limited and can serve different purposes. When the family uses them to produce goods, it gives up another use. It should consider the value of that option.
activities.prompt: If the family uses water and technology to produce goods rather than buy a holiday, what is the opportunity cost?
options: The value of the holiday given up.
The value of the goods produced, because they satisfy needs.
The market itself, because it is where buying and selling occur.
The family's desire for more wants after the choice.

why.The value of the goods produced, because: The goods produced are part of the chosen option, not the option given up.
why.The market itself, because it is where b: The market is a place where products and services are bought and sold.
why.The family's desire for more wants after: A later desire does not identify the value of the holiday given up.

activities.explanation: The holiday is the option given up when the family chooses production.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A business must often make economic choices between different alternatives.
Reason (R): Scarce resources can be used for many alternative purposes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The alternative uses of scarce resources explain why a business must choose between different alternatives.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Needs are important requirements such as food, water and shelter.
Reason (R): Wants are things people would like to have, such as gadgets, holidays or luxury items.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement about wants does not explain why needs are important requirements.

activities.prompt: Explain why families, businesses and governments must make economic choices.
activities.answer: Families, businesses and governments must often make economic choices because resources are limited, while human wants are unlimited and change over time. Scarce resources can be used for many alternative purposes, so using them for one purpose means giving up another possible use. The value of the option given up is the opportunity cost. People and economies therefore try to use scarce resources in the best possible way. Choices are necessary to decide which needs and wants will be met and how available resources will be used.
points: Links limited resources with unlimited and changing human wants.
Explains that scarce resources can have alternative uses.
Defines opportunity cost as the value of the option given up.
Explains why people try to use scarce resources in the best possible way.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A farmer decides to compare two plans. One plan grows more barley, while the other grows more wheat. The farmer records the possible combinations on a graph, with barley on the horizontal axis and wheat on the vertical axis. The points form a downward-sloping curve. The farmer uses this curve to choose a combination that makes efficient use of resources and avoids wasting resources.
activities.prompt: If the farmer chooses the plan with more barley, what must happen to wheat production?
options: Some wheat output must be forgone.
More wheat can be produced without reducing barley.
Barley and wheat output can both increase at the same time.
Barley can remain unchanged while wheat output increases.

why.More wheat can be produced without reduc: This ignores the trade-off between the two outputs.
why.Barley and wheat output can both increas: The PPC shows that increasing one output requires reducing the other.
why.Barley can remain unchanged while wheat: This describes changing wheat output rather than increasing barley.

activities.explanation: Growing more barley necessarily involves giving up some wheat.

activities.context: A farmer decides to compare two plans. One plan grows more barley, while the other grows more wheat. The farmer records the possible combinations on a graph, with barley on the horizontal axis and wheat on the vertical axis. The points form a downward-sloping curve. The farmer uses this curve to choose a combination that makes efficient use of resources and avoids wasting resources.
activities.prompt: Before making a production plan, how should an enterprise use the PPC?
options: Weigh the barley-wheat trade-off and select a point that avoids wastage.
Select the point with the most barley regardless of the wheat output.
Select the point with the most wheat regardless of the barley output.
Ignore the curve and plan only one of the two outputs.

why.Select the point with the most barley re: Choosing only the greatest barley output overlooks the wheat that must be given up.
why.Select the point with the most wheat reg: Choosing only the greatest wheat output overlooks the barley that must be given up.
why.Ignore the curve and plan only one of th: The PPC is intended to help enterprises compare possible combinations.

activities.explanation: This considers both the trade-off and efficient use of resources.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Producing more barley requires some wheat to be given up.
Reason (R): The wheat given up is the opportunity cost of growing more barley.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly identifies the cost of increasing barley production.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Every point on the PPC shows the greatest output possible without wasting resources.
Reason (R): The PPC helps enterprises and governments plan and make decisions.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain what each point represents.

activities.prompt: Explain how the PPC shows the trade-off between barley and wheat.
activities.answer: The PPC places barley on the horizontal axis and wheat on the vertical axis. Plotting the possible combinations creates a downward-sloping curve because producing more barley requires some wheat to be given up. The wheat given up is the opportunity cost of growing more barley. Therefore, the curve shows the trade-off between the two outputs. Each point represents the greatest output possible without wasting resources, and selecting such a point means resources are used efficiently.
points: Barley is on the horizontal axis and wheat is on the vertical axis.
Possible combinations create a downward-sloping curve.
More barley requires some wheat to be given up.
The curve shows the trade-off and efficient use of resources.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A household has limited money but several needs and wants. Family members consider buying a needed item, saving for another goal, or paying for a service. One member seeks information before deciding, while another urges the family to choose quickly. A producer watches how market prices are determined, while consumers compare sellers' prices. These decisions shape resource allocation and affect the well-being of people and society.
activities.prompt: What should the family do before choosing how to use its limited money?
options: Use relevant information to compare the choices and likely results.
Choose whichever option can be obtained most quickly.
Make the decision without comparing the available choices.
Select an option based only on personal preference.

why.Choose whichever option can be obtained: Speed alone does not show efficient resource use.
why.Make the decision without comparing the: Ignoring alternatives risks overlooking opportunity costs.
why.Select an option based only on personal: A preference alone may not account for other needs or possible outcomes.

activities.explanation: This supports a decision based on information and analysis.

activities.context: A household has limited money but several needs and wants. Family members consider buying a needed item, saving for another goal, or paying for a service. One member seeks information before deciding, while another urges the family to choose quickly. A producer watches how market prices are determined, while consumers compare sellers' prices. These decisions shape resource allocation and affect the well-being of people and society.
activities.prompt: If the household uses all its limited money for one goal, what is likely to happen?
options: Other goals will remain unmet, and possible benefits from alternatives will be forgone.
No competing use will be affected because one goal receives everything.
Only the chosen goal will be affected, with no effects on society.
The allocation will automatically become more efficient.

why.No competing use will be affected becaus: Allocating resources to one purpose can affect other possible uses.
why.Only the chosen goal will be affected, w: Resource allocation can affect the well-being of people and society.
why.The allocation will automatically become: Efficiency does not arise automatically from concentrating resources.

activities.explanation: Limited resources cannot satisfy every competing goal at once.

activities.context: A household has limited money but several needs and wants. Family members consider buying a needed item, saving for another goal, or paying for a service. One member seeks information before deciding, while another urges the family to choose quickly. A producer watches how market prices are determined, while consumers compare sellers' prices. These decisions shape resource allocation and affect the well-being of people and society.
activities.prompt: Before advising the household, what should an economist do?
options: Weigh what each choice would give up and consider possible results.
Give advice immediately because careful analysis is unnecessary.
Ignore other choices and focus on only one possible result.
Choose based on guesswork because information is not needed.

why.Give advice immediately because careful: Careful analysis supports a good economic decision.
why.Ignore other choices and focus on only o: Ignoring alternatives can conceal opportunity costs.
why.Choose based on guesswork because inform: Good decisions rely on data and analysis rather than guesswork.

activities.explanation: This involves alternatives, opportunity costs, and possible outcomes.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Economics studies how choices are made with limited resources.
Reason (R): Economics explains how consumers, producers, governments and financial institutions interact.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason describes economic interaction rather than explaining why economics studies choice.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Good economic decisions rely on data and analysis rather than guesswork.
Reason (R): Economists study alternatives, opportunity costs and possible outcomes before giving advice.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Studying alternatives, opportunity costs and possible outcomes is a way to apply data and analysis before advice is given.

activities.prompt: Explain why economics is important when resources are limited.
activities.answer: Economics helps people make good choices when resources are limited. Families, enterprises, and governments all have to decide how to use resources that could go to competing purposes. Economics studies these choices and resource allocation, including opportunity costs and possible outcomes. It also examines how consumers, producers, governments, and financial institutions interact, how people work and earn wages, and how market prices are determined. Good decisions rely on data and analysis rather than guesswork, so advice should compare alternatives and consider effects on the well-being of people and society.
points: Explains the need to choose among competing uses.
Links economics with resource allocation and opportunity costs.
Mentions interaction, work, wages, and market prices.
Shows why data and analysis are preferable to guesswork.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A farmer is deciding whether to grow sugarcane or millets and pulses for consumers over a given period. Sugarcane offers high profits and can support industries such as sugar, while millets and pulses save water, improve soil health and support sustainable agriculture. The farmer also knows that consumers differ in their needs, income levels, tastes and lifestyles, so the choice affects both current economic gains and long-term sustainability.
activities.prompt: If the farmer chooses sugarcane, what is an important opportunity cost to consider?
options: The profit earned from selling sugarcane.
The possible benefit from the water that millets and pulses could save.
The income received by consumers who purchase the goods.
The support provided to industries such as sugar.

why.The profit earned from selling sugarcane: This is a gain from the chosen crop rather than a benefit given up.
why.The income received by consumers who pur: Consumer income is related to the question of for whom to produce.
why.The support provided to industries such: This is a benefit of choosing sugarcane, not an opportunity cost.

activities.explanation: The possible benefit of saved water is included in the opportunity cost.

activities.context: A farmer is deciding whether to grow sugarcane or millets and pulses for consumers over a given period. Sugarcane offers high profits and can support industries such as sugar, while millets and pulses save water, improve soil health and support sustainable agriculture. The farmer also knows that consumers differ in their needs, income levels, tastes and lifestyles, so the choice affects both current economic gains and long-term sustainability.
activities.prompt: After deciding to grow sugarcane, what should the farmer do next?
options: Decide which consumers should receive the goods.
Change the product from sugarcane to millets and pulses.
Focus only on short-term profit and ignore long-term sustainability.
Choose how to produce it by combining land, labour, capital and technology suitably.

why.Decide which consumers should receive th: Choosing consumers is part of the question of for whom to produce.
why.Change the product from sugarcane to mil: Changing the crop would reopen the decision about what to produce.
why.Focus only on short-term profit and igno: A sound decision must balance economic gains with sustainability.

activities.explanation: After deciding what to produce, the producer must decide how to produce it.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The Problem of Choice

activities.title: The value of giving up
activities.prompt: Which option best explains opportunity cost?
options: The value of an option given up
The money paid for a choice
The number of choices available
The time used to make a choice
activities.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the option you give up when making a choice.

activities.title: Limited resource groups
activities.prompt: Natural resources are unlimited, while human-made resources are limited.
activities.explanation: Both natural and human-made resources are limited in quantity. This makes choices necessary.

activities.title: A natural resource
activities.prompt: Coal is a type of ______ resource.
activities.hint: Choose the resource group that comes from nature.
activities.explanation: Coal is a natural resource. Water is another natural resource.

activities.title: Match each idea
activities.prompt: Match each idea on the left with its meaning.
pairs: Important requirements such as food and shelter
Things people would like to have
A place where products and services are bought and sold
A central authority makes major economic decisions
Demand and supply guide most decisions
activities.explanation: Needs are requirements, while wants are desired items. Economic systems organise choices about goods, services and resources.

activities.title: Points on the PPC
activities.prompt: Which statement about the Production Possibility Curve is correct?
options: Output with resources left unused
Only the amount of wheat grown
Maximum output without wasting resources
A fixed total of barley and wheat
activities.explanation: Every point on the PPC shows the greatest output possible without wasting resources.

activities.title: The farmer's trade-off
activities.prompt: The ______ given up is the opportunity cost of growing more barley.
activities.hint: Think of the crop shown on the vertical axis.
activities.explanation: Producing more barley requires some wheat to be given up. That wheat is the opportunity cost.

activities.title: Who makes economic decisions?
activities.prompt: Which statement about economic systems is correct?
options: Major decisions are made by a central authority
Government makes every single economic decision
Private firms always replace market demand
A mixed economy has only planned features
activities.explanation: A central government authority makes major decisions in a planned economy. A mixed economy combines planned and market features.

activities.title: Changing wants
activities.prompt: Human wants stay the same over time.
activities.explanation: Human wants are unlimited and they change over time. People keep looking for new things to satisfy their wants.

activities.title: India's economic change
activities.prompt: India moved towards a market-oriented system while the government continued to play an important role.
activities.explanation: Reforms reduced excessive regulations and encouraged private enterprise. The government continued to play an important role.

chapters.title: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
chapters.summary: In this chapter: demand: meaning and the law of demand; other determinants of demand; supply and the law of supply; other determinants of supply.

lessons.title: Demand: Meaning and the Law of Demand

activities.prompt: Why do people usually buy more when something costs less?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Demand
activities.body: Demand means people are willing and able to buy at a particular price. A wish alone is not enough, because purchasing power is also needed. Price and quantity demanded have an inverse relationship. When price falls, quantity demanded rises. When price rises, quantity demanded falls. Individual demand shows how one consumer’s quantity changes at different prices. Market demand adds the quantities wanted by all potential buyers.
keyPoints: Demand needs willingness, ability, and purchasing power.
Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.
Market demand includes all potential buyers.
activities.explanation: These ideas explain what demand means and how it changes with price.

activities.prompt: Mangoes become cheaper when prices react to what people want and what is available. Will Srivalli buy more?
steps: Prices do not change randomly; they react to buyers' wants and availability.
Srivalli bought 2 kg when the price fell to ₹100 per kg.
Price and quantity demanded have an inverse relationship.
Therefore, a lower price can lead her to buy more mangoes.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A child wants a football but cannot buy it. What is missing for demand?
options: Willingness alone
Purchasing power
Random prices
More sellers
activities.explanation: A wish is not enough because demand also needs purchasing power.

activities.prompt: Demand means people are willing and ______ to buy at a particular price.
activities.hint: Think about what lets a person buy.
activities.explanation: Demand needs both willingness and the ability to buy.

activities.prompt: What usually happens when an item’s price falls?
options: Quantity demanded rises
Quantity demanded falls
Quantity demanded stays the same
The item’s supply disappears
activities.explanation: Falling price and rising quantity demanded show an inverse relationship.

activities.prompt: When mangoes fell to ₹100 per kg, how many did Srivalli buy?
options: 2 kg
2 bags
2 boxes
2 baskets
activities.explanation: Srivalli bought 2 kg of mangoes when their price fell to ₹100 per kg.

activities.prompt: Match each demand idea with its meaning.
pairs: One consumer’s quantity changes at different prices
Total quantity wanted by all potential buyers
Becomes a demand curve when shown graphically
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a demand idea with its meaning.

activities.prompt: One customer buys different amounts at different prices. Which demand is shown?
options: Individual demand
Market demand
Demand schedule
Purchasing power
activities.explanation: Individual demand shows one consumer’s quantity changes at different prices.

activities.prompt: Srivalli bought 2 kg of mangoes at ₹100 per kg. If the price rises, what happens?
options: The quantity she demands will fall.
The quantity she demands will rise.
The quantity she demands will stay the same.
The quantity she demands will change randomly.

This reverses the inverse relationship between price and quantity.
why.The quantity she demands will stay the s: This mistakes a higher price for a greater quantity demanded.
why.The quantity she demands will change ran: This assumes the law of demand cannot show the direction.

activities.explanation: A higher price lowers quantity demanded because their relationship is inverse.

activities.prompt: One graph shows one buyer's quantity demanded at different prices. Its line slopes downward. What relationship does it show?
options: Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.
Price and quantity demanded move together upward.
Price changes, but quantity never changes.
Quantity changes, but price never changes.

why.Price and quantity demanded move togethe: This mistakes an inverse relationship for a direct one.
why.Price changes, but quantity never change: This wrongly says one change never affects the other.
why.Quantity changes, but price never change: This treats price as fixed while allowing quantity to change.

activities.explanation: A downward graph shows price and quantity demanded changing oppositely.

activities.prompt: A table lists one buyer's quantities at different prices. Why plot the same pairs on graph paper?
options: To show how quantity changes as prices change clearly.
To add prices that the buyer never recorded before.
To include all potential buyers in one buyer's table.
To show that prices change without any clear reason.

why.To add prices that the buyer never recor: This wrongly suggests a graph creates new price information.
why.To include all potential buyers in one b: This confuses individual demand with market demand.
why.To show that prices change without any c: This mistakes a clear relationship for random price changes.

activities.explanation: Plotting prices and quantities turns the schedule into a demand curve.

activities.prompt: At one price, a shop adds every potential buyer's wanted quantity. What does this total show?
options: Market demand, because it includes all potential buyers.
Individual demand, because it studies only one buyer.
A demand curve, because it adds quantities at one price.
A buying wish, because ability to pay is not checked.

why.Individual demand, because it studies on: This wrongly uses market demand for one consumer's quantity.
why.A demand curve, because it adds quantiti: A demand curve is a graph, not a total quantity.
why.A buying wish, because ability to pay is: This confuses wanting with demand, which also needs purchasing power.

activities.explanation: Market demand is the total quantity wanted by all potential buyers.

activities.prompt: One market has many buyers who respond together to a price change. Another has only one buyer. Why is the first market's curve flatter?
options: Many buyers' responses make the total change less steep.
One buyer's response makes the total change less steep.
More buyers make each buyer want the same quantity.
Fewer prices make the total change less steep.

why.One buyer's response makes the total cha: One buyer's response cannot explain a flatter market curve.
why.More buyers make each buyer want the sam: This wrongly assumes every buyer wants the same quantity.
why.Fewer prices make the total change less: This blames the number of prices instead of buyers' responses.

activities.explanation: Many buyers responding together make the market curve flatter.

lessons.title: Other Determinants of Demand

activities.prompt: What makes you choose one snack instead of another?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Else Affects Demand?
activities.body: Demand does not depend only on price. A related good's price or availability can change demand. Substitute goods replace each other, while complementary goods are used together. Higher household income can help people buy more. Tastes and population also affect demand. Weather, festivals and cultural habits can shape seasonal demand. People get less extra usefulness as they consume more. What people expect about future prices can change buying time.
keyPoints: Substitute goods replace each other.
Complementary goods are used together.
Income, tastes and population affect demand.
Seasonal factors and price expectations affect buying.
Extra usefulness falls with more consumption.
activities.explanation: These are several important factors that can change demand.

activities.prompt: Coffee becomes more expensive. A family chooses tea instead. Why does this change their demand?
steps: Coffee and tea are substitutes because either can replace the other.
Coffee costs more, so people may switch from coffee to tea.
This price change affects demand because the goods can replace each other.
Therefore, a higher coffee price may increase demand for tea.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which pair contains substitute goods?
options: Smartphones and earphones
Tea and coffee
Cars and petrol
activities.explanation: Tea and coffee can replace each other, so they are substitute goods.

activities.prompt: When coffee becomes more expensive, people may switch to ______.
activities.hint: People may switch to it when coffee costs more.
activities.explanation: People may switch to tea when coffee becomes more expensive.

activities.prompt: What usually happens when household income rises?
options: Consumers usually buy fewer goods.
Consumers have fewer product choices.
Consumers can usually buy more.
Consumers stop buying related goods.
activities.explanation: Rising household income usually helps consumers afford more goods.

activities.prompt: Match each determinant with its effect on demand.
pairs: Its price or availability can affect demand
They influence which products are demanded
Demand depends on its size and composition
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a determinant with its effect on demand.

activities.prompt: Put the consumption sequence in order.
items: A person consumes some of a product
The person consumes more of it
The extra usefulness from the product declines
activities.explanation: As consumption increases, the product's extra usefulness declines.

activities.prompt: According to the lesson, what do consumers do when they expect prices to rise?
options: Postpone buying the goods.
Wait for better weather.
Choose fewer product types.
Buy the goods immediately.
activities.explanation: Consumers buy immediately when they expect prices to rise.

activities.prompt: Tea and coffee can replace one another. Coffee becomes more expensive. What may happen to demand for tea?
options: Demand for tea may increase because coffee is more expensive.
Demand for tea may decrease because coffee is more expensive.
Demand for tea may stay equal because coffee is more expensive.
Demand for tea may increase because tea and coffee are used together.

why.Demand for tea may decrease because coff: This reverses the effect of a higher price for a substitute.
why.Demand for tea may stay equal because co: This ignores that people may switch between substitute goods.
why.Demand for tea may increase because tea: This wrongly treats tea and coffee as complementary goods.

activities.explanation: People may switch from coffee to tea when coffee costs more.

activities.prompt: Smartphones and earphones are generally used together. Earphones become harder to find. What may happen to demand for smartphones?
options: Demand for smartphones may fall because earphones are harder to find.
Demand for smartphones may rise because earphones are harder to find.
Demand for smartphones may stay equal because earphones are harder to find.
Demand for smartphones may fall because earphones replace smartphones.

why.Demand for smartphones may rise because: This reverses the effect when a complementary good becomes harder to find.
why.Demand for smartphones may stay equal be: This ignores that a related good's availability can change demand.
why.Demand for smartphones may fall because: This wrongly treats earphones as substitutes for smartphones.

activities.explanation: Smartphones and earphones are complementary goods used together.

activities.prompt: Two countries have similar prices. One has more people who prefer fruit. What may be true about fruit demand?
options: It may be higher there because population size and tastes affect demand.
It may be lower there because population size and tastes affect demand.
It may be equal there because population size and tastes affect demand.
It may be higher there only because fruit is a substitute good.

why.It may be lower there because population: This reverses the possible effects of population size and tastes.
why.It may be equal there because population: This ignores that population size and tastes can change demand.
why.It may be higher there only because frui: This wrongly relies on substitution instead of population and preferences.

activities.explanation: More people and particular tastes can both affect demand.

activities.prompt: Two shoppers see the same item. One expects its price to fall. The other expects it to rise. What will they likely do?
options: The first waits, while the second buys immediately.
The first buys immediately, while the second waits.
Both wait, because expected prices do not affect buying.
Both buy immediately, because expected prices do not affect buying.

why.The first buys immediately, while the se: This swaps the effects of expected rising and falling prices.
why.Both wait, because expected prices do no: This wrongly says expected prices do not affect buying.
why.Both buy immediately, because expected p: This wrongly says expected prices do not affect buying.

activities.explanation: People wait for lower prices but buy when they expect prices to rise.

activities.prompt: A festival raises demand for a special food. As one person eats more, its extra usefulness falls. What may happen next?
options: Their demand may fall because the food gives less extra usefulness.
Their demand may rise because the food gives less extra usefulness.
Their demand stays equal because festivals always raise demand.
Their demand may fall because the food becomes a substitute good.

why.Their demand may rise because the food g: This reverses the effect of declining extra usefulness.
why.Their demand stays equal because festiva: This ignores that less extra usefulness can reduce demand.
why.Their demand may fall because the food b: This wrongly explains the fall using substitution instead of usefulness.

activities.explanation: Demand may fall as consuming more gives less extra usefulness.

lessons.title: Supply and the Law of Supply

activities.prompt: What happens to the mango supply when its price changes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How price changes supply
activities.body: The law of supply connects price and quantity supplied. Individual supply is the quantity one seller offers at different prices. Market supply is the sum of all individual supplies. When prices rise, producers gain more profit and offer more. They may also increase output, and new firms may enter the market. When prices fall, quantity supplied falls.
keyPoints: Higher prices encourage producers to supply more.
Individual supply comes from one seller.
Market supply includes every seller's supply.
activities.explanation: Price helps decide how much producers offer for sale.

activities.prompt: A mango seller gets a higher price for each mango. What should happen to the number of mangoes offered?
steps: First, the seller can earn more from each mango.
Then, the higher price makes selling more profitable.
So, the seller has a reason to offer more mangoes.
Therefore, quantity supplied increases as price increases.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: When price increases, quantity supplied also increases.
activities.explanation: Higher prices increase profitability. Producers respond by increasing output.

activities.prompt: When price rises, quantity supplied ______.
activities.hint: Think about what producers do when selling becomes more profitable.
activities.explanation: A higher price encourages producers to offer a larger quantity.

activities.prompt: Why are mangoes costly at the start of the season?
options: Supply is low
Supply is high
Demand is low
Demand is missing
activities.explanation: Mangoes are costly at the season's start because supply is low.

activities.prompt: Which meaning matches individual supply?
options: The quantity offered by one seller
The quantity bought by one buyer
The total quantity offered by all sellers
The quantity one seller offers at one price
activities.explanation: Individual supply is what one seller offers at different prices.

activities.prompt: Market supply equals the total of all individual supplies.
activities.explanation: Market supply is the sum of every seller's individual supply.

activities.prompt: Match each market situation to its result.
activities.explanation: Price changes affect supply. Supply and demand also influence market prices.

activities.prompt: A product's price rises. Which result best follows?
options: Supply and output both increase
Supply and output both decrease
Supply stays exactly the same
Output alone stays the same
activities.explanation: Higher prices encourage greater supply and output. New firms may also be attracted.

activities.prompt: Market supply is the sum of all ______ supplies.
activities.hint: Think about the supply provided by each seller.
activities.explanation: Each seller's individual supply adds to the market's total supply.

activities.prompt: Mangoes sell for more today. What will the seller offer?
options: The seller will offer more mangoes.
The seller will offer fewer mangoes.
The seller will offer the same mangoes.
The seller will stop selling mangoes.

This reverses the effect of a higher price on supply.
This ignores the reason producers increase output at higher prices.
This does not follow the direct relationship between price and supply.

activities.explanation: This matches the fact that higher prices encourage more output.

activities.prompt: A higher price makes selling profitable. What may happen next?
options: New firms may enter the market.
Existing firms may leave the market.
Supply may fall below demand.
Prices may fall below cost.

This mistakes an incentive to enter for an incentive to leave.
This focuses on a later balance, not the stated effect.
This adds a cost rule not given by the facts.

activities.explanation: Higher prices can attract new firms to the market.

lessons.title: Other Determinants of Supply

activities.prompt: What makes sellers offer more or less of a good?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why supply can change
activities.body: Supply can change for reasons other than a good's own price. High chickpea prices may make a farmer grow more chickpeas. Better technology can lower production costs. Drip irrigation and weather sensors can raise crop production. Cold storage helps farmers supply mangoes to distant markets. Suppliers also watch expected demand. They make more when demand may rise soon. Some hold back potatoes to sell later at higher prices.
keyPoints: Profitability and technology can affect supply.
Suppliers respond to expected demand.
Some suppliers delay selling for higher prices.
activities.explanation: These factors can change how much producers supply.

activities.prompt: A farmer wants more crops. Can drip irrigation and weather sensors help?
steps: The farmer wants more crops because lower costs allow more production.
Drip irrigation and weather sensors can raise crop production.
They use better technology, which can reduce production costs.
Lower costs allow producers to make more, so crop production may rise.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Different supply choices
activities.body: Suppliers plan around expected demand. They increase production when demand should rise soon. They reduce it when demand should fall. Potato wholesalers may delay selling to seek higher prices later. Technology can reduce costs, while irrigation and sensors can raise harvests. Cold storage can open distant mango markets. Supply choices can also reflect profitable alternatives.
keyPoints: Expected demand guides production decisions.
Technology and storage can increase supply.
Profitability can affect the choice to produce a good.
activities.explanation: These choices show how supply responds to prices, costs, technology, and expectations.

activities.prompt: More sellers can make supply exceed demand and push prices down.
activities.explanation: More sellers can add supply, and extra supply can push prices down.

activities.prompt: Better technology can reduce ______ and allow producers to make more.
activities.hint: Producers spend less when this falls.
activities.explanation: Better technology lowers costs, so producers can make more goods.

activities.prompt: Match each change with its possible result.
pairs: Supply can be lower than demand
activities.explanation: Each outcome follows from the matching change in sellers, technology, or storage.

activities.prompt: Put this production change in the correct order.
activities.explanation: The sequence shows how better technology can lead to greater production.

activities.prompt: What will suppliers do when they expect demand to fall soon?
options: They reduce production
They make more goods
They raise crop yields
They widen their markets
activities.explanation: Suppliers reduce production when they expect demand to fall soon.

activities.prompt: Why may potato wholesalers hold back their supply?
options: To sell later at higher prices
To reduce their production costs
To supply distant mango markets
To raise demand at once
activities.explanation: Wholesalers may wait for a chance to sell at higher prices.

activities.prompt: Chickpea prices are high. Should a farmer grow more chickpeas or potatoes?
options: More chickpeas, because their profitability may be higher.
More potatoes, because their profitability may be higher.
More chickpeas, because potato prices must also rise.
More potatoes, because chickpea prices must soon fall.

why.More potatoes, because their profitabili: This wrongly ignores chickpea profitability when choosing a crop.
why.More chickpeas, because potato prices mu: This wrongly links higher chickpea supply to potato prices.
why.More potatoes, because chickpea prices m: This wrongly assumes high chickpea prices will soon fall.

activities.explanation: High chickpea prices can make growing chickpeas more profitable.

activities.prompt: One market has many sellers. Another has few sellers. Where may prices be higher?
options: The market with few sellers, because supply may be lower.
The market with many sellers, because supply may be lower.
The market with few sellers, because demand may be lower.
The market with many sellers, because supply may exceed demand.

why.The market with many sellers, because su: This wrongly combines many sellers with lower supply.
why.The market with few sellers, because dem: This wrongly assumes fewer sellers mean lower demand.
why.The market with many sellers, because su: More sellers can make supply exceed demand, pushing prices down.

activities.explanation: Fewer sellers can leave supply below demand, pushing prices up.

activities.prompt: A farmer uses drip irrigation and weather sensors. What may happen to crop production?
options: It may rise because better technology lowers production costs.
It may fall because better technology raises production costs.
It may stay because production costs do not matter.
It may fall because better technology reduces crop production.

why.It may fall because better technology ra: This reverses the link between lower costs and more production.
why.It may stay because production costs do: This wrongly says production costs do not affect how much is produced.
why.It may fall because better technology re: This confuses better technology with less crop production.

activities.explanation: Better technology can reduce costs and allow producers to make more.

activities.prompt: One supplier expects rising demand. Another expects falling demand. Who produces more?
options: The first supplier, because expected demand supports more production.
The second supplier, because expected demand supports more production.
The first supplier, because expected demand supports less production.
The second supplier, because expected demand supports less production.

why.The second supplier, because expected de: This reverses how expected demand affects production.
why.The first supplier, because expected dem: The first supplier expects rising demand, which leads to more production.
why.The second supplier, because expected de: The second supplier expects falling demand, which leads to less production.

activities.explanation: Suppliers produce more when they expect demand to rise soon.

activities.prompt: Potato prices may rise later. What will wholesalers do with supply now?
options: They may hold back supply to sell later at higher prices.
They may add supply now to sell later at higher prices.
They may stop selling now to buy more potatoes later.
They may lower prices now to sell more potatoes today.

why.They may add supply now to sell later at: This misunderstands higher later prices as a reason to sell now.
why.They may stop selling now to buy more po: This wrongly treats waiting for higher prices as buying more.
why.They may lower prices now to sell more p: This wrongly uses today's lower price instead of waiting.

activities.explanation: Holding back supply can let wholesalers sell later at higher prices.
