lessons.title: Market Equilibrium and Changing Markets

activities.prompt: What makes a market price settle, and what happens when things change?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Markets Find Balance
activities.body: Buyers and sellers negotiate market prices. Demand means what buyers want to buy. Supply means what sellers offer to sell. Prices depend on how demand and supply interact. A low price can create excess demand. A high price can create excess supply. For mangoes, equilibrium is ₹100, with a quantity of 12 kg. At equilibrium, there is no pressure for price to change. Real markets keep moving as conditions change.
keyPoints: Prices depend on demand and supply.
Low prices create excess demand.
High prices create excess supply.
activities.explanation: This card shows how demand and supply affect prices in changing markets.

activities.prompt: Face mask demand rises rapidly during COVID-19. What changes in the market?
steps: Many buyers suddenly want face masks, so demand rises quickly.
This changes market conditions because demand has increased rapidly.
Demand and supply interact to determine prices in the market.
Therefore, changing demand can move the mask market’s equilibrium.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Negotiating Market Prices
activities.prompt: Which statement best explains how market prices are negotiated?
options: Buyers and sellers agree on prices.
Buyers pay whatever sellers ask for.
Sellers set prices without buyer agreement.
Market prices change without buyer-seller talks.
activities.explanation: Market prices are negotiated between what buyers will pay and sellers will accept.

activities.title: The Mango Quantity
activities.prompt: The equilibrium quantity of mangoes is ______ kg.
activities.hint: Find the equilibrium quantity for mangoes.
activities.explanation: At equilibrium, the quantity of mangoes demanded equals the quantity supplied.

activities.title: From Low Price to High Price
activities.prompt: Put these market states in order, from the lowest price to the highest price.
activities.explanation: A low price creates excess demand. A high price creates excess supply.

activities.title: Finding Equilibrium on a Graph
activities.prompt: On a demand and supply graph, where is equilibrium shown?
options: Where the two curves intersect.
Where demand alone moves upward.
Where supply alone moves downward.
Where the price line stays highest.
activities.explanation: The demand and supply curves meet at equilibrium. There is no pressure for price to change.

activities.title: A Sudden Change in Demand
activities.prompt: During COVID-19, what happened to demand for face masks?
options: It fell steadily.
It stayed unchanged.
It grew slowly.
It surged rapidly.
activities.explanation: During COVID-19, demand for face masks surged rapidly.

activities.title: Matching Market Examples
activities.prompt: Match each market example with its correct lesson detail.
activities.explanation: Hotel prices change with demand. Low prices create excess demand, while high prices create excess supply.

activities.prompt: The toy price is too low at a school fair. What happens?
options: Buyers want more toys than sellers offer.
Sellers offer more toys than buyers want.
Buyers and sellers want equal amounts of toys.
Buyers and sellers agree on one stable price.

why.Sellers offer more toys than buyers want: This reverses excess demand and excess supply.
why.Buyers and sellers want equal amounts of: Equal demand and supply occur at equilibrium, not at a very low price.
why.Buyers and sellers agree on one stable p: A very low price does not create a stable agreement.

activities.explanation: A price that is too low causes excess demand.

activities.prompt: One stall charges too much. Another charges too little. What is true?
options: The costly stall has excess supply; the cheap stall has excess demand.
The costly stall has excess demand; the cheap stall has excess supply.
Both stalls have excess demand because buyers keep wanting mangoes.
Both stalls have equal demand and supply at their different prices.

why.The costly stall has excess demand; the: This swaps the effects of prices that are too high and too low.
why.Both stalls have excess demand because b: This wrongly applies the low-price rule to both stalls.
why.Both stalls have equal demand and supply: This assumes unequal prices still give equal demand and supply.

activities.explanation: Too high a price causes excess supply, while too low causes excess demand.

activities.prompt: At ₹100, buyers want 12 kg of mangoes. Sellers also offer 12 kg. What follows?
options: The market is at equilibrium at ₹100.
The market has excess demand at ₹100.
The market has excess supply at ₹100.
The market price must change at ₹100.

Equal demand and supply show no excess demand.
Equal demand and supply show no excess supply.
This mistakes a balanced market for one needing change.

activities.explanation: Demand equals supply, so there is no pressure for price change.

activities.prompt: Hotel prices change with season and special situations. Why?
options: Prices respond to demand as market conditions change.
Prices ignore demand because sellers choose them alone.
Prices change only when the equilibrium quantity disappears.
Prices stay equal because buyers and sellers never interact.

why.Prices ignore demand because sellers cho: This wrongly assumes sellers act without buyers’ demand.
why.Prices change only when the equilibrium: This wrongly believes a changing quantity always removes equilibrium.
why.Prices stay equal because buyers and sel: This wrongly ignores the interaction between buyers and sellers.

activities.explanation: Hotel prices respond to demand, season and special situations.

lessons.title: Role of Government in the Economy

activities.prompt: How can government action help the economy without causing new problems?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Government Affects Markets
activities.body: Government can shape markets by limiting unfair practices and setting maximum prices for essential goods. A price floor is the lower limit on wages. Government can provide public goods, such as parks, and fund goods that benefit everyone. A monopoly may charge more and supply less. However, excessive intervention can harm markets. Low price limits can reduce supply, while heavy regulation and price controls can weaken investment in new ideas.
keyPoints: Government protects people and may set maximum prices.
Public goods can be provided or funded by government.
Too much control can reduce supply and investment.
activities.explanation: Government actions can help people, but they can also harm markets.

activities.prompt: A shop raises the price of medicine, and many families cannot afford it. What should the government do?
steps: The government can set a maximum price for essential medicines.
This can protect buyers from unfair prices.
But a price fixed below the market may reduce producers' supply.
So the government must balance protection for buyers with enough supply.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: During COVID-19, what did the government do to the maximum retail price of sanitisers?
options: Set a cap on it
Remove the price cap
Allow any selling price
Raise it without limit
activities.explanation: During COVID-19, the government capped the maximum retail price of sanitisers.

activities.prompt: The lower limit on wages is called a price ______.
activities.hint: Think of the lowest allowed level.
activities.explanation: The lower limit on wages is called a price floor.

activities.prompt: Every user of a public park must pay for its use.
activities.explanation: A family may hope to use a public park without paying if others pay.

activities.prompt: Match each example with its government role or possible effect.
pairs: May be used without paying if others pay
activities.explanation: Government actions protect people, provide shared goods and can sometimes affect market incentives.

activities.prompt: Which government action can require many regulations, licences and permits?
options: Excessive government intervention
Public funding for shared goods
Maximum medicine price caps
Rules against unfair practices
activities.explanation: Government intervention can require many regulations, licences and permits.

activities.prompt: Put this effect of a low price limit in order.
items: A price is fixed below market level
Producers' motivation to supply can fall
The market may receive less supply
activities.explanation: A below-market fixed price can weaken producers' motivation to supply.

activities.prompt: Medicine prices are fixed below market levels. What may happen next?
options: Producers may supply fewer medicines.
Buyers may buy many more medicines.
Shops may raise medicine prices freely.
Workers may demand more medicines daily.

It mistakes lower prices for a reason to buy much more.
A fixed price limits how high sellers may charge.
It wrongly links medicine prices to workers' daily demand.

activities.explanation: A price below the market can reduce producers' motivation to supply.

activities.prompt: One shop is the only battery seller. Compared with a competitive market, what may happen?
options: It may charge more and supply less.
It may charge less and supply less.
It may charge more and supply more.
It may charge less and supply more.

It wrongly combines lower prices with lower supply.
It wrongly combines higher prices with more supply.
It wrongly assumes monopoly power must lower prices.

activities.explanation: A monopoly can charge higher prices and supply less.

activities.prompt: COVID-19 sanitisers had a maximum price. What was this control for?
options: Stop sellers from charging unfair prices.
Stop sellers from selling any sanitisers.
Make the maximum price of every medicine fixed.
Make workers pay less for all goods.

why.Stop sellers from selling any sanitisers: A maximum price limits charges; it does not stop all sales.
why.Make the maximum price of every medicine: The cap applied to sanitisers, not every medicine.
A sanitiser price cap does not set prices for all goods.

activities.explanation: The cap protects consumers from unfair retail prices.

activities.prompt: A new product needs many permits. Its price is fixed below market levels. What may discourage investment?
options: Many rules and controls may reduce investment in new ideas.
Many rules and controls may attract many new sellers.
Many rules and controls may improve every product quickly.
Many rules and controls may remove the need for permits.

why.Many rules and controls may attract many: It wrongly assumes that more barriers attract more sellers.
why.Many rules and controls may improve ever: It wrongly assumes that more controls quickly improve every product.
why.Many rules and controls may remove the n: It wrongly assumes that controls make permits unnecessary.

activities.explanation: Heavy regulation and price controls can reduce incentives to invest.

activities.context: Srivalli wanted mangoes but needed enough purchasing power to buy them. When the price fell to ₹100 per kg, she bought 2 kg. She could buy more only if the price was lower and less if it were higher. Other buyers also changed how much they wanted when the price changed, so their responses together made the market demand curve flatter. Thus, the price and quantity demanded moved in opposite directions.
activities.prompt: If the price of mangoes rises above ₹100 per kg, what is likely to happen to the quantity Srivalli demands?
options: She will demand a smaller quantity of mangoes.
She will demand a larger quantity of mangoes.
She will demand exactly the same quantity of mangoes.
She will demand no mangoes at all.

why.She will demand a larger quantity of man: This reverses the effect of the price fall described in the case.
why.She will demand exactly the same quantit: This wrongly treats demand as unchanged when price changes.
This wrongly assumes that a price rise always reduces demand to zero.

activities.explanation: Price and quantity demanded have an inverse relationship.

activities.context: Srivalli wanted mangoes but needed enough purchasing power to buy them. When the price fell to ₹100 per kg, she bought 2 kg. She could buy more only if the price was lower and less if it were higher. Other buyers also changed how much they wanted when the price changed, so their responses together made the market demand curve flatter. Thus, the price and quantity demanded moved in opposite directions.
activities.prompt: Why is the market demand curve in this case flatter than an individual demand curve?
options: Many buyers respond to the same price change.
Only Srivalli responds to the price change.
Buyers do not respond to a change in price.
The total quantity wanted remains unchanged when price changes.

why.Only Srivalli responds to the price chan: This wrongly limits the market to one consumer.
why.Buyers do not respond to a change in pri: This wrongly denies the inverse relationship.
why.The total quantity wanted remains unchan: This wrongly ignores changes in the quantity wanted by buyers.

activities.explanation: The market demand curve is flatter because many buyers respond to the same price change.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Demand means being willing and able to buy at a particular price.
Reason (R): A wish to buy something is not enough without purchasing power.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains why willingness to buy must be supported by the ability to buy.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Market demand is the total quantity wanted by all potential buyers.
Reason (R): The market demand curve is flatter because only one buyer responds to a price change.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because many buyers, not only one, respond to a price change.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between individual demand and market demand, and state how a demand schedule becomes a demand curve.
activities.answer: Individual demand shows how one consumer’s quantity demanded changes at different prices. Market demand is the total quantity wanted by all potential buyers. A demand schedule shows an individual consumer’s quantities at different prices. When this schedule is shown graphically, it becomes a demand curve. The market demand curve is flatter because many buyers respond to the same price change, while individual demand concerns the response of only one consumer.
points: Individual demand concerns one consumer’s quantity demanded.
Market demand is the total quantity wanted by all potential buyers.
A demand schedule becomes a demand curve when shown graphically.
The market demand curve is flatter because many buyers respond to the same price change.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a festival week, a shop notices that demand for umbrellas changes with the weather. A household has bought a smartphone and needs matching earphones. Separately, coffee has become more expensive, so some consumers switch to tea. The shopkeeper wonders whether customers will buy umbrellas now or wait, because they expect the umbrella price to fall later.
activities.prompt: What may happen if coffee remains more expensive than before?
options: Many consumers may switch from coffee to tea.
More consumers may begin buying coffee as its price rises.
Tea and coffee may become a complementary pair.
Consumers may stop buying tea and coffee together.

why.More consumers may begin buying coffee a: A higher price does not automatically encourage consumers to buy more of that product.
why.Tea and coffee may become a complementar: Goods used as alternatives are substitutes, not complements.
why.Consumers may stop buying tea and coffee: Switching between substitutes does not mean that consumers stop buying both.

activities.explanation: Tea and coffee are substitute goods, so consumers can replace coffee with tea.

activities.context: During a festival week, a shop notices that demand for umbrellas changes with the weather. A household has bought a smartphone and needs matching earphones. Separately, coffee has become more expensive, so some consumers switch to tea. The shopkeeper wonders whether customers will buy umbrellas now or wait, because they expect the umbrella price to fall later.
activities.prompt: What should the shopkeeper expect if many customers expect umbrella prices to fall later?
options: Many customers may postpone buying umbrellas.
Many customers will buy umbrellas immediately.
All customers will buy umbrellas regardless of price expectations.
No customer will alter buying time because of expectations.

why.Many customers will buy umbrellas immedi: Buying immediately is more likely when consumers expect prices to rise.
why.All customers will buy umbrellas regardl: Price expectations can affect the timing of purchases.
why.No customer will alter buying time becau: Expectations about future prices can change buying decisions.

activities.explanation: Consumers usually postpone purchases when they expect prices to fall.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): When coffee becomes more expensive, some consumers may switch to tea.
Reason (R): Tea and coffee are substitute goods, so consumers can replace coffee with tea.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the relationship between tea and coffee explains the possible switch.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): When household income rises, consumers can usually afford to buy more.
Reason (R): Tastes and preferences have no influence on demand.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because tastes and preferences do influence demand.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between substitute goods and complementary goods, using suitable examples.
activities.answer: Substitute goods are products that consumers can use in place of one another, while complementary goods are products that consumers generally use together. Tea and coffee are substitutes because a consumer may switch to tea when coffee becomes more expensive. Smartphones and earphones are complementary goods because they are generally used together. Therefore, a change in the price or availability of either kind of related good can affect demand for the other product. This is why dearer coffee may lead to greater demand for tea.
points: Defines substitute goods correctly
Defines complementary goods correctly
Explains tea and coffee as substitutes
Explains smartphones and earphones as complements
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At the start of the mango season, mangoes are costly because supply is low. If the price rises, sellers can make more profit, so each seller may offer a larger quantity. The higher price may also encourage new sellers to enter the market. Market supply is therefore likely to grow, while the extra supply can eventually help bring prices down when supply exceeds demand.
activities.prompt: After the price of mangoes rises, what is the most likely change in the market?
options: The total quantity offered by sellers will increase.
The total quantity offered by sellers will decrease.
The total quantity offered by sellers will remain the same because only one seller's offer counts.
The total quantity offered by sellers will remain the same even if new firms enter the market.

why.The total quantity offered by sellers wi: This reverses the direct relationship between price and quantity supplied.
Market supply includes the supplies of all sellers, not only one.
New firms would add their own supplies to the market.

activities.explanation: Higher prices encourage greater output and may attract new firms.

activities.context: At the start of the mango season, mangoes are costly because supply is low. If the price rises, sellers can make more profit, so each seller may offer a larger quantity. The higher price may also encourage new sellers to enter the market. Market supply is therefore likely to grow, while the extra supply can eventually help bring prices down when supply exceeds demand.
activities.prompt: The mango price falls because supply exceeds demand. What change in the sellers' quantities should be expected?
options: The quantity each seller offers will fall.
The quantity each seller offers will rise.
The quantity each seller offers will stay unchanged because market supply exceeds demand.
The quantity each seller offers will stay unchanged because lower prices attract new firms.

why.The quantity each seller offers will ris: This reverses the law of supply.
why.The quantity each seller offers will sta: A change in price can change individual supply even when market supply exceeds demand.
It is higher prices, not lower prices, that can attract new firms.

activities.explanation: A decrease in price causes the quantity supplied to fall.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): As the market price rises, market supply tends to rise.
Reason (R): Higher prices make output more profitable and can attract new sellers.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the higher profitability and entry of sellers explain the rise in market supply.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): When price falls, individual supply rises.
Reason (R): A decrease in price reduces the quantity offered by a seller.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion reverses the law of supply, while the reason correctly states that lower prices reduce the quantity supplied.

activities.prompt: Explain how the law of supply connects price, quantity supplied, profitability, and the supply curve.
activities.answer: The law of supply describes a direct relationship between price and quantity supplied. When price increases, the quantity supplied increases; when price decreases, it falls. One reason is profitability: higher prices encourage producers to increase output. Higher prices can also attract new firms to the market, adding to the total quantity supplied. Therefore, a higher price tends to produce a greater supply and an upward-sloping supply curve.
points: The law of supply states a direct price–quantity relationship.
A higher price increases the quantity supplied.
A lower price reduces the quantity supplied.
Higher profitability and new firms increase supply, giving an upward-sloping curve.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Suppose chickpea prices are high, so a farmer may grow more chickpeas. A new drip irrigation system and weather sensors help the farmer raise crop production. Several sellers also bring chickpeas to the market. Some potato wholesalers hold back potatoes to sell later at higher prices. The farmer uses cold storage for mangoes, making it possible to supply mangoes to distant markets.
activities.prompt: If chickpea prices remain high, what may the farmer do next?
options: Increase chickpea production
Reduce chickpea production
Stop growing chickpeas
Keep production unchanged

why.Reduce chickpea production: Higher profitability can support increased output rather than reduced output.
why.Stop growing chickpeas: The case gives no reason for the farmer to stop growing chickpeas.
why.Keep production unchanged: High prices do not suggest that production should remain unchanged.

activities.explanation: High chickpea prices can encourage the farmer to grow more.

activities.context: Suppose chickpea prices are high, so a farmer may grow more chickpeas. A new drip irrigation system and weather sensors help the farmer raise crop production. Several sellers also bring chickpeas to the market. Some potato wholesalers hold back potatoes to sell later at higher prices. The farmer uses cold storage for mangoes, making it possible to supply mangoes to distant markets.
activities.prompt: How does cold storage change what the farmer can do with mangoes?
options: It lets the farmer supply mangoes to markets farther away.
It prevents the farmer from supplying mangoes outside the local area.
It limits mango supply to sellers in the local market.
It increases the number of mango sellers in distant markets.

why.It prevents the farmer from supplying ma: This reverses the stated effect of cold storage.
why.It limits mango supply to sellers in the: The case says cold storage expands the farmer's market reach.
why.It increases the number of mango sellers: Cold storage helps move supply; it does not create additional sellers.

activities.explanation: Cold storage helps farmers supply mangoes to distant markets.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A farmer may grow more chickpeas when chickpea prices are high.
Reason (R): High chickpea prices can make growing chickpeas more profitable.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why high chickpea prices may encourage greater production.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market

activities.title: What Shows Demand?
activities.prompt: Which situation shows demand?
options: A buyer wants and can buy at a price.
A buyer wants it but lacks purchasing power.
A seller offers goods at changing prices.
A shop keeps the same price for goods.
activities.explanation: Good choice. Demand needs both willingness and ability to buy.

activities.title: A Wish Is Enough
activities.prompt: Demand only needs a wish to buy something.
activities.explanation: Not quite. Demand also needs purchasing power.

activities.title: The Buying Power
activities.prompt: Demand needs purchasing ______, not only a wish to buy.
activities.hint: What helps a buyer actually pay?
activities.explanation: Well done. Willingness and purchasing power together create demand.

activities.title: Market Words
activities.prompt: Match each market idea with its correct meaning.
pairs: Total quantity wanted by potential buyers
Point where demand and supply intersect
activities.explanation: Great matching. These ideas help you compare buying and selling in a market.

activities.title: A Price That Is Too High
activities.prompt: At a price above equilibrium, what is likely to happen?
options: Excess supply appears and prices fall.
Excess demand appears and prices rise.
Supply equals demand without changing.
Producers face no price pressure.
activities.explanation: Yes. A high price creates excess supply, which pushes prices down.

activities.title: Price Pressure
activities.prompt: At market equilibrium, there is pressure for the price to change.
activities.explanation: False. At equilibrium, there is no pressure for the price to change.

activities.title: The Price Floor
activities.prompt: The lower limit on wages is called a price ______.
activities.hint: It is a minimum level, not a maximum.
activities.explanation: Correct. A price floor sets a lower limit on wages.

activities.title: Finding Market Equilibrium
activities.prompt: Put the steps towards finding market equilibrium in order.
items: Set out one seller's quantities at different prices
Add the supplies of all sellers
Find where supply and demand meet
activities.explanation: Perfect sequence. You moved from one seller to the whole market.

chapters.title: Oceans and Life
chapters.summary: In this chapter: ocean relief and the ocean floor; waves and coastal landforms; tides and their uses; ocean currents.

lessons.title: Ocean Relief and the Ocean Floor

activities.prompt: What hidden landscapes lie beneath the ocean’s waves?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Underwater Landforms
activities.body: The ocean floor has underwater landforms called submarine relief or ocean relief. These include underwater mountains, valleys, plateaus, and trenches. The Mariana Trench in the Pacific Ocean is the deepest place on Earth. The Mid-Ocean Ridge is the world’s longest mountain range. Mauna Kea in Hawai‘i is even taller than Mount Everest.
keyPoints: Submarine relief means underwater landforms.
Ocean relief includes mountains, valleys, plateaus, and trenches.
The Mariana Trench is the deepest place on Earth.
activities.explanation: The ocean floor has many remarkable landforms.

activities.prompt: A sea map shows flat, deep places beside long mountains. Why are they different?
steps: It looks flat because an abyssal plain is vast and flat.
It looks long because the Mid-Ocean Ridge is the world's longest range.
It marks great depth because the Mariana Trench is deepest on Earth.
They are ocean relief because they are underwater landforms.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Features of the Ocean Floor
activities.body: The continental shelf holds rich marine life, oil, and gas. The continental slope marks the true edge of a continent. An abyssal plain is the vast, flat, and deep ocean floor. Ocean trenches are the deepest parts of the ocean. A seamount rises from the ocean floor but does not reach the sea surface.
keyPoints: The continental shelf holds marine life, oil, and gas.
The continental slope marks the continent’s true edge.
An abyssal plain is vast, flat, and deep.
activities.explanation: These descriptions show different features of the ocean floor.

activities.prompt: Which place is the deepest place on Earth?
options: Mid-Ocean Ridge
Abyssal Plain
Mariana Trench
Continental Shelf
activities.explanation: The Mariana Trench is the deepest place on Earth.

activities.prompt: The Mid-Ocean Ridge is the world’s longest mountain range.
activities.explanation: The lesson tells you that this underwater range is the world’s longest.

activities.prompt: Match each ocean feature with its description.
pairs: Vast, flat, and deep ocean floor
activities.explanation: Each description matches a special fact about its ocean feature.

activities.prompt: Which description matches a guyot?
options: A flat-topped mountain formed from an old seamount
A mountain that reaches above the sea surface
The deepest part of the ocean
A long range formed by volcanic activity
activities.explanation: A guyot is a flat-topped underwater mountain formed from an old seamount.

activities.prompt: A seamount rises above the sea surface.
activities.explanation: A seamount rises from the ocean floor but does not reach the sea surface.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the Mid-Ocean Ridge is correct?
options: It is the world’s longest mountain range.
It is the deepest place on Earth.
It marks the true edge of a continent.
It is rich in marine life, oil, and gas.
activities.explanation: It is also an immense underwater mountain range formed by volcanic activity.

activities.prompt: A map shows the Mariana Trench and an abyssal plain. Which place is deepest?
options: The Mariana Trench is deeper than the abyssal plain.
The abyssal plain is deeper than the Mariana Trench.
Both places have exactly the same ocean depth.
The abyssal plain is not part of the ocean floor.

why.The abyssal plain is deeper than the Mar: Wrong, because this swaps the deep plain with the deeper trench.
why.Both places have exactly the same ocean: Wrong, because the two places do not have the same depth.
why.The abyssal plain is not part of the oce: Wrong, because an abyssal plain is part of the ocean floor.

activities.explanation: Right, because the Mariana Trench is the deepest place on Earth.

activities.prompt: Volcanic activity forms a huge underwater mountain range. What follows from this fact?
options: This range is the Mid-Ocean Ridge.
This range is a flat-topped guyot.
This range is a vast abyssal plain.
This range is the deepest ocean trench.

Wrong, because this mistakes a long range for a flat-topped mountain.
Wrong, because this mistakes a mountain range for the flat deep floor.
Wrong, because this mistakes a mountain range for a deep trench.

activities.explanation: Right, because the Mid-Ocean Ridge forms through volcanic activity.

activities.prompt: A map shows one feature with marine life, oil, and gas. Another marks a continent's true edge. Which pair fits?
options: The shelf has resources; the slope marks the true edge.
The slope has resources; the shelf marks the true edge.
The trench has resources; the ridge marks the true edge.
The plain has resources; the trench marks the true edge.

why.The slope has resources; the shelf marks: Wrong, because this swaps the continental shelf and slope.
why.The trench has resources; the ridge mark: Wrong, because this gives resources to a trench and an edge to a ridge.
why.The plain has resources; the trench mark: Wrong, because this gives resources to a plain and an edge to a trench.

activities.explanation: Right, because the shelf has those resources, and the slope marks the true edge.

lessons.title: Waves and Coastal Landforms

activities.prompt: What shapes a coastline as waves travel from the open ocean to shore?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Waves Shape Coasts
activities.body: Waves are the alternating rise and fall of the ocean’s surface. Winds across water mainly cause waves. Wave energy can travel across oceans. A crest is a high point. A trough is a low point. Erosion means wearing away. Sediment is loose material. Waves shape coasts through erosion and sediment movement. Wave deposits can form beaches. Wave erosion can form sea cracks, caves, arches, sea stacks, and stumps.
keyPoints: Winds blowing across water are the main cause of waves.
The crest is high, while the trough is low.
Waves shape coasts through erosion and sediment movement.
activities.explanation: These words help you describe waves and the coasts they shape.

activities.prompt: After a windy day at the sea, a child sees waves. Why can these waves change the coast?
steps: Winds blowing across water mainly cause waves.
These waves can carry energy across oceans over long distances.
At the coast, waves cause erosion and move sediment.
Therefore, strong storm winds can create huge waves that damage coasts.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Storm Waves and Tsunamis
activities.body: Strong storm winds can create huge waves that damage coastlines. Tsunamis are giant waves, mainly caused by underwater earthquakes. A run-up height shows how high tsunami water rises. The run-up height can reach 30 metres or even more. Large waves can carry energy across oceans over long distances.
keyPoints: Strong storm winds can create huge waves.
Underwater earthquakes mainly cause tsunamis.
A tsunami’s run-up height can reach 30 metres or even more.
activities.explanation: This card explains huge waves and the height a tsunami can reach.

activities.title: What Is a Wave?
activities.prompt: Which one describes a wave?
options: The ocean surface rising and falling
Sediment moving along a coast
Coastlines wearing away
Beaches forming from deposits
activities.explanation: A wave is the alternating rise and fall of the ocean’s surface.

activities.title: Match the Coastal Words
activities.prompt: Match each wave word to its meaning.
activities.explanation: You matched the high and low parts of waves with coastal features.

activities.title: What Causes Waves?
activities.prompt: Waves are mainly caused by movement of sediment.
activities.explanation: Winds blowing across water are the main cause of waves.

activities.title: The Main Cause of Tsunamis
activities.prompt: Tsunamis are giant waves mainly caused by underwater ______.
activities.hint: This event happens below the sea.
activities.explanation: Tsunamis are mainly caused by underwater earthquakes.

activities.title: Coastal Features from Wave Erosion
activities.prompt: Put the wave-erosion features in development order.
activities.explanation: Wave erosion can form these coastal features in this order.

activities.title: Spot the Correct Cause
activities.prompt: Which sentence about tsunamis is correct?
options: Underwater earthquakes mainly cause them.
Strong storm winds mainly cause them.
Wave deposits mainly create them.
Wave erosion mainly creates them.
activities.explanation: Tsunamis are giant waves mainly caused by underwater earthquakes.

activities.prompt: A beach is visible on a calm coast. Later, strong storm winds create huge waves there. What is most likely to happen to that coast?
options: Huge waves may damage the coastline.
More wave deposits will surely protect the coast.
An underwater earthquake will cause the waves.
The coast will remain completely unchanged.

why.More wave deposits will surely protect t: This mistake assumes deposits will protect the coast despite storm damage.
why.An underwater earthquake will cause the: This mistake uses the tsunami cause instead of the storm-wind cause.
why.The coast will remain completely unchang: This mistake ignores that waves shape coasts through erosion and sediment movement.

activities.explanation: This is right because strong storm winds can create huge waves that damage coastlines.

activities.prompt: A map shows caves, arches, and sea stacks along one coast. What process mainly made these features?
options: Wave erosion mainly made these features.
Wave deposition mainly made these features.
Strong winds mainly made these features.
Underwater earthquakes mainly made these features.

why.Wave deposition mainly made these featur: This mistake confuses deposition, which forms features such as beaches, with erosion.
This mistake skips the wave erosion process between storm winds and these features.
why.Underwater earthquakes mainly made these: This mistake mixes up the cause of tsunamis with the erosion that makes landforms.

activities.explanation: This is right because wave erosion can form sea cracks, caves, arches, and stacks.

activities.prompt: A wave erodes a coast. A long crack opens in it. What may form inside that crack?
options: A sea cave may form inside the crack.
A sea stack may stand beside the crack.
A beach may grow inside the crack.
A crest may rise inside the crack.

This mistake names a different erosion feature instead of following the crack-to-cave step.
This mistake confuses deposition with the erosion of a crack.
This mistake confuses a wave's high point with a coastal landform.

activities.explanation: This is right because wave erosion can form caves inside sea cracks.

lessons.title: Tides and Their Uses

activities.prompt: What makes ocean water rise and fall like a gentle heartbeat?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Tides
activities.body: Tides are the rhythmic rise and fall of ocean water. They occur twice a day in most parts of the world. High tide is the flood tide. Low tide is the ebb tide. Spring tides occur when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in a straight line. They produce unusually high and low tides. Neap tides occur during the Moon’s first- or third-quarter phase. Neap tides have smaller tidal differences.
keyPoints: High tide is the flood tide; low tide is the ebb tide.
Spring tides occur when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in a straight line.
Neap tides occur at the Moon’s first- or third-quarter phase.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the main ideas about tides.

activities.prompt: A cargo ship is about to enter a harbour. The water is rising. When should the captain plan the arrival?
steps: The rising water is moving towards high tide.
High tides help ships reach harbours more easily.
So the captain should plan the arrival near high tide.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What are tides?
options: The steady flow of seawater towards the shore
The rhythmic rise and fall of ocean water
The daily lifting and dropping of seabed
The regular warming and cooling of seawater
activities.explanation: This is the definition of tides in the lesson.

activities.prompt: High tide is also called the ______ tide.
activities.hint: Look for the other name of high tide.
activities.explanation: The flood tide is another name for high tide.

activities.prompt: Match each tide with its correct description.
pairs: Sun, Earth, and Moon in a straight line
Moon in its first- or third-quarter phase
activities.explanation: These pairs match each tide with its condition.

activities.prompt: How fast can tidal currents reach?
options: 5–6 knots
12 metres
Twice each day
activities.explanation: Tidal currents can reach speeds of 5–6 knots.

activities.prompt: Put these stages for spring tides in order.
items: Sun, Earth, and Moon are in a straight line
Unusually high and unusually low tides
activities.explanation: The straight-line alignment leads to spring tides. They produce unusually high and low tides.

activities.prompt: Which pair correctly describes neap tides?
options: Straight-line alignment; unusually high and low tides
First-quarter Moon; unusually high and low tides
Third-quarter Moon; smaller tidal difference
Straight-line alignment; smaller tidal difference
activities.explanation: Neap tides occur during the Moon’s first- or third-quarter phase. They have a smaller tidal difference.

activities.prompt: In most parts of the world, tides occur twice a day. A boat misses one high tide. What should it expect?
options: It can find another high tide later.
It must wait until the next day.
Low tide will replace the next high tide.
There will be no more tides that day.

This mistake treats one tide as the only tide that day.
why.Low tide will replace the next high tide: This mistake confuses high tide with low tide.
This mistake ignores the second tide in the day.

activities.explanation: Twice a day means another high tide can follow the missed one.

activities.prompt: The Sun, Earth, and Moon are in a straight line. What should happen to the tidal range?
options: It should become much larger than usual.
It should become much smaller than usual.
It should stay the same as usual.
It should vanish for one whole day.

why.It should become much smaller than usual: This mistake confuses spring tides with neap tides.
This mistake thinks a straight line has no tidal effect.
This mistake imagines that aligned positions remove all tidal movement.

activities.explanation: A straight line produces spring tides with an unusually large range.

activities.prompt: The Moon is in its first-quarter phase. What should happen to the difference between high and low tide?
options: It should become smaller than usual.
It should become larger than usual.
It should stay the same as usual.
It should change into no tide.

This mistake confuses neap tides with spring tides.
This mistake thinks the tide difference never changes.
This mistake thinks neap tides mean there are no tides.

activities.explanation: Neap tides have a smaller difference between high and low tide.

activities.prompt: The water is rising near a harbour. How should a sailor plan a ship's arrival?
options: The ship should arrive near high tide.
The ship should arrive near low tide.
The ship should arrive when the water falls.
The ship should ignore the tide.

This mistake confuses rising water with falling water.
why.The ship should arrive when the water fa: This mistake assumes low tide makes harbour entry easier.
This mistake ignores the effect of tides on ships.

activities.explanation: Rising water points towards high tide, which helps ships reach harbours.

activities.prompt: A map shows the Gulf of Khambhat. It says the tidal range is about 12 metres. What does this mean?
options: High and low tide differ by about 12 metres.
The height of high tide alone is 12 metres.
The height of low tide alone is 12 metres.
The two tides together rise about 12 metres.

why.The height of high tide alone is 12 metr: This mistake treats the whole range as only the high tide.
why.The height of low tide alone is 12 metre: This mistake treats the whole range as only the low tide.
why.The two tides together rise about 12 met: This mistake adds both tides instead of comparing them.

activities.explanation: A tidal range is the difference between high and low tide.

activities.prompt: A report says tidal currents can reach 5–6 knots. What does this tell a reader?
options: That speed is possible, but not always present.
That speed is present at all times.
That speed will never happen again.
That speed only happens near low tide.

This mistake adds a low-tide rule not given by the report.

activities.explanation: The word 'can' shows that this speed is possible.

lessons.title: Ocean Currents

activities.prompt: What makes ocean currents move in different directions?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Are Ocean Currents?
activities.body: Ocean currents are continuous streams of water moving in definite directions. Winds, Earth’s rotation, temperature, salinity and ocean shapes influence them. Currents from warmer regions are called warm currents. Maps usually show these in red and cold currents in blue. Ocean movements support marine life. They also aid fishing and travel. They influence climate.
keyPoints: Currents move continuously in definite directions.
Warm currents come from warmer regions.
They support marine life, fishing, travel and climate.
activities.explanation: Currents move continuously and affect ocean life and climate.

activities.prompt: A fishing family wants to find a sea place with many kinds of fish. What should it look for, and why?
steps: The family should look for a place where warm and cold currents meet.
This is because such places are important fishing grounds.
These fishing grounds contain nutrients.
Those nutrients support many kinds of fish, so the meeting place is a good choice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Is an Ocean Current?
activities.prompt: What is an ocean current?
options: Water moving continuously in definite directions
Water changing because of salinity
Water moving because of wind
Colours used on ocean maps
activities.explanation: An ocean current is a continuous stream of water moving in definite directions.

activities.title: The Colour of Cold Currents
activities.prompt: Maps usually show cold currents in red.
activities.explanation: Maps usually show cold currents in blue, not red.

activities.title: Match Currents and Places
activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct description.
pairs: Begins in the Gulf of Mexico
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a current or place with its correct description.

activities.title: Where Currents Meet
activities.prompt: What happens where warm and cold currents meet?
options: They become warm currents
They form important fishing grounds
They become cold currents
They stop moving
activities.explanation: Places where warm and cold currents meet are important fishing grounds.

activities.title: The Gulf Stream’s Journey
activities.prompt: Put these Gulf Stream steps in the correct order.
items: Begins in the Gulf of Mexico
activities.explanation: The Gulf Stream begins in the Gulf of Mexico before flowing towards Norway.

activities.title: The Cold Current Near Canada
activities.prompt: Which current carries freezing water along Canada’s east coast?
options: Warm current
Labrador Current
Cold current
Ocean current
activities.explanation: The Labrador Current carries freezing water along Canada’s east coast.

activities.title: Why Are These Fishing Grounds Important?
activities.prompt: Why are fishing grounds where warm and cold currents meet important?
options: Nutrients support many fish
Salinity blocks every fish
Temperature removes nutrients
Ocean shapes block fish
activities.explanation: These fishing grounds contain nutrients that support many kinds of fish.

activities.prompt: The Gulf Stream leaves the Gulf of Mexico for Norway. What will its water be like near Norway?
options: Relatively warm and still moving.
Freezing and moving north.
Freezing and stopped moving.
Salty and stopped moving.

This confuses the Gulf Stream with the freezing Labrador Current.
This mixes a warm current with a current that stops moving.
This confuses salinity with the temperature and movement of currents.

activities.explanation: says it keeps its water relatively warm, and says currents keep moving.

activities.prompt: Warm and cold currents meet near Canada’s east coast. What makes this place important for fishing?
options: The water has nutrients for many fish.
The water has no nutrients for fish.
The map’s red colour feeds the fish.
The warm current stops all fishing.

This mistakes a fishing ground for a place without nutrients.
This confuses a map colour with something that supports fish.
This confuses a warm current with the meeting of warm and cold currents.

activities.explanation: These meeting grounds contain nutrients that support many kinds of fish.

lessons.title: Cyclones, Tsunamis, and Early Warning Systems

activities.prompt: How can a warning reach us before disaster strikes?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Coastal Warnings Work
activities.body: Cyclones are large rotating storms. Tsunamis are giant waves caused by earthquakes. Early warning systems work like giant alarm systems for coastal areas. They detect hazards, predict disasters, and issue timely warnings. These systems must function continuously. India’s warning services monitor storms on both eastern and western coasts. Public awareness and training programmes matter as much as technology.
keyPoints: Cyclones are large rotating storms
Tsunamis are giant waves caused by earthquakes
Warnings detect, predict, and inform
Warning systems must work continuously
Training matters as much as technology
activities.explanation: These ideas explain how coastal warnings work.

activities.prompt: A coastal town gets one cyclone alert. Should its warning system shut down afterward? Explain why.
steps: Cyclones can threaten coastal areas, so the warning system must stay ready.
The system detects hazards, predicts disasters, and issues timely warnings.
It must work continuously because one alert cannot cover the whole storm.
Therefore, it should keep running instead of shutting down after one alert.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Spot the Cyclone
activities.prompt: Which statement describes a cyclone?
options: A large rotating storm
A giant earthquake wave
A coastal alarm system
A satellite phone service
activities.explanation: A cyclone is a large storm with winds that rotate.

activities.title: Complete the Warning
activities.prompt: These systems detect hazards, predict disasters, and issue ______ warnings.
activities.hint: This word means early enough to be useful.
activities.explanation: Timely warnings give people time to prepare for a disaster.

activities.title: Which Coasts Are Monitored?
activities.prompt: Where do India’s warning services monitor storms?
options: Eastern coast only
Western coast only
Both eastern and western coasts
Neither eastern nor western coast
activities.explanation: India’s warning services monitor storms on both coasts.

activities.title: When Must Warnings Work?
activities.prompt: When must effective early warning systems function?
options: Continuously
Only before a hazard
Only after a disaster
Only during training
activities.explanation: Continuous functioning helps warnings stay ready for coastal areas.

activities.title: Match the System to Its Work
activities.prompt: Match each system or programme with its work.
pairs: Builds cyclone shelters and improves responses
Forecasts storm surges and coastal flooding
Form a real-time tsunami detection network
activities.explanation: Each system has a special role in detecting, forecasting, warning, or preparing.

activities.title: Order the Warning Steps
activities.prompt: Put the three warning steps in the correct order.
activities.explanation: The system detects hazards, predicts disasters, and then issues timely warnings.

activities.prompt: An earthquake shakes the ground. What may follow near the coast, and why?
options: A giant wave, because earthquakes can cause tsunamis.
No wave, because only rotating storms make giant waves.
A giant wave, because every earthquake becomes a cyclone.
No wave, because giant waves happen only far inland.

why.No wave, because only rotating storms ma: This mistake confuses the causes of cyclones and tsunamis.
why.A giant wave, because every earthquake b: This mistake confuses an earthquake-caused tsunami with a cyclone.
why.No wave, because giant waves happen only: This mistake believes giant waves cannot occur near the coast.

activities.explanation: This is right because earthquakes can cause giant waves called tsunamis.

activities.prompt: Government says cyclone warnings must work continuously. What does this rule mean during a real storm?
options: Keep warning services running throughout the storm.
Start warning services only after the storm passes.
Run warning services for one short alert, then stop.
Stop warning services as soon as the storm develops.

why.Start warning services only after the st: This mistake treats continuous operation as something to begin after danger.
why.Run warning services for one short alert: This mistake thinks one short alert is the same as continuous work.
why.Stop warning services as soon as the sto: This mistake thinks warnings should stop when the storm develops.

activities.explanation: This is right because effective warning systems must function continuously.

activities.prompt: A map shows India's tsunami detection buoys. Another source shows satellite information sent to phones through Bluetooth. What do both sources show together?
options: Tsunamis can be detected at sea, and satellite information can reach phones.
Tsunamis can be detected at sea, but satellite information cannot reach phones.
Satellite information can reach phones, but tsunamis cannot be detected at sea.
Neither detection buoys nor phones can support warning work.

why.Tsunamis can be detected at sea, but sat: This mistake ignores the fact that Bluetooth sends satellite information to phones.
why.Satellite information can reach phones,: This mistake ignores the real-time network of tsunami detection buoys.
why.Neither detection buoys nor phones can s: This mistake mistakes useful warning tools for useless objects.

activities.explanation: This is right because buoys detect tsunamis and phones can receive satellite information.

activities.prompt: India's early cyclone prediction reduced the loss of human and animal lives. The NCRMP builds shelters and improves warnings and responses. What should a government do next?
options: Keep improving warnings, responses, shelters, and public training.
Stop all work because reduced losses mean cyclones cause no harm.
Use only shelters because warnings, responses, and training are unnecessary.
Use only technology because public awareness and training add nothing.

why.Stop all work because reduced losses mea: This mistake treats reduced losses as proof that no danger remains.
why.Use only shelters because warnings, resp: This mistake thinks one measure can replace the others.
why.Use only technology because public aware: This mistake thinks technology is more important than awareness and training.

activities.explanation: This is right because better prediction helps, while training remains equally important.

lessons.title: Marine Resources and Maritime Rules

activities.prompt: What lives beneath the waves, and who decides how we use them?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ocean Resources and Rules
activities.body: Marine resources are ocean features and materials with value. They include seafood, biodiversity, oil, gas, minerals, energy, tourism and coral reefs. They can be living or non-living resources. They support food security, economic activities and healthy environments. The Blue Economy means using ocean resources sustainably. Maritime law sets international rules for activities at sea.
keyPoints: Marine resources can be living or non-living.
The Blue Economy uses ocean resources sustainably.
Maritime law provides international rules for activities at sea.
activities.explanation: The ocean offers many resources, so clear rules help people use them responsibly.

activities.prompt: A coastal town wants to use seafood and tourism while keeping the sea healthy. How should it act?
steps: Seafood helps the town feed its people, so food security matters.
Tourism supports the town’s economy, so the sea is valuable.
Coral reefs and healthy environments matter, so use should protect them.
Using ocean resources sustainably fits the Blue Economy, so this is the best plan.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What are marine resources divided into?
options: Living and non-living
Seafood and oil
Minerals and gas
Tourism and coral reefs
activities.explanation: Marine resources have two main types: living and non-living resources.

activities.prompt: The Blue Economy means using ocean resources sustainably.
activities.explanation: This is the main meaning of the Blue Economy.

activities.prompt: A country's territorial ______ are the sea area closest to that country.
activities.hint: Think of the sea area nearest the country.
activities.explanation: Territorial waters cover the sea area closest to a country.

activities.prompt: How far does the contiguous zone extend from the baseline?
options: 24 nautical miles
200 nautical miles
The closest sea area
activities.explanation: The contiguous zone extends up to 24 nautical miles from the baseline.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct partner.
activities.explanation: Seafood is living, oil is non-living, and all countries enjoy equal rights on the high seas.

activities.prompt: Put these sea areas in order from the coast outwards.
activities.explanation: Territorial waters are closest. The contiguous zone reaches 24 nautical miles, while the EEZ reaches 200.

activities.prompt: Which statement about ocean rights is correct?
options: A country has special rights to use resources in its EEZ.
Every country has special rights over every EEZ.
Countries have equal rights within all coastal sea areas.
The high seas belong only to the nearest coastal country.
activities.explanation: A country has special rights to use ocean resources in its EEZ. All countries have equal rights on the high seas.

activities.prompt: Ships can ignore the rules of the road at sea.
activities.explanation: Ships must follow the rules of the road at sea to avoid collisions.

activities.prompt: A coastal town uses seafood, oil, gas, and tourism from its sea. Which benefit is clearest?
options: It supports food security and the town’s economy.
It makes all marine resources living resources.
It gives every country equal rights in the sea.
It makes territorial waters reach 200 nautical miles.

why.It makes all marine resources living res: This confuses living and non-living resources.
why.It gives every country equal rights in t: This confuses high-seas equality with the country’s special rights.
why.It makes territorial waters reach 200 na: This confuses an EEZ limit with territorial waters.

activities.explanation: Seafood supports food security, and sea activities support the economy.

activities.prompt: Two ships see each other at sea. Both want to avoid a collision. What should they do?
options: Both follow the rules of the road at sea.
Each follows its own route and ignores the other ship.
They sail faster even though their paths may cross.
They wait until the ships are much closer.

why.Each follows its own route and ignores t: This ignores the need for both ships to follow shared sea rules.
why.They sail faster even though their paths: This mistakes speed for the safe action needed to avoid collisions.
why.They wait until the ships are much close: This mistakes waiting for danger for preventing it.

activities.explanation: The rules of the road at sea help ships avoid collisions.

activities.context: A school expedition plans to examine a very deep place in the Pacific Ocean, a long underwater mountain range, and a broad, flat area of the ocean floor. A student also learns that some underwater mountains stop below the sea surface, while others have flattened tops. The team must decide which underwater landform matches each description and explain how the ocean floor can offer resources and mark a continent's true edge.
activities.prompt: The expedition finds the very deep place in the Pacific Ocean. Which location should it visit to reach the deepest place on Earth?
options: Mariana Trench
Mid-Ocean Ridge
Abyssal plain
Continental shelf

why.Mid-Ocean Ridge: The Mid-Ocean Ridge is a mountain range, not the deepest place.
why.Abyssal plain: An abyssal plain is deep and flat, but it is not the deepest place on Earth.
why.Continental shelf: The continental shelf is not the deepest place in the ocean.

activities.explanation: The Mariana Trench is correct because it is the deepest place on Earth.

activities.context: A school expedition plans to examine a very deep place in the Pacific Ocean, a long underwater mountain range, and a broad, flat area of the ocean floor. A student also learns that some underwater mountains stop below the sea surface, while others have flattened tops. The team must decide which underwater landform matches each description and explain how the ocean floor can offer resources and mark a continent's true edge.
activities.prompt: If an old underwater mountain has become flat-topped, which underwater landform is it?
options: Guyot
Seamount
Trench
Plateau

why.Seamount: A seamount may have a pointed top, so flat-topped describes a guyot.
why.Trench: A trench is a deep part of the ocean, not a flat-topped mountain.
why.Plateau: A plateau is an underwater landform, but this description identifies a guyot.

activities.explanation: A guyot is a flat-topped underwater mountain formed from an old seamount.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Mid-Ocean Ridge is an immense underwater mountain range formed by volcanic activity.
Reason (R): The Mid-Ocean Ridge is the world's longest mountain range.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but being the world's longest mountain range does not explain its formation by volcanic activity.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A guyot is a flat-topped underwater mountain formed from an old seamount.
Reason (R): A seamount rises from the ocean floor and reaches the sea surface.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The first statement is true, but the reason is false because a seamount does not reach the sea surface.

activities.prompt: Explain how a seamount, a guyot, and an ocean trench differ as forms of ocean relief.
activities.answer: The ocean floor has underwater landforms called submarine relief or ocean relief. These include underwater mountains, valleys, plateaus, and trenches. A seamount rises from the ocean floor but does not reach the sea surface. A guyot is a flat-topped underwater mountain formed from an old seamount. Ocean trenches are the deepest parts of the ocean. These examples show that ocean relief includes many different underwater landforms.
points: Defines ocean relief
Distinguishes a seamount from a guyot
Explains that a guyot comes from an old seamount
Identifies trenches as the deepest ocean parts
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Along a rocky coast, a coastal village lies beside a sandy beach. During a storm, strong winds blow across the water, and the ocean surface rises and falls in large waves. The waves strike the rocky shore, where cracks and caves have formed, while sediment has collected beside the beach. The villagers watch each wave rise to a high point and fall to a low point from the shore. Later, an underwater earthquake occurs offshore.
activities.prompt: The storm continues and its winds grow stronger. What is most likely to happen next?
options: The waves may become huge and damage the coastline.
The waves may become smaller and uncover more of the beach.
The waves may lose their energy before reaching the shore.
The waves may become even and stop damaging the coast.

why.The waves may become smaller and uncover: These huge waves can damage coastlines.
why.The waves may lose their energy before r: Stronger storm winds do not support smaller waves.
why.The waves may become even and stop damag: Waves can carry energy across oceans and continue reaching the shore.

activities.explanation: Strong storm winds can create huge waves.

activities.context: Along a rocky coast, a coastal village lies beside a sandy beach. During a storm, strong winds blow across the water, and the ocean surface rises and falls in large waves. The waves strike the rocky shore, where cracks and caves have formed, while sediment has collected beside the beach. The villagers watch each wave rise to a high point and fall to a low point from the shore. Later, an underwater earthquake occurs offshore.
activities.prompt: If wave erosion later leaves a tall block standing separately from the rest of the rocky coast, what could it be?
options: A sea stack.
A sea arch.
A sea cave.
A sea stump.

A sea arch is not a separate block of rock.
A sea cave is an opening rather than a standing block.
A sea stump is a later, smaller remnant.

activities.explanation: Wave erosion can form sea stacks.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Strong storm winds can create huge waves that damage coastlines.
Reason (R): Waves can carry energy across oceans over long distances.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but carrying energy over long distances does not explain why storm winds create huge waves.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Winds blowing across water are the main cause of waves.
Reason (R): Underwater earthquakes are the main cause of ordinary ocean waves.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but underwater earthquakes mainly cause tsunamis rather than ordinary waves.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between wave erosion and wave deposition.
activities.answer: Wave erosion and wave deposition both shape coastlines, but they act in different ways. Wave erosion can form sea cracks, caves, arches, sea stacks, and stumps as waves wear away coastal rock. Wave deposition occurs when waves move and leave sediment on the coast, and it can form features such as beaches. Therefore, erosion produces openings and remaining rock features, while deposition builds up deposited sediment such as beach sand.
points: Both processes shape coastlines.
Wave erosion forms cracks, caves, arches, stacks, and stumps.
Wave deposition forms features such as beaches.
Erosion and deposition act differently on the coast.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is assisting a cargo boat near the Gulf of Khambhat. The skipper plans to enter the harbour when the tide is high because the tidal range there is about 12 metres, and the boat must move through tidal currents that can reach 5–6 knots. The Moon is in its first-quarter phase. During the same visit, the student visits one of India’s major tidal-energy sites. The student wonders whether the Moon’s phase will affect the boat’s journey.
activities.prompt: Because the Moon is in its first-quarter phase, what should the student expect about the tides?
options: The difference between high and low water will be unusually large.
The difference between high and low water will be smaller than usual.
The boat will experience only one tide during the day.
The tidal currents will stop moving through the water.

why.The difference between high and low wate: This describes spring tides, not neap tides.
why.The boat will experience only one tide d: Tides occur twice a day in most parts of the world.
why.The tidal currents will stop moving thro: Nothing in the facts says that neap tides stop tidal currents.

activities.explanation: First- or third-quarter Moon produces neap tides with a smaller tidal difference.

activities.context: A student is assisting a cargo boat near the Gulf of Khambhat. The skipper plans to enter the harbour when the tide is high because the tidal range there is about 12 metres, and the boat must move through tidal currents that can reach 5–6 knots. The Moon is in its first-quarter phase. During the same visit, the student visits one of India’s major tidal-energy sites. The student wonders whether the Moon’s phase will affect the boat’s journey.
activities.prompt: If the Sun, Earth, and Moon later form a straight line, what change should the student expect?
options: The tidal range will become smaller.
The boat will find that high and low tides differ less than before.
The boat will experience unusually high and unusually low tides.
The tidal currents will stop moving through the water.

A smaller tidal difference is associated with neap tides.
why.The boat will find that high and low tid: Neap tides have a smaller difference between high and low tide.
why.The tidal currents will stop moving thro: The facts do not say that spring tides stop tidal currents.

activities.explanation: A straight line of the Sun, Earth, and Moon produces spring tides.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The cargo boat can reach the harbour more easily during high tide.
Reason (R): High tides help ships reach harbours more easily.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the reason directly explains the assertion.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Moon’s first-quarter phase produces unusually high and unusually low tides.
Reason (R): Neap tides occur when the Moon is in its first- or third-quarter phase.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true, but the assertion is false because first- or third-quarter Moon produces neap tides with a smaller tidal difference.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between spring tides and neap tides.
activities.answer: Spring tides and neap tides differ in both cause and effect. Spring tides occur when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in a straight line. They produce unusually high tides and unusually low tides, so the difference between high and low water is greater. Neap tides occur when the Moon is in its first-quarter or third-quarter phase. During neap tides, the difference between high and low tide is smaller. Therefore, a straight-line arrangement of the Sun, Earth, and Moon is associated with the wider tidal difference.
points: Spring tides occur when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in a straight line.
Spring tides produce unusually high and unusually low tides.
Neap tides occur at the Moon’s first- or third-quarter phase.
Neap tides have a smaller difference between high and low tide.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A fishing crew works at an important fishing ground where a warm current from a warmer region meets a cold current carrying freezing water. The crew uses a map in which the warm current is red and the cold current is blue. They notice many kinds of fish near the meeting point. One crew member wonders whether the colours show water temperature, while another asks why so many fish are present.
activities.prompt: If the warm current in the case became cold, how should the map represent it?
options: It should be coloured blue, because map colours identify warm and cold currents.
It should remain red, because maps use red for every moving body of water.
It should be coloured blue, because meeting currents create fishing grounds.
It should be coloured red, because salinity is the main feature represented by map colours.

why.It should remain red, because maps use r: Red is used for currents from warmer regions.
why.It should be coloured blue, because meet: Meeting currents do not determine map colours.
why.It should be coloured red, because salin: Salinity can influence currents but does not set the map colour.

activities.explanation: Blue is the usual colour for showing cold currents.

activities.context: A fishing crew works at an important fishing ground where a warm current from a warmer region meets a cold current carrying freezing water. The crew uses a map in which the warm current is red and the cold current is blue. They notice many kinds of fish near the meeting point. One crew member wonders whether the colours show water temperature, while another asks why so many fish are present.
activities.prompt: What effects could follow if ocean movements in this area changed?
options: Fishing and travel could be affected, and climate could change, because ocean movements support these purposes.
Only the map colours would change, because ocean movements have no effects on marine life.
The fish would lose their nutrients automatically, because nutrients depend on map colours.
Nothing would change, because currents move water but do not support marine life.

why.Only the map colours would change, becau: Map colours do not represent every effect of ocean movements.
why.The fish would lose their nutrients auto: Nutrients support fish independently of map colours.
why.Nothing would change, because currents m: Currents support marine life and have effects beyond moving water.

activities.explanation: Ocean movements aid fishing and travel and influence climate.

activities.context: A coastal community in India is reviewing its cyclone and tsunami preparations. Warning services monitor storms on both eastern and western coasts, detect hazards, predict disasters, and issue timely warnings. GEMINI receives satellite information and sends it to phones through Bluetooth. India has a real-time network of tsunami detection buoys. The SSEWS forecasts storm surges and coastal flooding. The NCRMP builds cyclone shelters and improves warnings and emergency responses. Public awareness and training programmes help people understand the warnings.
activities.prompt: After warning services detect a cyclone and predict where it may cause danger, what should they do next?
options: Issue a timely warning to people in the affected coastal area.
Wait until the cyclone has passed before warning anyone.
Use the tsunami detection buoys to confirm every cyclone.
Stop monitoring the eastern and western coasts until the warning is sent.

why.Wait until the cyclone has passed before: Delaying the warning would remove its timely purpose.
why.Use the tsunami detection buoys to confi: Buoys are for detecting tsunamis, not confirming cyclones.
why.Stop monitoring the eastern and western: Continuous monitoring is needed even while warnings are issued.

activities.explanation: Detected and predicted hazards must be communicated promptly.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Oceans and Life

activities.prompt: Which place is the deepest on Earth?
options: Mariana Trench
Mid-Ocean Ridge
Abyssal plain
Continental shelf
activities.explanation: The Mariana Trench lies in the Pacific Ocean. It is the deepest place on Earth.

activities.prompt: A seamount rises above the ocean’s surface.
activities.explanation: A seamount rises from the ocean floor. It does not reach the sea surface.

activities.prompt: Winds blowing across water are the main cause of ______.
activities.hint: They make the ocean’s surface rise and fall.
activities.explanation: Winds blowing across water are the main cause of waves.

activities.prompt: Match each term with its correct description.
pairs: A high point of a wave
A low point of a wave
The true edge of a continent
activities.explanation: A crest is high, while a trough is low. The other pairs match each term’s role.

activities.prompt: Which group can wave erosion form?
options: Cracks, caves, and arches
Beaches, shelves, and slopes
Ridges, trenches, and plains
Mountains, valleys, and plateaus
activities.explanation: Wave erosion can form sea cracks, caves, arches, sea stacks, and stumps.

activities.prompt: Spring tides occur when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in a straight line.
activities.explanation: Spring tides occur when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in a straight line.

activities.prompt: Put the early warning system’s actions in order.
activities.explanation: The system detects hazards first. It then predicts disasters and issues timely warnings.

activities.prompt: Where are important fishing grounds often found?
options: Where warm and cold meet
Where ocean trenches begin
Where shelf waters deepen
Where storm waves rise
activities.explanation: Warm and cold currents meet at important fishing grounds. These places contain nutrients that support fish.

activities.prompt: Match each sea zone or idea with its correct description.
pairs: Sea area closest to a country
activities.explanation: Territorial waters lie closest to a country. The other clues give each zone’s limit or meaning.

activities.prompt: Which action must ships take to avoid collisions?
options: Follow the rules of the road
Use only charts for direction
Keep close to the coast
Share equal rights at sea
activities.explanation: Ships must follow the rules of the road at sea. These rules help them avoid collisions.
