chapters.title: Life on Earth
chapters.summary: In this chapter: biomes and their variety; forests and grasslands; deserts and tundra; aquatic biomes and energy.

lessons.title: Biomes and Their Variety

activities.prompt: Why do different parts of Earth look and feel so different?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is a biome?
activities.body: Geography helps us see how climate, landforms and water shape life on Earth. A biome is a huge natural patch and a large natural region. Each biome is a broad environmental area. An ecosystem is like a neighbourhood within a biome. Biomes can be land-based or water-based. They support diverse plants and animals. Temperature, rainfall and main plant species help decide what can thrive.
keyPoints: Biomes are large natural regions.
An ecosystem is like a neighbourhood within a biome.
Climate and other conditions help shape life.
activities.explanation: Biomes are large natural regions where different kinds of life can thrive.

activities.prompt: Why do a green forest and hot desert have different life?
steps: Climate and landforms shape life because they affect the conditions around organisms.
Temperature, rainfall patterns, and main plant species help determine what can thrive.
The forest and desert therefore support different kinds of life.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Land-based biomes
activities.body: Biomes are grouped as land-based or water-based. Land-based biomes are also called terrestrial biomes. Their examples are forests, grasslands, deserts and tundra. Icy tundras, hot deserts, green forests and vast grasslands show biome variety. Each supports diverse plant and animal life. Temperature, rainfall patterns and main plant species help determine what can thrive.
keyPoints: Land-based biomes are called terrestrial biomes.
Forests, grasslands, deserts and tundra are examples.
Different biomes support diverse life.
activities.explanation: Terrestrial biomes have different conditions and support different kinds of life.

activities.prompt: Which meaning best describes a biome?
options: A large natural region
A narrow neighbourhood
A single climate pattern
A small ecosystem
activities.explanation: A biome is a large natural region of the world.

activities.prompt: A large natural region of the world is called a ______.
activities.hint: It is a huge natural patch.
activities.explanation: The lesson calls these huge natural patches biomes.

activities.prompt: An ecosystem is like a neighbourhood within a biome.
activities.explanation: The lesson compares an ecosystem to a neighbourhood within a biome.

activities.prompt: Match each description with the correct word.
activities.explanation: These descriptions explain biomes and the ecosystems found within them.

activities.prompt: Which set lists land-based biomes?
options: Forests, grasslands, deserts and tundra
Temperature, rainfall, landforms and water
Climate, ecosystems, neighbourhoods and regions
Water-based types, land-based types and biomes
activities.explanation: Forests, grasslands, deserts and tundra are terrestrial biomes.

activities.prompt: A child compares a hot desert and an icy tundra. Which idea fits the lesson best?
options: Their temperature, rainfall and plants can help explain their life.
Both must have exactly the same temperature, rainfall and plants.
Neither can support any plant or animal life.
They are always ecosystems within one broad biome.
activities.explanation: Temperature, rainfall and main plants help determine what can thrive. Biomes support diverse life.

activities.prompt: A child visits a green forest and a hot desert. Which plants should thrive in each?
options: The plants ignore climate because all biomes are similar.
The desert plants suit the forest's temperature and rainfall.
The forest plants suit the forest's temperature and rainfall.
Both places support exactly the same plant species.

why.The plants ignore climate because all bi: This wrongly treats climate as unimportant for plant growth.
why.The desert plants suit the forest's temp: This gives desert plants the forest's climate conditions.
why.Both places support exactly the same pla: This wrongly assumes that different biomes have identical life.

activities.explanation: This follows the rule that climate helps determine what can thrive.

activities.prompt: One place is an icy tundra, and another is a hot desert. Which comparison is best?
options: Their plants differ because temperature and rainfall patterns differ.
Their plants match because all large natural regions are alike.
Both have forest plants because green areas ignore climate.
Both have grassland plants because different climates still grow grass.

why.Their plants match because all large nat: This confuses the size of a biome with sameness.
why.Both have forest plants because green ar: This wrongly assumes that every tundra has forest plants.
why.Both have grassland plants because diffe: This wrongly assumes that different climates produce grassland plants.

activities.explanation: The right choice links different climates to different plants.

activities.prompt: A map shows a green forest and a broad hot desert. What can we compare?
options: The exact number of plants living in each region.
The daily weather changes inside each broad mapped region.
The names of every animal living in each region.
The kinds of plants suited to each region's climate.

why.The exact number of plants living in eac: A broad regional map cannot give an exact plant count.
why.The daily weather changes inside each br: A broad regional map does not show daily weather changes.
why.The names of every animal living in each: This map does not name every animal in either region.

activities.explanation: The biome clues help compare plants suited to each climate.

activities.prompt: A map shows a forest region and a water region. How should these biomes be grouped?
options: The forest is water-based, and the water region is land-based.
Both are land-based because both regions clearly contain living things.
The forest is land-based, and the water region is water-based.
Neither is grouped because only one region has living things.

why.The forest is water-based, and the water: This swaps the land and water biome groups.
why.Both are land-based because both regions: This wrongly assumes that all living things must live on land.
why.Neither is grouped because only one regi: This wrongly says that only one region can contain life.

activities.explanation: Forests are land-based, while water regions are water-based.

activities.prompt: Place A is hot and dry. Place B is green with regular rain. Which fits a hot desert?
options: Place B, because its green, wet conditions suit a desert.
Both places, because all biomes share the same climate.
Neither place, because climate cannot help identify a biome.
Place A, because its hot, dry conditions suit a desert.

why.Place B, because its green, wet conditio: This mistakes a green forest's conditions for desert conditions.
why.Both places, because all biomes share th: This wrongly treats all biomes as having the same climate.
why.Neither place, because climate cannot he: This overlooks that climate helps determine what can thrive.

activities.explanation: Hot, dry conditions fit the hot desert example.

lessons.title: Forests and Grasslands

activities.prompt: Ever wondered why forests and grasslands grow in such different places?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Where Forests and Grasslands Grow
activities.body: Tropical rainforests grow near the Equator and stay hot and wet all year. The Amazon Basin has the largest ones. Rainforests also cover the Congo Basin and parts of Southeast Asia. These regions hold the world's richest storehouse of biodiversity and are called a gene bank. Grasslands are open areas covered mainly with grass. Their rainfall is moderate but too little for dense forests. African tropical grasslands are called Savannas.
keyPoints: Rainforests lie between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.
A gene bank is another name for these rainforest regions.
Grasslands have moderate rainfall but too little for dense forests.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the main ideas about forests and grasslands.

activities.prompt: A map shows a hot, wet place near the Equator and another place with moderate rain. Which landscapes should we expect?
steps: Hot, wet places near the Equator have tropical rainforests, because these regions stay hot and wet all year.
Places with moderate rain have grasslands, because the rain is too little for dense forests.
People use grasslands for grazing, farming and livestock rearing, because grasslands support these activities.
Therefore, the first place should show a tropical rainforest, while the second should show an open grassland.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Near the Equator
activities.prompt: Tropical rainforests are found mainly near which place?
options: the Equator
the Amazon Basin
the Congo Basin
the Tropic of Cancer
activities.explanation: The lesson says tropical rainforests are found mainly near the Equator.

activities.title: Rainforest Weather
activities.prompt: Tropical rainforests stay ______ and wet throughout the year.
activities.hint: Think about the weather near the Equator.
activities.explanation: The lesson says these regions remain hot and wet throughout the year.

activities.title: Open Grasslands
activities.prompt: Grasslands are large open areas covered mainly with grass.
activities.explanation: This is exactly how the lesson describes grasslands.

activities.title: Match the Regions
activities.prompt: Match each place or region with its lesson description.
pairs: home of the largest tropical rainforests
has parts covered by tropical rainforests
activities.explanation: The Amazon Basin has the largest tropical rainforests, while African tropical grasslands are called Savannas.

activities.title: Grassland Rainfall
activities.prompt: Grasslands grow where rainfall is moderate but too little for dense forests.
activities.explanation: The lesson gives exactly this reason for the growth of grasslands.

activities.title: Forests and Oxygen
activities.prompt: Forests have no role in maintaining oxygen levels.
activities.explanation: Forests help maintain oxygen levels and balance the Earth's climate.

activities.prompt: A family visits a hot, wet land near the Equator. What should they expect to see?
options: A dense rainforest with hot, wet weather
An open grassland with moderate rainfall
A cold forest with dry, windy weather
A bare desert with very little rainfall

why.An open grassland with moderate rainfall: This mistake mixes up rainforests with grasslands.
why.A cold forest with dry, windy weather: This mistake uses cold and dry weather, which does not match the place.
why.A bare desert with very little rainfall: This mistake treats a hot, wet rainforest region like a dry, open area.

activities.explanation: This is right because tropical rainforests are found mainly near the Equator.

activities.prompt: Two maps show the Amazon Basin, Congo Basin, and Southeast Asia. What do these maps suggest?
options: These areas hold the world's richest biodiversity.
These areas have moderate rain and open grass.
These areas all lie very close to the Equator.
These areas are used only for livestock rearing.

why.These areas have moderate rain and open: This mistake confuses rainforests with grasslands.
why.These areas all lie very close to the Eq: This mistake assumes every rainforest area is near the Equator.
why.These areas are used only for livestock: This mistake ignores the many living things in rainforest regions.

activities.explanation: This is right because these rainforest areas together form the world's richest storehouse of biodiversity.

activities.prompt: A place has moderate rainfall but cannot support dense forests. What landscape fits this place?
options: An open grassland used for grazing animals.
A dense rainforest with hot, wet weather.
A rainforest region that stores biodiversity.
A tropical forest with moderate rainfall.

why.A dense rainforest with hot, wet weather: This mistake describes a hot, wet rainforest instead of grassland.
why.A rainforest region that stores biodiver: This mistake uses a forest benefit instead of a landscape clue.
why.A tropical forest with moderate rainfall: This mistake wrongly places a rainforest where rain is too low.

activities.explanation: This is right because grasslands grow where rain is moderate but too little for dense forests.

activities.prompt: A source describes African grassland where animals graze. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: It is a tropical grassland known as a Savanna.
It is a dense rainforest with moderate rainfall.
It is a hot, wet rainforest in the Amazon.
It is a forest area that stores oxygen levels.

why.It is a dense rainforest with moderate r: This mistake mixes up grassland and rainforest landscapes.
why.It is a hot, wet rainforest in the Amazo: This mistake gives an African place the Amazon's rainforest setting.
why.It is a forest area that stores oxygen l: This mistake chooses a forest benefit instead of the grassland clue.

activities.explanation: This is right because tropical grasslands in Africa are also known as Savannas.

lessons.title: Deserts and Tundra

activities.prompt: What surprises you most about places where life survives extreme dryness or cold?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Deserts and Tundra
activities.body: Deserts are the driest biomes and get very little rainfall. A desert can be hot, like the Sahara, or cold, like the Gobi. Desert plants and animals have special ways to survive heat and dryness. Some deserts have sandy soil and sparse plants. The Rann of Kutch is a large salt desert that becomes a marshy wetland during the monsoon. Tundra is the coldest biome. It has long, harsh winters, short summers, and frozen ground called permafrost.
keyPoints: Deserts receive very little rainfall and can be hot or cold.
Desert organisms store water and withstand heat and dryness.
Tundra is the coldest biome, with permafrost below its surface.
activities.explanation: Deserts and tundra have special conditions, so living things need special adaptations.

activities.prompt: A child sees a place with very little rain, sandy soil, and sparse plants. Is this place a desert?
steps: Very little rain fits a desert because deserts are the driest biomes.
Sandy soil and sparse plants also fit because deserts often have both.
Therefore, the place is likely a desert because several clues point to it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What are deserts?
options: The driest biomes
The wettest biomes
The coldest biomes
The rainiest biomes
activities.explanation: Deserts receive very little rainfall, so they are the driest biomes.

activities.prompt: The Rann of Kutch is one of the world's largest ______ deserts.
activities.hint: This kind of desert contains salt.
activities.explanation: The Rann of Kutch is one of the world's largest salt deserts.

activities.prompt: Which place is a cold desert?
options: The Gobi
The Sahara
The Rann of Kutch
The Tundra
activities.explanation: The Gobi is a cold desert. The Sahara is a hot desert.

activities.prompt: Match each place or biome with its description.
activities.explanation: Each place has a special desert or tundra description.

activities.prompt: Put the desert survival steps in order.
items: They store water and withstand heat and dryness.
activities.explanation: Harsh desert conditions lead to special adaptations. These help organisms survive.

activities.prompt: Why is it difficult for trees to grow in tundra?
options: The ground is frozen permafrost.
The soil is always very sandy.
The rainfall is always heavy.
The summers are long and hot.
activities.explanation: Frozen ground called permafrost makes it difficult for trees to grow.

activities.prompt: The Sahara is hot. The Gobi can be cold. Both are deserts. What does this show?
options: Deserts can have very different climates.
Deserts must always be extremely hot.
Only African deserts can feel cold.
Cold places receive much more rain.

This mistake thinks all deserts have hot climates.
This mistake confuses where deserts are with their climate.
This mistake links cold places with more rain, but deserts get little rain.

activities.explanation: This is right because deserts can be hot or cold.

activities.prompt: A map shows sandy soil, sparse plants, and very little rainfall in one region. What can we infer?
options: It is likely a desert region.
It is likely a tundra region.
It must be a sandy forest region.
It must be a marshy wetland region.

This mistake treats desert clues as signs of tundra.
This mistake thinks sandy soil proves the place is a forest.
This mistake thinks sparse plants show a marshy wetland.

activities.explanation: This is right because these clues match desert features.

activities.prompt: A family visits a tundra area in winter and summer. Which visit faces the longest harsh conditions?
options: The winter visit faces longer harsh conditions.
The summer visit faces longer harsh conditions.
Both visits face equally harsh conditions.
The spring visit faces the longest harsh conditions.

why.The summer visit faces longer harsh cond: This mistake focuses on short summers instead of harsh winters.
why.Both visits face equally harsh condition: This mistake assumes all tundra seasons are equally harsh.
why.The spring visit faces the longest harsh: This mistake ignores that winters are the harshest season.

activities.explanation: This is right because tundra winters are very long and harsh.

lessons.title: Aquatic Biomes and Energy

activities.prompt: How does energy flow through the watery homes of Earth?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Life in Aquatic Biomes
activities.body: Aquatic biomes cover about three-fourths of the Earth's surface. They are divided into freshwater and marine biomes. Freshwater biomes include rivers, lakes, ponds and wetlands. Marine biomes include oceans, seas and coral reefs. A biome pyramid is a picture showing how organisms relate. Plants and algae capture solar energy as producers. Less energy is available at higher levels.
keyPoints: Freshwater and marine are the two main aquatic biome groups.
Plants and algae are producers that capture solar energy.
Less energy is available at higher levels of a biome pyramid.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects aquatic biomes with the flow of energy.

activities.prompt: Why does a farm pond matter to people and other life?
steps: Ponds are freshwater because they belong with rivers, lakes, and wetlands.
This matters because freshwater biomes support farming and access to drinking water.
Energy starts there because plants and algae capture solar energy.
Living beings depend on one another, so the pond affects a wider system.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which group includes rivers, lakes, ponds and wetlands?
options: Freshwater biomes
Marine biomes
Biome pyramids
Coral reefs
activities.explanation: Rivers, lakes, ponds and wetlands are freshwater biomes.

activities.prompt: Freshwater biomes are important for farming and access to ______ water.
activities.hint: This water is needed for drinking.
activities.explanation: Freshwater biomes provide access to drinking water and support farming.

activities.prompt: Match each biome term with its correct description.
activities.explanation: Each term has a clear role or place within the lesson.

activities.prompt: What happens to organisms, biomass and available energy higher up a biome pyramid?
options: They increase
They decrease
They stay equal
They disappear
activities.explanation: The number of organisms, biomass and available energy decrease upward.

activities.prompt: Put these groups in order from the lowest to the highest level.
activities.explanation: Producers begin the pyramid, while top predators occupy its highest level.

activities.prompt: What does a biome pyramid show?
options: The colours of aquatic plants
The relationships between organisms
The dates of biome discoveries
The depth of every freshwater lake
activities.explanation: A biome pyramid is a graphical representation of relationships between organisms.

activities.prompt: A farmer needs farming and drinking water. Which biome fits best?
options: A freshwater biome, such as a river
A marine biome, such as an ocean
A coral reef in a marine biome
A pond in a marine biome

why.A marine biome, such as an ocean: Oceans are marine biomes, not freshwater biomes.
why.A coral reef in a marine biome: Coral reefs are marine, while these needs belong to freshwater biomes.
why.A pond in a marine biome: Ponds are freshwater biomes, so placing them in marine biomes is wrong.

activities.explanation: Freshwater biomes support farming and access to drinking water.

activities.prompt: Which level should have the most available energy in a biome pyramid?
options: Plants and algae at the producer level
Herbivores at the level above producers
Top predators at the highest level
Top predators at the lowest level

why.Herbivores at the level above producers: Herbivores are higher, where less available energy is shown.
why.Top predators at the highest level: Top predators are higher, where available energy is least.
why.Top predators at the lowest level: Top predators belong at the top, where less energy is available.

activities.explanation: Producers capture solar energy, and available energy decreases upward.

activities.prompt: Which pair shows one freshwater biome and one marine biome?
options: A river and a coral reef
An ocean and a sea
A pond and a lake
A sea and a coral reef

why.An ocean and a sea: An ocean and a sea are both marine biomes.
why.A pond and a lake: A pond and a lake are both freshwater biomes.
why.A sea and a coral reef: A sea and a coral reef are both marine biomes.

activities.explanation: A river is freshwater, while a coral reef is marine.

lessons.title: Biodiversity Conservation and Ecotourism

activities.prompt: What can we learn from places where wildlife thrives?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Protecting Variety of Life
activities.body: Biodiversity means the variety of life on Earth. It includes plants, animals, microorganisms and their ecosystems. Geography influences how organisms are protected and managed. Biodiversity is unevenly spread across Earth. The Himalaya and Western Ghats are biodiversity hotspots, places with much variety of life. Conservation strategies must suit their geographical setting. Sustainable practices can differ with geography. Ecotourism keeps environmental impact low. Forest ecotourism can balance tourism, protection and sustainable development.
keyPoints: Biodiversity includes many living things and their ecosystems.
Conservation strategies must suit the geographical setting.
Ecotourism aims for little environmental impact.
activities.explanation: Biodiversity needs care that fits each place.

activities.prompt: A river separates a village from a forest where animals live. Where should a crossing go?
steps: The river may block movement, so it can act as a barrier.
A crossing can connect the areas because the river separates them.
The crossing must suit the geography because strategies should fit each setting.
So place it on an animal route across the river.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does biodiversity mean?
options: The variety of life on Earth
The number of human homes
The height of mountain peaks
The amount of river water
activities.explanation: Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth.

activities.prompt: Biodiversity includes plants, animals, ______ and their ecosystems.
activities.hint: This is a tiny living organism.
activities.explanation: Microorganisms are living organisms, so they belong to biodiversity.

activities.prompt: Biodiversity includes ecosystems that living things inhabit.
activities.explanation: Ecosystems are part of the variety of life on Earth.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its correct meaning.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an idea with its role in conservation.

activities.prompt: Why must conservation strategies suit a geographical setting?
options: Because geography influences protection and management.
Because biodiversity is evenly spread everywhere.
Because every habitat needs an identical strategy.
Because ecotourism has no environmental impact.
activities.explanation: Geography affects how living organisms are protected and managed.

activities.prompt: Which statement about rivers, mountains and valleys is correct?
options: They can be barriers or corridors for wildlife.
They always serve as barriers for wildlife.
They always serve as corridors for wildlife.
They never affect the movement of wildlife.
activities.explanation: These landforms can act as barriers or corridors for wildlife.

activities.prompt: A map shows varied life in the Himalaya and Western Ghats. What does this suggest?
options: These hotspots show that biodiversity is unevenly spread.
The map shows equal biodiversity on every part of Earth.
Biodiversity exists only in these two mountain regions.
Only one of these areas really needs protection.

why.The map shows equal biodiversity on ever: This wrongly assumes every place has the same biodiversity.
why.Biodiversity exists only in these two mo: This wrongly thinks biodiversity exists only in mountain regions.
why.Only one of these areas really needs pro: This wrongly assumes only one hotspot needs protection.

activities.explanation: The Himalaya and Western Ghats are hotspots, showing uneven biodiversity.

activities.prompt: The Himalaya and Western Ghats have different geography. Should both use one plan?
options: No, because each conservation plan should suit its geography.
Yes, because one plan always works well everywhere.
No, because mountains never need conservation.
Yes, because geography never changes protection work.

why.Yes, because one plan always works well: This wrongly assumes one strategy works well in every place.
why.No, because mountains never need conserv: This wrongly treats mountains as areas without conservation needs.
why.Yes, because geography never changes pro: This wrongly assumes geography has no effect on protection.

activities.explanation: Conservation strategies must fit each area's geographical setting.

activities.prompt: A government sees a river between two animal areas. Where should a wildlife crossing go?
options: Near the river, because it can block animal routes.
Far from rivers, because water never affects animal movement.
Inside a tourist centre, because animals avoid open paths.
On every mountain, because valleys stop all wildlife.

why.Far from rivers, because water never aff: This wrongly assumes rivers never affect how animals move.
why.Inside a tourist centre, because animals: This wrongly assumes animal routes do not matter.
why.On every mountain, because valleys stop: This wrongly assumes valleys always stop all wildlife.

activities.explanation: A river can be a barrier, so a crossing should help movement.

activities.prompt: A forest tour crosses a route used by animals. What should guides do?
options: Keep routes clear and reduce the tour's environmental impact.
Make more noise so animals can hear the guides.
Block animal routes so tourists can walk freely.
Ignore routes and attract as many tourists as possible.

why.Make more noise so animals can hear the: This wrongly thinks noise helps protect animal routes.
why.Block animal routes so tourists can walk: This wrongly treats animal routes as unimportant to ecotourism.
why.Ignore routes and attract as many touris: This wrongly focuses on visitor numbers instead of low impact.

activities.explanation: Ecotourism should reduce impact and protect animal routes.

activities.prompt: A forest area wants tourist income and habitat protection. Which ecotourism plan is best?
options: One that balances visitors, protection, and sustainable development.
One that brings visitors but ignores habitat protection.
One that keeps all visitors out and stops tourism income.
One that raises visitor numbers even when the forest is damaged.

why.One that brings visitors but ignores hab: This wrongly thinks tourism matters more than forest protection.
why.One that keeps all visitors out and stop: This wrongly thinks protection means ending all forest tourism.
why.One that raises visitor numbers even whe: This wrongly ignores low impact and forest protection.

activities.explanation: The best plan balances tourism, protection, and sustainable development.

lessons.title: Forests and Human Communities

activities.prompt: How do forests shape the lives and traditions of forest communities?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Forests and Human Communities
activities.body: Forests provide food, fuel, fodder, medicine, shelter and timber. They also provide honey, fruits, nuts, resins and medicinal plants. Forest dwellers have a deep connection with forests. Their traditional knowledge passes through generations. Sacred groves are small forest patches protected by local communities. A Geographical Indication (GI) tag protects regional products and promotes cultural heritage. The Forest Rights Act recognises eligible communities’ rights over forest land.
keyPoints: Forests provide many useful products.
Forest dwellers pass traditional knowledge through generations.
GI tags and forest laws protect products, heritage and rights.
activities.explanation: Forests support people, culture and community rights in many ways.

activities.prompt: A forest community sells honey as a regional product. How can a GI tag help?
steps: The honey is a regional product, so GI tagging can protect it.
A GI tag is intellectual property, so it gives the product protection.
It also promotes cultural heritage, so the community's heritage is supported.
Therefore, the tag can protect the honey and promote cultural heritage.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Sacred Groves
activities.prompt: Sacred groves are small forest patches protected by local communities.
activities.explanation: Yes, local communities protect these small forest patches.

activities.title: Complete the Forest Products
activities.prompt: Forests provide food, fuel, fodder, medicine, shelter and ______.
activities.hint: Think of wood used to make things.
activities.explanation: Timber is another useful product provided by forests.

activities.title: Match the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each item on the left to its matching description.
pairs: Food, fuel, fodder, medicine, shelter and timber
Honey, fruits, nuts, resins and medicinal plants
Small forest patches protected by local communities
activities.explanation: Each description identifies an important forest idea from your lesson.

activities.title: What Does GI Tagging Do?
activities.prompt: What does GI tagging protect and promote?
options: Regional products and heritage
Forest fires and fuel
Healthcare and schooling
Water and sanitation
activities.explanation: GI tagging protects regional products and promotes cultural heritage.

activities.title: Ecological Commons
activities.prompt: What are forests, rivers, lakes, grazing lands, air and biodiversity called?
options: Ecological commons
Forest products
Non-timber products
Forest resources
activities.explanation: These shared natural examples are called ecological commons.

activities.title: Mendha Lekha
activities.prompt: Which statement about Mendha Lekha is true?
options: First village with forest-resource rights
First village with GI-tagged products
First village with sacred groves
First village with clean water
activities.explanation: Mendha Lekha became the first Indian village to gain forest-resource rights.

activities.prompt: A worker burns dry leaves beside a forest. What is the most likely result?
options: The fire may spread because people can cause forest fires
The fire cannot spread because dry leaves burn slowly
Animals will stop the fire before it reaches trees
Rain will stop the fire as soon as it starts

why.The fire cannot spread because dry leave: This wrongly assumes that dry leaves cannot spread a human-started fire.
why.Animals will stop the fire before it rea: Nothing in the fact says animals put out forest fires.
why.Rain will stop the fire as soon as it st: Nothing in the fact says rain always stops forest fires.

activities.explanation: Human-induced factors are among the main reasons for forest fires.

activities.prompt: One community protects a small forest patch. Another uses a larger forest. What follows?
options: The small patch is a sacred grove; the other may not be
The large forest must be sacred; the small patch is not
Both patches are sacred because local communities use forests
Neither patch is sacred because only timber makes a grove

why.The large forest must be sacred; the sma: It wrongly treats every large forest as a sacred grove.
why.Both patches are sacred because local co: It wrongly thinks forest use alone gives sacred-grove status.
why.Neither patch is sacred because only tim: It wrongly thinks timber, rather than local protection, defines a sacred grove.

activities.explanation: Sacred groves are small forest patches protected by local communities.

activities.prompt: A map marks forests, rivers, lakes, grazing lands and biodiversity. What does this map show?
options: These are all ecological commons in this area
These are only goods sold in local markets
These are all owned by one local family
These are all products made by forest fires

why.These are only goods sold in local marke: It wrongly treats ecological commons as only market goods.
why.These are all owned by one local family: It wrongly treats ecological commons as private family property.
why.These are all products made by forest fi: It wrongly treats ecological commons as products made by fires.

activities.explanation: Ecological commons include forests, rivers, lakes, grazing lands and biodiversity.

activities.prompt: An eligible community wants rights over forest land. What should the government do?
options: Recognise the community's rights over that forest land
Give one outsider rights over the community's forest land
Recognise only timber rights and leave land rights out
Wait until the community leaves its forest land

why.Give one outsider rights over the commun: It wrongly gives rights to an outsider instead of the eligible community.
why.Recognise only timber rights and leave l: It wrongly limits the Forest Rights Act to timber rights.
why.Wait until the community leaves its fore: It wrongly assumes the community must leave before rights can apply.

activities.explanation: The Forest Rights Act recognises eligible communities' rights over forest land.

activities.prompt: A community tags its regional honey and passes forest skills to children. Why can both actions protect its heritage?
options: The tag protects the product; shared knowledge passes heritage onward
The tag grants forest land; shared knowledge causes forest fires
The tag stops forest fires; shared knowledge replaces local services
The tag ends all needs; shared knowledge protects timber only

why.The tag grants forest land; shared knowl: GI tags do not give land rights; knowledge does not cause fires.
why.The tag stops forest fires; shared knowl: GI tags do not stop fires; knowledge does not remove basic needs.
why.The tag ends all needs; shared knowledge: GI tags protect products, and knowledge passes heritage through generations.

activities.explanation: GI tagging supports heritage, and shared knowledge passes it onward.

activities.prompt: Mendha Lekha is the first Indian village with forest-resource rights. What does this show?
options: The rule can give communities rights over forest land
Every community gains forest rights at the same time
Only individual forest workers can gain forest land rights
Forest rights cover products but not the forest land

why.Every community gains forest rights at t: Being first does not mean every community gained rights together.
why.Only individual forest workers can gain: The Act recognises communities, not only individual forest workers.
why.Forest rights cover products but not the: The rule is about forest land, not only forest products.

activities.explanation: The Forest Rights Act recognises eligible communities' rights over forest land.

activities.context: A student is comparing two large natural regions shown on a map. One has green forests, while the other has hot deserts. Each region contains smaller ecosystem neighbourhoods. The student learns that these huge natural patches are biomes and that each one is a broad environmental region. The student wonders why different kinds of biomes can support different life.
activities.prompt: If the rainfall pattern of the green forest changed, what should the student expect?
options: The plant and animal life able to thrive could change.
The region would no longer contain any ecosystems.
All its smaller neighbourhoods would support exactly the same life.
It would necessarily become a hot desert.

why.All its smaller neighbourhoods would sup: Different neighbourhoods need not support identical life.
why.It would necessarily become a hot desert: A rainfall change alone does not prove that a hot desert will result.

activities.explanation: Rainfall patterns help determine what can thrive.

activities.context: A student is comparing two large natural regions shown on a map. One has green forests, while the other has hot deserts. Each region contains smaller ecosystem neighbourhoods. The student learns that these huge natural patches are biomes and that each one is a broad environmental region. The student wonders why different kinds of biomes can support different life.
activities.prompt: Why can the green forest and the hot desert be classified as different biomes?
options: Differences in temperature, rainfall patterns and main plant species affect what can thrive.
Both are land-based types, so they must support exactly the same life.
Both are broad environmental regions, so they cannot support different life.
Their ecosystem neighbourhoods are larger than the biomes containing them.

why.Both are land-based types, so they must: Being land-based does not make all biomes identical.
why.Both are broad environmental regions, so: Broad environmental regions can support different life.
why.Their ecosystem neighbourhoods are large: An ecosystem is a neighbourhood within, not larger than, a biome.

activities.explanation: The three listed conditions help determine what can thrive.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A green forest and a hot desert are different biomes because different temperature, rainfall patterns and main plant species help determine what can thrive.
Reason (R): Temperature, rainfall patterns and main plant species help determine what can thrive in each biome.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains how different conditions can lead to different biomes and different life.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A vast grassland is a terrestrial biome.
Reason (R): All ecosystems are water-based types of biomes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The grassland is land-based, while the reason wrongly treats every ecosystem as water-based.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a biome and an ecosystem.
activities.answer: A biome is a large natural region of the world, also describable as a broad environmental region. An ecosystem is like a neighbourhood within a biome. The biome is therefore the wider natural area, while the ecosystem is the smaller unit used to describe part of it. This distinction also applies when biomes are grouped into land-based and water-based types. It helps organise geography by showing that a broad region and the neighbourhoods within it are not the same kind of unit.
points: A biome is a large natural region.
A biome is a broad environmental region.
An ecosystem is like a neighbourhood within a biome.
The biome is wider than its ecosystem neighbourhoods.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A community in the Amazon Basin plans to protect the surrounding tropical rainforest, which is hot and wet throughout the year. The forest is part of the world's richest storehouse of biodiversity and is also called a 'gene bank'. The community also keeps cattle in a nearby grassland where rainfall is moderate but too little for dense forests. The forest helps maintain oxygen levels and balance the Earth's climate, while the grassland supports grazing, farming and livestock rearing.
activities.prompt: What should the community do to protect the rainforest while continuing suitable activities on the grassland?
options: Keep the rainforest protected and use the grassland for livestock, crop farming and animal grazing.
Clear more rainforest so that cattle can graze beneath dense forest trees.
Plant dense forests across the grassland because its rainfall is moderate.
Stop all grassland activities even though animals can graze and people can farm there.

why.Clear more rainforest so that cattle can: Cattle do not need dense forest land.
why.Plant dense forests across the grassland: Moderate rainfall cannot support dense forests.
why.Stop all grassland activities even thoug: The grassland can support these activities.

activities.explanation: This balances forest protection with grassland use.

activities.context: A community in the Amazon Basin plans to protect the surrounding tropical rainforest, which is hot and wet throughout the year. The forest is part of the world's richest storehouse of biodiversity and is also called a 'gene bank'. The community also keeps cattle in a nearby grassland where rainfall is moderate but too little for dense forests. The forest helps maintain oxygen levels and balance the Earth's climate, while the grassland supports grazing, farming and livestock rearing.
activities.prompt: If the community protects the rainforest but continues appropriate activities in the grassland, what is the likely result?
options: The community can preserve the forest's rich biodiversity and climate functions while continuing animal grazing and agriculture on the grassland.
Biodiversity is protected, but the grassland can no longer support animal grazing or farming.
The forest will maintain oxygen levels, but moderate rainfall will turn the grassland into dense forest.
Animal grazing continues, but forest protection removes farming and grazing from the grassland.

why.Biodiversity is protected, but the grass: The two activities can continue in the grassland.
why.The forest will maintain oxygen levels,: Moderate rainfall is insufficient for dense forests.
why.Animal grazing continues, but forest pro: Protecting the forest does not remove grassland activities.

activities.explanation: This protects the forest without wasting the grassland.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Tropical rainforests lie mainly between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, close to the Equator.
Reason (R): These regions remain hot and wet throughout the year.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The year-round hot and wet climate explains why tropical rainforests are found in these equatorial regions.

activities.prompt: Explain why tropical rainforests are found mainly near the Equator between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.
activities.answer: Tropical rainforests are found mainly near the Equator, between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn. These regions remain hot and wet throughout the year, providing the conditions needed for tropical rainforests. The largest such forests are located in the Amazon Basin. They also cover the Congo Basin and parts of Southeast Asia. Together, these areas form the world's richest storehouse of biodiversity. For this reason, these rainforest regions are also known as a 'gene bank'.
points: Mainly near the Equator
Between the two tropics
Hot and wet throughout the year
Rich biodiversity or 'gene bank'
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a school field trip, a student visited the Rann of Kutch. Instead of the dry salt desert expected, the student walked through a marshy wetland during the monsoon. Around its edges, the ground was sandy and vegetation was sparse. A guide explained that desert organisms can store water and withstand heat and dryness. The student planned to compare the Rann with the cold Gobi in Asia and the hot Sahara in Africa.
activities.prompt: The monsoon ends. What is most likely to happen to the wetland at the Rann of Kutch?
options: The wet area would recede and dry, desert-like ground would return.
The wetland would remain unchanged because all deserts are permanently marshy.
The area would become densely wooded because sparse vegetation usually develops into forests.
The wetland would become tundra because deserts have long and severe winters.

why.The wetland would remain unchanged becau: This wrongly assumes that all deserts are permanently marshy.
why.The area would become densely wooded bec: Sparse vegetation does not mean that it must develop into dense forest.
why.The wetland would become tundra because: Long, harsh winters and permafrost are features of tundra, not deserts.

activities.explanation: The Rann becomes a marshy wetland during the monsoon.

activities.context: During a school field trip, a student visited the Rann of Kutch. Instead of the dry salt desert expected, the student walked through a marshy wetland during the monsoon. Around its edges, the ground was sandy and vegetation was sparse. A guide explained that desert organisms can store water and withstand heat and dryness. The student planned to compare the Rann with the cold Gobi in Asia and the hot Sahara in Africa.
activities.prompt: Which project would best show what the student learned about deserts?
options: Compare the Rann, Sahara, and Gobi to show differences in desert climate and the Rann's monsoon change.
Study only the Sahara and describe every desert as hot and dry without any wet season.
Compare the Rann with tundra and identify both as the world's driest biome.
Study minerals and oil in the Gobi while leaving out rainfall, temperature, and monsoon effects.

why.Study only the Sahara and describe every: This ignores the cold Gobi and the Rann's marshy period.
why.Compare the Rann with tundra and identif: Tundra is the coldest biome, while deserts are the driest biomes.
why.Study minerals and oil in the Gobi while: Mineral and oil resources are useful facts, but this project does not apply the lesson about desert climates.

activities.explanation: This comparison uses examples of hot and cold deserts and explains the Rann's marshy monsoon period.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Rann of Kutch is one of the world's largest salt deserts.
Reason (R): The Rann of Kutch becomes a marshy wetland during the monsoon.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but becoming a marshy wetland does not explain why the Rann is a large salt desert.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Trees have difficulty growing in tundra.
Reason (R): Frozen ground called permafrost makes tree growth difficult.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and permafrost directly explains the difficulty of tree growth in tundra.

activities.prompt: Explain how deserts and tundra make life difficult for plants and animals.
activities.answer: Deserts challenge life because they receive very little rainfall and often have sandy soil with sparse vegetation. Desert plants and animals have special adaptations for these harsh conditions. Organisms can store water and withstand heat and dryness. Tundra life faces different challenges because tundra is the coldest biome, with very long, harsh winters and short summers. Frozen ground called permafrost also makes it difficult for trees to grow. Thus, desert organisms must cope mainly with dryness, while tundra organisms experience severe cold and limited summer conditions.
points: Deserts receive very little rainfall.
Desert organisms store water and withstand heat and dryness.
Tundra has long, harsh winters and short summers.
Permafrost makes tree growth difficult.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A farming community gets drinking water from a pond and uses freshwater resources for its fields. Plants and algae in the pond capture solar energy, supporting herbivores, carnivores and top predators in the biome pyramid. A nearby ocean stores and distributes heat, affecting the Earth's climate. The community plans to remove some pond plants and must decide how this might affect the food relationships, freshwater needs and wider system of biomes.
activities.prompt: If the community removes some pond plants, what is the most likely effect on the biome pyramid?
options: Less energy will be available to organisms at higher levels.
More energy will become available to top predators.
Biomass will increase at every higher level.
The number of producers will rise automatically.

why.More energy will become available to top: Removing producers does not create a new energy source.
why.Biomass will increase at every higher le: Less energy is generally available at higher levels.
why.The number of producers will rise automa: Removing plants reduces rather than increases producers.

activities.explanation: Plants capture energy that can support higher-level organisms.

activities.context: A farming community gets drinking water from a pond and uses freshwater resources for its fields. Plants and algae in the pond capture solar energy, supporting herbivores, carnivores and top predators in the biome pyramid. A nearby ocean stores and distributes heat, affecting the Earth's climate. The community plans to remove some pond plants and must decide how this might affect the food relationships, freshwater needs and wider system of biomes.
activities.prompt: A student claims that reducing the heat stored by oceans cannot affect climate. Which response best corrects the student?
options: The claim is mistaken because marine biomes help regulate climate by spreading heat.
The claim is correct because organisms receive heat directly from the Sun.
The claim is correct because climate affects only plants, not marine life.
The claim is correct because a biome pyramid shows no relationships between organisms.

why.The claim is correct because organisms r: Solar energy is captured by producers and is not the stated cause of ocean heat storage.
why.The claim is correct because climate aff: Marine biomes contain relationships among different organisms.
why.The claim is correct because a biome pyr: A biome pyramid shows those relationships.

activities.explanation: Marine biomes affect climate by storing and distributing heat.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): If algae in a freshwater biome decrease, less energy will be available to organisms at higher levels.
Reason (R): Algae capture solar energy, and available energy decreases up the biome pyramid.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why fewer algae can mean less energy at higher levels.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Marine biomes are one of the two groups into which aquatic biomes are divided.
Reason (R): They affect the Earth's climate because their producers capture solar energy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but heat storage and distribution explain the climate effect.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Life on Earth

activities.prompt: Which statement about biomes is correct?
options: They are large natural regions.
They are tiny water neighbourhoods.
They contain only one plant type.
They cover every living thing.
activities.explanation: Biomes are large natural regions of the world. An ecosystem is like a neighbourhood within one.

activities.prompt: Tropical rainforests remain hot and wet throughout the year.
activities.explanation: Tropical rainforests lie between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.

activities.prompt: Match each biome with its description.
pairs: Hot and wet throughout the year
Large open areas covered mainly with grass
Driest biomes with very little rainfall
Coldest biome with very long, harsh winters
activities.explanation: Each description points to one of the main land-based biomes.

activities.prompt: Which group includes rivers, lakes, ponds and wetlands?
options: Freshwater biomes
Marine biomes
Terrestrial biomes
Desert biomes
activities.explanation: Freshwater biomes include rivers, lakes, ponds and wetlands.

activities.prompt: Put these groups in pyramid order, from the lowest level to the highest.
activities.explanation: Producers capture solar energy. Less energy is available at each higher level.

activities.prompt: Frozen ground called ______ makes it difficult for trees to grow.
activities.hint: This word starts with p.
activities.explanation: Permafrost is frozen ground. It makes tree growth difficult.

activities.prompt: Which option is a protected place for an important habitat?
options: A biosphere reserve
A river dam
A desert dune
A grazing field
activities.explanation: National parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves preserve important habitats.

activities.prompt: The Rann of Kutch stays dry throughout the monsoon.
activities.explanation: The Rann of Kutch becomes a marshy wetland during the monsoon.

activities.prompt: Which group of factors is a main reason for forest fires?
options: Human-induced factors
Ocean currents
Frozen ground
Salt deserts
activities.explanation: Human-induced factors are among the main reasons for forest-fire occurrences.

activities.prompt: Match each term with its correct description.
pairs: A type of intellectual property right
Small forest patches protected by local communities
Traditional knowledge passed down through generations
First Indian village to gain forest-resource rights
Forests, rivers, lakes, grazing lands, air and biodiversity
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a forest term with its description from the lesson.

chapters.title: Resistance and Resilience
chapters.summary: In this chapter: resistance and resilience: meaning and connection; rajputs and mewar: resistance and negotiation; ahoms and vijayanagara: endurance against expansion; marathas, sikhs and jats: building collective strength.

lessons.title: Resistance and resilience: meaning and connection

activities.prompt: How did communities protect their values while facing change and hardship?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding resistance and resilience
activities.body: India faced major changes between 1000 CE and 1700 CE. Resistance means actively opposing a force, authority or threat. It could include warfare, alliances, diplomacy or negotiation. Resilience means the ability to survive and adapt during hardship. Communities could resist invasions while protecting their core ideas, values and inherited traditions.
keyPoints: Resistance actively opposes a force, authority or threat.
Resistance can take military, political or cultural forms.
Resilience helps people survive, adapt and continue resisting.
activities.explanation: Resistance and resilience worked together during difficult times.

activities.prompt: A town faces war, unfair treatment, and outside rule. How can its people resist and stay resilient?
steps: The town can fight invaders, because resistance means opposing a threat.
Alliances and negotiation can resist threats without using weapons.
People can preserve core values, because resilience means surviving difficult situations.
Therefore, the town can resist, adapt customs, and keep its traditions.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How the ideas connect
activities.body: Resistance and resilience worked together. Resistance opposed invaders and other threats. Regional rulers and powers often resisted invaders entering their territories. Resilience gave people strength to continue resisting. Communities absorbed hardship, safeguarded core values and sometimes restored worship places or changed customs.
keyPoints: Regional rulers and powers often resisted invaders.
Resilience gave people strength to continue resisting threats.
Communities preserved traditions while adapting to new circumstances.
activities.explanation: Resilience helped communities and rulers continue resisting.

activities.title: Choose the meaning
activities.prompt: Which meaning best describes resistance?
options: Actively opposing a force or threat
Surviving and adapting through hardship
Joining others to protect shared values
Changing customs to suit new times
activities.explanation: Resistance means actively opposing a force, authority or threat.

activities.title: Two forms of resistance
activities.prompt: Resistance took both ______ and cultural forms.
activities.hint: This form of resistance involved warfare.
activities.explanation: Resistance included both military and cultural forms.

activities.prompt: Resilience is the capacity to survive and adapt in difficult situations.
activities.explanation: This is the meaning of resilience in your lesson.

activities.title: Match each idea
activities.prompt: Match each description with the correct idea.
activities.explanation: Resistance involves opposition, while resilience involves surviving and adapting.

activities.title: Why the connection matters
activities.prompt: Why does resilience help people keep resisting threats?
options: It gives people strength to continue resisting threats
It makes all threats disappear without any action
It removes the need for people to face hardship
It stops communities from adapting to new circumstances
activities.explanation: Resilience gives people the strength needed to continue resisting threats.

activities.title: Resilience in practice
activities.prompt: A community faces hardship. Which action best shows resilience?
options: It preserves traditions and adapts to new circumstances
It rejects all change and keeps customs unchanged
It uses only warfare and avoids community responses
It gives up its values whenever hardship increases
activities.explanation: They absorb hardship, preserve inherited traditions and adapt to new circumstances.

activities.prompt: A war brings fear and unfair treatment to a town. What response best shows resilience?
options: Restore places of worship and change some customs to suit new times.
Abandon every tradition and leave the town without any shared values.
Keep every custom unchanged and refuse to help the community.
End all cooperation and let the community fall apart completely.

why.Abandon every tradition and leave the to: This mistakes resilience for losing inherited traditions.
why.Keep every custom unchanged and refuse t: This mistakes preserving traditions for refusing to adapt.
why.End all cooperation and let the communit: This mistakes isolation for responding to hardship.

activities.explanation: This adapts to hardship while preserving inherited traditions.

activities.prompt: Region One meets invaders with soldiers. Region Two protects songs and beliefs. What do both show?
options: They show that both military and cultural resistance are possible.
They show that only military resistance can protect communities.
They show that only cultural resistance can protect communities.
They show that resistance must always involve a battle.

why.They show that only military resistance: This overlooks cultural resistance because no soldiers appear.
why.They show that only cultural resistance: This overlooks military resistance because no traditions appear.
why.They show that resistance must always in: This treats warfare as the only possible form of resistance.

activities.explanation: Military and cultural actions both oppose the invader or threat.

activities.prompt: A ruler faces an invader but cannot fight alone. What can the ruler do next?
options: Ask other powers for help and negotiate a peaceful agreement.
Stop all opposition and give up the region immediately.
Wait without action and hope the invader leaves soon.
Use threats alone and reject every possible agreement.

why.Stop all opposition and give up the regi: This mistakes avoiding opposition for a way to resist an invader.
why.Wait without action and hope the invader: This mistakes doing nothing for diplomacy or negotiation.
why.Use threats alone and reject every possi: This mistakes using threats for the wider choices resistance allows.

activities.explanation: This uses alliance and negotiation, both forms of resistance.

activities.prompt: A new exchange route brings together people with different beliefs. What response best shows lasting coexistence?
options: Develop lasting patterns of living together across religious lines.
End every shared custom so each group stays separate.
Remove all shared spaces and refuse any cooperation.
Change beliefs only when threats force communities to obey.

why.End every shared custom so each group st: This mistakes separation for responding to a new opportunity.
why.Remove all shared spaces and refuse any: This mistakes refusing cooperation for community resilience.
why.Change beliefs only when threats force c: This mistakes change under threats for lasting patterns across differences.

activities.explanation: This creates lasting coexistence across religious and cultural differences.

lessons.title: Rajputs and Mewar: resistance and negotiation

activities.prompt: How did Mewar find creative ways to resist and protect its freedom?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different ways to respond
activities.body: Different Rajput groups responded to Mughal power in different ways. Rāṇā Sāngā led a confederacy against Bābur at Khanua. A confederacy is a group joined for one aim. Some Rajputs, including Mewar, offered stiff resistance. The Kachhwāha Rajputs of Amber negotiated cooperation. Mahārāṇā Pratāp used guerrilla warfare, meaning surprise attacks, raids and ambushes. Mewar’s later resistance won recognition of its separate political position and autonomy.
keyPoints: Rāṇā Sāngā led a confederacy at Khanua.
Mewar resisted, while Amber negotiated cooperation.
Pratāp used guerrilla warfare and the Aravalli terrain.
activities.explanation: Mewar’s resistance and Pratāp’s strategy helped preserve its separate political position.

activities.prompt: A ruler wants Rajput support, but Mewar keeps resisting. What is the wise way forward?
steps: The Mughals wanted Rajputs because they offered military, political and administrative support.
The Kachhwāha Rajputs of Amber chose cooperation, so this was another possible approach.
Mewar’s route was different because its resistance remained strong, and Pratāp used guerrilla warfare in the Aravalli terrain.
Therefore, the ruler should negotiate a final treaty recognising Mewar’s continued autonomy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The leader at Khanua
activities.prompt: Who led the Rajput confederacy against Bābur at Khanua?
options: Rāṇā Sāngā
Mahārāṇā Pratāp
Bābur
Akbar
activities.explanation: Rāṇā Sāngā led the Rajput confederacy against Bābur at Khanua.

activities.title: Cooperation or resistance?
activities.prompt: The Kachhwāha Rajputs of Amber negotiated cooperative relationships.
activities.explanation: Yes. The Kachhwāha Rajputs of Amber chose negotiation with the Mughals.

activities.title: The rugged terrain
activities.prompt: Mahārāṇā Pratāp used the rugged ______ terrain to gain an advantage.
activities.hint: This rugged land helped Pratāp gain an advantage.
activities.explanation: Pratāp used the rugged Aravalli terrain to gain an advantage.

activities.title: Pratāp’s methods
activities.prompt: Which methods did Mahārāṇā Pratāp use against Mughal forces and their networks?
options: Long sieges at Chittor
Cooperation with Amber
Surprise attacks, raids and ambushes
Support for Mughal administration
activities.explanation: Pratāp used surprise attacks, raids and ambushes against Mughal forces and their networks.

activities.title: The siege of Chittor
activities.prompt: Mewar resisted Akbar’s siege of Chittor for less than five months.
activities.explanation: Mewar resisted the siege for more than five months, not less.

activities.title: Mewar’s resistance
activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: Mewar resisted Akbar’s siege of Chittor
He used the Aravalli terrain for surprise attacks
The Battle of Dewair helped bring down Mughal outposts
activities.explanation: The sequence moves from the siege to Pratāp’s strategy, attacks and Dewair.

activities.prompt: Akbar’s siege of Chittor lasted more than five months. Mewar kept resisting. What does this show?
options: Mewar was willing to resist Mughal authority for a long time.
Mewar gave up its resistance after a very short siege.
Mewar relied only on one direct battle against Akbar.
Mewar gained full Mughal support during the siege.

why.Mewar gave up its resistance after a ver: This ignores the siege lasting more than five months.
why.Mewar relied only on one direct battle a: Pratāp used guerrilla tactics, not only one direct battle.
why.Mewar gained full Mughal support during: The siege shows resistance, not Mughal support for Mewar.

activities.explanation: Long resistance supports Mewar’s refusal to accept Mughal authority.

activities.prompt: Bābur faced a Rajput confederacy at Khanua. Amber’s Kachhwāha Rajputs had cooperative Mughal ties. What pattern fits both events?
options: Rajput responses included both confederate resistance and negotiated cooperation.
All Rajputs used the same response to Mughal power everywhere.
Mughal power produced one identical response from every Rajput kingdom.
Mewar and Amber both ended all political contact with the Mughals.

why.All Rajputs used the same response to Mu: The two places showed different responses to Mughal power.
why.Mughal power produced one identical resp: One identical response cannot explain the different paths at Khanua and Amber.
why.Mewar and Amber both ended all political: It wrongly treats Amber as refusing Mughal cooperation.

activities.explanation: It correctly sees both confederate fighting and cooperative negotiation.

activities.prompt: A map marks Chittor in Mewar and rugged Aravalli hills nearby. Which plan fits Pratāp’s strategy?
options: Use the hills for surprise attacks, raids and ambushes.
Stay in one place and wait for a Mughal attack.
Avoid the hills and march through open ground.
Stop attacks and remove all military outposts.

why.Stay in one place and wait for a Mughal: Waiting in one place gives up the advantage of surprise.
why.Avoid the hills and march through open g: Avoiding the Aravalli terrain removes Pratāp’s geographical advantage.
why.Stop attacks and remove all military out: Ending attacks would remove the strategy’s pressure on Mughal networks.

activities.explanation: Pratāp used surprise attacks and ambushes in rugged terrain.

activities.prompt: The Mughals wanted Rajput military, political and administrative support. Which later policy best fits Mewar?
options: Recognise Mewar’s autonomy through a final treaty.
End Mewar’s separate status through an unconditional takeover.
Demand Mewar join a cooperative confederacy with Amber.
Keep Mewar outside all treaties and political relations.

why.End Mewar’s separate status through an u: The facts show negotiated recognition, not an unconditional takeover.
why.Demand Mewar join a cooperative confeder: Amber’s cooperation does not make Mewar’s treaty outcome the same.
why.Keep Mewar outside all treaties and poli: The final treaty shows political recognition, not complete separation.

activities.explanation: The final treaty recognised Mewar’s continued autonomy.

activities.prompt: Mewar used guerrilla warfare against Mughal forces and their networks. Why was this strategy useful?
options: It used surprise and terrain to weaken Mughal control.
It made fighting easier by avoiding all surprise attacks.
It helped Mughal forces reach more outposts safely.
It ended resistance by accepting Mughal authority at once.

why.It made fighting easier by avoiding all: Pratāp used surprise attacks, so this is false.
why.It helped Mughal forces reach more outpo: These attacks harmed Mughal networks rather than helping them.
why.It ended resistance by accepting Mughal: Mewar’s later resistance had not ended in Mughal acceptance.

activities.explanation: Surprise attacks and difficult terrain weakened Mughal control.

activities.prompt: Mewar’s military resistance continued until the final treaty recognised its autonomy. What does this sequence show?
options: Strong resistance could make the Mughals recognise Mewar’s separate position.
Any treaty proves the earlier resistance had no effect.
Mewar gained autonomy because it stopped resisting early.
The Mughals planned Mewar’s autonomy before any resistance.

why.Any treaty proves the earlier resistance: The treaty shows resistance affected the Mughal decision.
why.Mewar gained autonomy because it stopped: The sequence shows autonomy followed resistance, not an early surrender.
why.The Mughals planned Mewar’s autonomy bef: Nothing shows the Mughals planned autonomy before resistance.

activities.explanation: Mewar’s resistance forced recognition of its separate political position.

lessons.title: Ahoms and Vijayanagara: endurance against expansion

activities.prompt: How did clever leaders use nature to protect their kingdoms?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two kingdoms, strong defences
activities.body: The Ahom kingdom kept its independence from 1228 to 1826. Its commanders used forests, rivers, and monsoon cycles. Jayadhvaj Singha defied the Mughals, and Lachit Borphukan won at Saraighat in 1671. The Vijayanagara Empire arose in 1336 to stop Sultanate expansion into peninsular India. A river and rocky terrain protected it. Its capital was a major centre of trade, culture, and political power.
keyPoints: Ahom commanders used local terrain.
Lachit Borphukan defeated a Mughal fleet.
Vijayanagara had natural defences.
Its capital was an important trade centre.
activities.explanation: Both kingdoms used strong defences to protect their independence and power.

activities.prompt: How could commanders defend a kingdom without always meeting the enemy directly?
steps: The Ahoms knew about Assam’s forests, rivers and monsoon cycles.
They used local terrain because it avoided the need for direct confrontation.
Their 1671 victory over a Mughal fleet supports this strategy.
Local knowledge and terrain were therefore central to Ahom defence.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: For how long did the Ahom kingdom maintain its independence?
options: Almost two centuries
Almost four centuries
Almost six centuries
Almost eight centuries
activities.explanation: The Ahom kingdom remained independent from 1228 to 1826. This lasted almost six centuries.

activities.prompt: The Battle of Saraighat was fought in ______.
activities.hint: Think of the year when Lachit Borphukan defeated the Mughal fleet.
activities.explanation: Lachit Borphukan defeated a Mughal fleet at Saraighat in 1671.

activities.prompt: Match each person or place with its correct description.
activities.explanation: Each description shows a key action or meaning from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put these events in date order.
activities.explanation: The dates place each event in its correct place through time.

activities.prompt: Why did the Vijayanagara Empire arise?
options: To stop Sultanate expansion into peninsular India
To protect Assam’s forests and rivers
To control Mughal trade across India
To build a stronger Mughal fleet
activities.explanation: The empire arose in 1336 to stop the Sultanate expanding into peninsular India.

activities.prompt: Which statement describes Vijayanagara’s natural defence?
options: A river and rocky terrain aided defence
Forests and monsoon cycles aided defence
A Mughal fleet stopped its trade
A treaty ended its political power
activities.explanation: A river and rugged rocky terrain gave Vijayanagara a strong natural defence.

activities.prompt: Ahom commanders knew Assam’s forests, rivers and monsoon cycles. How could this knowledge help them in war?
options: They could use local terrain and avoid direct confrontation.
They could ignore the land and confront the enemy directly.
They could treat forests and rivers as unimportant.
They could rely on a treaty instead of knowing the land.

why.They could ignore the land and confront: This confuses knowing the land with choosing direct confrontation.
why.They could treat forests and rivers as u: This mistakes useful land knowledge for thinking land did not matter.
why.They could rely on a treaty instead of k: This confuses a treaty choice with the Ahoms’ land strategy.

activities.explanation: This is right because local terrain helped the Ahoms avoid direct fights.

activities.prompt: Ahoms knew forests, rivers, and monsoon cycles. Vijayanagara had a river and rocky terrain. Which plan uses each place’s strength?
options: Ahoms use familiar land; Vijayanagara uses natural barriers.
Ahoms ignore familiar land; Vijayanagara removes natural barriers.
Ahoms face enemies directly; Vijayanagara trades away its river.
Ahoms use a treaty; Vijayanagara relies on open ground.

why.Ahoms ignore familiar land; Vijayanagara: This reverses both strategies by removing their known advantages.
why.Ahoms face enemies directly; Vijayanagar: This confuses avoiding direct fights with meeting enemies directly.
why.Ahoms use a treaty; Vijayanagara relies: This confuses a treaty choice with each kingdom’s land defence.

activities.explanation: This is right because each plan uses its known land strength.

activities.prompt: Lachit Borphukan defeated a Mughal fleet at Saraighat in 1671. What does this suggest about Ahom methods?
options: Local terrain and knowledge helped the Ahoms win.
Direct confrontation was always the Ahom method.
The Ahoms knew little about Assam’s land.
No Mughal fleet could ever defeat the Ahoms.

why.Direct confrontation was always the Ahom: This mistakes one land-based victory for a rule about every battle.
why.The Ahoms knew little about Assam’s land: This confuses using land knowledge with knowing little about it.
why.No Mughal fleet could ever defeat the Ah: This turns one victory into a claim about every possible fleet.

activities.explanation: This is right because their land-based strategy worked at Saraighat.
