lessons.title: Marathas, Sikhs and Jats: building collective strength

activities.prompt: How did Marathas, Sikhs, and Jats turn challenges into collective strength?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different paths to collective strength
activities.body: Sovereignty means the right to rule. Maratha sovereignty was linked to Swarājya, meaning self-rule. Strategic alliances and forts helped them resist. Guru Nānak founded a movement that became Sikhism. It taught devotion to one God and equality for all. Guru Arjan Dev’s martyrdom, or death for his cause, became a turning point. The Sikhs chose firm resistance and resilience. Jats resisted heavy taxes and continued after Mughal victories.
keyPoints: Swarājya meant self-rule for the Marathas.
Strategic alliances and forts helped resistance.
Sikhs and Jats continued resisting despite hardship.
activities.explanation: Communities built strength through self-rule, alliances, faith and resistance.

activities.prompt: A village faces heavy taxes, and the revolt fails. What can the Jats’ experience teach us about collective strength?
steps: Heavy taxes and exploitation made Mughal rule unjust for the Jats.
Because of this injustice, the Jats rebelled under Gokul Jat in 1669.
The Mughals gained the upper hand, but Jat resistance continued.
This shows collective strength can survive a setback instead of ending at once.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Guru Nānak founded a spiritual movement that later became known as Sikhism.
activities.explanation: Guru Nānak founded this movement, which later became Sikhism.

activities.prompt: Match each community with its response.
activities.explanation: The Marathas used alliances, while the Sikhs and Jats chose resistance.

activities.prompt: An independent Maratha state was established in ______ with the rise of Chhatrapati Śhivājī.
activities.hint: Use the year given in your book.
activities.explanation: The independent Maratha state was established in 1674.

activities.prompt: Which forts helped the Marathas resist the Mughals?
options: Raigad and Gokul
Sinhagad and Gokul
Raigad and Sinhagad
Water and armouries
activities.explanation: Raigad and Sinhagad helped the Marathas resist the Mughals.

activities.prompt: Put the Jat resistance in the order described in your book.
activities.explanation: The Jats faced heavy taxes, rebelled in 1669, and continued resisting afterwards.

activities.prompt: After Guru Arjan Dev’s martyrdom, what did persecution lead the Sikhs to decide?
options: More heavy taxes and rituals
Strategic alliances and self-rule
Strong forts and large armouries
Firm resistance and resilience
activities.explanation: The Sikhs decided that persecution required firm resistance and resilience.

activities.prompt: Sikhism teaches one God, social equality and no rituals. A school event uses a special ritual and gives one group less respect. How should it change?
options: Remove the ritual and give every group equal respect.
Keep the ritual, but treat every group equally.
Remove the ritual, but keep one group lower.
Keep the ritual and let one group lead it.

why.Keep the ritual, but treat every group e: This notices equality but forgets Sikh rejection of rituals.
why.Remove the ritual, but keep one group lo: This removes rituals but misunderstands social equality.
why.Keep the ritual and let one group lead i: This treats ritual and special status as more important than Sikh teaching.

activities.explanation: This follows both Sikh equality and rejection of rituals.

activities.prompt: Maratha sovereignty was linked to Swarājya, or self-rule. Marathas used strategic alliances to extend control. Two regions want to work together without giving up self-rule. What should they do?
options: Form a strategic alliance and keep their own self-rule.
Give up self-rule so one region can control both.
Avoid all alliances so each region stays independent.
Join an alliance but remove every local ruler.

why.Give up self-rule so one region can cont: This thinks an alliance requires losing self-rule.
why.Avoid all alliances so each region stays: This thinks alliances contradict Maratha ideas of sovereignty.
why.Join an alliance but remove every local: This confuses joining an alliance with ending self-rule.

activities.explanation: This combines Maratha self-rule with the use of strategic alliances.

activities.prompt: Heavy taxes led Jats to rebel under Gokul Jat in 1669. A Maratha state began in 1674. Jat resistance continued after the Mughals gained the upper hand. What summary is correct?
options: Jats rebelled first, and Jat resistance continued after Mughal victory.
Marathas acted first, and Jat resistance ended after Mughal victory.
Both groups acted together, and Jat resistance ended at once.
Jats acted later, but Maratha control continued after Mughal victory.

why.Marathas acted first, and Jat resistance: This reverses the order and wrongly ends Jat resistance after victory.
why.Both groups acted together, and Jat resi: This wrongly puts both events in the same year and ends resistance.
why.Jats acted later, but Maratha control co: This reverses the order and confuses Jat resistance with Maratha control.

activities.explanation: The Jat revolt was in 1669, and Jat resistance continued after Mughal success.

lessons.title: Bhakti, Sulh-i-kul and temples: preserving traditions

activities.prompt: How did people preserve devotion and build community when temples were not possible?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Devotion, Peace and Temples
activities.body: Bhakti was personal devotion to the divine, expressed through hymns. It taught inclusion, equality, simplicity, and a connection with everyday life. It offered spiritual refuge. Community singing, called sankīrtan, brought people together and bridged social divisions. Local languages strengthened shared identities. Akbar adopted Sulh-i-kul as a government policy. It meant peace with all. Temples supported local life, workers, and rulers.
keyPoints: Bhakti expressed personal devotion through hymns.
Community singing and local languages built shared identities.
Sulh-i-kul meant peace with all.
Temples supported workers and gained ruler support.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how devotion, peace, and temples supported communities.

activities.prompt: Your town wants a place for devotion, but cannot build a temple. How can people show devotion and build unity?
steps: Bhakti is personal devotion expressed through hymns, so singing fits its meaning.
When temples cannot be built, devotees can use nām kīrtan instead.
Sankīrtan brings people together and builds a shared sense of community.
Using local languages can strengthen identity, so shared songs can create solidarity.
Therefore, the town can hold community hymn gatherings without building a temple.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Was Bhakti?
activities.prompt: Which description fits Bhakti?
options: A tradition of devotion expressed through hymns
A policy of peace and universal toleration
A system for managing land grants
A method of providing specialised jobs
activities.explanation: Bhakti was a tradition of personal devotion to the divine. People expressed it through hymns.

activities.title: When Temples Could Not Be Built
activities.prompt: What did devotees use when temples could not be built?
options: Nonmaterial forms such as nām kīrtan
Land grants that employed temple workers
Political support from nearby rulers
Local languages for shared identities
activities.explanation: Devotees used nonmaterial forms such as nām kīrtan. This helped them practise devotion without temples.

activities.title: The Name for Community Singing
activities.prompt: Community singing called ______ brought large gatherings and fostered a shared sense of community.
activities.hint: Use the lesson’s name for community singing.
activities.explanation: Sankīrtan was community singing. It brought large gatherings and fostered community.

activities.title: The Meaning of Sulh-i-kul
activities.prompt: What did Sulh-i-kul mean?
options: Peace with all and universal toleration
Personal devotion to the divine
Community singing and shared identity
Land grants and specialised employment
activities.explanation: Sulh-i-kul meant peace with all, universal toleration and absolute peace.

activities.title: Matching Traditions and Meanings
activities.prompt: Match each tradition or term with its meaning.
pairs: A nonmaterial form when temples could not be built
activities.explanation: Each pair shows the meaning given in the lesson.

activities.title: Order of Topics
activities.prompt: Put these topics in their page order in your book.
items: Bhakti as personal devotion through hymns
activities.explanation: The pages move from Bhakti and community singing to Sulh-i-kul and temples.

activities.prompt: People from different social groups join a community hymn gathering. What result did Bhakti saints seek?
options: It bridged social divisions.
It made everyone follow one ruler.
It removed the need for devotion.
It ended the need for community singing.

This confuses shared community with political rule.
This mistakes singing for abandoning devotion.
This confuses the gathering's result with its purpose.

activities.explanation: This is right because singing helped bridge social divisions.

activities.prompt: A village temple employs many workers and manages land. Another village holds large hymn gatherings without a temple. How do their main roles differ?
options: The temple village creates jobs; the other builds community through singing.
The temple village builds unity; the other manages land grants.
The temple village provides land grants; the other creates many jobs.
The temple village builds singing communities; the other supports temple workers.

why.The temple village builds unity; the oth: This swaps the roles of temples and hymn gatherings.
why.The temple village provides land grants;: This overlooks the land grants managed by temples.
why.The temple village builds singing commun: This assigns temple workers to a hymn gathering.

activities.explanation: This is right because temples provided jobs and singing built community.

activities.prompt: A temple record lists land grants and specialised workers. What can we understand from this source?
options: The temple shaped the local economy.
The temple only served the ruler.
The temple ended all community life.
The temple relied only on hymns.

It reverses support: rulers supported temples, not the reverse.
It mistakes economic work for the absence of community life.
It confuses hymns with the work done by temples.

activities.explanation: This is right because temples managed land and employed many workers.

activities.prompt: During the later part of his reign, Akbar adopts Sulh-i-kul. Which action best follows it?
options: Accept all faiths and keep universal peace.
Allow only one faith in the whole region.
Use temples to control every local worker.
Make state peace depend on temple grants.

why.Allow only one faith in the whole region: This mistakes toleration for forcing one faith.
why.Use temples to control every local worke: This confuses temple jobs with the meaning of toleration.
why.Make state peace depend on temple grants: This confuses temple grants with the meaning of state peace.

activities.explanation: This is right because Sulh-i-kul means peace with all and universal toleration.

activities.prompt: Some devotees cannot build a temple. They use nām kīrtan instead. Why might they choose it?
options: It lets them show devotion without a building.
It makes devotion depend on temple land.
It removes the need for a spiritual refuge.
It makes community singing less useful.

This reverses the relation between devotion and temple buildings.
why.It removes the need for a spiritual refu: It confuses a spiritual refuge with losing one.
It overlooks how community singing brings people together.

activities.explanation: This is right because nonmaterial forms were used when temples could not be built.

activities.prompt: People sing sacred hymns in their own local language. Why did this strengthen their shared identity?
options: They found common words and felt more united.
They rejected the need for everyday devotion.
They stopped sharing hymns with other people.
They gained control over temple land grants.

why.They rejected the need for everyday devo: It mistakes language use for rejecting everyday life.
why.They stopped sharing hymns with other pe: It confuses local identity with ending shared singing.
why.They gained control over temple land gra: It confuses cultural solidarity with temple administration.

activities.explanation: This is right because local languages strengthened identities and solidarity.

lessons.title: Agriculture, trade and the Indian Ocean

activities.prompt: How did farming, trade, and money shape life around the Indian Ocean?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Farming, finance and trade
activities.body: Agriculture supported the state, and land revenue was its main income source. Some Delhi Sultans took land tax as high as 50 per cent of farm production. Irrigation means supplying water to fields. New irrigation methods helped farming, while small-scale irrigation shaped the Vijayanagara economy. A hunḍī was a financial instrument for large deals. Inland trade grew with towns, and India became a major Indian Ocean trading centre.
keyPoints: Land revenue was the main source of state income.
Water-supplying technologies increased farm output.
Small-scale irrigation shaped the Vijayanagara economy.
Hunḍīs supported large deals and trading grew.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how farming, finance and trade supported a strong economy.

activities.prompt: How can a trader make a big deal without carrying heavy money?
steps: The trader wants a large business deal, not heavy cash.
A hunḍī works because it allows large deals without carrying large money.
Sarrāfs and their agents operate hunḍīs, giving the trader a money network.
Thus, the trader can use hunḍīs instead of carrying heavy cash.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The state's main income
activities.prompt: Which income source was the main one for the state?
options: Coastal commerce
Hunḍī dealings
Land revenue
Indian Ocean trade
activities.explanation: Land revenue was the main source of state income.

activities.title: A financial instrument
activities.prompt: A ______ was widely used as a financial instrument.
activities.hint: It helped with large business deals without carrying money.
activities.explanation: A hunḍī was widely used as a financial instrument.

activities.title: Using a hunḍī
activities.prompt: What could a merchant do with a hunḍī?
options: Handle large deals without carrying money
Collect land tax from farm producers
Control coastal trade under local rulers
Supply water to fields through irrigation
activities.explanation: Hunḍī transactions allowed large business deals without carrying large amounts of money.

activities.title: Match ideas with terms
activities.prompt: Match each idea to its matching term.
pairs: Ways to supply water to fields
activities.explanation: Each term matches the correct economic activity in the lesson.

activities.title: The money-changers' network
activities.prompt: Money-changers called sarrāfs and their agents run a network. Which instrument do they operate?
options: A rope pulley
A hunḍī
A Persian wheel
Land revenue
activities.explanation: Sarrāfs and their agents operated networks of hunḍīs.

activities.title: A strong economy
activities.prompt: Which statement best shows the economy's strength after invasions and unrest?
options: The economy stopped, and communities lost all strength
The economy stayed dynamic, with resources for resistance
Coastal commerce ended under regional rulers
Inland trade shrank when towns grew
activities.explanation: The economy remained dynamic despite invasions and unrest. Its strength gave communities resources to resist political and cultural threats.

activities.prompt: Some Delhi Sultans take half of production as tax. Which result follows?
options: Half of farm production becomes land revenue for the state.
Half of farm production stays with regional rulers and communities.
Half of farm production becomes income for money-changers.
Half of farm production becomes income for inland trade networks.

why.Half of farm production stays with regio: This confuses state land revenue with regional rulers' income.
why.Half of farm production becomes income f: This confuses land revenue with money-changers' income.
This confuses land revenue with income from inland trade.

activities.explanation: This is right because land revenue was the main state income.

activities.prompt: A trader needs a large deal. Which plan avoids carrying much money?
options: Use a hunḍī through sarrāfs and their agents for the deal.
Use a hunḍī to collect land tax directly from farmers.
Use a Persian wheel to move money between trading towns.
Use a rope pulley to carry coins through inland towns.

why.Use a hunḍī to collect land tax directly: This confuses hunḍīs with tools for collecting land tax.
why.Use a Persian wheel to move money betwee: This confuses irrigation technology with a financial instrument.
why.Use a rope pulley to carry coins through: This confuses irrigation technology with a way to carry coins.

activities.explanation: This is right because sarrāfs and agents operated hunḍīs for large deals.

activities.prompt: A map shows many trade routes around India. What does this suggest?
options: India had become a major centre of Indian Ocean trade.
India had stopped all trade with nearby coastal regions.
India mainly earned money from land tax and no trade.
India's coastal trade stayed only with regional rulers.

why.India had stopped all trade with nearby: This mistakes map links for a complete end of coastal trade.
why.India mainly earned money from land tax: This mistakes trading connections for a land-revenue-only economy.
why.India's coastal trade stayed only with r: This confuses local coastal control with the whole Indian Ocean network.

activities.explanation: This is right because India became a major centre of this trading network.

activities.context: Between 1000 CE and 1700 CE, invasions and wars brought political and social distress to many parts of India. In one region, the ruler formed alliances and negotiated while local groups also took up arms against invaders. The attacks included religious discrimination and damaged places of worship. Yet communities rebuilt their worship places, preserved inherited traditions, and changed some customs. Over time, patterns of coexistence developed across religious and cultural lines.
activities.prompt: What is the most suitable next step for the ruler when invasions continue and civilians face distress?
options: Seek allied support and negotiate safer terms for the community.
Rely only on armed defence and refuse every agreement.
Avoid organised defence and wait without preparing.
Stop opposing the invaders and give up the community's core values.

why.Rely only on armed defence and refuse ev: A belief that only warfare is possible overlooks other forms of resistance.
why.Avoid organised defence and wait without: Doing nothing would not protect the community from continuing hardship.
why.Stop opposing the invaders and give up t: Giving up core values would not safeguard what helped the community remain resilient.

activities.explanation: The case shows that resistance can include both alliances and negotiation.

activities.context: Between 1000 CE and 1700 CE, invasions and wars brought political and social distress to many parts of India. In one region, the ruler formed alliances and negotiated while local groups also took up arms against invaders. The attacks included religious discrimination and damaged places of worship. Yet communities rebuilt their worship places, preserved inherited traditions, and changed some customs. Over time, patterns of coexistence developed across religious and cultural lines.
activities.prompt: If the community wants to adjust to new circumstances while protecting its civilisation's core ideas, what should it do?
options: Safeguard core values while changing customs where circumstances require it.
Change all core values so that no inherited tradition remains.
Keep every custom unchanged and refuse to adjust to new circumstances.
Avoid adapting and stop restoring the community's places of worship.

why.Change all core values so that no inheri: Changing everything would weaken the inherited traditions that need protection.
why.Keep every custom unchanged and refuse t: Unchanging every custom would prevent the adaptation required in new circumstances.
why.Avoid adapting and stop restoring the co: Stopping restoration would not allow the community to recover from hardship.

activities.explanation: Indian civilisation remained resilient by safeguarding its core ideas and values.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Communities restored places of worship after invasions caused social distress.
Reason (R): Restoring places of worship was an active military campaign against the invaders.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The restoration is stated, but it was a community response rather than a military campaign against the invaders.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The ruler could oppose the invaders through both warfare and negotiation.
Reason (R): Resistance can include alliances, diplomacy, negotiation and warfare, so using different methods fits its meaning.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains why several methods of opposition can all be forms of resistance.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between resistance and resilience, and show how they are connected.
activities.answer: Resistance and resilience are related but not the same. Resistance means actively opposing a force, authority or threat. It can be military, such as warfare, or involve alliances, diplomacy and negotiation. Resilience is the capacity to survive and adapt in difficult conditions. It can give people the strength to continue resisting. For example, a community might fight invaders through an alliance and also preserve its traditions, restore a place of worship, and change some customs. The active opposition shows resistance, while surviving hardship while adapting and safeguarding inherited traditions shows resilience.
points: Defines resistance as actively opposing a threat.
Identifies warfare, alliances, diplomacy and negotiation as forms of resistance.
Defines resilience as the capacity to survive and adapt.
Explains that resilience can give people the strength to continue resisting.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After Akbar’s siege of Chittor, which lasted for more than five months, Mahārāṇā Pratāp changed his strategy. He used the rugged Aravalli terrain to gain an advantage. Surprise attacks, raids and ambushes were used against Mughal forces and their networks. The Battle of Dewair helped bring down important Mughal outposts in Mewar. Later, Mewar’s military resistance made the Mughals recognise its separate political position, and the final treaty clearly recognised its continued autonomy.
activities.prompt: If a Mughal force entered the rugged Aravalli area during Pratāp’s campaign, what response would best apply guerrilla warfare and Mewar’s use of the terrain?
options: Exploit the Aravalli terrain for an advantage and disrupt Mughal forces and networks through unexpected attacks and raids.
Avoid the rugged ground and seek one long, fixed confrontation with the Mughal force.
Wait for the Mughal force to withdraw and rely only on holding the outposts already captured.
Offer cooperation and stop military resistance even though Mewar is maintaining stiff resistance.

why.Avoid the rugged ground and seek one lon: This surrenders the terrain advantage central to Pratāp’s strategy.
why.Wait for the Mughal force to withdraw an: This ignores surprise attacks, raids and continuing resistance.
why.Offer cooperation and stop military resi: Cooperation suited some other Rajputs, but not Mewar’s resistant strategy.

activities.explanation: This directly applies guerrilla warfare and the use of terrain.

activities.context: After Akbar’s siege of Chittor, which lasted for more than five months, Mahārāṇā Pratāp changed his strategy. He used the rugged Aravalli terrain to gain an advantage. Surprise attacks, raids and ambushes were used against Mughal forces and their networks. The Battle of Dewair helped bring down important Mughal outposts in Mewar. Later, Mewar’s military resistance made the Mughals recognise its separate political position, and the final treaty clearly recognised its continued autonomy.
activities.prompt: After the Battle of Dewair brought down important Mughal outposts, what should Mewar do to continue its resistance?
options: Continue guerrilla warfare, use the terrain for advantage and disrupt remaining Mughal forces and networks through unexpected attacks and raids.
End military resistance and rely only on the earlier success at Dewair.
Keep the troops in one place for a long siege and avoid raids or ambushes.
Negotiate a cooperative relationship with the Mughals while keeping the captured outposts.

why.End military resistance and rely only on: Ending resistance contradicts Mewar’s continuing struggle.
why.Keep the troops in one place for a long: A fixed siege avoids the mobile methods that helped Mewar resist.
why.Negotiate a cooperative relationship wit: Cooperation does not continue Mewar’s military resistance.

activities.explanation: This continues the guerrilla methods associated with Pratāp’s strategy.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Kachhwāha Rajputs of Amber negotiated a cooperative relationship with the Mughals.
Reason (R): The Mughals valued Rajputs for the military, political and administrative support they offered.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The second statement explains why cooperative relationships with Rajputs were useful to the Mughals.

activities.prompt: Explain how Mahārāṇā Pratāp’s change in strategy helped Mewar resist Mughal power.
activities.answer: Mahārāṇā Pratāp changed his strategy by adopting guerrilla warfare. He used the rugged Aravalli terrain to gain an advantage. Surprise attacks, raids and ambushes were directed at Mughal forces and their networks. The Battle of Dewair helped bring down important Mughal outposts in Mewar. This continuing military resistance forced the Mughals to recognise Mewar’s separate political position. The final treaty then clearly recognised Mewar’s continued autonomy.
points: Pratāp adopted guerrilla warfare.
The rugged Aravalli terrain gave him an advantage.
He used surprise attacks, raids and ambushes.
Resistance eventually brought recognition of Mewar’s autonomy.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school activity, students must recommend strategies for rulers facing attacks. The Ahom side studies Jayadhvaj Singha’s rejection of a Mughal treaty and Lachit Borphukan’s victory over a Mughal fleet at Saraighat. Ahom commanders knew Assam’s forests, rivers and monsoon cycles and relied on local terrain. The Vijayanagara side must protect its capital, the ‘City of Victory’ near present-day Hampi, where a river and rugged rocky terrain provide natural defence. Students must explain how local advantages support endurance.
activities.prompt: What should the Ahom side recommend when planning to meet an attack?
options: Choose ground where forests, rivers and the monsoon can slow an approaching force.
Form an open line in the nearest clearing and face the attackers directly.
Choose routes without considering water or weather because terrain is unimportant.
Wait for the monsoon to end before deciding how the commanders should move.

why.Form an open line in the nearest clearin: This contradicts their reliance on terrain instead of direct confrontation.
why.Choose routes without considering water: This ignores the local conditions that their commanders knew.
why.Wait for the monsoon to end before decid: Their knowledge of monsoon cycles should guide the timing of movement.

activities.explanation: This applies their knowledge of forests, rivers and monsoon cycles.

activities.context: At a school activity, students must recommend strategies for rulers facing attacks. The Ahom side studies Jayadhvaj Singha’s rejection of a Mughal treaty and Lachit Borphukan’s victory over a Mughal fleet at Saraighat. Ahom commanders knew Assam’s forests, rivers and monsoon cycles and relied on local terrain. The Vijayanagara side must protect its capital, the ‘City of Victory’ near present-day Hampi, where a river and rugged rocky terrain provide natural defence. Students must explain how local advantages support endurance.
activities.prompt: If the Vijayanagara side is advised to leave its natural defences and meet attackers in the open, what should the students recommend instead?
options: Keep the army close to the river and rocks so attackers face difficult ground.
Move away from the river and rocky areas so the army can fight on level ground.
Leave the capital undefended while concentrating only on trade.
Relocate the capital without considering the river or rocky terrain.

why.Move away from the river and rocky areas: This sacrifices the strong defence provided by the river and rocks.
why.Leave the capital undefended while conce: This neglects the capital’s strong natural defence.
why.Relocate the capital without considering: Any move should consider the river and rugged rocky terrain.

activities.explanation: This makes effective use of the capital’s natural protection.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Ahom commanders relied on local terrain instead of direct confrontation.
Reason (R): They knew about Assam’s forests, rivers and monsoon cycles.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Their knowledge of these local conditions made reliance on terrain a suitable strategy.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Vijayanagara means ‘City of Victory’ and was established near present-day Hampi.
Reason (R): The name ‘City of Victory’ means that its capital was never attacked.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement about the name and location is correct, but the proposed meaning is false.

activities.prompt: Explain how knowledge of local conditions helped the Ahoms resist attacks and maintain independence.
activities.answer: The Ahom commanders did not depend on direct confrontation. Because they knew about Assam’s forests, rivers and monsoon cycles, they could use local terrain when planning how to meet threats. This approach helped them preserve independence for almost six centuries, from 1228 to 1826. Jayadhvaj Singha showed determination by defying the Mughals and rejecting their treaty within a year. Lachit Borphukan defeated a Mughal fleet at the Battle of Saraighat in 1671. Their endurance therefore rested on knowledge of local conditions as well as strong resistance to outside power.
points: Use of local terrain rather than direct confrontation.
Knowledge of forests, rivers and monsoon cycles.
Independence maintained from 1228 to 1826.
Examples of resistance under Jayadhvaj Singha and Lachit Borphukan.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After Guru Nānak founded a spiritual movement that later became known as Sikhism, the movement taught devotion to one God, social equality and rejection of rituals. The community faced persecution, and the martyrdom of Guru Arjan Dev became a major turning point. From then, the Sikhs decided that persecution required firm resistance and resilience, even when the struggle was difficult.
activities.prompt: If persecution against the Sikh community continues, what response best applies the decision described in the case?
options: Stop resisting and wait for the pressure to pass.
Replace collective resistance with separate individual acts of devotion.
Continue the struggle with determination despite the pressure.
Accept unequal treatment to keep the community together.

why.Stop resisting and wait for the pressure: This abandons the lesson that persecution required firm resistance.
why.Replace collective resistance with separ: The Sikh response involved collective resilience, not only individual devotion.
why.Accept unequal treatment to keep the com: Accepting unequal treatment contradicts Sikhism's teaching of social equality.

activities.explanation: This matches the decision to keep resisting despite persecution.

activities.context: After Guru Nānak founded a spiritual movement that later became known as Sikhism, the movement taught devotion to one God, social equality and rejection of rituals. The community faced persecution, and the martyrdom of Guru Arjan Dev became a major turning point. From then, the Sikhs decided that persecution required firm resistance and resilience, even when the struggle was difficult.
activities.prompt: If a Sikh community faces pressure to accept unequal treatment, which principle should guide its response?
options: The community should accept unequal treatment if conflict is reduced.
The community should defend equal treatment because Sikhism supports social equality.
The community should limit the faith to one person.
The community should insist on public rituals before treating people equally.

why.The community should accept unequal trea: Social equality does not make unequal treatment acceptable.
why.The community should limit the faith to: Devotion to one God does not mean that only one person may belong to the faith.
why.The community should insist on public ri: Sikhism rejects rituals, and equality is not conditional on them.

activities.explanation: Sikhism supports social equality, so it guides the response to unequal treatment.

activities.context: A community unable to build temples begins gathering for nām kīrtan, expressing personal devotion through hymns in its local language. Community singing draws large gatherings, and people from different social divisions join together. By sharing devotion and using their familiar language, they find a spiritual refuge, strengthen their shared identity and create solidarity. Akbar later adopts Sulh-i-kul as state policy, supporting peace with all and universal toleration.
activities.prompt: If the community replaced its local language in these gatherings with a language people did not use in everyday life, what would be the likely effect?
options: Shared identities and solidarity would weaken.
Shared identities and solidarity would strengthen.
Shared identities and solidarity would remain completely unchanged.
Shared identities and solidarity would disappear altogether.

why.Shared identities and solidarity would s: The change would remove an important source of solidarity.
why.Shared identities and solidarity would r: No fact suggests that identity and solidarity remain unchanged.
why.Shared identities and solidarity would d: The effect would be weakening, not complete disappearance.

activities.explanation: Local languages strengthened shared identities.

activities.context: A community unable to build temples begins gathering for nām kīrtan, expressing personal devotion through hymns in its local language. Community singing draws large gatherings, and people from different social divisions join together. By sharing devotion and using their familiar language, they find a spiritual refuge, strengthen their shared identity and create solidarity. Akbar later adopts Sulh-i-kul as state policy, supporting peace with all and universal toleration.
activities.prompt: What should Akbar do to put Sulh-i-kul into practice?
options: Accept people across social divisions and maintain peaceful relations.
Give preference to people from one social division.
Require all public gatherings to use a single language.
Use state power to restrict peaceful gatherings.

why.Give preference to people from one socia: Excluding one division would contradict universal toleration.
why.Require all public gatherings to use a s: A single language was not the stated meaning of the policy.
why.Use state power to restrict peaceful gat: Restricting peaceful gatherings would work against absolute peace.

activities.explanation: Sulh-i-kul required peace with all and universal toleration.

chapters.title: Governance and Public Policy
chapters.summary: In this chapter: governance and government; how governance evolved in india; good governance and its challenges; e-governance for better governance.

lessons.title: Governance and Government

activities.prompt: How can a community make decisions that truly work for everyone?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Democracy Works
activities.body: Governance is the process of making, implementing and monitoring decisions. Government means the institutions that exercise political power. Democracy needs more than elections. It needs transparent institutions, responsible representatives and citizens taking part. Transparent work can be seen clearly. Accountable representatives answer for their duties. Good governance makes public policies effective and responsive. Effective policies work well. Responsive governance answers people's needs. Democratic governance focuses on people and their welfare.
keyPoints: Government means institutions that exercise political power.
Governance includes making, implementing and monitoring decisions.
Democratic governance places citizens at the centre of political life.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how decisions, institutions and citizens work together in democracy.

activities.prompt: A town votes for representatives, but people cannot see decisions or ask representatives to answer. Is this strong democratic governance?
steps: Voting lets people choose representatives, but elections alone cannot make democracy work well.
When decisions and representatives cannot be checked, transparency and accountability are weak.
Democratic governance also needs citizen participation and the rule of law.
Therefore, strong democracy needs open institutions, responsible representatives and active citizens.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Is Governance?
activities.prompt: Which statement describes governance?
options: The process of making, implementing and monitoring decisions
The institutions responsible for exercising political power
Only the voting that takes place during elections
Public problems that citizens and institutions need to solve
activities.explanation: Governance includes making, implementing and monitoring decisions.

activities.title: Government and Political Power
activities.prompt: Government refers to the institutions that exercise ______ power.
activities.hint: This kind of power is exercised by institutions.
activities.explanation: Government refers to institutions that exercise political power.

activities.title: Needs of a Strong Democracy
activities.prompt: Besides voting, what does a strong democracy need?
options: Regular elections without any shared rules
Transparent institutions and responsible representatives
Political power without citizen participation
Street-light repairs without public feedback
activities.explanation: A strong democracy needs transparent institutions and responsible representatives.

activities.title: Ideas and Their Meanings
activities.prompt: Match each idea to its description.
pairs: Placing citizens at the centre of political life
Planning, maintenance, reporting faults and receiving feedback
Policies that are transparent, accountable, effective and responsive
activities.explanation: Matching them helps you connect each idea with its meaning.

activities.title: Citizens at the Centre
activities.prompt: Democratic governance places ______ at the centre of political life.
activities.hint: These people take part in decisions.
activities.explanation: Democratic governance places citizens at the centre of political life.

activities.title: Stages of Governance
activities.prompt: Put the stages of governance in order.
activities.explanation: Governance involves making, implementing and monitoring decisions in this order.

activities.prompt: A town holds elections. Citizens cannot see council decisions or question representatives. What is the likely effect?
options: People may distrust local government because transparency and accountability are weak.
People may trust local government because elections give them political power.
Representatives will become more accountable because elections alone are enough.
Public problems will disappear because citizens selected the representatives.

why.People may trust local government becaus: This mistake assumes that elections automatically make representatives accountable.
why.Representatives will become more account: This mistake assumes that voting by itself is enough for democracy.
why.Public problems will disappear because c: This mistake assumes that choosing representatives will remove all public problems.

activities.explanation: This is right because hidden decisions and weak checks harm transparency and accountability.

activities.prompt: Place A shows decisions openly and answers citizens. Place B hides decisions and ignores feedback. Which place shows stronger governance and why?
options: Place A, because transparency, accountability and feedback support responsible governance.
Place B, because secrecy and silence make public institutions stronger.
Place A, because voting alone makes public institutions work well.
Place B, because hidden decisions help citizens take part.

why.Place B, because secrecy and silence mak: This mistake treats secrecy and ignored feedback as signs of strong governance.
why.Place A, because voting alone makes publ: This mistake believes voting alone can make democracy work well.
why.Place B, because hidden decisions help c: This mistake thinks secrecy helps citizens participate in decisions.

activities.explanation: This is right because openness, answers and feedback support democratic governance.

activities.prompt: A public board shows planned street lights, completed repairs, reported faults and citizen feedback. What does this source show?
options: It shows governance because institutions and citizens work together on public problems.
It shows only voting because elections involve choosing people for office.
It shows only government because institutions exercise political power.
It shows no governance because decisions are neither made nor monitored.

why.It shows only voting because elections i: This mistake confuses elections with the whole process of making and monitoring decisions.
why.It shows only government because institu: This mistake confuses government institutions with the wider process of governance.
why.It shows no governance because decisions: This mistake wrongly treats monitoring and citizen feedback as unrelated to governance.

activities.explanation: This is right because the board shows institutions and citizens solving public problems together.

activities.prompt: A local council plans a new street light. It publishes the plan, names the responsible officer, and invites feedback. Which choice follows good governance?
options: The council publishes the plan, accepts feedback, and monitors the work.
The council hides the plan and ignores all feedback.
The council votes once and never checks the work.
The council keeps the plan secret because representatives decide alone.

why.The council hides the plan and ignores a: This mistake treats secrecy and ignored feedback as signs of good governance.
why.The council votes once and never checks: This mistake believes that one vote can replace implementation and monitoring.
why.The council keeps the plan secret becaus: This mistake believes representatives should work without citizen participation.

activities.explanation: This is right because transparency, responsibility, feedback and monitoring support good governance.

activities.prompt: A resident finds a broken street light. The resident reports it and sends feedback. Why might the resident do this?
options: To help institutions and citizens solve a public problem together.
To replace elections with a new system of choosing representatives.
To keep public problems hidden from local institutions.
To show that transparency and accountability do not matter.

why.To replace elections with a new system o: This mistake thinks reporting faults is meant to replace elections.
why.To keep public problems hidden from loca: This mistake believes public problems should stay hidden from institutions.
why.To show that transparency and accountabi: This mistake sees transparency and accountability as unimportant to citizens.

activities.explanation: This is right because reporting faults and feedback help solve public problems together.

activities.prompt: A town first holds an election. Later, residents help review a public project and check its results. Which choice best supports strong democracy?
options: Choose representatives, then allow citizens to take part and check decisions.
Choose representatives, then stop citizens from taking part in decisions.
Avoid representatives, because only direct citizen action supports democracy.
Hold one vote, then ignore how institutions use political power.

why.Choose representatives, then stop citize: This mistake treats excluding citizens from decisions as democratic participation.
why.Avoid representatives, because only dire: This mistake assumes participation means citizens must replace representatives for every decision.
why.Hold one vote, then ignore how instituti: This mistake thinks voting alone is enough for democracy to work well.

activities.explanation: This is right because democracy needs representatives, participation, transparency and accountability.

lessons.title: How Governance Evolved in India

activities.prompt: How did traditional ideas shape the way modern India is governed?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Traditions and Modern Governance
activities.body: Many societies used local and organic systems before colonial rule. These were local systems that grew within society. Colonial institutions influenced independent societies. India preserved pre-colonial knowledge and framed its Constitution around Indian values. Institutions joined traditional ideas with modern democracy. Governance was a sacred responsibility. The Sengol was a sign of righteous governance. Rām Rājya stressed honesty, transparency, compassion and welfare. Good governance brought peace, prosperity, justice and well-being.
keyPoints: India preserved pre-colonial knowledge while colonial influence continued.
Traditional governance values shaped modern democratic institutions.
Good governance meant social peace, prosperity, justice and well-being.
activities.explanation: India combined preserved traditions with modern democratic governance.

activities.prompt: A village changes rules after independence. What should guide the new rules?
steps: Many societies used organic local systems, so older self-government already existed.
Colonial institutions often influenced society after independence, so old habits remained.
India preserved old traditions, so its Constitution followed Indian values.
Modern institutions adapted old ideas to democracy, so rules should respect both.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Governance Before Colonial Rule
activities.prompt: What helped many societies govern themselves before colonial rule?
options: Local systems
Colonial institutions
Modern democracy
National mottos
activities.explanation: Before colonial rule, many societies governed themselves through local and organic systems.

activities.title: Systems That Grew Within Society
activities.prompt: Before colonial rule, many societies used ______ and organic systems.
activities.hint: These systems were based within local communities.
activities.explanation: Local and organic systems helped societies govern themselves before colonial rule.

activities.title: Match Governance Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its description.
activities.explanation: India preserved old knowledge, while colonial influence continued. Its motto and traditions also shaped governance.

activities.title: The Duty of an Ideal King
activities.prompt: Which duty belonged to an ideal king?
options: Protecting people and honouring duty
Preserving power and personal status
Keeping wealth and public rank
Choosing comfort and easy choices
activities.explanation: An ideal king's foremost duty was to protect people and uphold righteous duty.

activities.title: Order the Historical Periods
activities.prompt: Put these historical periods in time order.
activities.explanation: Local and organic systems existed before colonial rule. Colonial institutions then influenced societies. India adopted its national motto after Independence.

activities.title: The Ruler and the People
activities.prompt: Kauṭilya linked the ruler’s happiness with the happiness of the ______.
activities.hint: Think about those governed by the ruler.
activities.explanation: Kauṭilya linked the ruler’s happiness with the happiness of the people.

activities.prompt: A kind ruler hides facts and neglects welfare. Which qualities are missing?
options: Transparency, welfare, and a people-centred approach.
Personal power and strict punishment.
Isolation and secrecy in governance.
Private wealth without public responsibility.

This mistakes rule for power and punishment, not welfare.
This praises secrecy, although Rām Rājya values transparency.
why.Private wealth without public responsibi: This treats private wealth as enough, although public welfare matters.

activities.explanation: Rām Rājya includes transparency, welfare, and a people-centred approach.

activities.prompt: A display shows India’s motto, Constitution, and Sengol. What does it show?
options: India copied only colonial ways of governing.
India rejected all pre-colonial governance ideas.
India treated governance as only personal power.
India joined old traditions with modern democracy.

why.India copied only colonial ways of gover: This wrongly assumes modern institutions copied only colonial ways.
why.India rejected all pre-colonial governan: This wrongly assumes the Constitution and Sengol reject old ideas.
why.India treated governance as only persona: This wrongly treats governance as power, not a sacred responsibility.

activities.explanation: India’s motto, Constitution, and Sengol reflect Indian values and traditions.

activities.prompt: A ruler has wealth, but people suffer conflict. Is this good governance?
options: Yes, because the ruler has wealth.
No, because governance concerns only the ruler.
No, because social peace is missing.
Yes, because rulers hold all power.

This mistakes the ruler’s wealth for the people’s well-being.
why.No, because governance concerns only the: This wrongly treats good governance as the ruler’s private concern.
This wrongly assumes power proves good governance.

activities.explanation: Social peace is one test of good governance, and conflict harms it.

activities.prompt: A ruler feels happy while people suffer. What does Kauṭilya teach?
options: The ruler's happiness depends on the people's happiness.
The ruler's happiness depends mainly on personal wealth.
The ruler's happiness matters more than the people's happiness.
The ruler's happiness is separate from the people's happiness.

why.The ruler's happiness depends mainly on: This mistakes personal success for the people’s happiness.
why.The ruler's happiness matters more than: This wrongly treats ruler and people as having separate interests.
why.The ruler's happiness is separate from t: This denies the connection Kauṭilya drew between ruler and people.

activities.explanation: Kauṭilya linked the ruler’s happiness with the people’s happiness.

activities.prompt: A leader calls governance only power. How should this leader understand it?
options: As personal power to control other people.
As a duty only during difficult times.
As a reward for the leader's higher status.
As a sacred responsibility to protect people.

why.As personal power to control other peopl: This mistakes governance for personal power over other people.
This wrongly treats a continuing sacred duty as temporary.
why.As a reward for the leader's higher stat: This wrongly treats sacred responsibility as a reward for status.

activities.explanation: Tradition calls governance sacred, and the ruler must protect people.

lessons.title: Good Governance and Its Challenges

activities.prompt: How can good governance make our communities safer and fairer?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Good Governance
activities.body: Good governance affects daily life. It helps maintain law and order, so people can live safely. It protects citizens’ rights and freedom. It supports education, healthcare, transport and other public services. Good governance promotes justice, fairness and trust. It also needs cooperation, responsiveness, transparency, participation and the rule of law. Weak coordination, unequal access, misuse of offices and misinformation can harm it.
keyPoints: Governance supports safety, rights and public services.
Good governance promotes justice, fairness and trust.
Challenges include weak coordination, unequal access, office misuse and misinformation.
activities.explanation: Good governance improves public life while facing serious challenges.

activities.prompt: A town opens a clinic, but some families cannot reach it. What should be done?
steps: Governance helps people obtain healthcare, so the clinic matters to the community.
If some families cannot reach it, access to this service is unequal.
Unequal access can leave some communities behind, which is unfair.
Therefore, government and citizens should cooperate so services reach people fairly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Governance affects only special events, not daily life.
activities.explanation: Governance affects many parts of our daily life.

activities.prompt: What helps good governance work?
options: Unequal access to public services
Misuse of public offices
Cooperation between government and citizens
Misinformation and fake news
activities.explanation: Good governance depends on government and citizens working together.

activities.prompt: Good governance depends on ______ between government and citizens.
activities.hint: People and government working together.
activities.explanation: Good governance depends on this shared effort.

activities.prompt: Match each governance action with its result.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a clear result of good governance.

activities.prompt: What can weak coordination between institutions cause?
options: Coordination between institutions can improve
Citizen-government trust can grow
Government programme implementation can be harmed
Public office misuse can increase
activities.explanation: Weak coordination can harm how government programmes are implemented.

activities.prompt: Which situation can stop resources and benefits from reaching people?
options: Misuse of public offices
Unequal access to services
Misinformation and fake news
Weak coordination between institutions
activities.explanation: Misuse of public offices can block resources and benefits.

activities.prompt: A clinic is open, but remote families cannot reach it. What may happen?
options: Some communities may fall behind in getting services.
All communities may receive services equally soon.
Public offices may stop resources from reaching people.
Citizens may stop cooperating with the government.

why.All communities may receive services equ: One open clinic does not give every community equal access.
why.Public offices may stop resources from r: This confuses misuse of public offices with unequal access.
why.Citizens may stop cooperating with the g: A service-access problem does not necessarily end cooperation.

activities.explanation: Unequal access can leave some communities behind.

activities.prompt: A town improved citizen-government cooperation. What may now grow between them?
options: Trust between citizens and the government.
Conflict between citizens and the government.
Unequal access to public services.
More misuse of public offices.

why.Conflict between citizens and the govern: Better cooperation does not necessarily create conflict.
Improved cooperation does not show unequal access to services.
The situation does not mention misuse of public offices.

activities.explanation: Cooperation between citizens and government helps build trust.

activities.prompt: A map shows one village has a school. Another village has none. What does this suggest?
options: Equal access to education may not exist.
Different citizens may have different rights.
Law and order may be weak in the second village.
Government and citizens may not cooperate.

why.Different citizens may have different ri: A school map does not show differences in citizens’ rights.
why.Law and order may be weak in the second: A school map does not show the strength of law and order.
why.Government and citizens may not cooperat: The map does not show whether citizens and government cooperate.

activities.explanation: The map suggests that access to education may be unequal.

activities.prompt: A council publishes its budget and invites residents to meetings. What should this build?
options: Trust between citizens and the council.
More conflict between citizens and the council.
The rule of law may become weaker.
Fewer public services in the town.

why.More conflict between citizens and the c: Openness and participation support trust rather than conflict.
Nothing here shows that participation weakens the rule of law.
The situation does not show any change in public services.

activities.explanation: Transparency and participation can help build trust between citizens and government.

activities.prompt: An official misuses school funds. What may happen to children's meals?
options: School meal benefits may not reach the children.
School meal benefits may reach more children.
Schools may become more responsive to families.
Trust may grow among families and officials.

why.School meal benefits may reach more chil: Misusing funds does not help benefits reach more children.
why.Schools may become more responsive to fa: Responsiveness does not remove the harm caused by misused funds.
why.Trust may grow among families and offici: Misuse of public offices does not support good governance or trust.

activities.explanation: Misuse can stop resources and benefits from reaching people.

activities.prompt: A fake message says free healthcare will end. Why can it harm good governance?
options: It can mislead people about healthcare access.
It can guarantee fair healthcare for every family.
It can make transport services more responsive.
It can remove citizens' freedom to choose.

why.It can guarantee fair healthcare for eve: Spreading false information does not guarantee fairness in healthcare.
why.It can make transport services more resp: False messages do not make transport services more responsive.
why.It can remove citizens' freedom to choos: False messages challenge good governance rather than removing freedom.

activities.explanation: Misinformation can mislead people about access to public services.

lessons.title: E-Governance for Better Governance

activities.prompt: How could digital tools make government services easier for everyone?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Is E-Governance?
activities.body: E-governance means using information and communication technology by governments. Digital technology has changed how the government interacts with people. Governments use it to provide services and share information. It can make governance more transparent, so people can understand government actions better. It can make services easier to reach and use. This reduces paperwork and can save office visits. It also helps services arrive efficiently and quickly across large areas.
keyPoints: E-governance uses information and communication technology.
Governments provide services and share information.
It improves transparency, access and convenience.
It reduces paperwork and speeds up service delivery.
Digital access needs devices, reliable internet and useful skills.
Digital services must remain inclusive and accessible to everyone.
activities.explanation: Digital tools can make government services easier for everyone to use.

activities.prompt: What if a person can get a government service without visiting an office?
steps: E-governance uses digital tools for government services and information.
This can reduce paperwork and let people avoid government offices.
It can make governance more transparent, accessible and convenient.
However, people need devices, internet and skills, so access must stay inclusive.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Does E-Governance Use?
activities.prompt: Which statement about e-governance is correct?
options: It uses information and communication technology.
Only paper records are used by governments.
Information sharing is stopped completely.
Every service needs an office visit.
activities.explanation: Good choice. Governments use digital information and communication technology.

activities.title: A Changed Way of Interacting
activities.prompt: Digital technology has changed how the government interacts with people.
activities.explanation: Correct. Digital technology has changed the government's interaction with people.

activities.title: A Service From Home
activities.prompt: Your family wants a government service from home. What can e-governance help them do?
options: Access the service without visiting an office.
Handle more paper work at home.
Visit more government offices.
Wait for every service to close.
activities.explanation: Yes. Many services can be accessed without visiting government offices.

activities.title: Less Paper Work
activities.prompt: E-governance reduces the amount of ______ that citizens must handle.
activities.hint: This is the paper that citizens no longer need to handle.
activities.explanation: Correct. E-governance reduces the paperwork handled by citizens.

activities.title: Match the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each e-governance idea with its meaning.
pairs: Services reach large areas efficiently and quickly
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an important idea with what it means.

activities.title: Services for Everyone
activities.prompt: The government wants e-governance to work for all people. What must it do?
options: Keep digital services inclusive and accessible.
Allow only people with digital skills.
Limit services to places with reliable internet.
Raise the cost of every digital service.
activities.explanation: Correct. Digital services must stay inclusive and accessible to everyone.

activities.prompt: A person needs a government service. The service is available online. What is likely to happen?
options: The person handles less paperwork and may avoid an office visit.
The person must visit every office to receive the service.
The person receives no service because online services do not work.
The person must learn every government process before using the service.

why.The person must visit every office to re: This mistake assumes that people must always visit offices.
why.The person receives no service because o: This mistake thinks online services do not provide real services.
why.The person must learn every government p: This mistake believes digital use requires knowing every process first.

activities.explanation: This is right because e-governance reduces paperwork and can save office visits.

activities.prompt: One area has internet, devices and skills. Another lacks them. How will e-governance likely work?
options: The first area can use more digital services.
The second area can use every service equally.
Both areas will work well because the government uses technology.
The first area needs no reliable internet for digital services.

why.The second area can use every service eq: This mistake assumes technology works equally without these needs.
why.Both areas will work well because the go: This mistake ignores the different access available in each area.
why.The first area needs no reliable interne: This mistake believes reliable internet is unnecessary for digital services.

activities.explanation: This is right because people need devices, internet and useful skills.

activities.prompt: A digital service helps some people, but others lack internet or skills. What should the government do?
options: Keep the service inclusive and accessible to everyone.
Close the service so only skilled users can use it.
Assume everyone has the same devices and internet.
Remove support for people who cannot use the service.

why.Close the service so only skilled users: This mistake thinks access matters only for skilled users.
why.Assume everyone has the same devices and: This mistake ignores differences in devices and internet access.
why.Remove support for people who cannot use: This mistake believes people who cannot use it should lose support.

activities.explanation: This is right because government services must include and support everyone.

activities.prompt: A citizen chooses an online government service instead of an office visit. Why?
options: It can reduce paperwork and save an office trip.
It hides the service from people without internet.
It makes government information harder to share.
It prevents the government from improving its processes.

why.It hides the service from people without: This mistake thinks online services exclude people without internet.
why.It makes government information harder t: This mistake believes digital services make information harder to share.
why.It prevents the government from improvin: This mistake assumes e-governance stops administrative improvement.

activities.explanation: This is right because e-governance reduces paperwork and office visits.

activities.prompt: Before e-governance, a citizen handled papers and visited offices. What changes with it?
options: Paperwork can shrink, and many services need no office visit.
Citizens must handle more papers for the same services.
Government communication with citizens becomes less useful.
Large areas can receive slower and less efficient service.

why.Citizens must handle more papers for the: This mistake thinks digital services increase paperwork for citizens.
why.Government communication with citizens b: This mistake believes e-governance weakens government communication.
why.Large areas can receive slower and less: This mistake ignores the faster and more efficient delivery possible across large areas.

activities.explanation: This is right because e-governance reduces paperwork and office visits.

lessons.title: Public Policy and Public Welfare

activities.prompt: How does a small idea become a policy that helps everyone?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Public Policy Is
activities.body: Public policy is a planned course of government action to solve public problems. Public means everyone in a society or community. It explains what the government wants and why. It also explains who will act and how work will be done. It includes a way to measure success. Monitoring checks progress, while evaluation judges results. A feedback loop uses results to guide actions. Needed changes are made.
keyPoints: Public policies can quietly shape everyday life.
Public institutions carry out policies for public benefit.
Feedback from success checks guides needed changes.
activities.explanation: This card explains how public policy is planned, checked and changed.

activities.prompt: Rubbish lies around a housing area. How should the government improve it?
steps: First, it identifies rubbish as a public problem because it affects everyone.
Next, it plans how to remove rubbish because policy must be planned.
Then, it names who will act and how, because policy explains both.
Finally, feedback checks results, so needed changes can make the policy better.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In public policy, who does “public” refer to?
options: People living in one family
Government officers only
Everyone in a society or community
People who receive one benefit
activities.explanation: “Public” means everyone living in a society or community. It does not mean only one group.

activities.prompt: Public policies are often financed with public money collected through taxes.
activities.explanation: Public policies are often financed with public money. This money is collected through taxes.

activities.prompt: Public policy is a ______ course of government action to solve public problems.
activities.hint: Look for the word in the lesson’s definition.
activities.explanation: The lesson defines public policy as a planned course of government action.

activities.prompt: How can people help shape public policy?
options: By identifying problems, raising concerns and giving suggestions
By keeping every concern private and making no suggestions
By choosing every policy decision without public views
By ignoring problems and refusing to suggest changes
activities.explanation: People help shape policies by identifying problems, raising concerns and giving suggestions.

activities.prompt: Put the policy checking steps in the correct order.
activities.explanation: Monitoring checks progress, and evaluation judges the results. Needed changes guide the next action.

activities.prompt: A policy’s results show that changes are needed. What should happen next?
options: Make the needed changes
Keep the policy unchanged
Stop checking all results
Measure results without acting
activities.explanation: Changes are made when a policy needs them. The results then guide later action.

activities.prompt: A government plans pipe repairs for everyone. Why is this public policy?
options: It is government action planned to solve a shared problem.
It is a random act with no plan for a shared problem.
It is a private plan aimed at solving one household's problem.
It is a government plan without any public purpose.

why.It is a random act with no plan for a sh: This mistakes an unplanned reaction for a planned government course.
why.It is a private plan aimed at solving on: This wrongly treats a shared public problem as one family's issue.
why.It is a government plan without any publ: This wrongly assumes government plans need no public purpose.

activities.explanation: It is a planned government action to solve a problem affecting everyone.

activities.prompt: After checking results, new bins were added. Why?
options: The policy needed a change to improve its results.
The bins were added only to collect more taxes.
The policy had never included any way to measure success.
Only private groups could ask for needed policy changes.

why.The bins were added only to collect more: This wrongly makes taxes the only reason for changing policy.
why.The policy had never included any way to: This wrongly assumes checking results is not part of policy.
why.Only private groups could ask for needed: This wrongly places needed policy changes only in private hands.

activities.explanation: The feedback loop shows when needed changes can improve a policy.

activities.prompt: A map shows waste service in some areas only. Why worry?
options: The service may not reach everyone who should benefit.
Only areas with waste should receive any public service.
People outside the areas should not count as the public.
The map proves that no public policy exists anywhere.

why.Only areas with waste should receive any: This wrongly treats public service as needed in only some areas.
why.People outside the areas should not coun: This wrongly excludes people who also live in the society.
why.The map proves that no public policy exi: This wrongly assumes unequal coverage means no policy exists.

activities.explanation: Public includes everyone, so leaving some areas out raises a concern.

activities.prompt: Residents report unsafe swings. Which government plan is complete?
options: Set safe-swing goals and reasons, assign workers, choose methods, and measure results.
Repair swings only, and leave workers, reasons, and methods unnamed.
Name workers only, and forget the swing goal, reasons, and method.
Measure results only, and skip the goal, reasons, workers, and method.

why.Repair swings only, and leave workers, r: This wrongly leaves important parts of the policy unnamed.
why.Name workers only, and forget the swing: This wrongly thinks the goal and reasons can be left out.
why.Measure results only, and skip the goal,: This wrongly thinks measuring results can replace action.

activities.explanation: A complete policy explains its aim, reasons, workers, method, and measure.

activities.prompt: People report broken streetlights and suggest better lights. What can this do?
options: It can help shape a policy change that addresses the problem.
It can stop the government from making any policy.
It can change policy only after private money is raised.
It can affect only the people who reported the problem.

why.It can stop the government from making a: This wrongly assumes public concerns stop government action.
why.It can change policy only after private: This wrongly makes private funding a condition for policy change.
why.It can affect only the people who report: This wrongly limits policy effects to the people who complained.

activities.explanation: People can shape policies by raising concerns and giving suggestions.

activities.prompt: A reading programme uses tax money. Who should it mainly benefit?
options: Everyone in the public, because the policy is for public benefit.
One private family, because tax money can serve private needs.
Only government workers, because they implement the policy.
Only people who suggested it, because they shaped the policy.

why.One private family, because tax money ca: This wrongly assumes one private family should receive public benefit.
why.Only government workers, because they im: This wrongly treats public money as benefit for government workers only.
why.Only people who suggested it, because th: This wrongly assumes only people who give ideas should benefit.

activities.explanation: This is right because public policy serves everyone and uses public money.
