lessons.title: Stakeholders and the Policy Process

activities.prompt: How do people turn a public problem into a policy that works?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Who Makes Public Policy?
activities.body: Public policy is made and implemented by many people and organisations. Citizens spot problems, vote, join discussions and give feedback. Elected representatives raise issues, make laws and approve budgets. Government officials prepare policies, deliver services and check progress. Civil society groups, experts and the media study problems, suggest solutions and create awareness.
keyPoints: Citizens help by voting, participating and giving feedback.
Government officials prepare policies and deliver services.
Many groups study problems and suggest solutions.
activities.explanation: Public policy depends on the work of many people and organisations.

activities.prompt: A street light is broken. Which stakeholders should work together to solve it?
steps: Citizens identify the problem because policy starts when a public need appears.
Experts, civil society groups and the media suggest solutions because they study problems.
Elected representatives raise public issues before officials prepare an approved policy.
Many stakeholders must work together because they make and implement public policy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which group helps make and implement public policy?
options: Citizens and organisations
Only one government official
Only businesses and shops
Only people who make laws
activities.explanation: Many people and organisations work together throughout the policy process.

activities.prompt: In policy-making, the government collects information and consults ______.
activities.hint: People who study problems and suggest solutions.
activities.explanation: The government consults experts, stakeholders and the public.

activities.prompt: After a policy is approved, what happens next?
options: Programmes and schemes are made.
The policy stays only as a draft.
The policy replaces programmes and schemes.
All monitoring of the policy ends.
activities.explanation: An approved policy is turned into programmes and schemes.

activities.prompt: Put the policy-making process in order.
items: A public need or problem is recognised.
Information is collected and consultations take place.
A draft policy is prepared, reviewed and approved.
The policy becomes programmes and schemes.
activities.explanation: The policy moves from recognition to approval, action and continuous checking.

activities.prompt: Which statement about monitoring is correct?
options: Implementation is checked continuously.
Implementation is checked only before approval.
Implementation is checked only after approval.
Implementation is never evaluated.
activities.explanation: Policy implementation is continuously monitored and evaluated.

activities.prompt: Residents report a dangerous footpath. Which next step supports a fair policy decision?
options: Collect information and consult experts, stakeholders and the public.
Approve a final plan before anyone studies the reported danger.
Deliver new services without deciding on any public policy.
Wait for citizens to solve the danger without government action.

why.Approve a final plan before anyone studi: This reverses the order by approving before gathering information.
why.Deliver new services without deciding on: This confuses later service delivery with earlier policy-making.
why.Wait for citizens to solve the danger wi: This wrongly treats citizens as the only group that can act.

activities.explanation: This correctly puts information and consultation before policy approval.

activities.prompt: Residents recognise a public need. Which action should come first in policy-making?
options: Government gathers information and consults experts, stakeholders and the public.
Authorities prepare, review and approve a draft without consultation.
Officials turn an approved policy into programmes and schemes.
Officials monitor implementation and evaluate progress before delivery.

why.Authorities prepare, review and approve: This skips the earlier consultation that should come first.
why.Officials turn an approved policy into p: This skips earlier consultation, preparation and policy approval.
why.Officials monitor implementation and eva: This mistakes monitoring for the first policy-making step.

activities.explanation: This correctly begins by gathering facts and consulting different groups.

activities.prompt: Few people know why a new scheme was created. What should experts and media do?
options: Study the problem and suggest solutions to create awareness.
Approve the budget and make laws for the scheme.
Prepare and review the draft policy by themselves.
Monitor delivery and evaluate the scheme without explaining it.

why.Approve the budget and make laws for the: This confuses representatives' duties with experts' and media work.
why.Prepare and review the draft policy by t: This confuses authorities' duties with experts' and media work.
why.Monitor delivery and evaluate the scheme: This confuses officials' monitoring duty with the need for awareness.

activities.explanation: This matches the role of studying problems, suggesting solutions and creating awareness.

activities.prompt: A council has a safer-road policy and a programme plan. What should the scheme do?
options: Put the planned road work into action.
Set the general direction for safer roads.
Arrange the full plan for road work.
Check the results after road work begins.

why.Set the general direction for safer road: This confuses the scheme's action role with the policy's direction role.
This confuses the programme's planning role with the scheme's action role.
why.Check the results after road work begins: This confuses monitoring with the scheme's action role.

activities.explanation: This follows the rule that schemes put programme plans into action.

activities.context: A neighbourhood has reported that some street-lights are not working. The local government institution records the faults, repairs the lights and asks residents to report further problems. Residents identify dark areas and suggest where maintenance is needed. The institution publishes how decisions are made and explains the action taken. Although elections allow citizens to choose representatives, those representatives must still make decisions, implement them and monitor whether public problems are being solved.
activities.prompt: If residents stop reporting faults and giving feedback, what is the most likely result?
options: Citizen involvement would decline, so the institution might miss problems needing attention.
The institution would gain better information and could plan maintenance more effectively.
Representative responsibility would disappear because citizens would participate less.
Street-light maintenance would become more transparent because fewer reports would need recording.

why.The institution would gain better inform: Less feedback can leave institutions without useful information about problems.
why.Representative responsibility would disa: Participation and responsible representatives both support democracy.
why.Street-light maintenance would become mo: Transparency comes from openness, not from fewer citizen reports.

activities.explanation: Feedback helps institutions identify problems and improve maintenance.

activities.context: A neighbourhood has reported that some street-lights are not working. The local government institution records the faults, repairs the lights and asks residents to report further problems. Residents identify dark areas and suggest where maintenance is needed. The institution publishes how decisions are made and explains the action taken. Although elections allow citizens to choose representatives, those representatives must still make decisions, implement them and monitor whether public problems are being solved.
activities.prompt: After an election, a representative ignores citizens' requests and refuses to explain a decision. What should citizens do?
options: Ask the representative to explain the decision and accept responsibility for checking the result.
Accept the decision without challenge because election victory settles all responsibility.
Stop participating in decisions because elected representatives have political authority.
Make and implement a new decision alone without involving the institution or other citizens.

why.Accept the decision without challenge be: An election alone does not remove the need for responsible representatives.
why.Stop participating in decisions because: Democratic governance requires continuing citizen participation.
why.Make and implement a new decision alone: Decisions should involve institutions and citizens working together rather than one person acting alone.

activities.explanation: Responsible representatives should explain their decisions and be accountable for the results.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Transparency and accountability are central to governance in a democracy.
Reason (R): Democratic governance focuses on people and their welfare.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain why transparency and accountability are central.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Receiving feedback is part of street-light governance.
Reason (R): Governance requires institutions and citizens to work together on public problems.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Citizen feedback enables institutions and citizens to work together in solving public problems.

activities.prompt: Explain why voting in elections alone is not enough to make a democracy work well.
activities.answer: Voting in elections alone is not enough because a strong democracy needs transparent institutions and responsible representatives. Democratic governance rests on transparency, accountability, participation and the rule of law. It places citizens at the centre of political life and focuses on people and their welfare. Voting gives people a way to take part, but institutions and citizens must continue working together to make, implement and monitor decisions. Good governance must also make public policies transparent, accountable, effective and responsive. Therefore, elections alone do not provide all the institutions, rules, practices and participation needed for democracy to work well.
points: Elections alone are insufficient.
A strong democracy needs transparency, accountability, participation and the rule of law.
Institutions and citizens must work together to make, implement and monitor decisions.
Democratic governance focuses on people, their welfare and responsive public policies.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In modern India, a community is considering how its local institutions should work. Its leaders know that many communities were governed through local and organic systems before colonial rule, and that colonial institutions continued to influence society after independence. They also recognise that India preserved much of its pre-colonial knowledge and adapted traditional ideas of governance to modern democracy. A new leader wants the system to reflect Rām Rājya and the duties of an ideal king.
activities.prompt: If the leader is deciding what counts as successful governance, which approach best follows the ideas described in the case?
options: Make the ruler's happiness the main measure, separate from the people's happiness.
Treat social peace, prosperity, justice and well-being as signs of good governance.
Use government power mainly to serve the ruler's own interests.
Judge governance only by the ruler's ability to preserve personal authority.

why.Make the ruler's happiness the main meas: This wrongly separates the ruler's happiness from the people's happiness.
why.Use government power mainly to serve the: This wrongly treats governance as serving the ruler rather than the people.
why.Judge governance only by the ruler's abi: This wrongly makes personal authority the only measure of success.

activities.explanation: This matches the traditional measures of good governance.

activities.context: In modern India, a community is considering how its local institutions should work. Its leaders know that many communities were governed through local and organic systems before colonial rule, and that colonial institutions continued to influence society after independence. They also recognise that India preserved much of its pre-colonial knowledge and adapted traditional ideas of governance to modern democracy. A new leader wants the system to reflect Rām Rājya and the duties of an ideal king.
activities.prompt: How should an ideal leader act when personal authority conflicts with the welfare of the people?
options: Give personal authority priority because the leader controls the government.
Follow the ruler's wishes even when the people are unhappy.
Protect the people and uphold righteous duty, linking the ruler's happiness with the people's happiness.
Treat governance as a means of gaining power without accepting responsibility.

why.Give personal authority priority because: This wrongly makes the ruler's authority more important than the people.
why.Follow the ruler's wishes even when the: This wrongly separates the ruler's happiness from the people's happiness.
why.Treat governance as a means of gaining p: This wrongly treats governance as power without responsibility.

activities.explanation: This follows the ideal king's duty and Kauṭilya's link between the two kinds of happiness.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): After Independence, India rejected all pre-colonial institutions and traditions.
Reason (R): India preserved much of its knowledge of pre-colonial institutions and traditions.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because the reason is true and states that India preserved, rather than rejected, this knowledge.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Good governance in Indian tradition was judged by social peace, prosperity, justice and well-being.
Reason (R): An ideal king's foremost duty was to protect people and uphold righteous duty.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The ruler's duty to protect people explains why governance was judged by peace, prosperity, justice and well-being.

activities.prompt: Explain how pre-colonial traditions and modern democracy are connected in India's governance.
activities.answer: India's governance grew from both continuity and adaptation. Before colonial rule, many societies used local and organic systems. After independence, colonial institutions could still influence society, so modern institutions did not simply erase the past. India preserved much of its knowledge of pre-colonial institutions and traditions, and its Constitution was framed according to India's own values and ideals. Indian institutions therefore adapted traditional ideas of governance to modern democracy, making older traditions relevant within modern democratic governance.
points: Pre-colonial societies used local and organic systems.
India preserved much pre-colonial institutional knowledge.
The Constitution reflected India's own values and ideals.
Traditional ideas were adapted to modern democracy.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A town’s education, healthcare and transport programmes are delivered by different institutions. The institutions do not coordinate properly, so government programmes are not implemented effectively. Some communities also have less access to these services than others. Meanwhile, a false message about a public service programme is spreading online. Citizens are unsure which information to trust, while some public offices are being misused so that resources do not reach people.
activities.prompt: If the institutions began coordinating properly, what would be the most likely result?
options: Government programmes would be implemented more effectively.
Unequal access would increase because services would become less fair.
Public offices would be misused more often because resources would be harder to distribute.
Citizens would have less reason to cooperate with the government.

why.Unequal access would increase because se: Better coordination would not be expected to make services less fair.
why.Public offices would be misused more oft: The misuse of offices is a separate problem from weak coordination.
why.Citizens would have less reason to coope: Good governance depends on cooperation between citizens and the government.

activities.explanation: Proper coordination removes a challenge that can harm programme implementation.

activities.context: A town’s education, healthcare and transport programmes are delivered by different institutions. The institutions do not coordinate properly, so government programmes are not implemented effectively. Some communities also have less access to these services than others. Meanwhile, a false message about a public service programme is spreading online. Citizens are unsure which information to trust, while some public offices are being misused so that resources do not reach people.
activities.prompt: Why are the misused public offices a problem for the people in the town?
options: They stop resources and benefits from reaching people.
They make citizens more likely to cooperate with the government.
They ensure that public services reach every community equally.
They help institutions coordinate their work properly.

why.They make citizens more likely to cooper: Misuse does not build cooperation between citizens and the government.
why.They ensure that public services reach e: Misuse can have the opposite effect of equal access to services.
why.They help institutions coordinate their: Misuse does not improve coordination between institutions.

activities.explanation: Misuse can prevent resources and benefits from reaching people.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Misinformation and fake news are serious challenges for good governance.
Reason (R): Good governance includes responsiveness, transparency, participation and the rule of law.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason does not directly explain why misinformation is a challenge.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Weak coordination between institutions can harm the implementation of government programmes.
Reason (R): When institutions do not coordinate properly, government programmes may not reach people effectively.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains how weak coordination can harm programme implementation.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between good governance and the challenges that weaken it?
activities.answer: Good governance is a way of governing that includes responsiveness, transparency, participation and the rule of law. It promotes justice and fairness, protects citizens’ rights and freedom, and helps provide education, healthcare, transport and other public services. The challenges are conditions that can weaken this process. Weak coordination can harm programme implementation, unequal access can leave communities behind, misuse of public offices can stop benefits from reaching people, and misinformation and fake news are serious challenges for good governance. Both cooperation and trust are therefore important.
points: Good governance includes responsiveness, transparency, participation and the rule of law.
Good governance promotes justice, fairness, rights and public services.
Weak coordination, unequal access and misuse of offices weaken governance.
Misinformation and fake news are serious challenges for good governance.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A local government uses information and communication technology to provide services and share information. Citizens can apply for or obtain many services without visiting government offices, so less paperwork is needed from them. This helps the government communicate more easily, improve administrative processes, and deliver services efficiently across the area. However, a resident who lacks reliable internet or useful digital skills may still find it difficult to use these services.
activities.prompt: Why can a citizen obtain a government service without making a physical visit to a government office?
options: The service can be completed through the digital channel, so an office visit is not needed.
The office visit will still be necessary because digital services do not reduce travel.
The citizen will need to handle more paperwork because digital services add extra steps.
The service will take longer because online delivery cannot cover large areas.

why.The office visit will still be necessary: This is incorrect because many services can be accessed without visiting offices.
why.The citizen will need to handle more pap: This is incorrect because e-governance reduces the paperwork citizens must handle.
why.The service will take longer because onl: This is incorrect because e-governance supports efficient and quick delivery across large areas.

activities.explanation: This correctly connects digital service delivery with avoiding an office visit.

activities.context: A local government uses information and communication technology to provide services and share information. Citizens can apply for or obtain many services without visiting government offices, so less paperwork is needed from them. This helps the government communicate more easily, improve administrative processes, and deliver services efficiently across the area. However, a resident who lacks reliable internet or useful digital skills may still find it difficult to use these services.
activities.prompt: What should a citizen who wants to use digital services but lacks useful digital skills do?
options: The citizen should practise and learn the skills needed to use digital services.
The citizen should try to use the services without learning any skills.
The citizen should rely on internet alone because skills become unnecessary.
The citizen should stop using digital services until a new device is provided.

why.The citizen should try to use the servic: This is incorrect because people need useful skills for digital services.
why.The citizen should rely on internet alon: This is incorrect because internet access and useful skills are both needed.
why.The citizen should stop using digital se: This is incorrect because the immediate skills gap can be addressed by learning.

activities.explanation: This correctly identifies the preparation needed to use digital services.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): E-governance can reduce the amount of paperwork that citizens must handle.
Reason (R): Governments use information and communication technology to provide services and share information digitally.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and digital service delivery explains why less paperwork is required from citizens.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Governance and Public Policy

activities.prompt: What does governance involve in a democracy?
options: Institutions and citizens working together to solve public problems
Institutions working alone to make every important decision
Citizens voting without taking any other part
Political power being used only for private benefit
activities.explanation: Governance joins institutions and citizens. They work together to solve public problems.

activities.prompt: Voting in elections alone is enough to make a democracy work well.
activities.explanation: Voting is useful, but it is not enough. A democracy needs more than elections.

activities.prompt: Misinformation and fake news are serious challenges for good governance.
activities.explanation: Misinformation and fake news can harm good governance and public decisions.

activities.prompt: Public policies are often financed with public money collected through ______.
activities.hint: People pay this to government institutions.
activities.explanation: Public policies are often financed this way. The money is called public money.

activities.prompt: Which qualities does Rām Rājya combine?
options: Secrecy, isolation, punishment, trade and a leader-centred approach
Profit, speed, secrecy, trade and a market-centred approach
Probity, transparency, compassion, welfare and a people-centred approach
Force, status, secrecy, distance and an elite-centred approach
activities.explanation: Rām Rājya includes probity, transparency, compassion, welfare and a people-centred approach.

activities.prompt: Match each group with its role.
pairs: Identify problems, vote, participate and give feedback
Raise public issues, make laws and approve budgets
Prepare policies, deliver services and monitor progress
Civil society groups, experts and media
Study problems, suggest solutions and create awareness
activities.explanation: Each group has a different role. Together, they help make and implement public policy.

activities.prompt: Put the public policy-making process in order.
items: Recognise a public need or problem
Collect information and consult experts, stakeholders and the public
Prepare, review and approve a draft policy
Turn the approved policy into programmes and schemes
activities.explanation: This is the policy-making sequence. Monitoring and evaluation continue after implementation begins.

activities.prompt: Which change can e-governance bring?
options: It can make governance more transparent, accessible and convenient
It can make governance less accessible and less convenient
It can stop governments from communicating with citizens
It can make public services slower across large areas
activities.explanation: E-governance can improve access and convenience. It also supports quicker service delivery across large areas.

activities.prompt: Which statement about India's governance heritage is correct?
options: Indian institutions avoided all traditional ideas of governance
The Constitution ignored India's own values and ideals
Indian institutions adapted traditional ideas to modern democracy
India kept colonial institutions without any adaptation
activities.explanation: India kept much pre-colonial knowledge. Its institutions also adapted traditional ideas to modern democracy.

activities.prompt: Why are public policies monitored and evaluated through feedback?
options: So policies stop affecting everyone in society
So changes can be made when they are needed
So public institutions stop implementing the work
So public problems are no longer recognised
activities.explanation: Public policies include ways to measure success. Feedback helps guide needed changes.

chapters.title: Managing Your Personal Finances
chapters.summary: In this chapter: personal finance, income and the five pillars; budgeting and its four steps; saving, investing and compounding; common investment options.

lessons.title: Personal Finance, Income and the Five Pillars

activities.prompt: Curious how you can build a smart money plan for your future?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Money and Income
activities.body: Personal finance means planning and managing your own money for needs and wants. The five pillars are income, budgeting, saving, investing and protection. Income is money received regularly or sometimes for products or services. It is essential because money cannot be spent, saved or invested without it. Examples include a teacher's salary, a shopkeeper's profits and an investor's interest.
keyPoints: Personal finance means managing your own money.
The five pillars guide personal finance.
Income supports spending, saving and investing.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you understand how careful money management begins with income.

activities.prompt: A teacher wants to buy a house in five years. How should they prepare?
steps: Buying a house in five years requires good money management.
The teacher's monthly salary provides regular income.
Income comes first, because money cannot be saved or invested without it.
So, the teacher should manage the salary carefully to prepare.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Different Ways to Receive Income
activities.body: Income can reach people in different ways. A teacher receives a monthly salary. A shopkeeper receives profits from running a business. An investor can receive interest from bank deposits. Income is essential because money cannot be spent, saved or invested without it.
keyPoints: A monthly salary is income for a teacher.
Business profits and bank interest are also income.
Income makes spending, saving and investing possible.
activities.explanation: Different people receive income through different arrangements.

activities.prompt: What does personal finance mean?
options: Handling cash for a different organisation
Planning and managing your own money
Buying products for other people's needs
Saving money for another person
activities.explanation: Personal finance means planning and managing your own money for needs and wants.

activities.prompt: Income can arrive regularly, or only sometimes for products or services.
activities.explanation: Income may arrive regularly or sometimes for products or services.

activities.prompt: Match each person with the income they can receive.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a different way that income can be received.

activities.prompt: Why is income essential for personal finance?
options: It lets you avoid managing all your money.
It only helps when you buy something for yourself.
It lets you spend, save and invest money.
It makes every purchase affordable for you.
activities.explanation: Money cannot be spent, saved or invested without income.

activities.prompt: A teacher receives income as a ______ salary.
activities.hint: This income arrives every month.
activities.explanation: A teacher receives a monthly salary as income.

activities.prompt: Put the five pillars in the order taught in this lesson.
activities.explanation: These are the five pillars of personal finance named in the lesson.

activities.prompt: You plan for a house in five years. Which set shows all five pillars?
options: Salary, prices, saving, trading and safety
Budgeting, income, loans, spending and security
Profits, expenses, interest, loans and risks
Income, budgeting, saving, investing and protection
activities.explanation: These are the five pillars. Managing money well helps with plans like buying a house.

activities.prompt: Someone plans to buy a house in five years. Which choice best shows personal finance?
options: Manage income now, because the house goal needs planning.
Plan only later, because five years is enough time.
Spend on wants now, because future needs can wait.
Stop planning, because a distant house feels less urgent.

why.Plan only later, because five years is e: This puts planning after the years when it should happen.
why.Spend on wants now, because future needs: This confuses present wants with planning for a future goal.
why.Stop planning, because a distant house f: This assumes time makes careful money management unnecessary.

activities.explanation: This is right because the house goal requires good money management.

activities.prompt: A person wants to save and invest but has no income. What can happen?
options: They can save money without income.
They can invest money without income.
They cannot save or invest money.
They should stop planning their money.

This confuses wanting to save with being able to save.
This confuses choosing to invest with having money to invest.
This mistakes giving up planning for solving the money problem.

activities.explanation: Right: money cannot be saved or invested without income.

lessons.title: Budgeting and Its Four Steps

activities.prompt: How can you make your money last without giving up your goals?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How to Make a Budget
activities.body: Budgeting means planning in advance how income will be spent. A budget is a written plan that balances income with expenses. List all monthly expenses, including small ones. Set a savings goal with an amount and purpose. Track spending by comparing it with the budget. Review the budget when income, expenses or goals change. Budgeting controls excessive eating out. Balancing income and expenditure helps you live within your means.
keyPoints: List all monthly expenses.
Set a savings goal.
Track and review spending.
activities.explanation: A clear budget helps you plan, save and control your spending.

activities.prompt: An unexpected medical bill arrives. How should the family change its budget?
steps: List all expenses, large and small, because this is the first step.
Review the budget because the medical bill changes expenses.
Change spending choices so income and expenditure stay balanced.
The revised budget should fit the new medical situation.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Meaning of Budgeting
activities.prompt: What does budgeting mean?
options: Planning income spending before it happens
Planning income spending after it happens
Writing down only large monthly expenses
Keeping every rupee without a plan
activities.explanation: Budgeting means planning in advance how income will be spent.

activities.title: A Balanced Budget
activities.prompt: A budget balances income with expenses.
activities.explanation: A budget is a written plan that balances income with expenses.

activities.title: Monthly Savings
activities.prompt: To save ₹3,000 in six months, you must save ______ each month.
activities.hint: Share the total savings equally between the months.
activities.explanation: Saving ₹500 each month gives ₹3,000 over six months.

activities.title: Choosing What Matters
activities.prompt: A family wants to choose between different needs. What should guide the choice?
options: The family's financial goals
The length of their shopping list
The number of shops nearby
The colour of their budget paper
activities.explanation: Financial goals help people decide which needs and choices matter most.

activities.title: An Unexpected Expense
activities.prompt: An unexpected medical bill arrives. What may the family need to do?
options: Change the budget
Remove every savings goal
Stop tracking all spending
Keep the budget unchanged
activities.explanation: Unexpected medical expenses may require changes to the budget.

activities.title: Why Balance the Budget?
activities.prompt: Why does balancing income and expenditure help?
options: It helps people live within their means
It removes the need for a written plan
It guarantees that no expense will occur
It makes every goal affordable
activities.explanation: Balancing income and expenditure helps people live within their means.

activities.prompt: An unexpected medical bill has arrived. What should the family do with its budget?
options: Review the budget and change planned spending.
Keep the budget unchanged because it was already written.
Remove small expenses from the budget before starting.
Use a savings goal instead of listing expenses.

why.Keep the budget unchanged because it was: This ignores that changed expenses require a budget review.
why.Remove small expenses from the budget be: All expenses, even small ones, belong in the first step.
why.Use a savings goal instead of listing ex: A savings goal does not replace listing all expenses.

activities.explanation: Medical costs can change expenses, so the budget needs review.

activities.prompt: Your goal is to save ₹3,000 in six months. Which monthly plan fits it?
options: Save ₹500 every month.
Save ₹3,000 every month.
Save ₹500 only once.
Save ₹500 in some months.

This treats the whole six-month goal as a monthly amount.
This does not set aside the planned amount every month.
This leaves some months without the planned saving.

activities.explanation: Saving ₹3,000 over six months means saving ₹500 each month.

activities.prompt: Your income stays the same, but your goals change. What should you do with the budget?
options: Review it so the budget matches the changed goals.
Keep it unchanged because only income affects the budget.
Add new expenses without checking the current plan.
Stop comparing spending because the goals have changed.

why.Keep it unchanged because only income af: This wrongly thinks income is the only reason to review a budget.
why.Add new expenses without checking the cu: A changed budget should be checked, not changed without thought.
why.Stop comparing spending because the goal: Tracking spending remains useful after goals change.

activities.explanation: A budget should be reviewed when goals change.

activities.prompt: Your monthly spending is more than your income. Which budgeting aim addresses this?
options: Balancing income and expenditure to live within your means.
Listing every expense before making a spending plan.
Choosing which needs and spending choices matter most.
Comparing actual spending with the written budget.

why.Listing every expense before making a sp: Listing expenses is only the first step of budgeting.
why.Choosing which needs and spending choice: Priorities help choices, but balancing addresses spending above income.
why.Comparing actual spending with the writt: Tracking compares spending with the plan but does not balance it.

activities.explanation: Balancing income and expenditure helps people live within their means.

lessons.title: Saving, Investing and Compounding

activities.prompt: How can Dhruv make his money work harder for his future?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Your Money Can Grow
activities.body: Saving means keeping income aside for later. Savings form a financial surplus, or money kept aside, that grows over time. They help with emergencies and investments. Investing places savings in assets to protect and grow value. Investments can earn returns. Liquidity means how easily you can use money. Cash savings are more liquid than investments. Compounding reinvests earnings to earn more. Early investments have longer to earn returns.
keyPoints: Saving keeps income aside for later.
Investing protects value and can earn returns.
Compounding reinvests earnings to earn more.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how saving and investing can help your money grow.

activities.prompt: Aarav has money after paying his needs. Should he keep it as cash, invest it, or do both?
steps: He keeps some as savings, because saving means setting income aside for future use.
This creates a financial surplus, because saved money can grow over time.
He invests part in assets, because investing protects and grows the money's value.
He keeps cash for emergencies and invests some savings, because cash is more liquid and investments can build wealth.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Saving means keeping some income aside for future use.
activities.explanation: Saving means keeping some income aside for future use.

activities.prompt: Saving forms a financial ______ that grows over time.
activities.hint: This means money kept aside.
activities.explanation: Savings form a financial surplus that grows over time.

activities.prompt: Match each money idea to its meaning.
activities.explanation: Each idea is joined to its meaning from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Which statement about liquidity is correct?
options: Investments provide greater liquidity
Cash and investments have equal liquidity
Cash savings provide greater liquidity
Only investments provide liquidity
activities.explanation: Cash savings provide greater liquidity than investments.

activities.prompt: Early investments have less time to earn returns.
activities.explanation: Early investments have longer to earn returns and produce further returns.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of investment growth in order.
activities.explanation: Compounding happens when investment earnings are reinvested to earn more.

activities.prompt: At age 65, Dhruv has only about ______ as much money as Bhavisha.
activities.hint: Think of the share of Bhavisha's amount.
activities.explanation: At age 65, Dhruv has only about 40% as much money as Bhavisha.

activities.prompt: Sita's phone suddenly stops working. Why did saving some income help her?
options: It gave her money for an unexpected need.
It made her phone impossible to break.
It turned her savings into an investment.
It stopped all emergencies from happening.

This wrongly assumes saving prevents an emergency.
why.It turned her savings into an investment: This confuses keeping money with investing it.
why.It stopped all emergencies from happenin: This wrongly assumes saving stops emergencies.

activities.explanation: This is right because emergencies can happen and savings help with them.

activities.prompt: Your family needs to buy groceries today. Which choice gives easier access to money?
options: Keep the money as cash savings.
Put all the money into investments.
Save nothing until the shop closes.
Move the money into another asset.

This confuses easy access with protection from losing value.
This wrongly assumes there is no need for savings today.
This wrongly assumes another asset is easier to use than cash.

activities.explanation: This is right because cash savings have greater liquidity.

lessons.title: Common Investment Options

activities.prompt: What makes some investments feel safer while others offer more chances to grow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ways to invest money
activities.body: Fixed deposits are common and safe. You place money together for a fixed period. This is called a lump sum. Its interest rate stays unchanged. Bonds let you lend to governments or companies. Bondholders receive regular interest. Buying shares makes you part-owner. Shareholders may gain through dividends and price rises. Fluctuating prices make shares riskier. Mutual funds collect money from many investors. Professional managers choose investments. Different assets reduce risk.
keyPoints: Fixed deposits keep the interest rate unchanged.
Bonds allow lending and give regular interest to bondholders.
Shares offer ownership, but fluctuating prices mean higher risk.
Mutual funds use different assets to reduce risk.
activities.explanation: Each option offers a different way to invest money.

activities.prompt: One child saved one lump sum. What should they choose for safety?
steps: They choose a fixed deposit because it is among the safest options.
One lump sum fits because the deposit lasts for a fixed period.
Their rate stays unchanged because the deposit rate is fixed.
Therefore, a fixed deposit fits the wish for safety and one rate.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which option is among the most common and safest?
options: Fixed deposits
Company shares
Government bonds
Mutual funds
activities.explanation: Fixed deposits are among the most common and safest investment options.

activities.prompt: A fixed deposit's interest rate can change during the investment.
activities.explanation: The interest rate remains unchanged during the investment.

activities.prompt: The interest rate stays ______ during a fixed deposit.
activities.hint: It always stays the same.
activities.explanation: A fixed deposit keeps the same interest rate throughout the investment.

activities.prompt: Match each investment with what it involves.
pairs: Lump sum for a fixed period
activities.explanation: Each pair shows what the investment involves.

activities.prompt: Which statement about bondholders is correct?
options: They receive regular interest
They own part of a company
They choose mutual fund investments
They collect money from many investors
activities.explanation: Bondholders receive regular interest from their bonds.

activities.prompt: Mutual fund money can be invested only in company shares.
activities.explanation: Mutual fund investments can include shares, bonds and other financial assets.

activities.prompt: A family wants a safe option with one rate. What should they choose?
options: A fixed deposit, because it is safe and keeps one rate.
A company share, because it is safe and keeps one rate.
A mutual fund, because it is safe and keeps one rate.
A government bond, because it is safe and keeps one rate.

why.A company share, because it is safe and: This mistakes higher-risk shares for a safe, fixed-rate investment.
why.A mutual fund, because it is safe and ke: This wrongly assumes mutual funds keep one unchanged interest rate.
why.A government bond, because it is safe an: This wrongly assumes a bond's price is always fixed.

activities.explanation: Fixed deposits are among the safest options, and their rates stay unchanged.

activities.prompt: A ₹10,000 bond pays 5% for one year. What interest comes?
options: The holder receives ₹500 in interest.
The holder owns ₹500 of the company.
The holder manages ₹500 for many investors.
The holder lends ₹500 to many companies.

Receiving interest does not make a bondholder part-owner.
why.The holder manages ₹500 for many investo: Managing investments is the work of mutual fund managers.
This wrongly treats one bond like lending to many companies.

activities.explanation: The holder receives ₹500 because 5% of ₹10,000 is ₹500.

lessons.title: Protection, Insurance, Borrowing and Risk

activities.prompt: How can you protect your family’s future while making smart money choices?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Staying safe with money
activities.body: Protection means safeguarding income, savings and assets, or things you own, against risks. Insurance is a legal contract. You pay regularly, and the company gives compensation for covered losses or expenses. It works by sharing risk through a common pool of payments. Borrowing can help with productive purposes, but misuse can harm you. Responsible borrowing means taking necessary loans and repaying them on time. An EMI is the fixed monthly loan payment.
keyPoints: Protection safeguards income, savings and assets.
Insurance shares risk through a common pool.
Responsible borrowing needs timely repayment.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you face risks and borrow responsibly.

activities.prompt: An illness brings a large hospital bill. How can a family protect its money?
steps: An illness can cause financial loss because hospital care costs money.
Health insurance helps because it pays for covered treatment, medicines and tests.
A common pool helps because it shares risk among premium payers.
Therefore, health insurance protects the family's income, savings and assets.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose the meaning
activities.prompt: Which word means safeguarding income, savings and assets against risks?
options: Investment
Protection
Borrowing
EMI
activities.explanation: Protection keeps your money and belongings safer from risks.

activities.title: Unexpected losses
activities.prompt: Unexpected events can cause significant financial losses.
activities.explanation: Yes, unexpected events can harm your money.

activities.title: The monthly loan payment
activities.prompt: An ______ is the fixed monthly amount used to repay a loan.
activities.hint: These are the initials used for this monthly loan payment.
activities.explanation: An EMI is the same fixed amount each month for repaying a loan.

activities.title: Insurance basics
activities.prompt: Which statement about insurance is correct?
options: You pay regularly for a legal contract.
You receive payment without regular payments.
The company keeps every risk alone.
Every loss is covered without limits.
activities.explanation: Insurance is a legal contract, so you pay regularly for cover.

activities.title: Match each idea
activities.prompt: Match each insurance or borrowing idea with its correct description.
pairs: Helps pay for hospital treatment, medicines and tests
Gives financial support to a family after the policyholder's death
Covers losses involving vehicles, homes and other property
Fixed monthly amount used to repay a loan
Can help, but can harm when misused
activities.explanation: Each insurance type has a different purpose, while borrowing needs care.

activities.title: How insurance works
activities.prompt: Put the steps of insurance in order.
activities.explanation: Regular payments support the common pool, which helps cover losses.

activities.title: Responsible borrowing
activities.prompt: Responsible borrowing means taking any loan and repaying it when convenient.
activities.explanation: It means taking necessary loans and repaying them on time.

activities.title: Choosing an investment
activities.prompt: Which set should guide your investment choices?
options: Risk, return, time horizon and liquidity
Risk, return, time horizon and savings
Risk, return, time horizon and assets
Risk, return, time horizon and borrowing
activities.explanation: Good investment choices consider risk, return, time horizon and liquidity.

activities.prompt: Premiums go into one pool. What happens when one member has a covered loss?
options: The insurer compensates the covered loss from the shared pool.
The insurer keeps the covered loss separate from all members.
Every member receives a payment for one person's loss.
Only the member who paid most receives a payment.

why.The insurer keeps the covered loss separ: A common pool combines risks rather than keeping each loss separate.
why.Every member receives a payment for one: Sharing risk does not mean every member receives money.
why.Only the member who paid most receives a: Payment does not depend only on who paid the most premium.

activities.explanation: The insurer provides compensation from a pool that shares risk.

activities.prompt: A car is damaged and a policyholder dies. Which statement applies correctly?
options: General insurance covers the car; life insurance supports the family.
Life insurance covers the car; general insurance supports the family.
Health insurance covers the car; life insurance supports the family.
General insurance covers the car; health insurance supports the family.

why.Life insurance covers the car; general i: This reverses the roles of general insurance and life insurance.
why.Health insurance covers the car; life in: Health insurance helps with medical costs, not vehicle damage.
why.General insurance covers the car; health: Life insurance, not health insurance, supports the family after death.

activities.explanation: General insurance covers vehicles, while life insurance supports the family after death.

lessons.title: Income Tax and Responsible Money Management

activities.prompt: How does income tax help us, and how can we manage our money wisely?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding taxes
activities.body: Taxes are compulsory payments made by people and businesses to the government. They help fund schools, hospitals, transport, defence and other public services. Direct taxes are paid on income or profits. Indirect taxes are added to prices. Income tax uses slabs, and different income portions have different rates. You should pay taxes honestly and on time. Managing money wisely means making careful financial decisions at every stage.
keyPoints: Taxes fund public services
Direct and indirect taxes work differently
Income tax uses different rates
activities.explanation: Taxes are an important part of responsible money management.

activities.prompt: A worker’s yearly income rises above the tax limit. How will income tax change?
steps: Income tax is paid on the income a person earns in a year.
Below the limit, that person is exempt from paying income tax.
Income tax uses slabs, so different portions have different rates.
Therefore, as the income rises, the income tax payable also rises.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What are taxes?
activities.prompt: Which one describes taxes?
options: Optional gifts to schools
Compulsory government payments
Payments only to shops
Prices paid by every shopper
activities.explanation: Taxes are compulsory payments made by people and businesses to the government.

activities.title: Match each idea
activities.prompt: Match each tax or money idea with its meaning.
pairs: Added to the price of goods
Paid on income earned in a year
activities.explanation: Direct taxes concern income or profits, while indirect taxes appear in prices. Slabs apply different rates to income portions.

activities.title: Where is an indirect tax paid?
activities.prompt: Where is an indirect tax paid?
options: In the price of goods
Directly on personal income
Directly on business profits
activities.explanation: Indirect taxes are added to the price of goods and services.

activities.title: Complete the sentence
activities.prompt: Taxes are ______ payments made to the government.
activities.hint: People and businesses must make these payments.
activities.explanation: The word “compulsory” shows that taxes must be paid.

activities.title: How income tax is calculated
activities.prompt: Put the steps for calculating income tax in order.
items: Income tax is calculated using slabs
Different portions of income are separated
Each portion is taxed at a different rate
Tax payable rises as income rises
activities.explanation: Income tax uses slabs with different rates. Higher income means more income tax is payable.

activities.title: A responsible tax decision
activities.prompt: Which action best follows responsible money management?
options: Paying tax at any convenient time
Choosing tax rates for each person
Paying tax honestly and on time
Making tax payments without care
activities.explanation: Paying taxes honestly and on time is an important responsibility. Managing money wisely needs careful financial decisions.

activities.prompt: A café adds tax to the price of a meal. Who pays that tax through the price?
options: The customer, because the tax is added to the price.
The café, because every tax is paid only after buying.
The customer, because the tax comes from yearly profits.
The driver, because transport taxes pay for every meal.

why.The café, because every tax is paid only: This wrongly treats buying a meal as the time to pay income tax.
why.The customer, because the tax comes from: This confuses indirect taxes with direct taxes on yearly profits.
why.The driver, because transport taxes pay: This wrongly links buying a meal to transport funding.

activities.explanation: This is right because an indirect tax is added to the price.

activities.prompt: One worker earns less than the limit. Another earns more than the limit. What is true?
options: The lower earner is exempt; the higher earner pays tax.
Both are exempt, because all income is untaxed.
Both pay tax, because every income earns the same tax.
Only the lower earner pays, because lower incomes are taxed.

why.Both are exempt, because all income is u: This wrongly treats every income as tax-free.
why.Both pay tax, because every income earns: This wrongly assumes that every income pays the same tax.
why.Only the lower earner pays, because lowe: This reverses the rule that lower incomes can be exempt.

activities.explanation: This is right because low incomes can be exempt from income tax.

activities.prompt: Income is divided into slabs, and each slab has a rate. How is tax found?
options: Each portion of income is taxed at its own rate.
Every portion of income is taxed at one highest rate.
No income portion is taxed, because slabs remove all tax.
Only the lowest portion is taxed, because others are free.

why.Every portion of income is taxed at one: This wrongly uses one rate for every income portion.
why.No income portion is taxed, because slab: This wrongly assumes that tax slabs remove all income tax.
why.Only the lowest portion is taxed, becaus: This wrongly assumes income above the lowest portion is untaxed.

activities.explanation: This is right because different income portions have different rates.

activities.prompt: A worker can pay income tax now but chooses to wait. What should they do?
options: Pay honestly and on time, because tax is a responsibility.
Wait longer, because paying on time is not important.
Pay only part, because any part removes the duty.
Choose not to pay, because taxes are only suggestions.

why.Wait longer, because paying on time is n: This mistakes a responsibility for something that can be delayed.
why.Pay only part, because any part removes: This wrongly believes that partial payment removes the duty.
why.Choose not to pay, because taxes are onl: This wrongly treats compulsory tax as an optional suggestion.

activities.explanation: This is right because honest and timely payment is a responsibility.

activities.context: A person plans to buy a house in five years and must manage money well to prepare. The person receives a monthly salary and sometimes money for products or services. Personal finance involves planning and managing this money. The person makes a budget, saves part of the income, considers investing, and thinks about protection. These activities connect the five pillars: income, budgeting, saving, investing and protection.
activities.prompt: If the person stops budgeting and saving after receiving income, what is most likely to happen next?
options: They will be less prepared to buy the house.
They will be better prepared because their income remains unchanged.
They will need to make fewer financial decisions.
They will have more money available for investing.

why.They will be better prepared because the: Unchanged income does not remove the need to budget and save.
why.They will need to make fewer financial d: Stopping these activities can increase, not reduce, financial decisions.
why.They will have more money available for: Money not budgeted or saved does not automatically become available for investing.

activities.explanation: This is the likely result of not managing money well.

activities.context: A person plans to buy a house in five years and must manage money well to prepare. The person receives a monthly salary and sometimes money for products or services. Personal finance involves planning and managing this money. The person makes a budget, saves part of the income, considers investing, and thinks about protection. These activities connect the five pillars: income, budgeting, saving, investing and protection.
activities.prompt: What should the person do when they receive money for a product or service?
options: Add that income to their financial plan.
Ignore it because only a salary counts as income.
Spend it immediately without making a budget.
Use it only for the house and ignore other needs and wants.

why.Ignore it because only a salary counts a: Income is not limited to a monthly salary.
why.Spend it immediately without making a bu: Personal finance requires planning and managing money.
why.Use it only for the house and ignore oth: The budget must account for needs, wants and future aims.

activities.explanation: Money for products or services is also income.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A teacher's monthly salary is income.
Reason (R): The teacher receives that money regularly as a salary.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains why a monthly salary is regular income.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A shopkeeper's profit from running a business counts as income.
Reason (R): Business profits cannot count as income because they are not received regularly.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement is true, but the reason is false because income may also be received sometimes.

activities.prompt: How does the meaning of income differ from the wider idea of personal finance?
activities.answer: Income means money received regularly or sometimes for products or services. A teacher's monthly salary is regular income. A shopkeeper's profit comes from running a business, while an investor can receive interest from bank deposits. A shareholder can receive dividends and interest from securities. These examples show that income is not limited to one source. However, personal finance is broader than receiving money: it also includes budgeting, saving, investing and protection. Managing these parts well is especially important for someone planning to buy a house in five years.
points: Income is money received regularly or sometimes.
A monthly salary and business profits are different sources.
Interest and dividends can also provide income.
Personal finance includes planning and managing money through five pillars.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student writes a monthly budget that balances income with expenses and lists every large and small expense. The student chooses a savings goal of saving ₹3,000 in six months for a future need. After shopping and eating out, the student compares actual spending with the budget. When an unexpected medical expense arises, the student reviews the budget because expenses have changed.
activities.prompt: After the unexpected medical expense arises, what should the student do next?
options: Review the budget and change planned spending if needed.
Keep the budget unchanged because it was written in advance.
Ignore the medical expense and continue the old plan.
Remove the savings goal without checking income and expenses.

why.Keep the budget unchanged because it was: A written budget may need changes after new expenses.
why.Ignore the medical expense and continue: Ignoring an expense would leave the plan unbalanced.
why.Remove the savings goal without checking: Removing a goal should follow a careful review.

activities.explanation: A change in expenses calls for a budget review.

activities.context: A student writes a monthly budget that balances income with expenses and lists every large and small expense. The student chooses a savings goal of saving ₹3,000 in six months for a future need. After shopping and eating out, the student compares actual spending with the budget. When an unexpected medical expense arises, the student reviews the budget because expenses have changed.
activities.prompt: After tracking spending, the student notices that frequent eating out has made actual spending exceed the budget. What is the best response?
options: Reduce excessive eating out to keep spending within the budget.
Continue eating out the same way because the budget lists expenses.
Eat out more because the spending has already been compared.
Stop tracking spending and make no changes to the plan.

why.Continue eating out the same way because: Listing expenses does not mean every spending choice should continue.
why.Eat out more because the spending has al: Tracking helps identify and control unnecessary choices.
why.Stop tracking spending and make no chang: Tracking should continue so spending can be compared with the budget.

activities.explanation: Reducing unnecessary spending helps control the budget.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A budget should be reviewed when income changes.
Reason (R): A change in income can affect the plan for balancing income with expenses.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the change in income explains why the budget should be reviewed.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A savings goal only needs to say what the money is for, not how much to save.
Reason (R): A good savings goal states both how much to save and what it is for.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because a good savings goal must include an amount as well as a purpose.

activities.prompt: Explain why budgeting helps a person control spending and live within their means.
activities.answer: Budgeting is useful because it plans in advance how income will be spent and balances income with expenses. Listing all monthly expenses, including both large and small ones, gives the student a clear view of where money is going. Tracking spending then compares actual spending with the budget, so unnecessary choices such as excessive eating out can be spotted and controlled. A budget should be reviewed when income, expenses or goals change. For example, an unexpected medical expense may require changes. This review helps balance income and expenditure so that people live within their means.
points: Plans spending in advance
Balances income with expenses
Tracks actual spending against the budget
Reviews the budget when circumstances change
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Dhruv keeps some of his income aside for emergencies and places the rest in investments. He reinvests the returns he earns, so those earnings can earn further returns. Dhruv began investing later than Bhavisha. By age 65, Dhruv has only about 40% as much money as Bhavisha.
activities.prompt: If Dhruv continues reinvesting his investment earnings, what can happen next?
options: His reinvested earnings may generate additional returns.
His cash savings will become less liquid than his investments.
His financial surplus will stop growing over time.
His investments will no longer protect their value.

why.His cash savings will become less liquid: Cash savings have greater liquidity than investments.
why.His financial surplus will stop growing: A financial surplus can continue growing over time.

activities.explanation: Reinvesting earnings allows them to earn further returns.

activities.context: Dhruv keeps some of his income aside for emergencies and places the rest in investments. He reinvests the returns he earns, so those earnings can earn further returns. Dhruv began investing later than Bhavisha. By age 65, Dhruv has only about 40% as much money as Bhavisha.
activities.prompt: Which feature of the case best explains why Dhruv has less money than Bhavisha by age 65?
options: His investments had fewer years to earn returns and generate further returns.
He began later, so he never had a financial surplus to invest.
He kept all his money as cash, so no investment earnings were possible.
His emergency savings were larger, leaving less money for assets.

why.He began later, so he never had a financ: A later start does not mean he had no surplus.
why.He kept all his money as cash, so no inv: The case says he did invest in assets.
why.His emergency savings were larger, leavi: No evidence links larger emergency savings to the gap.

activities.explanation: His later start left less time for returns to grow.

activities.context: Dhruv keeps some of his income aside for emergencies and places the rest in investments. He reinvests the returns he earns, so those earnings can earn further returns. Dhruv began investing later than Bhavisha. By age 65, Dhruv has only about 40% as much money as Bhavisha.
activities.prompt: Dhruv receives additional income. What should he do to prepare for emergencies and future growth?
options: Keep some as cash savings and place some into assets.
Keep all of it as cash and make no future investment.
Spend all of it now and create no financial surplus.
Place all of it in assets and keep no cash for emergencies.

why.Keep all of it as cash and make no futur: Cash alone does not prepare money for future investment.
why.Spend all of it now and create no financ: Spending everything prevents a surplus from forming.
why.Place all of it in assets and keep no ca: Keeping no cash reduces emergency liquidity.

activities.explanation: This balances emergency savings with investment.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Cash savings provide greater liquidity than investments.
Reason (R): Cash savings are less liquid than investments.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason directly contradicts it.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between saving and investing, and how does saving help with investing?
activities.answer: Saving means keeping some income aside for future use. It creates a financial surplus that can grow over time and gives people money to meet emergencies. Investing means placing savings in assets to protect and grow their value and generate returns. Cash savings have greater liquidity than investments, so keeping some in cash is useful when money is needed. Saving also prepares money for future investment. Investing can increase wealth, protect money from losing value, and allow it to grow faster than inflation.
points: Defines saving and financial surplus
Explains emergency use and liquidity
Defines investing in assets
Links saving with future investment
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A shareholder may gain through dividends and a rise in the share price.
Reason (R): Share prices can fluctuate, so investing in shares involves higher risk.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but fluctuating share prices explain the higher risk rather than the possible gains.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Buying a bond makes a person part-owner of the company that issued it.
Reason (R): Bonds allow people to lend money to governments or companies for a fixed period.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true, but a bondholder lends money rather than becoming a part-owner.

activities.prompt: How does a fixed deposit differ from a bond, and how does the investor earn through each?
activities.answer: A fixed deposit starts with one lump sum placed for a fixed period, and its interest rate stays unchanged throughout the investment. A bond instead means lending money to a government or company for a fixed period, so the investor acts as a lender. The bondholder receives regular interest. Thus, both involve earning interest, but the fixed deposit is based on depositing a lump sum, while the bond is based on lending money.
points: A fixed deposit uses one lump sum for a fixed period.
The fixed-deposit interest rate remains unchanged.
A bond means lending money to a government or company.
A bondholder receives regular interest.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Managing Your Personal Finances

activities.title: The Five Pillars
activities.prompt: Which set contains all five pillars of personal finance?
options: Income, budgeting, saving, investing and protection
Income, borrowing, saving, insurance and shopping
Expenses, loans, profits, taxes and liquidity
Wages, budgeting, lending, stocks and security
activities.explanation: The five pillars are income, budgeting, saving, investing and protection.

activities.title: Teacher Income
activities.prompt: A teacher receives income as a monthly salary.
activities.explanation: A monthly salary is regular income received by a teacher.

activities.title: A Money Plan
activities.prompt: A written plan that balances income with expenses is called a ______.
activities.hint: It is a plan for spending your income.
activities.explanation: A budget is a written plan that balances income with expenses.

activities.title: Sources of Income
activities.prompt: Match each person with their source of income.
activities.explanation: Income may arrive as salary, business profits, interest, dividends or other returns.

activities.title: Mutual Fund Manager
activities.prompt: Who decides where to invest money collected by a mutual fund?
options: A mutual fund shareholder
A bank deposit investor
A bond lending company
A professional fund manager
activities.explanation: Professional fund managers decide where to invest mutual fund money.

activities.title: Compounding Steps
activities.prompt: Put the stages of compounding in the correct order.
activities.explanation: Compounding happens when investment earnings are reinvested to earn more.

activities.title: Bond Interest
activities.prompt: A ₹10,000 bond paying 5% interest gives ₹______ after one year.
activities.hint: Multiply ₹10,000 by 5%.
activities.explanation: The interest is ₹500, because ₹10,000 multiplied by 5% gives ₹500.

activities.title: Types of Insurance
activities.prompt: Match each insurance type with what it helps cover.
pairs: Financial support for a policyholder’s family
Losses involving vehicles, homes and property
activities.explanation: Each insurance type helps with different losses, expenses or family support.

activities.title: Direct and Indirect Taxes
activities.prompt: Direct taxes are added to the price of goods and services.
activities.explanation: Indirect taxes are added to prices. Direct taxes are paid on income or profits.

activities.title: Responsible Borrowing
activities.prompt: Which action shows responsible borrowing?
options: Taking unnecessary loans and skipping repayments
Repaying necessary loans on time
Taking extra loans and delaying each repayment
Taking loans only for unnecessary spending
activities.explanation: Responsible borrowing means taking necessary loans and repaying them on time. An EMI is the fixed monthly amount used to repay a loan.
