chapters.title: From Ideas to Startups
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what entrepreneurship means; turning ideas into successful ventures; the oberoi entrepreneurial journey; preparing a business plan.

lessons.title: What Entrepreneurship Means

activities.prompt: What makes an idea become a business, and how can it help others?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ideas become businesses
activities.body: Entrepreneurship means turning an idea into a business venture. A venture means starting a business. Running businesses need planning, organising and learning. Profit is money left after paying production and selling costs. Entrepreneurs notice opportunities and use new ways to solve problems. Factors of production are different things entrepreneurs combine. They create value for society through innovations, driven by passion. They accept risks by investing money and time.
keyPoints: Ideas become business ventures through planning, organising and learning.
Profit comes after production and selling costs are paid.
Entrepreneurs notice opportunities, solve problems and combine factors.
Entrepreneurs accept risks and create value for society.
activities.explanation: This card connects ideas, business work, profit and entrepreneur actions.

activities.prompt: A young person sees a problem that others see as a challenge. She finds a new solution and starts a business. Is she an entrepreneur, and why?
steps: She notices an opportunity where others see a challenge.
She turns her idea into a venture and invests money and time.
This means she takes a risk while building the business.
Her innovative solution solves the problem, so she creates social value as an entrepreneur.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Starting a business
activities.prompt: What does an entrepreneur turn into a business venture?
options: An idea
A challenge
A production cost
A business plan
activities.explanation: Entrepreneurship turns an idea into a business venture.

activities.title: Running a business
activities.prompt: Running a business involves ______, organising and learning through experience.
activities.hint: This word comes before organising and learning.
activities.explanation: Planning is part of running a business.

activities.title: Understanding profit
activities.prompt: Profit is money earned after paying production and selling costs.
activities.explanation: Profit is the money earned after both production and selling costs are paid.

activities.title: Business words and meanings
activities.prompt: Match each business word with its meaning.
pairs: A new way to solve a problem
activities.explanation: These pairs connect business words with their meanings.

activities.title: An entrepreneur at work
activities.prompt: An entrepreneur notices an opportunity and solves a problem. The entrepreneur also invests money and time. What does this show?
options: Careful planning without any innovation
Opportunity seeking and risk taking
Profit seeking without solving problems
Learning through experience without investment
activities.explanation: The entrepreneur notices opportunities, solves problems and takes risks.

activities.title: Entrepreneurs and society
activities.prompt: Which statement best describes an entrepreneur's wider role?
options: Earning profits without solving any real problems
Taking risks without investing money or time
Creating value for society through their innovations
Learning through experience without creating new solutions
activities.explanation: Entrepreneurs wish to create value for society. Their innovations contribute to society.

activities.prompt: One business earns more money from sales. It also pays higher production and selling costs. Another earns less and pays less. Which one has more profit?
options: Neither one can be known from these facts.
The first business must have more profit.
The second business must have more profit.
Both businesses must have the same profit.

why.The first business must have more profit: This confuses higher sales money with higher profit.
why.The second business must have more profi: This confuses lower costs with a sure higher profit.
why.Both businesses must have the same profi: This assumes equal profits without knowing either business.

activities.explanation: Right: profit needs both sales money and all costs.

activities.prompt: People say a problem cannot be solved well. An entrepreneur studies it and finds a new solution. Why does she act this way?
options: She wants the problem to remain a challenge.
She thinks others must solve it without innovation.
She hopes the new solution creates more problems.
She is determined to solve it with innovation.

why.She wants the problem to remain a challe: This wrongly treats the problem as something to keep.
why.She thinks others must solve it without: This wrongly thinks innovation should not solve the problem.
why.She hopes the new solution creates more: This wrongly hopes innovation will create more problems.

activities.explanation: Right: determination leads her to solve the problem with innovation.

activities.prompt: An entrepreneur creates an innovative solution to a real problem. How can this innovation contribute to society?
options: It can create value through a better solution.
It can create more problems through a new method.
It can remove the need for passion and planning.
It can replace planning with constant business risks.

why.It can create more problems through a ne: This reverses innovation's contribution to society.
why.It can remove the need for passion and p: This confuses business work with the meaning of social contribution.
why.It can replace planning with constant bu: This confuses taking risks with contributing to society.

activities.explanation: Right: innovations can contribute value to society.

lessons.title: Turning Ideas into Successful Ventures

activities.prompt: What turns an ordinary idea into a successful business and a better community?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: From Ideas to Success
activities.body: A poor young man used intelligence, dedication and hard work to build wealth. He shared half his fortune with a merchant and helped city communities. Seven homemakers from a Mumbai chawl began making papads in 1959. They had grit and unity despite having no special degrees or investors. Their cooperative grew to more than 45,000 women members by 2023. It helped thousands become financially independent through a self-reliant business.
keyPoints: Hard work and intelligence can turn an idea into wealth.
Grit and unity helped seven homemakers build a cooperative.
The cooperative shared ownership and profits equally.
activities.explanation: The lesson shows how hard work, grit and unity can turn ideas into success.

activities.prompt: Can women start a successful business without special degrees or investors?
steps: They began making papads because they wanted extra money.
They had grit and unity because these helped them work together.
They formed a cooperative so every member became an equal owner.
They shared profits equally and built a self-reliant business that helped women become financially independent.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The First Goal
activities.prompt: What was the women’s first goal when making papads?
options: Earn extra money
Attract investors
Gain special degrees
Reach 45,000 members
activities.explanation: Their first goal was to earn extra money by making and selling papads.

activities.title: Equal Ownership
activities.prompt: Every cooperative member was an equal ______.
activities.hint: Each person had the same ownership status.
activities.explanation: Every member of the cooperative became an equal owner.

activities.title: People and Achievements
activities.prompt: Match each person or group with the related fact.
activities.explanation: The young man shared his fortune and also used his wealth to help city communities.

activities.title: Members of the Cooperative
activities.prompt: What did every member of the cooperative become?
options: An equal owner
A paid investor
A senior manager
An outside supplier
activities.explanation: Every member became an equal owner, and profits were shared equally.

activities.title: How the Cooperative Worked
activities.prompt: Match each cooperative feature with its detail.
activities.explanation: The cooperative combined equal ownership, equal profits and a completely self-reliant business.

activities.title: A Wider Achievement
activities.prompt: Which result best describes the organisation’s wider achievement?
options: Financial independence and a self-reliant business
Special degrees and outside investors
Equal seniority and unequal profits
Extra money and no business
activities.explanation: It helped thousands of women become financially independent and built a completely self-reliant business.

activities.prompt: Four women form a cooperative. One has worked there longest. How should profits be shared?
options: Each woman receives equal profits because every owner has an equal share.
Each woman receives more profits because she has worked there longer.
The oldest worker receives all profits because she trained the others.
Profits are split by degrees because more study always adds more value.

why.Each woman receives more profits because: This wrongly treats longer service as a reason for unequal ownership.
why.The oldest worker receives all profits b: This wrongly gives one member control over everyone else's profits.
why.Profits are split by degrees because mor: This wrongly assumes that degrees decide profit shares in this cooperative.

activities.explanation: Equal profit sharing follows the cooperative's equal ownership rule.

activities.prompt: A photo shows seven women making papads in 1959. A map shows members in 2023. What can we compare?
options: The cooperative grew much larger and reached many more women.
Each woman's income stayed exactly the same across these two years.
The women no longer needed to earn extra money.
The cooperative became less important to women in the city.

why.Each woman's income stayed exactly the s: The sources do not provide enough information about each woman's income.
why.The women no longer needed to earn extra: The later membership does not show that the original need disappeared.
why.The cooperative became less important to: The large membership shows continuing importance, not declining importance.

activities.explanation: The different sources show growth from seven members to over 45,000.

activities.prompt: A 2023 map marks cooperative members across many places. What can the map show best?
options: Where cooperative members lived, but not each woman's income.
Whether every member shared profits equally.
How much money each woman earned.
Why women first began making papads.

why.Whether every member shared profits equa: The map does not explain how profits were shared among members.
The map shows where members lived, not how much money they earned.
The map can show members' places, but not their original reasons.

activities.explanation: A map can show locations, but it cannot show each member's income.

activities.prompt: A merchant inspired the poor young man to seek his fortune. What best explains giving half the fortune?
options: He wanted to thank the merchant for the inspiration that helped him.
He wanted to become poor again after becoming wealthy.
He believed merchants should receive every part of someone's fortune.
He needed the merchant to hide his wealth from other people.

why.He wanted to become poor again after bec: The facts show generosity, not a wish to lose his wealth.
why.He believed merchants should receive eve: This wrongly turns his thanks into a rule for giving away everything.
why.He needed the merchant to hide his wealt: Nothing in the facts suggests that he needed help hiding his wealth.

activities.explanation: He gave half because the merchant had inspired his successful journey.

activities.prompt: A group has grit and unity but no special degrees or investors. What can we reasonably predict?
options: They may build a self-reliant business through steady effort.
They must fail because they lack formal qualifications.
They will automatically earn more than every other business.
They need investors before they can begin working together.

why.They must fail because they lack formal: The women's success shows that special degrees are not necessary.
why.They will automatically earn more than e: Nothing in the facts guarantees that they will earn more than every business.
why.They need investors before they can begi: The women began without investors, so investors are not required first.

activities.explanation: The women's experience shows that grit and unity can support a self-reliant business.

lessons.title: The Oberoi Entrepreneurial Journey

activities.prompt: What can one entrepreneur teach us about turning a dream into a business?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: From a Small Job to a Big Business
activities.body: Mohan Singh Oberoi was born in Punjab in 1898. His first job paid ₹50 monthly. He learned hotel work. In 1934, he mortgaged his wife's jewellery to follow his vision. He used savings to buy a small hotel. He turned struggling hotels into successful businesses and built a hotel chain. He founded a hotel management school. Entrepreneurship means running a business. It needs more than a good idea.
keyPoints: He learned hotel work and bought a small hotel.
He built a chain, expanded worldwide and founded a hotel management school.
The Government of India awarded him the Padma Bhushan.
activities.explanation: His journey shows that entrepreneurship needs planning, teamwork, decision making and effective management.

activities.prompt: Born in Punjab in 1898, Mohan Singh Oberoi faced early difficulties. His first hotel job paid ₹50 each month. How did he build one of India's largest hotel chains?
steps: Early difficulties and low pay showed that ideas alone were not enough.
Learning every part of hotel work gave him useful business skills.
Mortgaging jewellery and using savings showed strong commitment to his vision.
His planning, teamwork, decisions and management built one of India's largest chains.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What was Mohan Singh Oberoi's first hotel job?
options: Hotel teacher
Bank clerk
Desk clerk
Shop owner
activities.explanation: His first hotel job was as a desk clerk.

activities.prompt: In 1934, he mortgaged his wife's ______ to follow his business vision.
activities.hint: He used something valuable from his wife.
activities.explanation: He mortgaged his wife's jewellery in 1934.

activities.prompt: What did he buy with all his savings?
options: A hotel chain
A management school
A worldwide business
A small hotel
activities.explanation: He used all his savings to buy a small hotel.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its partner from Oberoi's journey.
activities.explanation: These pairs show his job, learning, hotel work and school.

activities.prompt: Put these stages of Oberoi's business journey in order.
items: Learn every part of hotel operations
Use savings to buy a small hotel
Change struggling hotels into successful businesses
Build one of India's largest hotel chains
activities.explanation: He learned hotel work before buying and growing his business.

activities.prompt: What honour did the Government of India award Mohan Singh Oberoi?
options: A small hotel
The Padma Bhushan
A hotel chain
A hotel management school
activities.explanation: The Government of India awarded him the Padma Bhushan.

activities.prompt: Mohan Singh Oberoi first earned ₹50 each month as a desk clerk. Later, he built one of India's largest hotel chains. What explains this change?
options: He learned hotel operations and became skilled at managing hotels.
He stopped learning after his first desk clerk job.
He relied on his first idea without learning hotel work.
He changed only hotels that were already successful.

why.He stopped learning after his first desk: This wrongly assumes that he quit learning after his first job.
why.He relied on his first idea without lear: This wrongly assumes that a good idea alone was enough.
why.He changed only hotels that were already: This wrongly assumes that he ignored struggling hotels.

activities.explanation: This is right because learning hotel operations helped him improve struggling hotels.

activities.prompt: A small hotel bought by Mohan Singh Oberoi is struggling. What would he most likely try to do next?
options: Learn every part of its work and improve its business.
Leave it alone because he already had a good business idea.
Change only its billing and ignore all other work.
Sell it before trying to understand its problems.

why.Leave it alone because he already had a: This wrongly assumes that ideas alone were enough.
why.Change only its billing and ignore all o: This wrongly assumes that learning one part of hotel work was enough.
why.Sell it before trying to understand its: This wrongly assumes that selling hotels was part of his successful method.

activities.explanation: This is right because he learned all hotel operations to improve hotels.

activities.prompt: His first hotel job taught him service, billing and administration. How could this help him later?
options: It could help him turn struggling hotels into successful businesses.
It could help him stop making decisions about hotels.
It could turn one small hotel into a large chain immediately.
It could remove the need for planning and effective management.

why.It could help him stop making decisions: This wrongly assumes that learning stopped him from making decisions.
why.It could turn one small hotel into a lar: This wrongly assumes that one small hotel could become large immediately.
why.It could remove the need for planning an: This wrongly assumes that learning removed the need for management.

activities.explanation: This is right because his hotel knowledge helped him improve struggling hotels.

activities.prompt: A child has a good business idea but no plan. Which action best follows Oberoi's entrepreneurship lesson?
options: Make a plan, take decisions, manage well and work with others.
Start quickly because a good idea makes planning unnecessary.
Work alone and avoid making difficult business decisions.
Wait and hope that problems will solve themselves.

why.Start quickly because a good idea makes: This wrongly assumes that a good idea makes planning unnecessary.
why.Work alone and avoid making difficult bu: This wrongly assumes that teamwork and decision making are not needed.
why.Wait and hope that problems will solve t: This wrongly assumes that problems will disappear without action.

activities.explanation: This is right because entrepreneurship needs planning, teamwork, decisions and management.

activities.prompt: A biography says the Government of India awarded Oberoi the Padma Bhushan. What can the reader mainly learn from this?
options: The Government of India recognised his business achievements.
The Government of India gave him his first hotel job.
The Government of India bought and expanded his hotel chain.
The Government of India taught him all hotel operations.

why.The Government of India gave him his fir: This confuses the award with his first hotel job.
why.The Government of India bought and expan: This wrongly assumes the government bought his hotel chain.
why.The Government of India taught him all h: This wrongly assumes the award was training in hotel operations.

activities.explanation: This is right because the award shows government recognition of his achievements.

lessons.sceneCaption: A group photograph including Mr. Mohan Singh Oberoi and others.

lessons.title: Preparing a Business Plan

activities.prompt: What would you want to know before turning your big idea into a business?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What a Business Plan Does
activities.body: A business plan is a written blueprint. It shows a business’s goals and the steps for reaching them. It guides you from the first stage of a business idea. The plan supports decisions and helps you stay organised. It covers users, money, costs, places, workers, skills, prices, profit, advertising and threats. A strong financial start is needed before the business begins.
keyPoints: A written blueprint for goals and steps
Guidance for decisions and organisation
Details about users, money, workers, advertising and threats
activities.explanation: This blueprint guides a business idea and supports organised decisions.

activities.prompt: A child wants to sell lunch. The child does not know where to sell it. The child also does not know the costs. Why write a business plan first?
steps: The child writes down the goal and the steps. This gives the business idea a clear path.
The child lists who will buy the lunch. This identifies the people who will use the product.
The child lists equipment, rent, salaries, ingredients and packaging. This calculates the money needed and the costs.
The plan also decides where lunch is made and sold. Together, these choices make the business plan clear.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is a business plan?
options: A written blueprint for business goals
A record of past sales without any plans
A list of workers’ favourite foods
A guide for choosing a daily route
activities.explanation: A business plan is a written blueprint. It shows the business’s goals and steps.

activities.prompt: A business plan calculates money needs but does not list costs.
activities.explanation: The statement is false because the plan lists the costs.

activities.prompt: A business plan is a written ______ of a business’s goals and steps.
activities.hint: It shows the business’s goals and the steps towards them.
activities.explanation: A blueprint shows the goals and the steps for reaching them.

activities.prompt: Match each business plan detail with what it identifies or decides.
pairs: People who will use the product or service
Where the product will be made and sold
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a detail identified or decided by the plan.

activities.prompt: A business plan supports decisions and helps entrepreneurs remain organised.
activities.explanation: Both decision support and organisation are benefits of the plan.

activities.prompt: Which set contains details included in a business plan?
options: Money needs, costs, price and profit estimate
Worker birthdays, lunch tastes and rest days
Holiday plans, road maps and weather reports
Product colours, font choices and wall designs
activities.explanation: The plan calculates money needs and lists costs. It also sets the price and estimates possible profit.

activities.prompt: One food business plan lists only ingredients. Another also lists equipment, rent, salaries and packaging. Why is the second stronger?
options: It shows all the money the business needs.
It shows only the cost of the ingredients.
It tells workers which skills they must learn.
It explains how the food will be advertised.

why.It shows only the cost of the ingredient: This mistake treats one cost as the whole budget.
why.It tells workers which skills they must: This mistake focuses on workers instead of financial needs.
why.It explains how the food will be adverti: This mistake focuses on advertising instead of financial needs.

activities.explanation: The stronger plan lists all the costs in the financial plan.

activities.prompt: A seller has a product idea. The seller has no goals or steps. What should the seller do first?
options: Write a business plan with goals and steps.
Buy all the needed equipment straight away.
Choose all workers without checking needed skills.
Set the selling price without estimating possible profit.

why.Buy all the needed equipment straight aw: Buying first skips checking the money needed and costs.
why.Choose all workers without checking need: Choosing workers first skips planning the skills needed.
why.Set the selling price without estimating: Setting a price first skips estimating the possible profit.

activities.explanation: Writing a plan first gives the seller clear goals and steps.

activities.prompt: A business plan cannot pay for all costs. What should the business do before starting?
options: It should strengthen its financial start first.
It should choose its advertising first.
It should add workers straight away.
It should choose the sale place first.

This choice focuses on advertising, not the financial start.
This choice focuses on staffing, not the financial start.
Choosing a place does not provide the needed money.

activities.explanation: A business needs a strong financial start before it begins.

activities.prompt: Plan A sets a price. Plan B sets a price and estimates possible profit. Which plan gives more financial guidance?
options: Plan B, because it includes both price and profit.
Plan A, because setting a price is enough.
Plan B, because it lists every business cost.
Plan A, because possible profit can stay unknown.

why.Plan A, because setting a price is enoug: This mistake thinks a price alone is enough for financial planning.
why.Plan B, because it lists every business: This mistake thinks an estimate of profit is the same as a cost list.
why.Plan A, because possible profit can stay: This mistake leaves possible profit outside the business plan.

activities.explanation: The business plan sets the price and estimates possible profit.

lessons.title: The Four Functional Areas of a Business

activities.prompt: What helps a business turn big dreams into smooth, everyday growth?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Four Areas, One Business
activities.body: A successful business has four key pillars that turn goals into growth. These areas are management and operations, finance and accounting, human resources, and marketing and sales. Each area has a special job. Together, they improve decisions and use resources properly.
keyPoints: The four areas work together to help a business grow.
Each area has a special function.
Together, they improve decisions and use resources properly.
activities.explanation: These four areas work together to keep a business running smoothly.

activities.prompt: A shop wants to grow. How should its four business areas work together?
steps: Management should guide resources because this moves work towards business goals.
Operations should deliver goods or services on time because this keeps work efficient.
Finance, accounting, people and sales should manage their special work because each area has a clear function.
Together, the four areas improve decisions and use resources properly, turning goals into growth.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Managing Business Money
activities.prompt: Which area manages the money needed to operate and grow a business?
options: Management and operations
Finance and accounting
Human resources
Marketing and sales
activities.explanation: Finance manages the money needed to operate and grow a business.

activities.title: Persuading Customers
activities.prompt: The marketing and sales team attracts customers and persuades them to ______.
activities.hint: Think about what persuaded customers do.
activities.explanation: Marketing and sales attracts customers and persuades them to buy.

activities.title: Area and Function
activities.prompt: Match each functional area with its special function.
pairs: Plans and guides resources towards goals
Attracts customers and persuades them to buy
activities.explanation: Each area has a special function that helps the business run smoothly.

activities.title: Profit or Loss
activities.prompt: What does a profit and loss account show?
options: Profit or loss for the business
Staff needs for the workforce
Customers for the sales team
Delivery plans for operations
activities.explanation: A profit and loss account shows whether the business has made a profit or loss.

activities.title: Management Tasks
activities.prompt: Put the management tasks in the order shown in your book.
activities.explanation: Management involves planning, organising and guiding resources towards business goals.

activities.title: Late Deliveries
activities.prompt: A business often delivers goods late. Which area should improve this?
options: Management and operations
Finance and accounting work
Human resources work
Marketing and sales work
activities.explanation: Operations delivers goods or services efficiently and on time.

activities.prompt: A shop's goods arrive late, and customers wait. Which work needs fixing?
options: Producing and delivering goods on time
Recording and reporting financial transactions
Managing the workforce and its tasks
Attracting customers and persuading them to buy

why.Recording and reporting financial transa: This mistake treats recording money as fixing late delivery.
why.Managing the workforce and its tasks: This mistake thinks workers cause delivery delays.
why.Attracting customers and persuading them: This mistake thinks customer attraction fixes delivery delays.

activities.explanation: This is right because operations deliver goods and services on time.

activities.prompt: A business lacks money for its work. Which work is most needed?
options: Managing money for operating and growing
Recording and reporting financial transactions
Delivering goods and services efficiently
Attracting customers and persuading them to buy

why.Recording and reporting financial transa: This mistake thinks recording money provides needed funds.
why.Delivering goods and services efficientl: This mistake thinks a money shortage is an operations problem.
why.Attracting customers and persuading them: This mistake thinks attracting buyers solves a money shortage.

activities.explanation: This is right because finance manages money for operating and growing.

activities.prompt: Workers need managing at a business. Which work is most needed?
options: Managing the people who work there
Delivering goods and services on time
Managing money for business growth
Attracting customers and persuading them

why.Delivering goods and services on time: This mistake treats a workforce issue as an operations issue.
why.Managing money for business growth: This mistake treats a workforce issue as a finance issue.
why.Attracting customers and persuading them: This mistake treats a workforce issue as a marketing issue.

activities.explanation: This is right because human resources manages the workforce.

activities.prompt: A business makes goods, but few know them. Which work is most needed?
options: Attracting customers and persuading them to buy
Recording and reporting financial transactions
Managing money for business growth
Managing people and the workforce

why.Recording and reporting financial transa: This mistake thinks recording money attracts customers.
why.Managing money for business growth: This mistake thinks managing money attracts customers.
why.Managing people and the workforce: This mistake thinks managing workers attracts customers.

activities.explanation: This is right because marketing and sales persuade customers to buy.

activities.prompt: Business A manages all four areas well. Business B manages only marketing and sales. What may follow?
options: A may improve decisions and use resources
B must attract more customers and persuade buyers
A must have more workers and resources
B must need less money and fewer workers

why.B must attract more customers and persua: This mistake assumes only marketing must outperform all four areas.
why.A must have more workers and resources: This mistake thinks better management means adding more resources.
why.B must need less money and fewer workers: This mistake assumes marketing can replace the other three areas.

activities.explanation: This is right because all four areas improve decisions and resource use.

activities.prompt: Records show more money in than out. What should the account show?
options: A profit for the business
A loss for the business
Only the number of workers
A plan for future work

why.A loss for the business: This mistake reverses the meaning of revenue above expenses.
why.Only the number of workers: This mistake sees financial records as workforce records.
why.A plan for future work: This mistake treats an account as a future plan.

activities.explanation: This is right because revenue above expenses means a profit.

lessons.title: Traditional Enterprise and Modern Startups

activities.prompt: How can the wisdom of traditional entrepreneurs inspire today’s startups?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Old Skills and New Ideas
activities.body: Traditional communities pass business skills through generations. Self-employment means working for yourself. Innovation means making ideas work. The Chettiar community of Tamil Nadu traded, lent money and kept records. They were known for business ethics. They reinvested profits in trade, education and community welfare. Failure can teach entrepreneurs, or business starters, and build stronger ideas. India's ecosystem for new businesses ranks third worldwide. The Startup India scheme supports Atmanirbhar Bharat.
keyPoints: Traditional communities passed business skills through generations.
Chettiars traded, lent money and reinvested profits.
Failure can help entrepreneurs build stronger ideas.
activities.explanation: This lesson links traditional business skills with India's modern startup ecosystem.

activities.prompt: A Chettiar teenager asks an older relative how to run the family business. What should they learn?
steps: Older members pass skills to younger ones because entrepreneurial knowledge survives across generations.
These skills support India's local economy because they include self-employment, innovation, and trade.
Chettiars build borrower trust because strong ethics and trust-based lending guide them.
The community benefits because profits are reinvested in trade, education, and welfare.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which community is named as traditional and entrepreneurial?
options: The Chettiar community
The moneylender group
The trader guild
activities.explanation: The Chettiar community of Tamil Nadu is the named traditional entrepreneurial community.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its partner from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a lesson detail about Chettiars with their work, values or profits.

activities.prompt: Chettiars were traders, bankers and ______.
activities.hint: They lent money to people.
activities.explanation: Moneylenders lent money, and this was one Chettiar occupation.

activities.prompt: What did Chettiars do with their profits?
options: Keep all profits permanently unused
Stop investing in trade and learning
Reinvest them in trade, education and welfare
End all support for their community
activities.explanation: The lesson says Chettiars reinvested profits in trade, education and community welfare.

activities.prompt: Put the path from failure to stronger ideas in order.
activities.explanation: Failure comes first, teaches entrepreneurs and helps them build stronger ideas.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the Startup India scheme is correct?
options: It supports the return of old lending.
It supports the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat.
It supports the end of local trade.
It supports only older business methods.
activities.explanation: The Startup India scheme supports the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat.

activities.prompt: Entrepreneurs can learn from failure and build stronger ideas. A young entrepreneur's first business fails. What should the entrepreneur do next?
options: Repeat the same plan because changing it would look weak.
Accept that every idea will fail before trying another one.
Avoid new ideas because one failure proves failure always.
Study the failure to learn and build a stronger next idea.

why.Repeat the same plan because changing it: This mistakes avoiding change for learning from failure.
why.Accept that every idea will fail before: This wrongly turns one failure into the fate of every idea.
why.Avoid new ideas because one failure prov: This assumes failure cannot lead to stronger ideas.

activities.explanation: This is right because failure can teach and help build stronger ideas.

activities.prompt: India is the world's third-largest startup ecosystem. A 2025 map shows around 120 unicorns. What can these sources support?
options: India's startup ecosystem had reached third-largest world scale.
Traditional Chettiar loans were counted among these unicorns.
The map proved which community first invented local trade.
The map showed every startup failed before reaching 2025.

why.Traditional Chettiar loans were counted: This wrongly treats traditional lenders as modern startup unicorns.
why.The map proved which community first inv: This mistakes a modern startup map for evidence about historical invention.
why.The map showed every startup failed befo: This wrongly assumes the map records universal startup failure.

activities.explanation: This is right because the rank and unicorn count show India's startup scale.

activities.prompt: Startup India supports the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat. A startup builder requests help. What should the government office support?
options: Block the startup and give help only to old traders.
Count unicorns but refuse all help to startup builders.
Support the startup if its work follows the Atmanirbhar Bharat vision.
Use the scheme to stop all new businesses from forming.

why.Block the startup and give help only to: This mistakes backing old traders for backing the scheme's startup vision.
why.Count unicorns but refuse all help to st: This wrongly assumes counting is more important than enterprise support.
why.Use the scheme to stop all new businesse: This confuses government support for startups with blocking all new businesses.

activities.explanation: This is right because the scheme supports ventures aligned with Atmanirbhar Bharat.

activities.context: A student noticed that a shop owner was struggling to keep stock and serve customers. The student saw this difficulty as an opportunity and developed an idea for a delivery service. She planned the work, organised the resources, and learned through experience. The venture required money and time, but she was determined to solve the problem innovatively. She hoped to earn profit and create value for society.
activities.prompt: Why was taking a risk reasonable for the student?
options: A business venture can require an entrepreneur to risk money and time.
Any idea becomes a business venture without investment.
Profit can be earned before production and selling costs are paid.
Careful planning removes the need to accept business risks.

why.Any idea becomes a business venture with: Turning an idea into a venture requires planning and resources.
why.Profit can be earned before production a: Profit comes only after production and selling costs are paid.
why.Careful planning removes the need to acc: Planning does not remove the risks involved in running a business.

activities.explanation: Investing money and time is a form of risk-taking.

activities.context: A student noticed that a shop owner was struggling to keep stock and serve customers. The student saw this difficulty as an opportunity and developed an idea for a delivery service. She planned the work, organised the resources, and learned through experience. The venture required money and time, but she was determined to solve the problem innovatively. She hoped to earn profit and create value for society.
activities.prompt: If one factor needed for the original plan were unavailable, what should the student do?
options: Continue with the same plan because changing it would be too difficult.
Treat planning as a replacement for every missing factor.
Reorganise the venture by combining available factors in a workable way.
Stop the venture because factors of production can never be rearranged.

why.Continue with the same plan because chan: Keeping an unsuitable plan ignores the need to organise resources.
why.Treat planning as a replacement for ever: Planning cannot replace the factors needed for production.
why.Stop the venture because factors of prod: Entrepreneurs can adjust their organisation when circumstances change.

activities.explanation: Entrepreneurs combine different factors of production.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The entrepreneur took a risk by investing money and time.
Reason (R): Turning the idea into a business venture required a commitment of both money and time.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why investing money and time was a risk taken for the venture.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): An entrepreneur combines different factors of production.
Reason (R): A single factor is enough to produce and sell.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement about combining factors is true, but the suggested reason is false.

activities.prompt: How can an entrepreneur turn an idea into a business venture and contribute to society?
activities.answer: To turn an idea into a business venture, the entrepreneur should plan, organise the work, combine different factors of production, and learn through experience. The entrepreneur will also need to take risks by investing money and time. To contribute to society, the entrepreneur should be determined to solve a problem with an innovative solution and create value for society. These actions show how an idea can become a venture while producing benefits for others.
points: The idea is developed through planning and organising.
Different factors of production are combined.
Learning through experience guides the venture.
Innovation, social value and investment are important.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A poor man saw a dead mouse as the start of a fortune. Through intelligence, dedication and hard work, he became wealthy. He gave half his fortune to the merchant who inspired him and used his wealth to help communities. Seven homemakers in a Mumbai chawl began making papads in 1959 to earn extra money. Although they had no degrees or investors, they had grit and unity. Their cooperative made every member an equal owner and shared profits equally.
activities.prompt: If the cooperative changed its practice and began sharing profits unequally, what would most directly happen?
options: The organisation would immediately lose its self-reliant character.
Some members could gain more than others from the business.
Membership growth would certainly stop.
Every woman in the business would become financially independent.

why.The organisation would immediately lose: Unequal sharing would not automatically end self-reliance.
Unequal rewards do not necessarily stop the organisation from growing.
why.Every woman in the business would become: Financial independence would not be guaranteed for every member.

activities.explanation: The new practice could give some members greater rewards.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The cooperative's practice of sharing profits equally regardless of seniority fitted its equal-owner structure.
Reason (R): Every member of the cooperative became an equal owner.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Equal ownership supported the decision to treat every member equally when profits were divided.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The women's lack of special degrees stopped the cooperative from becoming a large business.
Reason (R): The women had grit and unity.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion reverses the outcome because the cooperative became a large business despite their lack of special degrees.

activities.prompt: Explain how the young man's use of his wealth showed that success should involve responsibility as well as earning.
activities.answer: The young man did more than become wealthy. Intelligence, dedication and hard work helped him turn the possibility of a fortune connected with a dead mouse into actual wealth. He then showed responsibility towards the person who had inspired him by giving half his fortune to the merchant. He also used his wealth to help communities in the city. His story therefore presents success as more than personal earnings. It also includes generosity towards an inspiration and support for other people, showing how wealth could be used to help others.
points: Intelligence, dedication and hard work led to his wealth.
He gave half his fortune to the merchant who inspired him.
He used his wealth to help city communities.
The story connects personal success with responsibility and generosity.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After facing difficulties early in life, Mohan Singh Oberoi took a hotel job as a desk clerk for ₹50 a month. He learned service, billing and administration, then mortgaged his wife's jewellery in 1934 and used his savings to buy a small hotel. He turned struggling hotels into successful businesses, built one of India's largest hotel chains, founded a hotel management school and expanded worldwide. The Government of India later awarded him the Padma Bhushan.
activities.prompt: After becoming a desk clerk, Oberoi realised that knowing only hotel service would not be enough to run a business. What should he do next?
options: Remain focused only on service and leave all other duties aside.
Learn only billing and administration because financial work is more useful.
Choose either service or administration but avoid learning the whole hotel system.
Study the complete hotel system, including service, billing and administration.

why.Remain focused only on service and leave: Service alone would give him an incomplete understanding of hotel work.
why.Learn only billing and administration be: Billing and administration were important, but neither covered the full system.
why.Choose either service or administration: Avoiding other duties would leave major gaps in his knowledge.

activities.explanation: Understanding every part of operations prepared him to manage hotels.

activities.context: After facing difficulties early in life, Mohan Singh Oberoi took a hotel job as a desk clerk for ₹50 a month. He learned service, billing and administration, then mortgaged his wife's jewellery in 1934 and used his savings to buy a small hotel. He turned struggling hotels into successful businesses, built one of India's largest hotel chains, founded a hotel management school and expanded worldwide. The Government of India later awarded him the Padma Bhushan.
activities.prompt: Oberoi transformed a struggling hotel into a successful business and later expanded his chain worldwide. Which approach should guide such continued growth?
options: Rely only on the original business idea and avoid making new decisions.
Expand rapidly while paying no attention to planning or daily management.
Use planning, teamwork, sound decisions and effective management together.
Transfer every decision to others so that leadership no longer matters.

why.Rely only on the original business idea: A good idea alone was not enough for Oberoi's entrepreneurial success.
why.Expand rapidly while paying no attention: Expansion without planning or management could weaken the business.
why.Transfer every decision to others so tha: Avoiding decisions and leadership would remove effective management.

activities.explanation: These were the qualities shown by Oberoi's successful journey.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Oberoi's entrepreneurial journey required more than simply having a good idea.
Reason (R): The journey required planning, teamwork, decision making and effective management.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why a good idea by itself was insufficient.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Oberoi's first hotel job paid a high monthly salary.
Reason (R): He learned every part of hotel operations, from service to billing and administration.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because the job paid only ₹50 a month, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why Oberoi's journey shows that entrepreneurship needs more than a good idea.
activities.answer: Oberoi did not succeed merely because he recognised a business opportunity. As a desk clerk earning ₹50 a month, he learned service, billing and administration, gaining a broad understanding of hotel operations. In 1934, he mortgaged his wife's jewellery and used all his savings to buy a small hotel. He then turned struggling hotels into successful businesses, built one of India's largest hotel chains, founded a hotel management school and expanded worldwide. His example shows that an idea becomes an enterprise through planning, teamwork, decision making and effective management.
points: Learned every part of hotel operations
Took financial risks to follow his business vision
Turned struggling hotels into successful businesses
Used planning, teamwork, decision making and effective management
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A young entrepreneur wants to sell food in a shop. She writes a business plan that identifies customers, the money needed for equipment, rent, salaries, ingredients and packaging, and where the food will be made and sold. The plan sets prices, estimates possible profit, states which worker skills are required, and explains how the food will be advertised. It also identifies threats that could cause loss. Before starting, she checks that the plan gives the business a strong financial start.
activities.prompt: What should the entrepreneur do if the people she planned for do not want the food?
options: Revise the customer part of the plan before proceeding
Begin buying equipment without checking whether the product is wanted
Change only the advertising method and keep every other decision
Raise the price even though the intended customers do not want the food

why.Begin buying equipment without checking: Buying equipment before checking the intended customers could weaken the financial start.
why.Change only the advertising method and k: Changing advertising alone does not correct the mistake in identifying customers.
why.Raise the price even though the intended: Changing the price cannot make unwilling customers want the product.

activities.explanation: The plan must identify the people who will use the product.

activities.context: A young entrepreneur wants to sell food in a shop. She writes a business plan that identifies customers, the money needed for equipment, rent, salaries, ingredients and packaging, and where the food will be made and sold. The plan sets prices, estimates possible profit, states which worker skills are required, and explains how the food will be advertised. It also identifies threats that could cause loss. Before starting, she checks that the plan gives the business a strong financial start.
activities.prompt: If the rent in the financial plan changes, what should the entrepreneur do?
options: Recalculate the money needed and update the list of costs
Keep the same estimate because the other costs remain unchanged
Remove rent from the financial plan after choosing the shop
Replace the entire cost list with worker salaries

why.Keep the same estimate because the other: One changed cost can affect the total amount required.
why.Remove rent from the financial plan afte: Rent is a required cost and should remain in the financial plan.
why.Replace the entire cost list with worker: Salaries are only one of the costs that must be included.

activities.explanation: The plan calculates how much money is needed and lists the costs.

activities.context: A young entrepreneur wants to sell food in a shop. She writes a business plan that identifies customers, the money needed for equipment, rent, salaries, ingredients and packaging, and where the food will be made and sold. The plan sets prices, estimates possible profit, states which worker skills are required, and explains how the food will be advertised. It also identifies threats that could cause loss. Before starting, she checks that the plan gives the business a strong financial start.
activities.prompt: What should the entrepreneur do if she finds a possible cause of loss before the business begins?
options: Record it as a threat and review the affected costs and profit estimate
Leave it out because a strong financial start prevents every possible loss
Remove the threat from the plan once operations begin
Treat it only as an advertising issue and leave the financial plan unchanged

why.Leave it out because a strong financial: A strong financial start does not remove the need to identify possible losses.
why.Remove the threat from the plan once ope: Threats should be considered before the business begins.
why.Treat it only as an advertising issue an: Some causes of loss can affect costs and the possible profit.

activities.explanation: The plan identifies threats to operations or causes of loss.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: From Ideas to Startups

activities.prompt: What does an entrepreneur do with an idea?
options: Turns it into a business venture.
Only pays workers after a profit.
Changes it into a customer.
Creates jobs without using money.
activities.explanation: Entrepreneurship turns an idea into a business venture.

activities.prompt: Profit is the money earned after paying production and selling costs.
activities.explanation: Profit remains after production and selling costs are paid.

activities.prompt: Entrepreneurs notice ______ that others may see as challenges.
activities.hint: Entrepreneurs often see chances where others see problems.
activities.explanation: They notice opportunities that others may treat as challenges.

activities.prompt: Match each business area with its main job.
pairs: Planning and guiding resources towards goals
Attracting customers and persuading them to buy
activities.explanation: Each area has a special function. Together, they help the business run smoothly.

activities.prompt: Put these accounting steps in the correct order.
items: Record money coming in as revenue.
Record money going out as expenses.
Show whether there is a profit or loss.
activities.explanation: Accounting tracks incoming and outgoing money. The profit and loss account shows the result.

activities.prompt: What is a business plan?
options: A written blueprint of goals and steps.
A list of customers' favourite colours.
A record of daily worker conversations.
A guide to changing business goals.
activities.explanation: A business plan shows a business's goals and the steps for reaching them.

activities.prompt: Cooperative members shared profits equally, whatever their seniority.
activities.explanation: Every member became an equal owner. Members shared profits equally, whatever their seniority.

activities.prompt: Seven homemakers from a Mumbai chawl started making papads in ______.
activities.hint: This year is given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Seven Mumbai homemakers started making papads in 1959.

activities.prompt: Match each entrepreneur's quality with its meaning.
pairs: Solving a problem with an innovative solution
activities.explanation: Entrepreneurs take risks, solve problems creatively and create value for society.

activities.prompt: What does Mohan Singh Oberoi's journey show about entrepreneurship?
options: It needs planning and effective management.
It needs only a good business idea.
It needs only a small hotel.
It needs no learning or teamwork.
activities.explanation: His journey shows entrepreneurship needs more than a good idea. It also needs planning, teamwork, decision making and effective management.
